questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Cell injury, adaptation, necrosis vs apoptosis
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man dies 24 hours after an acute anterior myocardial infarction. Microscopy of the infarcted myocardium shows preserved 'ghost' tissue outlines with loss of nuclei and increased cytoplasmic eosinophilia. This appearance represents which type of necrosis?
questions.concept: Ischemic necrosis of all solid organs except the brain produces coagulative necrosis: protein denaturation preserves the cellular outline while the nucleus is lost. Brain infarcts undergo liquefactive necrosis. Caseous necrosis is typical of TB granulomas.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Cell injury, adaptation, necrosis vs apoptosis
questions.stem: In experimental ischemia, which finding best marks the transition from REVERSIBLE to IRREVERSIBLE cell injury?
options: Severe plasma-membrane damage with mitochondrial permeability transition and massive calcium influx
Detachment of ribosomes from rough ER
questions.concept: Reversible injury shows swelling, blebs, and ribosomal detachment. Irreversibility is defined by severe membrane damage, profound mitochondrial dysfunction (permeability transition pore opening), and massive cytosolic calcium influx that activate degradative enzymes.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 20-year-old undergoes appendicectomy for acute appendicitis. Which inflammatory cell predominates in the appendiceal wall during the first 24 hours of acute inflammation?
questions.concept: Neutrophils are the hallmark of acute inflammation (first 24 hours), recruited by chemotaxis. Macrophages and lymphocytes dominate chronic inflammation; eosinophils suggest allergic or parasitic processes.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Lung biopsy in pulmonary tuberculosis shows granulomas with central caseation and Langhans giant cells. Which cytokine, secreted mainly by Th1 lymphocytes, is most important in activating macrophages to form epithelioid cells?
questions.concept: Granuloma formation is a type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity response. Th1 cells secrete IFN-gamma, the key macrophage-activating cytokine that drives transformation into epithelioid and Langhans giant cells. IL-4/IL-5 drive Th2/eosinophilic responses; IL-10 is anti-inflammatory.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with abdominal distension is found to have a complex ovarian mass. Which serum tumor marker is most useful for monitoring epithelial ovarian carcinoma?
questions.concept: CA-125 is the standard marker for epithelial (serous) ovarian carcinoma, used for monitoring response and recurrence. CEA is used for colorectal cancer, AFP for hepatocellular/yolk-sac tumors, and CA 19-9 for pancreatic cancer.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: In oncology, which statement best defines the STAGING of a malignant tumor?
options: Degree of differentiation of tumor cells
Extent of tumor spread — size, nodal involvement, and metastasis
The mitotic rate per high-power field
questions.concept: Staging describes anatomic extent of spread (TNM: Tumor size, Node status, Metastasis) and is the single most important prognostic factor. Grading describes differentiation (how closely tumor resembles normal tissue), reflecting aggressiveness.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has a testicular mass; serum AFP is elevated. An elevated AFP essentially EXCLUDES which of the following as a PURE germ cell tumor?
questions.concept: Pure seminoma does NOT produce AFP; a raised AFP indicates a non-seminomatous element (classically yolk-sac tumor). Beta-hCG may be mildly elevated in some seminomas (syncytiotrophoblasts), but AFP elevation reclassifies the tumor as non-seminomatous, which changes management.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has a malar rash, arthralgia and proteinuria; ANA and anti-dsDNA are positive. Renal biopsy shows granular ('lumpy-bumpy') immune-complex deposits. This glomerular injury represents which hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.concept: SLE nephritis is a type III hypersensitivity: antigen-antibody (immune) complexes deposit in glomeruli, fixing complement and causing granular immunofluorescence. Type II is direct antibody binding to fixed cell/tissue antigens; type IV is T-cell mediated.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: IMAGE-DESCRIBED: A renal biopsy stained with Congo red and viewed under polarized light shows apple-green birefringence in glomeruli and vessel walls. The deposited protein is arranged in which configuration?
questions.concept: Amyloid is defined by a beta-pleated sheet conformation, which produces the characteristic apple-green birefringence with Congo red under polarized light regardless of the precursor protein (AL, AA, etc.).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has Hb 8 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, low serum ferritin and high total iron-binding capacity (TIBC). The most likely diagnosis is?
questions.concept: Iron deficiency anemia is microcytic-hypochromic with LOW ferritin, HIGH TIBC and low transferrin saturation. Anemia of chronic disease has low TIBC with normal/high ferritin. Thalassemia has a normal/high red-cell count with disproportionately low MCV and normal ferritin.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 60-year-old strict vegetarian has macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils AND paresthesias with loss of vibration and proprioception. Which laboratory finding differentiates vitamin B12 deficiency from folate deficiency?
questions.concept: Both B12 and folate deficiency raise homocysteine and cause megaloblastic changes. Only B12 deficiency raises methylmalonic acid and only B12 deficiency causes neurological disease (subacute combined degeneration of the cord).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: IMAGE-DESCRIBED: A 10-year-old with jaundice, splenomegaly and anemia has a peripheral smear showing small, round, densely staining red cells lacking central pallor, and increased osmotic fragility. The underlying defect involves which structure?
questions.concept: Hereditary spherocytosis results from defects in membrane cytoskeletal proteins (spectrin, ankyrin, band 3), producing spherocytes with increased osmotic fragility that are trapped and destroyed in the spleen. Splenectomy is curative for symptoms.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 4-year-old presents with fever, bruising and lymphadenopathy. Marrow shows more than 20% lymphoblasts that are TdT-positive and CD10-positive. The most likely diagnosis is?
questions.concept: ALL is the commonest childhood leukemia; lymphoblasts express TdT (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase) and, in B-ALL, CD10 and CD19. TdT positivity distinguishes lymphoblasts from myeloblasts.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: IMAGE-DESCRIBED: A 35-year-old with pancytopenia and mucosal bleeding has a marrow smear showing abnormal promyelocytes packed with pink, needle-like Auer rods, some in bundles ('faggot cells'). The genetic lesion and specific therapy are?
questions.concept: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (AML-M3) carries t(15;17) forming the PML-RARA fusion. It causes DIC (bleeding), and the blocked promyelocytes are driven to differentiate by ATRA (all-trans retinoic acid), often with arsenic trioxide.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: IMAGE-DESCRIBED: A 22-year-old with painless cervical lymphadenopathy has a node biopsy showing large binucleate cells with prominent 'owl-eye' inclusion-like nucleoli within a mixed inflammatory background. These diagnostic cells are typically positive for?
questions.concept: The binucleate 'owl-eye' cell is the Reed-Sternberg cell of classical Hodgkin lymphoma; it is characteristically CD15+ and CD30+ (and CD45-negative). B-cell markers CD20 are usually negative in classical Hodgkin.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which feature favors HODGKIN lymphoma over non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: Extranodal presentation with non-contiguous, unpredictable spread
Orderly contiguous nodal spread with Reed-Sternberg cells
Frequent leukemic phase in peripheral blood
Typical involvement of Waldeyer ring and mesenteric nodes
questions.concept: Hodgkin lymphoma arises in a single axial nodal group and spreads contiguously to adjacent nodes, contains Reed-Sternberg cells, and rarely has a leukemic phase. NHL is often multifocal, non-contiguous, and more commonly extranodal.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy develops painful knee swelling (hemarthrosis) after minor trauma. Tests show prolonged aPTT, normal PT, normal platelet count and normal bleeding time, with low factor VIII activity. The diagnosis is?
questions.concept: Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) is X-linked, causing deep tissue and joint bleeds with a prolonged aPTT but normal PT, platelet count and bleeding time. Von Willebrand disease would also prolong the bleeding time / affect platelet function.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which coronary artery is most frequently involved in acute myocardial infarction?
questions.concept: The LAD is involved in roughly 40-50% of MIs (anterior wall and anterior septum), RCA in ~30-40% (inferior/posterior wall), and LCx in ~15-20% (lateral wall).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient dies suddenly 5 days after an acute MI with cardiac tamponade found at autopsy. This is due to which complication, occurring at the phase of maximal ventricular wall weakness?
questions.concept: During days 3-7, macrophage-mediated removal of necrotic debris maximally weakens the infarcted wall — the peak window for rupture. Free-wall rupture causes hemopericardium and tamponade; septal rupture causes a VSD; papillary rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 6-year-old has periorbital edema, proteinuria of 4 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, normal blood pressure and no hematuria. Light microscopy is normal; electron microscopy shows diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes. The diagnosis is?
questions.concept: Minimal change disease is the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children: heavy selective proteinuria, normal light microscopy and immunofluorescence, with foot-process effacement on EM. It is highly steroid-responsive.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: An 8-year-old develops smoky, cola-colored urine, periorbital puffiness and hypertension 2 weeks after a sore throat; serum C3 is low. Electron microscopy of the glomerulus would most likely show?
options: Linear IgG along the basement membrane
questions.concept: Post-streptococcal (post-infectious) glomerulonephritis is a nephritic syndrome appearing 1-3 weeks after group A strep infection, with low C3, RBC casts, and subepithelial electron-dense 'humps' on EM. Wire-loops suggest lupus nephritis; linear IgG suggests anti-GBM disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A chronic alcoholic has ascites, splenomegaly, dilated periumbilical veins (caput medusae) and esophageal varices. These findings are all direct consequences of?
questions.concept: Cirrhosis raises portal venous pressure, opening porto-systemic collaterals: esophageal/gastric varices, caput medusae, and hemorrhoids, plus splenomegaly and ascites. These are the classic manifestations of portal hypertension.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient has painless progressive jaundice, dark urine, pale (clay-colored) stools, pruritus and markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase. This pattern indicates which type of jaundice?
questions.concept: Obstructive jaundice gives conjugated hyperbilirubinemia: bilirubin appears in urine (dark urine), stools become pale (no urobilinogen), and there is pruritus with a markedly raised ALP/GGT. Hemolytic jaundice is unconjugated with NO bilirubinuria.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: IMAGE-DESCRIBED: MRI of a 60-year-old shows a heterogeneous, ring-enhancing mass crossing the corpus callosum in a 'butterfly' pattern. Biopsy shows pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation. The diagnosis is?
questions.concept: Glioblastoma is the commonest primary malignant brain tumor in adults; its histological hallmarks are pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular (endothelial) proliferation, and it characteristically crosses the corpus callosum ('butterfly glioma').

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes ZERO-order kinetics of drug elimination?
options: A constant FRACTION of drug is eliminated per unit time
A constant AMOUNT of drug is eliminated per unit time
Half-life is constant and independent of dose
It applies to most drugs at ordinary therapeutic doses
questions.concept: Zero-order (saturation) kinetics eliminates a constant amount of drug per unit time because metabolizing enzymes are saturated; half-life is NOT constant. Classic examples are phenytoin, ethanol, and high-dose aspirin. First-order kinetics (most drugs) eliminates a constant fraction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A drug undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism when taken orally. What is its bioavailability by the intravenous route?
questions.concept: Intravenous administration bypasses absorption and first-pass metabolism, so bioavailability is 100% (the reference standard). Drugs with high first-pass effect (propranolol, GTN, lignocaine, morphine) have low ORAL bioavailability.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A woman on combined oral contraceptive pills starts anti-tubercular therapy and later discovers she is pregnant. Which drug most likely caused contraceptive failure via hepatic enzyme induction?
questions.concept: Rifampicin is a potent inducer of cytochrome P450 (CYP3A4), accelerating metabolism of oestrogen/progestogen and causing OCP failure; it similarly lowers levels of warfarin, phenytoin and antiretrovirals. Isoniazid, by contrast, is an enzyme INHIBITOR.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 16-year-old on long-term antiepileptic therapy develops gum hypertrophy, hirsutism and coarsening of the facial features. Which drug is responsible?
questions.concept: Phenytoin characteristically causes gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, coarse facies, megaloblastic anemia (folate interference), and cerebellar signs at toxic levels. It follows zero-order kinetics near therapeutic doses.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A farmer presents with pinpoint pupils, excessive salivation and lacrimation, bradycardia and muscle fasciculations after spraying an insecticide. Which drug specifically REACTIVATES acetylcholinesterase?
questions.concept: Organophosphate poisoning is treated with atropine (blocks muscarinic effects) PLUS pralidoxime, an oxime that reactivates inhibited acetylcholinesterase if given early, before enzyme 'aging'. Physostigmine/neostigmine would worsen cholinergic excess.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which anticholinesterase crosses the blood-brain barrier and is therefore used to treat the CENTRAL effects of anticholinergic (atropine) toxicity?
questions.concept: Physostigmine is a tertiary amine (lipid-soluble) that crosses the blood-brain barrier, so it reverses central anticholinergic toxicity. Neostigmine, pyridostigmine and edrophonium are quaternary compounds acting only peripherally (used in myasthenia gravis / reversing neuromuscular block).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Minutes after a penicillin injection a patient develops urticaria, wheeze, angioedema and hypotension. The immediate drug of choice is?
questions.concept: Anaphylaxis is treated first with intramuscular adrenaline: alpha-1 vasoconstriction reverses hypotension/angioedema, beta-2 relieves bronchospasm, and beta-1 supports the heart. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts, not first-line.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: During preoperative preparation of a patient with pheochromocytoma, which principle must be followed to avoid a hypertensive crisis?
options: Start a beta-blocker first, then add an alpha-blocker
Achieve alpha-blockade (e.g. phenoxybenzamine) BEFORE giving any beta-blocker
questions.concept: In pheochromocytoma, alpha-blockade must precede beta-blockade. Giving a beta-blocker first leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, precipitating a severe hypertensive crisis. Phenoxybenzamine (irreversible alpha-blocker) is used first.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A hypertensive patient on enalapril develops a persistent, irritating dry cough. This adverse effect is due to accumulation of?
questions.concept: ACE (kininase II) also degrades bradykinin; ACE inhibitors therefore raise bradykinin, causing dry cough and (rarely) angioedema. Switching to an angiotensin-receptor blocker (ARB), which does not affect bradykinin, resolves the cough.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A woman at 30 weeks gestation has blood pressure 160/105 mmHg. Which antihypertensive is CONTRAINDICATED because of fetal renal dysgenesis and skull hypoplasia?
questions.concept: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are teratogenic (fetal renal failure, oligohydramnios, skull ossification defects) and are contraindicated in pregnancy. Safe agents include methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine and hydralazine.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: An elderly patient on digoxin and furosemide develops nausea, yellow-green visual halos and an arrhythmia. Which electrolyte disturbance most predisposed him to digoxin toxicity?
questions.concept: Loop/thiazide diuretics cause hypokalemia, which increases digoxin binding to the Na/K-ATPase and precipitates toxicity (GI upset, xanthopsia/yellow vision, arrhythmias). The antidote for severe toxicity is digoxin-specific antibody (Fab) fragments.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi 8e, Ch. Cardiac Glycosides / CHF

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient on long-term amiodarone for a ventricular arrhythmia needs periodic monitoring for toxicity of which TWO organs most characteristically affected?
questions.concept: Amiodarone (iodine-rich, class III) characteristically causes thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyper-) and pulmonary fibrosis; other effects include hepatotoxicity, corneal microdeposits, and blue-grey skin. Thyroid and lung function are monitored.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient is brought in generalized convulsive status epilepticus. The first-line drug to abort the seizure is?
questions.concept: First-line treatment of status epilepticus is an intravenous benzodiazepine (lorazepam or diazepam) to abort seizures rapidly; this is followed by a longer-acting agent (fosphenytoin/phenytoin, valproate, or levetiracetam) to prevent recurrence.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A child has brief staring spells with eyelid flutter; EEG shows 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges. Which statement about drug therapy is correct?
options: Ethosuximide is preferred; carbamazepine may WORSEN the seizures
Carbamazepine is preferred; valproate worsens them
Phenytoin is preferred; ethosuximide worsens them
Vigabatrin is preferred; valproate worsens them
questions.concept: This is childhood absence epilepsy. Ethosuximide (or valproate) is first-line. Carbamazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin and vigabatrin can paradoxically AGGRAVATE absence and myoclonic seizures — a classic 'twisted' exam point.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient started on haloperidol develops high fever, 'lead-pipe' muscular rigidity, altered sensorium and a markedly raised creatine kinase. The diagnosis and management are?
options: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; stop the drug and give dantrolene/bromocriptine
questions.concept: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome results from dopamine (D2) blockade: hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability and raised CK. Management is stopping the antipsychotic, supportive cooling/fluids, and dantrolene or bromocriptine (a dopamine agonist).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient stable on lithium for bipolar disorder is started on a thiazide diuretic and becomes confused with coarse tremor and ataxia. Why did lithium toxicity develop?
options: The thiazide increased lithium renal clearance
The thiazide increased proximal sodium (and lithium) reabsorption, raising lithium levels
Both drugs are eliminated by the liver
questions.concept: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and is handled like sodium by the kidney. Thiazides (and NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, dehydration) reduce lithium clearance, raising levels and causing tremor, ataxia, confusion and seizures.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi 8e, Ch. Drugs for Mood Disorders

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: When performing a digital (finger) nerve block, lignocaine should NOT be combined with adrenaline. The classical reason is?
options: Adrenaline shortens the duration of anaesthesia
Vasoconstriction of end-arteries risks digital ischemia and gangrene
Adrenaline is chemically inactivated by lignocaine
questions.concept: The classical teaching is to avoid adrenaline with local anaesthetics in end-artery regions (fingers, toes, penis, tip of nose, ear pinna) because vasoconstriction can cause ischemic necrosis. Adrenaline is otherwise added to prolong action and reduce systemic absorption.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient on gentamicin for gram-negative sepsis develops a rising serum creatinine and new hearing loss. These two dose-related toxicities are characteristic of which antibiotic class?
questions.concept: Aminoglycosides characteristically cause nephrotoxicity (usually reversible) and ototoxicity (often irreversible), plus neuromuscular blockade. They are concentration-dependent bactericidals, favoring once-daily dosing with monitoring.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antibiotic is contraindicated in pregnant women and in children under 8 years because it causes permanent tooth discoloration and affects bone growth?
questions.concept: Tetracyclines (including doxycycline) chelate calcium and deposit in developing teeth and bone, causing permanent yellow-brown tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia; they are avoided in pregnancy and in children under 8 years.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A hospitalized patient grows methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) in blood cultures. The drug of choice is vancomycin, which acts by?
options: Binding the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus to block peptidoglycan cell-wall synthesis
questions.concept: Vancomycin (a glycopeptide) binds the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala of peptidoglycan precursors, inhibiting cell-wall synthesis; it is the drug of choice for serious MRSA infection. Rapid infusion releases histamine causing 'red-man' syndrome.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient on antitubercular therapy develops numbness and tingling of the feet (peripheral neuropathy). Which drug is responsible and how is it prevented?
questions.concept: Isoniazid interferes with pyridoxine metabolism, causing peripheral neuropathy, especially in the malnourished, diabetics, alcoholics and HIV patients; prophylactic/therapeutic pyridoxine (B6) prevents and treats it.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi 8e, Ch. Antitubercular Drugs; grounded via PMC/StatPearls on INH toxicity

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A tuberculosis patient reports decreasing visual acuity and difficulty distinguishing red from green. Which drug is responsible and requires monthly visual monitoring?
questions.concept: Ethambutol causes dose-dependent optic (retrobulbar) neuritis with loss of visual acuity and red-green color discrimination; it is usually reversible if the drug is stopped promptly, so visual acuity/color vision are monitored. Streptomycin damages the vestibulo-cochlear nerve instead.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi 8e, Ch. Antitubercular Drugs; grounded via Frontiers/PMC on ethambutol optic neuropathy

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: To achieve radical cure of Plasmodium vivax malaria (eradicating the liver hypnozoites and preventing relapse), which drug is added — and must be avoided/screened for in G6PD deficiency?
questions.concept: Primaquine (and tafenoquine) kill the dormant hepatic hypnozoites of P. vivax/ovale, giving radical cure and preventing relapse. Being oxidant drugs, they cause acute hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, so G6PD status should be checked first.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A newly diagnosed obese type-2 diabetic is started on metformin as first-line therapy. Its main mechanism of action and characteristic serious adverse effect are?
options: Reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis; can cause lactic acidosis
Blocks intestinal glucose absorption; causes flatulence
Increases renal glucose excretion; causes urinary infections
questions.concept: Metformin (a biguanide) reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves peripheral insulin sensitivity; it does not cause hypoglycemia or weight gain, which is why it is first-line. Its rare but serious adverse effect is lactic acidosis, so it is avoided in significant renal/hepatic impairment.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi 8e, Ch. Drugs for Diabetes Mellitus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The most reliable method to sterilize culture media and heat-stable surgical instruments, effective even against bacterial spores, is autoclaving at?
options: 121 C at 15 lb/sq inch for 15 minutes
Dry heat at 100 C for 1 hour
questions.concept: Autoclaving uses saturated steam at 121 C and 15 psi for 15 minutes; moist heat kills spores by coagulating proteins. Sterilization is checked with Bacillus stearothermophilus (Geobacillus) spore strips as the biological indicator.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which staining technique demonstrates Mycobacterium tuberculosis, exploiting the mycolic acid in its cell wall?
questions.concept: The Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast stain uses hot carbol fuchsin with acid-alcohol decolorization; mycobacteria resist decolorization due to their mycolic-acid-rich wall and appear red on a blue background. Albert stain is for Corynebacterium metachromatic granules.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin crosses the placenta to provide passive immunity to the newborn?
questions.concept: IgG is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta, giving passive immunity in early infancy. IgM (a pentamer) is the first antibody in a primary response and cannot cross the placenta; secretory IgA protects mucosal surfaces and breast milk.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient with recurrent disseminated Neisseria (meningococcal and gonococcal) infections most likely has a deficiency of which complement components?
options: Terminal complement components C5-C9 (membrane attack complex)
questions.concept: Deficiency of the terminal complement components (C5-C9), which form the membrane attack complex, specifically predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections. C1-esterase-inhibitor deficiency instead causes hereditary angioedema.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: About four hours after eating cream-filled pastries at a party, several people develop acute vomiting and diarrhea. The most likely cause is a PREFORMED enterotoxin produced by?
questions.concept: Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin is preformed in the food and heat-stable, giving rapid-onset (1-6 hour) vomiting-predominant food poisoning. Its short incubation (toxin already present) distinguishes it from invasive causes like Salmonella.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A rising anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titre following pharyngitis supports recent infection with?
questions.concept: ASO antibodies rise after Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal (S. pyogenes) infection and are used to support a diagnosis of rheumatic fever or post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. S. pyogenes is bacitracin-sensitive.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: On MacConkey agar, Salmonella and Shigella appear as colorless (pale) colonies whereas E. coli forms pink colonies. This is because Salmonella and Shigella are?
questions.concept: MacConkey agar differentiates by lactose fermentation: fermenters (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter) produce acid and appear pink; non-fermenters (Salmonella, Shigella, Proteus) remain colorless/pale. This is a classic identification step.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan & Paniker 10e, Ch. Enterobacteriaceae / Culture Media

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient in a cholera outbreak has profuse painless 'rice-water' stools and severe dehydration. The single most important, life-saving intervention is?
questions.concept: Cholera kills through dehydration, so rapid fluid and electrolyte replacement (ORS or IV fluids) is life-saving. Cholera toxin raises intracellular cAMP causing massive chloride/water secretion; antibiotics (e.g. doxycycline) are only an adjunct to shorten shedding.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Under India's NTEP, the recommended INITIAL rapid diagnostic test for presumptive pulmonary TB, which also detects rifampicin resistance, is?
questions.concept: Nucleic-acid amplification tests (CBNAAT/GeneXpert, Truenat) are rapid, sensitive and simultaneously detect rifampicin resistance, so they are used upfront under NTEP's universal drug-susceptibility strategy. LJ culture is the gold standard but slow; the Mantoux test only indicates exposure, not active disease.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan & Paniker 10e, Ch. Mycobacterium; NTEP guidelines

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A leprosy patient has numerous symmetrical skin nodules, a 'leonine facies', abundant acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smears, and a negative lepromin test. This represents which pole of the disease?
questions.concept: Lepromatous leprosy reflects poor cell-mediated immunity: multibacillary, symmetric lesions, leonine facies, and a NEGATIVE lepromin test. Tuberculoid leprosy has good CMI — paucibacillary, few asymmetric lesions, and a positive lepromin test.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A blood donor's hepatitis B panel shows: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc negative. This pattern most likely indicates?
questions.concept: Vaccination produces isolated anti-HBs positivity WITH anti-HBc negative (the vaccine contains only surface antigen). Immunity from natural infection shows anti-HBs AND anti-HBc positive; a carrier is HBsAg positive.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient with recent acute hepatitis is HBsAg negative AND anti-HBs negative. Which single serological marker confirms recent hepatitis B infection during this 'window period'?
questions.concept: In the window period HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared; anti-HBc IgM is the only positive marker and confirms recent/acute infection. This is a classic exam trap.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan & Paniker 10e, Ch. Hepatitis B Serology

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which hepatitis virus is transmitted feco-orally and carries a high risk of fulminant hepatitis and mortality specifically in PREGNANT women?
questions.concept: Hepatitis E (an RNA virus, feco-orally transmitted) is notorious for causing fulminant hepatic failure with high mortality (around 20%) in pregnant women, especially in the third trimester. Hepatitis A is also feco-oral but rarely fulminant.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: To diagnose HIV infection in a 2-month-old infant born to an HIV-positive mother, the appropriate test is?
questions.concept: Maternal IgG antibody crosses the placenta and can persist up to ~18 months, so antibody tests are unreliable in infants. A virological test (HIV DNA or RNA PCR) is required to diagnose HIV in babies under 18 months.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan & Paniker 10e, Ch. Human Immunodeficiency Virus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: An HIV patient with a CD4 count of 150 cells/uL develops progressive exertional dyspnea, a dry cough, bilateral perihilar infiltrates and a markedly raised serum LDH. The most likely opportunistic infection is?
questions.concept: PCP typically occurs when CD4 falls below 200: insidious dry cough, exertional dyspnea, diffuse interstitial infiltrates and a high LDH. Cotrimoxazole is used for treatment and for prophylaxis once CD4 is below 200. CMV/MAC usually occur at CD4 below 50.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan & Paniker 10e, Ch. HIV / Opportunistic Infections

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: IMAGE-DESCRIBED: A blood smear from a febrile traveler shows crescent- (banana-) shaped gametocytes and red cells containing multiple small ring forms; no mature schizonts are seen in the peripheral blood. The species is?
questions.concept: Banana/crescent-shaped gametocytes and multiply-infected red cells showing only ring forms are characteristic of P. falciparum; its schizogony occurs in deep capillaries (hence no peripheral schizonts), producing sequestration and cerebral malaria.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient has fever paroxysms recurring every 72 hours (quartan periodicity). Which Plasmodium species is most likely?
questions.concept: P. malariae causes quartan (72-hour) fever cycles. P. vivax and P. ovale cause benign tertian (48-hour) fever, and P. falciparum causes malignant tertian malaria. Periodicity reflects the erythrocytic schizogony cycle length.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A diabetic in ketoacidosis develops a black necrotic eschar on the palate and nasal turbinates with orbital swelling. KOH mount of tissue shows broad, aseptate hyphae branching at right angles. The organism is?
questions.concept: Mucormycosis (Rhizopus/Mucor) causes rhino-orbito-cerebral disease in diabetic ketoacidosis and immunocompromise; hyphae are broad, aseptate and branch at right angles. Treatment is amphotericin B, surgical debridement, and correcting the DKA. Aspergillus has septate hyphae branching at 45 degrees.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has crushing retrosternal chest pain radiating to the left arm for 40 minutes; ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Which immediate drug most reduces mortality and should be given (chewed) at once?
questions.concept: This is an inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF). Chewable aspirin (antiplatelet) reduces mortality and is given immediately; definitive therapy is reperfusion by primary PCI or thrombolysis. Nitrates, morphine and oxygen provide symptomatic relief but do not reduce mortality.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21e, Acute MI

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with acute chest pain has ST elevation in leads V1 to V4. This localizes the infarct to which wall, supplied by which coronary artery?
options: Anteroseptal wall; left anterior descending artery
questions.concept: V1-V4 ST elevation indicates an anteroseptal infarct supplied by the LAD. Inferior wall (II, III, aVF) maps to the RCA, and lateral leads (I, aVL, V5-V6) map to the left circumflex.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21e, ECG in MI

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A young woman with exertional dyspnea and hemoptysis has a loud first heart sound, an opening snap, and a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble best heard at the apex in the left lateral position. The lesion is?
questions.concept: Mitral stenosis (usually rheumatic) produces a loud S1, an opening snap and an apical mid-diastolic rumble; complications include atrial fibrillation, hemoptysis and left-atrial enlargement. Aortic stenosis gives an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21e, Valvular Heart Disease

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 20-year-old has episodic wheeze and breathlessness that is worse at night, fully relieved by salbutamol, with normal spirometry between attacks. The most likely diagnosis is?
questions.concept: Asthma is a reversible airway obstruction: episodic, nocturnal, often atopic, and fully relieved by bronchodilators with normal spirometry between attacks. COPD, in contrast, is largely fixed obstruction in older smokers.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21e / GINA guidelines

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 60-year-old smoker with chronic cough and dyspnea has a POST-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.6 with little reversibility. This spirometry confirms?
options: An obstructive pattern consistent with COPD
questions.concept: A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 that is not fully reversible defines COPD (GOLD). Restrictive disease shows reduced lung volumes with a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Under India's current NTEP, a newly diagnosed patient with drug-sensitive pulmonary TB receives which treatment regimen?
options: 2 months of HRZE (intensive) followed by 4 months of HRE (continuation), given daily
2 months of HRE followed by 7 months of HR
questions.concept: NTEP uses daily fixed-dose combinations by weight band: intensive phase 2 months of HRZE (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol), then continuation phase 4 months of HRE — a total of 6 months. Pyrazinamide is dropped in the continuation phase.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is defined as resistance to at least which drugs?
questions.concept: MDR-TB is defined as resistance to at least isoniazid AND rifampicin, the two most potent first-line drugs. Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB adds resistance to fluoroquinolones and other key second-line agents.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: According to standard criteria, diabetes mellitus is diagnosed by a FASTING plasma glucose of at least?
questions.concept: Diagnostic thresholds are fasting plasma glucose 126 mg/dL or more, 2-hour OGTT 200 or more, HbA1c 6.5% or more, or random glucose 200 with symptoms. A fasting glucose of 100-125 mg/dL denotes impaired fasting glucose (prediabetes).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 19-year-old type-1 diabetic presents with vomiting, deep rapid breathing, fruity breath, glucose 480 mg/dL, ketonuria and pH 7.1. After starting IV fluids and insulin, which electrolyte must be closely monitored and replaced to prevent a fatal arrhythmia?
questions.concept: In diabetic ketoacidosis, insulin drives potassium into cells and can precipitate dangerous hypokalemia. Potassium must be monitored and replaced (insulin is withheld if K+ is below 3.3 mEq/L) to prevent cardiac arrhythmias.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The earliest clinical indicator of diabetic nephropathy, which warrants starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB for renoprotection, is?
questions.concept: Microalbuminuria (30-300 mg/day albumin) is the earliest sign of diabetic nephropathy. ACE inhibitors or ARBs reduce intraglomerular pressure and slow progression, and are started at this stage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has weight loss, palpitations, heat intolerance, fine tremor, a diffuse goiter and bulging eyes (exophthalmos). The most likely diagnosis is?
questions.concept: Graves disease is autoimmune hyperthyroidism caused by TSH-receptor-stimulating antibodies: diffuse goiter, ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos) and pretibial myxedema, with suppressed TSH and raised T3/T4. The eye signs are specific to Graves.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and a firm goiter; TSH is high, free T4 low, and anti-thyroid-peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies are strongly positive. The diagnosis is?
questions.concept: Hashimoto (chronic autoimmune) thyroiditis is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas; anti-TPO antibodies are positive and there is lymphocytic infiltration. It carries a small long-term risk of thyroid lymphoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A chronic kidney disease patient has serum potassium 7.2 mEq/L with tall peaked T waves on ECG. Which drug should be given FIRST to stabilize the cardiac membrane?
questions.concept: In severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes, IV calcium gluconate is given first to stabilize the myocardium (it does not lower potassium). Insulin-dextrose, salbutamol and bicarbonate then shift potassium intracellularly, while resins/dialysis remove it from the body.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient has arterial pH 7.28, HCO3 12 mEq/L and a calculated anion gap of 24 (a HIGH anion-gap metabolic acidosis). Which of the following is a recognized cause?
questions.concept: High anion-gap metabolic acidosis (mnemonic MUDPILES) includes methanol, uremia, DKA, propylene glycol, INH/iron, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol and salicylates. Diarrhea, RTA and saline cause a NORMAL (hyperchloremic) anion-gap acidosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 65-year-old presents 2 hours after sudden right-sided hemiparesis and aphasia. Before giving intravenous thrombolysis (tPA), which immediate investigation is essential?
options: Non-contrast CT of the head to exclude hemorrhage
questions.concept: A non-contrast CT head must exclude intracranial hemorrhage before thrombolysis, because tPA is contraindicated in hemorrhagic stroke. IV tPA is given for ischemic stroke within about 4.5 hours if there is no contraindication.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A young adult has fever, severe headache and neck rigidity. CSF shows high neutrophils, LOW glucose and high protein. The most likely diagnosis is?
questions.concept: Pyogenic bacterial meningitis gives turbid CSF with neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose and high protein. Viral meningitis is lymphocytic with normal glucose; tuberculous meningitis is lymphocytic with low glucose, high protein and a cobweb clot.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient in a dengue-endemic area has high fever, retro-orbital pain, thrombocytopenia, and now a RISING hematocrit with a narrowing pulse pressure. The rising hematocrit indicates?
options: Plasma leakage, a warning sign for dengue shock
questions.concept: Plasma leakage in severe dengue causes hemoconcentration (rising hematocrit), a narrowing pulse pressure and serous effusions — key warning signs of impending dengue shock syndrome. Management is careful fluid therapy; platelets are not routinely transfused.
questions.reference: Harrison's 21e / NCVBDC dengue guidelines (renamed from NVBDCP)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient has one week of stepwise rising fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal discomfort and rose spots on the trunk. Which test is MOST useful for confirmation during the first week of illness?
questions.concept: In enteric (typhoid) fever, blood culture is positive and most useful in the first week; stool and urine cultures become positive later (2nd-3rd week). The Widal test is less specific and can give false positives.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A cirrhotic patient develops confusion and asterixis (flapping tremor) with a raised blood ammonia after a gastrointestinal bleed. The mainstay drug to reduce the nitrogenous load is?
questions.concept: Hepatic encephalopathy is treated with lactulose, which acidifies the colon (trapping ammonia as ammonium) and acts as a cathartic; rifaximin is added if needed. Precipitants such as GI bleed, infection, constipation and electrolyte disturbance must also be corrected.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: To study risk factors for a RARE cancer efficiently, which study design is most appropriate, and which measure of association does it yield?
options: Randomized controlled trial; number needed to treat
questions.concept: A case-control (retrospective) study is efficient for rare diseases: it starts with cases and controls and looks back at exposures, yielding an odds ratio. Cohort studies measure incidence and relative risk but are inefficient for rare outcomes.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive & Social Medicine 27e, Epidemiology

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The number of NEW cases of a disease occurring in a defined population over a specified period is called?
questions.concept: Incidence counts new cases over a period; prevalence counts all existing (old plus new) cases at a point or period. They are linked approximately by Prevalence = Incidence x Duration, so chronic diseases have high prevalence.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A screening test is applied to 1000 people. Of 100 truly diseased, 90 test positive; of 900 non-diseased, 810 test negative. The SENSITIVITY of the test is?
questions.concept: Sensitivity = true positives / (true positives + false negatives) = 90/100 = 90%. (Specificity here would be 810/900 = 90%.) Sensitivity measures the ability to correctly identify those WITH disease.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A test with fixed high sensitivity and specificity is applied to a population with VERY LOW disease prevalence. What happens to the positive predictive value (PPV)?
questions.concept: PPV depends on prevalence: when prevalence is low, most positive results are false positives, so PPV falls even for a good test. Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic to the test and do not change with prevalence; NPV rises when prevalence is low.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e, Screening / Validity

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: For a good SCREENING test (to detect disease early in apparently healthy people), which characteristic is most desirable?
questions.concept: Screening tests should be highly sensitive so that few true cases are missed (few false negatives). Confirmatory/diagnostic tests emphasize high specificity. Screening also follows the Wilson-Jungner criteria (important disease, latent stage, suitable test, accepted treatment, facilities available).

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: To compare the PROPORTION of fully vaccinated children between two districts (categorical data), the appropriate test of significance is?
questions.concept: The chi-square test compares proportions/categorical (qualitative) data across groups. The t-test compares the means of two groups (quantitative data), and ANOVA compares means across more than two groups.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Under India's National Immunization Schedule (Universal Immunization Programme), which vaccines are given AT BIRTH?
options: BCG, OPV-0 (zero dose) and Hepatitis B birth dose
questions.concept: At birth the UIP gives BCG, oral polio zero dose (OPV-0), and the Hepatitis B birth dose (ideally within 24 hours). Pentavalent, fIPV, rotavirus and PCV begin at 6 weeks.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The pentavalent vaccine used in India's UIP protects against five diseases. Which combination is correct?
options: Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Hepatitis B and Haemophilus influenzae type b
Measles, Mumps, Rubella, Polio and Tuberculosis
Cholera, Typhoid, Tetanus, Diphtheria and Polio
Hepatitis A, B, C, D and E
questions.concept: Pentavalent vaccine = DPT (diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus) + Hepatitis B + Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). It is given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks under the UIP.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Under the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, vector-control activities against malaria specifically target which vector?
questions.concept: Malaria is transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito. Aedes aegypti transmits dengue and chikungunya; Culex transmits filariasis and Japanese encephalitis; the sandfly (Phlebotomus) transmits kala-azar.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e, Malaria / Vector-borne diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In the epidemiology of tuberculosis, the most important source of infection in the community is?
options: A sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB patient
questions.concept: A sputum smear-positive ('open') pulmonary TB case is the most infectious source, spreading Mycobacterium tuberculosis via droplet nuclei. Prompt diagnosis and treatment of such cases is the cornerstone of TB control.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In 2020 the RNTCP was renamed to reflect India's goal of eliminating tuberculosis. Its current name is?
questions.concept: The Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) was renamed the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) in 2020, in line with India's target to eliminate TB by 2025 (ahead of the global 2030 SDG target).

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Control of dengue, malaria, filariasis, kala-azar, chikungunya and Japanese encephalitis in India falls chiefly under which national programme?
options: National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP)
questions.concept: The NVBDCP covers the six vector-borne diseases: malaria, dengue, chikungunya, lymphatic filariasis, kala-azar and Japanese encephalitis. Note: the programme's directorate has recently been reorganised as the National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC) — verify the current name against the latest MoHFW source.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e, National Health Programmes

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A malnourished 3-year-old has difficulty seeing in dim light and foamy, triangular (Bitot) spots on the conjunctiva. The deficient nutrient is?
questions.concept: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness (earliest sign), Bitot spots, xerophthalmia and, if untreated, keratomalacia; it is a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness. India runs a Vitamin A prophylaxis programme for under-fives.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A 2-year-old has bilateral pedal edema, a 'moon face', hepatomegaly, sparse discolored hair and 'flaky-paint' skin desquamation, with weight about 70% of expected. The diagnosis is?
options: Nutritional marasmus with severe wasting only
questions.concept: Kwashiorkor is severe protein deficiency with edema, hepatomegaly (fatty liver), dermatosis ('flaky paint'), hair changes and weight 60-80% of expected WITH edema. Marasmus is severe energy deficit with gross wasting, no edema, and weight below 60%.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e, Protein-Energy Malnutrition

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) is best defined as the number of deaths of infants under one year of age per?
options: 1000 live births in the same year
questions.concept: IMR = infant deaths (under 1 year) per 1000 live births in a given year; it is a sensitive indicator of a population's socioeconomic development and maternal-child health. Maternal mortality ratio (MMR) instead uses a denominator of 100,000 live births.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e, Demography & Vital Statistics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: As per India's Biomedical Waste Management Rules (2016), used needles and other sharps should be discarded into which color-coded container?
questions.concept: Under the 2016 color code: Yellow = human/anatomical, soiled and expired-drug waste; Red = contaminated recyclable plastic (tubing, catheters, IV sets); White (translucent) = sharps (needles, scalpels); Blue = broken glass and metallic implants.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e / Biomedical Waste Management Rules 2016

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: VIDEO-DESCRIBED: A ward video shows a patient who suddenly cries out and becomes rigid with all four limbs extended (tonic phase) for about 20 seconds, then develops rhythmic jerking of all limbs (clonic phase) with frothing at the mouth and tongue-biting, followed by a period of confusion and drowsiness. This semiology is most consistent with?
questions.concept: A tonic stiffening phase followed by clonic jerking of all limbs, with loss of awareness, tongue-biting and a post-ictal confusional state, defines a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Absence seizures are brief staring spells with no post-ictal phase; focal aware seizures preserve awareness; psychogenic events lack true post-ictal drowsiness and typical injury.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease has this ECG. Which metabolic abnormality is the most likely cause?
questions.concept: The strip shows tall, narrow, PEAKED (tented) T waves with flattened P waves - the classic early ECG of hyperkalaemia, common in CKD. Progression is peaked T then wide QRS then sine-wave. Emergency Rx: IV calcium gluconate (membrane stabiliser) first, then insulin+glucose / beta-agonist to shift K+ intracellularly.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 55-year-old with 40 minutes of crushing chest pain has this ECG. The finding indicates?
questions.concept: Elevated ST segments in a patient with ischaemic chest pain = acute ST-elevation MI (transmural ischaemia). Needs immediate reperfusion - primary PCI or thrombolysis - plus antiplatelets/anticoagulation. 'Time is muscle'.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with palpitations has this rhythm strip. The most likely diagnosis is?
questions.concept: Irregularly irregular R-R intervals with absent discrete P waves = atrial fibrillation. Management: rate control (beta-blocker/CCB) or rhythm control, plus anticoagulation guided by CHA2DS2-VASc.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Adding Drug Y shifts Drug X's dose-response curve to the RIGHT with the SAME maximal response (see graph). Drug Y is a?
questions.concept: A parallel rightward shift with UNCHANGED Emax is the signature of a competitive (surmountable) antagonist - more agonist overcomes it. A non-competitive antagonist instead LOWERS Emax and cannot be surmounted.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: In this graph, Drug Y lowers Drug X's maximal response and the reduction is NOT overcome by increasing the dose. Drug Y is a?
questions.concept: A reduced Emax that cannot be surmounted by more agonist = non-competitive antagonist (binds irreversibly or at an allosteric site). Contrast with competitive antagonism (right shift, preserved Emax).

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: This epidemic curve shows a single sharp peak with all cases clustered together. It is most consistent with which type of outbreak?
questions.concept: A single peak with all cases arising within one incubation period = point/common-source outbreak (e.g., a contaminated meal). A propagated outbreak shows successive peaks about one incubation period apart.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: For this normal distribution, approximately what percentage of observations lie within +/- 2 standard deviations of the mean?
questions.concept: Empirical rule: about 68% lie within +/-1 SD, 95% within +/-2 SD, and 99.7% within +/-3 SD. This underpins 95% confidence intervals and laboratory reference ranges.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: This flow-volume loop shows a scooped (concave) expiratory limb with reduced peak flow. The pattern is?
questions.concept: A concave/scooped expiratory limb with reduced flows (and FEV1/FVC < 0.7) = obstructive disease (asthma/COPD). Restrictive disease gives a narrow, tall loop with reduced volumes but a preserved/high ratio.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: This peripheral blood smear is from a child with chronic haemolytic anaemia and recurrent painful crises. The abnormal cells indicate?
questions.concept: Elongated crescent/sickle-shaped RBCs on smear, with haemolytic anaemia and vaso-occlusive crises = sickle cell disease (HbS: glutamate->valine at beta-6). Confirm with Hb electrophoresis; target cells and Howell-Jolly bodies (autosplenectomy) may coexist.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: This Gram stain shows purple (Gram-positive) cocci arranged in grape-like clusters. The most likely organism is?
questions.concept: Gram-positive cocci in clusters = Staphylococcus (catalase-positive). Streptococci form chains/pairs (catalase-negative). Coagulase separates S. aureus (+) from coagulase-negative staph such as S. epidermidis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: This lymph-node preparation shows a large binucleate cell with prominent eosinophilic 'owl-eye' nucleoli. It is characteristic of?
questions.concept: The binucleate 'owl-eye' Reed-Sternberg cell (CD15+, CD30+, CD20-) is diagnostic of classical Hodgkin lymphoma. RS cells are few, set in a reactive background of lymphocytes/eosinophils.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with chronic cough, evening fever and weight loss has a chest X-ray showing an upper-lobe cavitary lesion. The most likely diagnosis is?
questions.concept: Upper-lobe cavitation with constitutional symptoms strongly suggests reactivation pulmonary TB (high bacillary load, highly infectious). Confirm with sputum AFB/CBNAAT; treat per NTEP (2HRZE / 4HRE).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The dorsal (posterior) column–medial lemniscus pathway of the spinal cord is chiefly responsible for carrying which of the following sensory modalities?
options: Fine (discriminative) touch, vibration and conscious proprioception
Unconscious proprioception destined for the cerebellum
questions.concept: The dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) carry fine discriminative touch, vibration, two-point discrimination and conscious joint-position sense. Fibers ascend ipsilaterally, synapse in the gracile/cuneate nuclei of the medulla, then cross as the internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus. Pain and temperature instead travel in the lateral spinothalamic tract, and unconscious proprioception in the spinocerebellar tracts.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord and Ascending Tracts

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The lateral spinothalamic tract is the principal ascending pathway for which of the following sensations?
questions.concept: The lateral spinothalamic tract conveys pain and temperature. First-order fibers enter and travel a short distance in the dorsolateral tract of Lissauer and synapse in the dorsal horn; second-order fibers cross in the anterior white commissure and ascend contralaterally to the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus. Because the fibers cross close to their level of entry, a cord lesion causes contralateral pain/temperature loss beginning one to two segments below.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord and Ascending Tracts

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 55-year-old strict vegetarian with megaloblastic anaemia reports tingling in the feet, an unsteady gait that is worse in the dark, and stiff weak legs. Examination shows loss of vibration and joint-position sense, brisk knee jerks and extensor plantar responses. Which combination of spinal tracts is degenerating?
options: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
Lateral spinothalamic and anterior corticospinal tracts
Spinocerebellar tracts and anterior horn cells
Dorsal columns and lateral spinothalamic tracts
questions.concept: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration, which simultaneously demyelinates the dorsal columns (sensory ataxia, positive Romberg, loss of vibration/position sense) and the lateral corticospinal tracts (spastic weakness, brisk reflexes, extensor plantar responses). The combination of a proprioceptive sensory ataxia with upper-motor-neuron signs — sometimes alongside absent ankle jerks from an associated peripheral neuropathy — is characteristic.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — Diseases of the Spinal Cord

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with untreated syphilis has a broad-based stamping gait, lightning-like shooting pains in the legs, and falls when he closes his eyes while washing his face. He has absent ankle jerks and small irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react to light. The primary site of spinal cord damage is:
options: The dorsal columns and dorsal (posterior) nerve roots
questions.concept: Tabes dorsalis is a form of tertiary neurosyphilis that degenerates the dorsal roots and dorsal columns, producing sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia, a positive Romberg sign, lightning pains, areflexia, and loss of vibration and joint-position sense. Argyll Robertson pupils — small, irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react to light — are the classic associated finding.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord (Clinical Notes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: During repair of a thoracic aortic aneurysm a patient wakes with flaccid paraplegia and complete loss of pain and temperature sensation below the umbilicus, yet vibration and joint-position sense in the toes are entirely preserved. Which territory has been infarcted?
options: The anterior spinal artery territory, sparing the dorsal columns
The posterior spinal artery territory, sparing the corticospinal tracts
The entire cross-section of the cord at that level
A single dorsal root entry zone
questions.concept: Anterior spinal artery syndrome infarcts the anterior two-thirds of the cord: the corticospinal tracts (motor) and the spinothalamic tracts (pain/temperature) are lost bilaterally below the level, whereas the dorsal columns — supplied by the paired posterior spinal arteries — are spared, so vibration and proprioception remain intact. It is a recognised complication of aortic cross-clamping and profound hypotension.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — Vascular Diseases of the Spinal Cord

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: In the dorsal columns, the fasciculus gracilis (lying most medially) carries proprioceptive and fine-touch information from which region of the body?
options: The lower limb and lower trunk (below about the sixth thoracic segment)
The upper limb and upper trunk
questions.concept: The dorsal columns are somatotopically organised: the medially placed fasciculus gracilis carries fibers from the lower limb and lower trunk (below about T6), while the more lateral fasciculus cuneatus (present only above T6) carries fibers from the upper limb and upper trunk. A useful mnemonic is 'gracilis = ground/legs, and it lies medial'.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy — Spinal Cord: Ascending Pathways

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Second-order neurons of the pain and temperature pathway cross the midline within the spinal cord at which structure, and how far do they usually ascend before crossing?
options: The anterior (ventral) white commissure, ascending one to two segments before crossing
The posterior grey commissure, crossing within the same segment
The pyramidal decussation in the medulla
The internal arcuate fibers of the medulla
questions.concept: In the spinothalamic (anterolateral) system the second-order fibers cross in the anterior white commissure, typically ascending one to two segments above their level of entry before crossing. This delayed, oblique crossing explains why a cord hemisection produces contralateral pain/temperature loss beginning a segment or two below the lesion, and why a central (syrinx) lesion first interrupts these decussating fibers.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord and Ascending Tracts

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Approximately 85–90% of corticospinal (pyramidal) fibers cross the midline to form the lateral corticospinal tract at which anatomical site?
options: The pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla
The anterior white commissure of the spinal cord
The posterior limb of the internal capsule
The midbrain at the level of the red nucleus
questions.concept: Most corticospinal fibers decussate at the junction of the medulla and spinal cord (the pyramidal decussation) and descend as the crossed lateral corticospinal tract, which controls contralateral limb musculature. The uncrossed minority continues as the anterior corticospinal tract and crosses segmentally in the anterior white commissure to supply axial and proximal muscles.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Descending Tracts of the Spinal Cord

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: An elderly man with cervical spondylosis falls forward, striking his forehead in a hyperextension injury. He now has marked weakness and a 'burning' sensory disturbance in both hands and forearms, but his legs are only mildly affected and he can still walk. Which pattern of cord injury best explains this?
options: Central cord syndrome, damaging the central grey and the medially placed cervical corticospinal fibers
questions.concept: Acute central cord syndrome, typical of a hyperextension injury in a spondylotic cervical spine, damages the central grey matter and the medially situated cervical (arm) fibers of the lateral corticospinal tract — arm fibers lie medial to leg fibers in the tract. The result is disproportionately greater weakness and sensory disturbance in the upper limbs than the lower limbs, often with a cape-like dissociated sensory loss.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord (Clinical Notes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has progressive painless weakness with wasting and fasciculations of the hands, together with spasticity, brisk reflexes and extensor plantar responses in the legs. Sensation is entirely normal and there are no sphincter or eye-movement problems. Which structures are affected?
options: The lateral corticospinal tracts together with the anterior horn cells, with sensory tracts spared
The dorsal columns and spinocerebellar tracts
The dorsal roots and posterior columns
questions.concept: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a motor neuron disease that combines upper-motor-neuron signs (lateral corticospinal tract degeneration → spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantars) with lower-motor-neuron signs (anterior horn cell loss → wasting and fasciculations). Sensation is preserved because the ascending sensory tracts are not involved — a key clue that distinguishes it from myelopathies such as subacute combined degeneration.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis and Other Motor Neuron Diseases

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: An unimmunised child develops fever followed by rapidly progressive asymmetric flaccid weakness of one leg, with loss of tendon reflexes and later muscle wasting, but no sensory loss. The spinal structure selectively destroyed is:
questions.concept: Poliovirus has a selective tropism for the anterior horn (lower motor neuron) cells of the spinal cord, producing a pure lower-motor-neuron picture: asymmetric flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, areflexia and wasting, with completely preserved sensation because the sensory tracts and dorsal roots are spared. Involvement is typically patchy and asymmetric.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord (Clinical Notes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A teenager has progressive gait and limb ataxia, loss of vibration and joint-position sense, absent knee and ankle jerks but extensor plantar responses, along with pes cavus and scoliosis. This combination reflects degeneration of which set of spinal tracts?
options: Spinocerebellar tracts, dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
Anterior horn cells and lateral spinothalamic tracts
Dorsal roots and the anterior white commissure
questions.concept: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal-recessive GAA trinucleotide-repeat disorder that degenerates the spinocerebellar tracts (limb and gait ataxia), the dorsal columns (loss of vibration and position sense, sensory ataxia) and the corticospinal tracts (extensor plantar responses despite paradoxically absent tendon jerks). Pes cavus, scoliosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are characteristic associated features.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — The Hereditary Ataxias

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: In the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway, where does the first-order (primary) sensory neuron synapse onto the second-order neuron?
options: In the nucleus gracilis or nucleus cuneatus of the medulla
In the dorsal horn at the segmental level of entry
In the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus
questions.concept: Uniquely among the major sensory pathways, the first-order neuron of the dorsal column system ascends ipsilaterally the entire length of the cord before synapsing in the gracile or cuneate nucleus of the medulla. The second-order neuron then crosses as the internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus and terminates on the third-order neuron in the VPL of the thalamus, which projects to the primary sensory cortex.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy — Spinal Cord: Ascending Pathways

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A patient stands steadily with the eyes open but sways and nearly falls the moment the eyes are closed (a positive Romberg sign). This finding localises the lesion to which spinal pathway?
questions.concept: A positive Romberg sign indicates a sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia due to dorsal column dysfunction. With the eyes open, vision compensates for the lost joint-position sense; on closing the eyes that visual compensation is removed and the patient sways. A cerebellar ataxia, by contrast, is present even with the eyes open, so Romberg's test is negative in cerebellar disease.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord (Clinical Notes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A knife wound hemisects the left half of the spinal cord at the C6 level. Which of the following findings is expected below the lesion?
options: Loss of pain and temperature on the RIGHT side of the body, beginning a few segments below the lesion
Loss of pain and temperature on the LEFT side of the body
Loss of vibration and proprioception on the RIGHT side of the body
Flaccid paralysis of the right lower limb
questions.concept: In Brown-Séquard (cord hemisection) the spinothalamic fibers have already crossed, so pain and temperature are lost contralaterally (on the right), beginning one to two segments below the lesion. The dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts are still uncrossed at this level, so vibration/proprioception loss and spastic weakness are ipsilateral (on the left). Hence the expected finding is contralateral (right-sided) pain and temperature loss.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord (Clinical Notes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: To relieve intractable cancer pain in the right leg, a neurosurgeon divides the left anterolateral quadrant of the spinal cord (an anterolateral cordotomy). Which tract is being deliberately interrupted?
options: The lateral spinothalamic tract, carrying already-crossed pain and temperature fibers
questions.concept: Because pain and temperature fibers cross within the cord and then ascend in the contralateral lateral spinothalamic tract, cutting the left anterolateral quadrant abolishes pain and temperature sensation on the right side of the body below the lesion — the anatomical principle behind anterolateral cordotomy. Touch, vibration and proprioception are preserved because the dorsal columns are untouched.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord and Ascending Tracts

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A young adult with a known cervical syrinx, who already had a cape-like loss of pain and temperature over the shoulders, now develops wasting, weakness and areflexia of the small muscles of both hands. This new finding is due to the expanding cavity now involving:
options: The anterior horn cells at the affected cervical segments
The lateral spinothalamic fibers that have already crossed and ascended
questions.concept: A syrinx begins centrally and first interrupts the decussating spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure, producing dissociated 'cape' sensory loss (pain/temperature lost, touch/proprioception spared). As the cavity enlarges ventrolaterally it destroys the anterior horn cells, causing lower-motor-neuron wasting, weakness and areflexia of the hands; still later, lateral corticospinal involvement adds spastic weakness of the legs.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord (Clinical Notes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The dorsal (posterior) spinocerebellar tract, which arises from the nucleus dorsalis of Clarke, conveys which type of information, and does it cross the midline?
options: Unconscious proprioception from the lower limb, ascending uncrossed (ipsilateral) to the cerebellum
Conscious proprioception, crossing in the medulla
Pain and temperature, crossing in the spinal cord
Voluntary motor commands descending to the cerebellum
questions.concept: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract originates in the nucleus dorsalis of Clarke (roughly C8–L2/3) and carries unconscious proprioceptive information from muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs of the lower limb and trunk. It remains uncrossed (ipsilateral) and enters the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle, providing the input needed for coordination of posture and fine limb movement.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy — Spinal Cord: Ascending Pathways

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A discrete lesion damages only the lateral corticospinal tract on the right side of the spinal cord at the T8 level. On which side, and with what features, will the resulting motor deficit appear below the lesion?
options: On the right (ipsilateral) side, with spastic weakness, hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response
On the left (contralateral) side, with flaccid weakness and absent reflexes
On the right side, with flaccid paralysis and fasciculations
questions.concept: The corticospinal fibers have already decussated in the medulla, so within the spinal cord the lateral corticospinal tract carries fibers destined for the ipsilateral (same-side) muscles. A right-sided cord lesion therefore produces right-sided upper-motor-neuron signs below the level — spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response — not contralateral or flaccid weakness.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Descending Tracts of the Spinal Cord

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which set of clinical signs indicates an upper motor neuron (corticospinal tract) lesion rather than a lower motor neuron lesion?
options: Spasticity, hyperreflexia and an extensor (upgoing) plantar response
Flaccidity, prominent fasciculations and marked early muscle wasting
Absent tendon reflexes with fully preserved power
Loss of pain and temperature with normal muscle power
questions.concept: Upper motor neuron (corticospinal) lesions produce spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, an extensor plantar (positive Babinski) response and only minimal (disuse) wasting. Lower motor neuron lesions instead cause flaccid weakness, hypotonia, hyporeflexia or areflexia, marked wasting and fasciculations. Correctly separating these two patterns is the first step in localising a lesion along the motor pathway.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Descending Tracts of the Spinal Cord

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The ventral (anterior) spinocerebellar tract is unusual in that its fibres cross the midline twice before reaching the cerebellum. Through which cerebellar peduncle does it finally enter the cerebellum?
questions.concept: The ventral (anterior) spinocerebellar tract arises from spinal border cells, crosses the midline in the cord, ascends, and then crosses back a second time within the cerebellum, entering through the superior cerebellar peduncle. The dorsal spinocerebellar tract from Clarke's column stays uncrossed and enters via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Both carry unconscious proprioception from the lower limb.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: For both the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway and the spinothalamic pathway, the third-order neuron that projects to the primary somatosensory cortex has its cell body located in which structure?
options: Ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus
Substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn
questions.concept: For both the dorsal column–medial lemniscus and spinothalamic systems the third-order neuron lies in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus (the face is relayed by VPM). Its axon passes through the posterior limb of the internal capsule to the postcentral gyrus. The nucleus gracilis houses second-order DCML cell bodies, and dorsal root ganglia contain the first-order neurons.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: On entering the spinal cord, first-order pain and temperature fibres ascend or descend one to two segments before synapsing in the dorsal horn. Within which structure do they travel during this short course?
questions.concept: Thinly myelinated and unmyelinated pain and temperature (and crude touch) fibres travel one to two segments up or down in the dorsolateral tract of Lissauer before synapsing on second-order neurons in the dorsal horn, chiefly the substantia gelatinosa (Rexed lamina II). This is why the spinothalamic sensory level often lies a segment or two below the actual level of a cord lesion.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has a slowly enlarging intramedullary spinal cord tumour in the thoracic region. He has lost pain and temperature sensation over the trunk and both lower limbs, yet sensation over the perineum and perianal 'saddle' area is strikingly preserved. This 'sacral sparing' is explained by which feature of the spinothalamic tract?
options: Sacral fibres are laminated most laterally and are spared by a centrally expanding lesion
Sacral fibres decussate only in the medulla
Sacral sensation is carried entirely in the dorsal columns
Sacral dermatomes have dual (bilateral) cord innervation
questions.concept: In the lateral spinothalamic tract fibres are somatotopically laminated, with sacral segments lying most laterally (superficially) and cervical segments most medially.
