A centrally arising intramedullary tumour or syrinx therefore destroys the medial cervical/thoracic fibres first while the laterally placed sacral fibres are spared, producing 'sacral sparing.' An extramedullary compressive lesion tends instead to involve sacral sensation early.
questions.reference: Vishram Singh, Textbook of Clinical Neuroanatomy, 3rd ed., Ch. 6 (Spinal Cord)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The fasciculus cuneatus is present in the dorsal columns only above the mid-thoracic (approximately T6) level. Which information does it convey?
options: Fine touch, vibration and conscious proprioception from the upper limb, upper trunk and neck
Pain and temperature from the lower limb
Conscious proprioception from the lower limb and lower trunk
Voluntary motor commands to the upper limb
questions.concept: The dorsal columns comprise a medial fasciculus gracilis and a lateral fasciculus cuneatus. The cuneatus is added at about the T6 level and carries discriminative touch, vibration and conscious proprioception from the upper limb, upper trunk and neck; below T6 only the gracilis (lower limb and lower trunk) is present. Cuneatus fibres synapse in the nucleus cuneatus of the medulla.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A comatose patient after a midbrain haemorrhage shows extension and internal rotation of all four limbs (decerebrate posturing). Loss of which descending influence, leaving vestibulospinal and pontine reticulospinal drive to the extensors unopposed, best explains this posture?
options: Rubrospinal tract facilitation of flexor tone
Lateral corticospinal tract control of the hands
questions.concept: Decerebrate rigidity (extension of all four limbs) follows a brainstem lesion below the level of the red nucleus. Removing the rubrospinal tract's facilitation of flexor muscle tone leaves the extensor drive of the lateral vestibulospinal and pontine reticulospinal tracts unopposed, so extensor tone dominates. A lesion above the red nucleus (e.g., internal capsule) spares rubrospinal flexor facilitation and instead produces decorticate posturing with arm flexion.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The largest neurons contributing axons to the corticospinal tract, the giant Betz cells, are found in which layer of the primary motor cortex?
questions.concept: Only about 30% of corticospinal fibres arise from the primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4), with the rest from premotor and sensory areas. The giant Betz cells, the largest neurons of the primary motor cortex, lie in cortical layer V (the internal pyramidal layer) and contribute the fastest-conducting, largest-diameter corticospinal axons, though they form only a small fraction of the tract's total fibres.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A patient with a cervical syrinx develops a right-sided Horner's syndrome (partial ptosis, miosis and facial anhidrosis). Damage to which grey-matter structure, the origin of pre-ganglionic sympathetic fibres, accounts for this?
options: Intermediolateral cell column (lateral horn) at C8–T2
questions.concept: Pre-ganglionic sympathetic neurons occupy the intermediolateral cell column (lateral horn) of spinal segments T1–L2, and those supplying the head and eye emerge from C8–T2 (the ciliospinal centre of Budge). A cervical syrinx expanding into this lateral horn interrupts the oculosympathetic outflow, producing an ipsilateral Horner's syndrome of partial ptosis, miosis and facial anhidrosis.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 24-year-old man develops an episode of visible (gross) hematuria within 1-2 days of an upper respiratory tract infection, and similar episodes recur with subsequent infections. Renal biopsy immunofluorescence shows mesangial deposits of which immunoglobulin?
questions.concept: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. Synpharyngitic gross hematuria (concurrent with, not 1-2 weeks after, a mucosal infection) with mesangial IgA and C3 deposits distinguishes it from poststreptococcal GN, where hematuria follows the infection by weeks.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has nephrotic-range proteinuria, and renal biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall with subepithelial deposits producing a 'spike and dome' pattern on silver stain. Circulating autoantibodies against which podocyte antigen are most characteristic?
questions.concept: Primary membranous nephropathy is a leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults and older Caucasians; roughly 70% are driven by autoantibodies to the podocyte antigen PLA2R. Subepithelial immune-complex deposits with reactive GBM spikes give the silver-stain 'spike and dome' appearance.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 40-year-old African-American man with HIV infection develops heavy proteinuria and full nephrotic syndrome. Renal biopsy shows sclerosis involving portions (segments) of some (focal) glomeruli, with the rest appearing normal on light microscopy. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, especially in people of African descent and in HIV, heroin use, sickle cell and obesity. Light microscopy shows sclerosis of segments of some glomeruli; unlike minimal change disease it causes non-selective proteinuria and often responds poorly to steroids.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a malar rash, arthralgia and positive anti-dsDNA develops hematuria and proteinuria. Renal biopsy shows diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with thickened, homogeneous eosinophilic capillary loops ('wire-loop' lesions) and a 'full-house' immunofluorescence pattern. This corresponds to which class of lupus nephritis?
questions.concept: Class IV diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis is the most common and most severe form. Subendothelial immune-complex deposits produce 'wire-loop' capillary loops, and immunofluorescence shows 'full-house' staining (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q). It carries the worst renal prognosis and drives aggressive immunosuppression.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A young adult presents with a mixed nephrotic-nephritic picture and persistently low serum C3. Renal biopsy shows a thickened glomerular basement membrane with a 'tram-track' (double-contour) appearance caused by mesangial cell interposition. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Membranoproliferative GN presents with a combined nephrotic/nephritic picture and low complement. Duplication/splitting of the GBM from mesangial cell interposition and new basement-membrane synthesis gives the classic 'tram-track' double-contour appearance on silver/PAS stain.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has recurrent hematuria, progressive sensorineural hearing loss and anterior lenticonus. Electron microscopy of the glomerular basement membrane shows irregular thinning and thickening with 'basket-weave' splitting of the lamina densa. The defective protein is:
questions.concept: Alport syndrome is a hereditary nephritis, most often X-linked, caused by mutations in type IV collagen (alpha-3/4/5 chains). The clinical triad is hematuria progressing to renal failure, sensorineural deafness and ocular defects (anterior lenticonus), with a pathognomonic 'basket-weave' GBM on electron microscopy.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has persistent asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with normal renal function, normal hearing and no significant proteinuria; several relatives have similar isolated hematuria. Electron microscopy shows diffuse uniform thinning of the glomerular basement membrane. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Thin basement membrane disease (benign familial hematuria)
questions.concept: Thin basement membrane disease (benign familial hematuria) causes lifelong isolated microscopic hematuria with an excellent prognosis; EM shows diffusely thinned GBM (roughly 150-250 nm versus the normal ~350-400 nm). Unlike Alport syndrome it lacks deafness, ocular lesions and progression to renal failure.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with rapidly progressive renal failure and hemoptysis. Renal biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis, but immunofluorescence reveals NO immune deposits (pauci-immune). Which serologic test is most likely to be positive?
questions.concept: Pauci-immune crescentic (RPGN type III) glomerulonephritis lacks glomerular immune deposits and is associated with ANCA — c-ANCA/PR3 in granulomatosis with polyangiitis and p-ANCA/MPO in microscopic polyangiitis and EGPA. Anti-GBM disease (type I) instead shows linear IgG, and immune-complex RPGN (type II) shows granular deposits.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — Glomerular Diseases

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient develops acute kidney injury after prolonged hypotension from septic shock. Urinalysis shows muddy-brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Ischemic acute tubular necrosis is the commonest cause of intrinsic AKI. Sloughed necrotic tubular epithelium forms pathognomonic 'muddy-brown' granular casts; unlike prerenal azotemia the FENa is greater than 2% and urine osmolality is low because injured tubules cannot concentrate or reabsorb sodium.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 58-year-old diabetic woman with a long history of analgesic (NSAID/phenacetin) abuse develops flank pain, gross hematuria and passes sloughed tissue fragments in her urine; imaging shows destruction of the renal papillae. This complication is:
questions.concept: Renal papillary necrosis is classically caused by Diabetes mellitus, Analgesic abuse (NSAIDs/phenacetin), Sickle cell disease, and severe pyelonephritis/obstruction. Ischemic coagulative necrosis of the papillae produces flank pain, hematuria and sloughed papillary tissue passed in the urine.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 62-year-old smoker presents with painless hematuria, dull flank pain and a palpable abdominal mass; CT shows a solid renal mass extending into the renal vein. Histology shows nests of cells with clear, lipid- and glycogen-laden cytoplasm. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma, linked to VHL gene inactivation and smoking, is the commonest renal malignancy in adults. The classic triad is hematuria, flank pain and a palpable mass; it characteristically invades the renal vein and can cause paraneoplastic syndromes (polycythemia, hypercalcemia, Cushing).
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient with nephrotic syndrome suddenly develops acute flank pain and worsening proteinuria; imaging confirms renal vein thrombosis. Urinary loss of which protein best explains this thrombotic tendency?
questions.concept: Nephrotic syndrome produces a hypercoagulable state largely from urinary loss of antithrombin III and other anticoagulant regulators, predisposing to renal vein thrombosis and venous thromboembolism. Membranous nephropathy has the strongest association with renal vein thrombosis among the nephrotic pathologies.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — Glomerular Diseases

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which combination of findings best characterizes the NEPHRITIC syndrome, as opposed to the nephrotic syndrome?
options: Hematuria with RBC casts, hypertension and sub-nephrotic proteinuria
Proteinuria over 3.5 g/day with hypoalbuminemia and generalized edema
Massive selective proteinuria without any hematuria
Isolated lipiduria with oval fat bodies and no hematuria
questions.concept: Nephritic syndrome reflects glomerular inflammation: hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts, oliguria, hypertension and mild-to-moderate (sub-nephrotic) proteinuria. Nephrotic syndrome, by contrast, is defined by proteinuria over 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia/lipiduria.
questions.reference: Robbins Basic Pathology — The Kidney and Its Collecting System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A child develops acute nephritic syndrome about two weeks after impetigo. Which finding best supports poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis and its typically favorable prognosis?
options: Raised anti-DNase B / ASO titer with a low C3 that normalizes in about 8 weeks
Linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane
Persistently low C3 lasting beyond 3 months
questions.concept: Poststreptococcal GN follows pharyngitis or skin infection (impetigo) by 1-3 weeks. Evidence of recent streptococcal infection (raised ASO or anti-DNase B) with a transiently low C3 that recovers within about 8 weeks supports the diagnosis. Prognosis is excellent in children; EM shows subepithelial 'humps'.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A child has persistent hypocomplementemia and nephritic features; renal biopsy shows ribbon-like, intensely electron-dense deposits within the glomerular basement membrane itself. This finding is most associated with which autoantibody?
questions.concept: Dense deposit disease (formerly MPGN type II, now a C3 glomerulopathy) shows dense intramembranous deposits transforming the lamina densa into a ribbon. It is driven by C3 nephritic factor, an autoantibody that stabilizes the alternative-pathway C3 convertase, causing unregulated complement consumption and persistently very low C3.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with a large, smooth, unilateral abdominal mass that does not cross the midline, along with hematuria and hypertension. Histology shows a triphasic pattern of blastemal, primitive epithelial (tubular) and stromal elements. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is the commonest primary renal malignancy of childhood, peaking at 2-5 years, and is associated with WT1 mutations (WAGR, Denys-Drash) and WT2/Beckwith-Wiedemann. It forms a triphasic blastemal-epithelial-stromal mass. Neuroblastoma, its main mimic, characteristically crosses the midline and encases vessels.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops nephrotic-range proteinuria. Renal biopsy stained with Congo red shows mesangial and vascular deposits that display apple-green birefringence under polarized light. These deposits are:
questions.concept: Renal amyloidosis (AA type in chronic inflammation such as rheumatoid arthritis; AL type in plasma-cell dyscrasias) deposits beta-pleated-sheet protein in the mesangium and vessel walls, causing nephrotic syndrome. Congo red staining is pathognomonic, showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: What is the earliest clinical indicator of diabetic nephropathy?
questions.concept: The earliest clinically detectable sign of diabetic nephropathy is microalbuminuria (urinary albumin 30-300 mg/day), reflecting early glomerular injury before overt proteinuria or a rise in creatinine. Structurally, GBM thickening and mesangial expansion precede the nodular Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions; ACE inhibitors/ARBs are renoprotective at this stage.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — Diabetic Nephropathy

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy develops palpable purpura over the buttocks and lower legs, colicky abdominal pain, arthralgia and hematuria following a viral illness. Skin and renal mesangial biopsies show deposition of which immunoglobulin?
questions.concept: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) is the most common systemic vasculitis of childhood. IgA immune-complex deposition in small vessels and the glomerular mesangium produces the tetrad of palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal (GI) pain and glomerulonephritis; the renal lesion is histologically identical to IgA nephropathy.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which is the most common cause of the nephrotic syndrome in children?
questions.concept: Minimal change disease accounts for the majority of nephrotic syndrome in children. It produces highly selective proteinuria, responds dramatically to corticosteroids, shows normal light microscopy, and reveals only diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement on electron microscopy. Membranous nephropathy predominates in adults.
questions.reference: Robbins Basic Pathology — The Kidney and Its Collecting System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient with nephrotic syndrome has 'oval fat bodies' in the urine that display a 'Maltese cross' appearance under polarized light. This finding reflects urinary loss of which substance?
questions.concept: Heavy glomerular protein loss in nephrotic syndrome is accompanied by hyperlipidaemia and lipiduria. Filtered lipoproteins are taken up by tubular cells and shed as 'oval fat bodies' and fatty casts; under polarized light the cholesterol esters produce the characteristic 'Maltese cross' birefringence. This confirms the lipiduria of nephrotic syndrome rather than loss of red cells or immunoglobulins.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Ch. 20 (The Kidney)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which glomerular disease is now the most common cause of primary (idiopathic) nephrotic syndrome in adults, especially among African-Americans?
questions.concept: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) has become the most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults, particularly among African-Americans, and its incidence is rising. Membranous nephropathy is the classic cause in older Caucasian adults, whereas minimal change disease predominates in children. FSGS shows sclerosis of segments of some glomeruli with foot-process effacement and is frequently steroid-resistant.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Ch. 20 (The Kidney)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is newly diagnosed with membranous nephropathy on renal biopsy. In an adult of this age, which underlying condition most importantly needs to be actively excluded as a secondary cause?
options: An occult solid-organ malignancy (e.g., lung or colon carcinoma)
questions.concept: Membranous nephropathy is primary (anti-PLA2R antibody mediated) in about three-quarters of cases, but in an older adult secondary causes must be sought — above all an occult solid-organ malignancy (lung, colon, breast, prostate), plus infections such as hepatitis B, autoimmune disease (SLE) and drugs (NSAIDs, penicillamine, gold). Age-appropriate cancer screening is therefore indicated in a newly diagnosed older patient.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Ch. 20 (The Kidney)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: In rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, the crescents that fill Bowman's space are composed predominantly of which elements?
options: Proliferating parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating macrophages, with fibrin
questions.concept: In rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, breaks in the glomerular capillary wall let fibrin and plasma proteins into Bowman's space, triggering proliferation of parietal epithelial cells together with infiltrating monocytes/macrophages to form cellular crescents that compress the tuft. If untreated they organise into fibrous crescents with irreversible loss of function. Crescents are the histological hallmark whatever the immunologic type (I anti-GBM, II immune-complex, III pauci-immune).
questions.reference: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology, 7th ed., Ch. 22 (The Kidney and Lower Urinary Tract)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient presents with a nephritic picture. Which of the following is characteristically associated with a NORMAL serum complement (C3) level, helping distinguish it from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.concept: Serum complement helps classify glomerulonephritis. Normocomplementaemic (normal C3) nephritides include IgA nephropathy, Henoch-Schonlein purpura, anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease, ANCA-associated pauci-immune GN and Alport syndrome. Hypocomplementaemic (low C3) causes include post-streptococcal GN, membranoproliferative GN/dense deposit disease, lupus nephritis, cryoglobulinaemia and endocarditis-associated GN. A normal C3 in a nephritic patient therefore points away from PSGN toward IgA nephropathy.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Ch. 20 (The Kidney)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: In diabetic nephropathy, what is the earliest detectable histological (structural) glomerular change, appearing before the pathognomonic Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules?
options: Diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with mesangial matrix expansion
Cellular crescent formation in Bowman's space
Wire-loop lesions of the capillary loops
questions.concept: The earliest structural glomerular lesion of diabetic nephropathy is diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, detectable within a couple of years of disease onset, accompanied by progressive mesangial matrix expansion. Only later do the pathognomonic nodular Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions and hyaline arteriolosclerosis appear. Clinically the earliest marker is microalbuminuria, but histologically the earliest change is GBM thickening.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Ch. 20 (The Kidney)

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Which of the following is the use of the Mallampatti classification?
options: To evaluate the risk of surgery
To evaluate the pros and cons of surgery
To evaluate the fitness of the patient
questions.concept: The Mallampati classification grades visibility of the oropharyngeal structures (soft palate, uvula, pillars) with the mouth open, and is used to predict the difficulty of laryngoscopy and endotracheal intubation - it is an airway assessment, not an overall surgical-risk score.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Which of the following topical local anesthetics is commonly used in cataract surgery?
questions.concept: Proparacaine 0.5% is a rapid-onset topical ester anaesthetic routinely instilled for ocular surface anaesthesia in cataract surgery and tonometry; bupivacaine is an injectable local anaesthetic, and halothane/nitrous oxide are inhalational general anaesthetics.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Lower limb: femoral/sciatic nerve, foot drop
questions.stem: A surgical procedure is performed on the great saphenous vein, around 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus. Which of the following structures is most likely to be injured?
questions.concept: The saphenous nerve (terminal sensory branch of the femoral nerve) travels with the great saphenous vein just anterior to the medial malleolus, so it is the structure most at risk during saphenous vein surgery at the ankle; the sural nerve accompanies the small saphenous vein posterolaterally.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Zellweger syndrome is associated with which cellular organelle?
questions.concept: Zellweger (cerebrohepatorenal) syndrome is the prototype peroxisomal biogenesis disorder, so the organelle involved is the peroxisome. NOTE: the scraped answer key said 'Nucleosomes' (B), but that is medically incorrect - the correct organelle is the peroxisome (A).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A 3-month-old baby presents with severe hepatomegaly, cataracts in both eyes, lethargy, and hypotonia. Based on these symptoms, which enzyme deficiency is most likely involved?
questions.concept: Classic galactosemia is caused by galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT) deficiency, producing hepatomegaly, bilateral cataracts, lethargy/hypotonia and E. coli sepsis; galactokinase deficiency causes isolated cataracts without the hepatic and neurologic features.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A child with a sore throat starts developing skin lesions as in the image below. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Guttate psoriasis appears as sudden crops of small, drop-like (guttate) scaly papules a week or two after a streptococcal sore throat, classically in children and young adults; the post-strep history is the key pointer even without the image.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A truck driver reports multiple painful genital ulcers on his scrotum following unprotected sexual intercourse, accompanied by painful lymph nodes. What is the most likely cause?
questions.concept: Multiple painful genital ulcers with tender, suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo) are characteristic of chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi); the syphilitic chancre is a solitary painless ulcer with painless adenopathy, and donovanosis is a painless beefy-red ulcer.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A patient with a history of trauma presents with hearing loss. A High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) scan was performed. Which of the following structures is not typically visualized on HRCT?
questions.concept: HRCT of the temporal bone resolves bony and air-containing structures (cochlea, vestibule, semicircular canals) but cannot show the microscopic soft-tissue organ of Corti within the cochlear duct.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: What is the most commonly used test for newborn hearing screening?
questions.concept: Otoacoustic emissions (OAE) are the standard first-line universal newborn hearing screen - quick, non-invasive and objective; BERA is used as the confirmatory second-tier test in babies who fail OAE.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: During measurement of a rifled barrel weapon, the caliber depends on?
questions.concept: The calibre (bore) of a rifled firearm is the distance between two diametrically opposite lands (the raised ridges left after the barrel is grooved), not between the grooves.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A farmer presents with a painful snakebite wound on his right foot. There are two fang marks with swelling and bleeding at the bite site. What is the first step in management?
options: Sling or splint leading to immobilization
See the snake brought by a relative
questions.concept: First aid for snakebite follows the R.I.G.H.T. approach - Reassure, Immobilise the bitten limb (splint, keep below heart level) and get to hospital; anti-snake venom is definitive but is given in hospital only once features of systemic envenomation appear, so immobilisation is the correct first step. (Venom suction and tourniquets are harmful and contraindicated.)

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: For how long is exclusive breastfeeding recommended?
questions.concept: WHO/UNICEF recommend exclusive breastfeeding (breast milk only, no water or other foods) for the first 6 months of life, with complementary feeding started thereafter while breastfeeding continues up to 2 years.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct definition of postpartum pyrexia?
questions.concept: Puerperal (postpartum) pyrexia is a temperature of 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees C) or more on two occasions 24 hours apart within the first 10 days postpartum, excluding the first 24 hours - so the fever counted is that arising after the first 24 hours.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 46-year-old male presents to the outpatient department with a history of lower back pain and painful urination. Upon investigation, he is found to have normocytic normochromic anemia and hypercalcemia. Serum protein electrophoresis reveals an M-spike in the gamma region. Which of the following tests is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis of multiple myeloma?
questions.concept: Multiple myeloma is confirmed by demonstrating monoclonal free light chains (Bence Jones protein) in urine alongside the serum M-spike, marrow plasmacytosis, hypercalcaemia, anaemia and lytic bone lesions; ordinary urine dipstick/UACR misses light chains.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A young woman presents with recurrent headaches, easy bruising, and episodes of visual blurring. Her platelet count is elevated, while her red blood cell (RBC) and white blood cell (WBC) counts are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Isolated, sustained thrombocytosis with normal RBC and WBC counts causing microvascular symptoms (headache, visual disturbance) plus a bleeding/thrombosis tendency points to essential thrombocythemia, a myeloproliferative neoplasm; polycythemia vera would raise the haematocrit and CML/AML the WBC count.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which of the following microorganisms is likely responsible for causing bilateral infiltrates in an HIV-positive patient?
questions.concept: In an HIV patient with a low CD4 count, bilateral diffuse perihilar interstitial infiltrates are classically due to Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), the commonest AIDS-defining opportunistic pneumonia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which nerve defect causes lagophthalmos?
questions.concept: Lagophthalmos (inability to fully close the eye) results from facial nerve (CN VII) palsy, which paralyses orbicularis oculi, the muscle that closes the eyelids.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle?
questions.concept: The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve (CN VI) - remember 'LR6 SO4': lateral rectus = 6th, superior oblique = 4th, and all other extraocular muscles = oculomotor (3rd).

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: The diagnosis in a patient who is unable to do internal and external rotation of the hip is?
questions.concept: A hip that cannot be internally or externally rotated points to a dislocation, where the femoral head is locked out of the acetabulum producing a fixed deformity; fractures around the hip usually permit some (painful) movement rather than a rigid rotational block.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In the context of a new onset of a morbid disease, how does the change in incidence affect the prevalence of the disease?
options: Prevalence is not related to incidence
Incidence will increase, and prevalence will decrease
Prevalence will increase with a decrease in the incidence
questions.concept: Prevalence is approximately incidence multiplied by average disease duration; when a new disease emerges and incidence rises (with duration unchanged), prevalence rises too, so both increase together.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A gym owner observes that individuals who drink iced tea during their workouts tend to lose more weight. What is the nature of this relationship?
questions.concept: This is an indirect association: the real association is entirely explained by a common confounder (the exercise/health-consciousness that accompanies iced-tea drinking drives the weight loss), so iced tea is not the direct cause. A spurious association would be a false one arising from chance or bias.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which of the following organs is a primary lymphoid organ?
questions.concept: Primary (central) lymphoid organs - the bone marrow and thymus - are where lymphocytes are produced and mature; lymph node, spleen and MALT are secondary lymphoid organs where antigen-driven responses take place.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the earliest marker to rise in a case of myocardial infarction (MI)?
questions.concept: Heart-type fatty acid binding protein (H-FABP) is a small cytosolic protein released within 1-3 hours of myocardial injury, rising even earlier than CK-MB and troponin, making it the earliest of the listed markers; troponin remains the most specific/confirmatory.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: What condition is likely in a newborn presenting with dry, rough skin, a big tongue and rough hair?
questions.concept: A neonate with coarse dry skin, macroglossia (large tongue), coarse hair, hypotonia and prolonged jaundice suggests congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism); untreated it causes irreversible intellectual disability, which is why newborn TSH screening exists.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: What is the likely age of a child who can ride a tricycle, walk up stairs with alternate steps, but cannot hop?
questions.concept: Riding a tricycle and climbing stairs with alternating feet are ~3-year gross-motor milestones, whereas hopping on one foot appears around 4 years; a child with the former but not yet hopping is about 3-3.5 years old.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: What is the mechanism of action of Ethosuximide?
options: Inhibits calcium channels in thalamic neurons
questions.concept: Ethosuximide, the drug of choice for absence (petit mal) seizures, works by blocking T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons, interrupting the thalamocortical rhythm underlying 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A female patient with a history of bronchial asthma has developed an acute attack of migraine. Which drug should be avoided?
questions.concept: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker (used for migraine prophylaxis) that must be avoided in asthmatics because beta-2 receptor blockade precipitates bronchospasm; the other listed agents are not contraindicated by asthma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: What is the typical Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) in a healthy adult?
questions.concept: Normal glomerular filtration rate in a healthy adult is about 125 mL/min (roughly 180 L/day), conventionally estimated using inulin or creatinine clearance.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: What renal function is represented by the formula UV/P?
questions.concept: Renal clearance is calculated as (U x V)/P - urine concentration times urine flow rate divided by plasma concentration - giving the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per unit time.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: What is the medical term for a person who fears seeing tall buildings and looking down from heights?
questions.concept: Acrophobia is the specific phobia of heights; agoraphobia is fear of open or crowded places from which escape is difficult, claustrophobia of enclosed spaces, and nomophobia of being without a mobile phone.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: A 45-year-old male presented with severe abdominal pain following alcohol intake. Make a diagnosis based on the given X-ray.
questions.concept: Free gas under the diaphragm on an erect film indicates pneumoperitoneum, most often from a perforated peptic ulcer - a recognised cause of sudden severe abdominal pain in a patient after alcohol. NOTE: this is an image-dependent question and the X-ray itself was not available to review; the answer follows the scraped key and the text (abdominal, not chest, pain favours perforated ulcer over Boerhaave-related pneumomediastinum), so it is left unverified.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: Ga-68 PSMA PET scan is used to diagnose which of the following conditions?
questions.concept: Ga-68 PSMA (prostate-specific membrane antigen) PET/CT targets PSMA that is over-expressed on prostate cancer cells, and is used to stage and detect biochemically recurrent prostate cancer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman, 10 years after mastectomy, notices gradual swelling and heaviness in her right upper limb without pain. On examination, bluish nodules on the skin with no infections are noted. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.concept: Long-standing post-mastectomy lymphoedema of the arm that later develops bluish/purple cutaneous nodules is Stewart-Treves syndrome - a lymphangiosarcoma arising within the chronically lymphoedematous limb.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which of the following inhalation agents has a blood-gas partition coefficient similar to nitrous oxide?
questions.concept: Desflurane's blood-gas partition coefficient (~0.42) is closest to that of nitrous oxide (~0.47); a low coefficient means low blood solubility, giving rapid induction and recovery. Isoflurane (1.4) and halothane (2.3) are far more soluble.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: In epidural anesthesia, which of the following layers is least likely to be punctured during the procedure?
questions.concept: In an epidural the needle stops in the epidural (extradural) space, so it crosses skin, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments and ligamentum flavum but does NOT pierce the dura or arachnoid mater; arachnoid puncture occurs only in spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthesia. (Option D 'Infraspinous' is a mis-transcription of the interspinous ligament.)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which muscle movements are related to the Abducens nerve?
questions.concept: The abducens nerve (CN VI) supplies only the lateral rectus, which abducts the eye; its palsy causes a convergent (medial) squint with failure of abduction.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which substance is involved in the conjugation process in the liver?
questions.concept: Hepatic phase-II conjugation uses UDP-glucuronic acid (a glucose-derived uronic-acid-pathway product) to glucuronidate bilirubin, drugs and hormones for excretion; glucuronic acid is the conjugating moiety.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A 7-year-old child of short stature presents with skin patches and learning difficulties. Diagnostic workup indicates a defect in DNA repair specifically related to double-strand breaks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Bloom syndrome is caused by a defective BLM RecQ helicase needed for homologous-recombination repair of double-strand breaks, producing chromosomal instability, marked short stature, photosensitive facial erythema/cafe-au-lait patches and cancer predisposition. XP and Cockayne are nucleotide-excision-repair defects and Lynch is a mismatch-repair defect, so the 'double-strand break' clue uniquely selects Bloom.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following deficiencies causes follicular hyperkeratosis?
questions.concept: Follicular hyperkeratosis (phrynoderma, 'toad skin') is the classic cutaneous sign of vitamin A deficiency, reflecting keratinising metaplasia of the follicular epithelium.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: What nutritional deficiency is commonly associated with a chronic alcoholic presenting with a pruritic, eczematous rash on the neck and dorsum of the hands?
questions.concept: A photosensitive, eczematous rash over sun-exposed skin (neck = Casal's necklace, dorsa of hands) in an alcoholic is pellagra from niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency - the classic 3 D's: dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 50-year-old male presents with right-sided serous otitis media and a history of cervical lymphadenopathy. The probable diagnosis is?
questions.concept: New-onset unilateral serous otitis media in an adult (from Eustachian-tube obstruction) together with cervical lymphadenopathy is nasopharyngeal carcinoma until proven otherwise.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A person who was mentally unsound at the time of committing a crime is exempt from liability if they were unaware of the nature of their actions or its consequences. What is this principle called?
questions.concept: The McNaughton (M'Naghten) rule is the legal test of insanity: a person is not criminally liable if, due to unsoundness of mind, they did not know the nature of the act or that it was wrong.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Acute liver failure is a clinical feature of which of the following?
questions.concept: Amanita phalloides ('death cap') contains amatoxins that inhibit RNA polymerase II, producing hepatocellular necrosis and acute (fulminant) liver failure. OP poisoning gives a cholinergic crisis, belladonna an anticholinergic picture and morphine respiratory depression.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Identify the option with the least risk of TOLAC (trial of labor after cesarean)?
questions.concept: A prior low-segment transverse (Kerr) uterine incision carries the lowest risk of scar rupture and is the best candidate for a trial of labour after caesarean; a previous classical (upper-segment vertical) incision is a contraindication to TOLAC.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which among the following hormones acts on post ovulatory endometrium?
questions.concept: After ovulation the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which converts the oestrogen-primed proliferative endometrium into the secretory phase to support implantation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 27-year-old pregnant female in her first trimester presents to the OPD for a regular antenatal checkup. During blood type screening, potential ABO incompatibility is discussed. The healthcare provider explains that certain antibody types are less concerning than others during pregnancy. ABO incompatibility does not occur due to which antibody in her case?
questions.concept: ABO haemolytic disease of the newborn is caused by maternal IgG anti-A/anti-B crossing the placenta; naturally occurring ABO isohaemagglutinins are IgM, and IgD is not a blood-group antibody at all, so incompatibility never arises from IgD. NOTE: the wording is ambiguous - the inferred key is IgD (the isotype never involved in ABO antibodies), but a reader focused on placental transfer could defensibly pick IgM (does not cross the placenta), so this item is flagged for manual review.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: An 8-year-old child with a history of GTCS came with an episode of convulsions for more than 45 minutes. What will be the appropriate management for this patient?
questions.concept: A convulsion lasting more than 5 minutes is status epilepticus; first-line therapy is an IV benzodiazepine (lorazepam) and, if seizures persist, a second-line agent such as levetiracetam (or valproate/fosphenytoin) is added.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient having hypertension is on thiazides and is complaining of fatigue and hypokalemia. Which of the following drugs can prevent potassium loss?
questions.concept: Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic (it blocks the ENaC sodium channel in the collecting duct) and, added to a thiazide, offsets thiazide-induced hypokalaemia. Furosemide, acetazolamide and indapamide all waste potassium.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy presents with recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. He is diagnosed with severe combined immunodeficiency due to an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Which enzyme deficiency is responsible?
questions.concept: The commonest autosomal-recessive severe combined immunodeficiency is adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency; accumulated deoxyadenosine/dATP is toxic to both T and B lymphocytes, causing recurrent bacterial, viral and fungal infections. (HGPRT deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan; OTC deficiency causes hyperammonaemia.)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 32-year-old patient presents with blurred vision, photophobia, and mild ocular pain. Examination reveals aqueous flares and keratic precipitates in the anterior chamber. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Keratic precipitates with aqueous flare and cells in the anterior chamber indicate anterior uveitis, i.e. iridocyclitis (inflammation of the iris and ciliary body); intermediate, posterior and toxoplasma uveitis instead involve the vitreous or chorioretina, not the anterior chamber.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Optic nerve glioma is seen in?
questions.concept: Optic nerve (pathway) glioma - a pilocytic astrocytoma - is the classic CNS tumour of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1); bilateral vestibular (acoustic) schwannomas characterise NF-2 instead.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Identify the type of fracture in a patient who sustained a road traffic accident resulting in fractures of both the tibia and fibula.
questions.concept: A 'bumper' (fender) fracture is a fracture of the tibia/fibula produced when a car bumper strikes the leg of a standing pedestrian, classically fracturing the proximal tibia.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Rukmini is attending the village health nutrition and sanitation program day. How frequently is this conducted?
questions.concept: The Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Day (VHSND) is held once every month at the Anganwadi centre to deliver maternal-child health, immunisation and nutrition services under the National Health Mission.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Arrange the order of the Disaster management cycle:
questions.concept: Park's disaster-management cycle proceeds impact -> response (rescue/relief) -> rehabilitation (recovery/reconstruction) -> mitigation/prevention for future events. NOTE: phase nomenclature and ordering vary between sources, but this matches the standard Park sequence.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Iron absorption is decreased in which of the following?
questions.concept: Tannins/polyphenols in tea (and coffee) chelate non-haem iron and reduce its absorption, whereas the vitamin C in amla, lemon and sprouted grains enhances iron absorption.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Marriage and mortality belong under?
questions.concept: Fertility, mortality, migration and marriage are the demographic processes that determine population size and structure; demographic dividend/bonus/window instead describe the economic benefit of a large working-age population.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: What is the ANMOL program for auxiliary nurse midwives?
questions.concept: ANMOL ('ANM Online') is a tablet-based application that lets auxiliary nurse-midwives record and update beneficiary service data in real time.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the investigation of choice for CML?
questions.concept: CML is defined by the BCR-ABL fusion arising from t(9;22) (Philadelphia chromosome); FISH detects this fusion sensitively and is the investigation of choice among the given options. NOTE: conventional karyotyping is the traditional confirmatory test and RT-PCR (not listed) is the most sensitive method for diagnosis/monitoring; LAP score only distinguishes CML from a leukaemoid reaction.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: All of the following are correct about NETs except?
questions.concept: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are webs of decondensed chromatin studded with antimicrobial proteins, formed by NETosis (which requires PAD4-mediated citrullination of arginine residues on histones) and implicated in sepsis and in exposing autoantigens that drive SLE. They trap microbes extracellularly and are NOT a form of phagocytosis - hence the 'except'.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A child with diarrhea was eager to drink, and the skin pinch went back slowly. Which of the following categories is the child classified into as per IMNCI?
questions.concept: A child who is restless/eager to drink with a skin pinch that goes back slowly has 'some dehydration', which is the Yellow IMNCI category (needs ORS/facility treatment); severe dehydration (lethargic, drinking poorly, very slow pinch) is Pink and no dehydration is Green.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Conjunctival xerosis is caused by which vitamin deficiency?
questions.concept: Conjunctival xerosis and Bitot's spots are early ocular signs of vitamin A deficiency (xerophthalmia), which can progress to keratomalacia and irreversible blindness.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient was given an antipsychotic drug, haloperidol and the patient developed acute dystonia. Which is the next best step?
questions.concept: Acute dystonia from a high-potency antipsychotic (haloperidol) is an extrapyramidal reaction treated with an anticholinergic such as benztropine (or IV diphenhydramine); switching to or adding another dopamine blocker would not help.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A group of people are travelling to the mountains, and a girl starts complaining of mountain sickness. What is the drug of choice?
questions.concept: Acetazolamide, a carbonic-anhydrase-inhibitor diuretic, is the drug of choice for prevention and treatment of acute mountain (high-altitude) sickness; it induces a mild metabolic acidosis that stimulates ventilation and speeds acclimatisation. Promethazine and dimenhydrinate treat motion sickness, not AMS.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which of the following oxygen-sensitive channels is present in peripheral chemoreceptors?
questions.concept: Hypoxia in the glomus (type I) cells of the peripheral chemoreceptors inhibits oxygen-sensitive potassium (K+) channels, causing depolarisation, voltage-gated Ca2+ influx and neurotransmitter release that increases ventilation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which type of ion channel is affected by mutations in the CFTR gene?
questions.concept: The CFTR gene encodes a cAMP-regulated chloride channel; its mutation (commonly the delta-F508 deletion) causes cystic fibrosis, with defective epithelial chloride transport and abnormally thick secretions.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Atypical antipsychotic with the least metabolic side effects?
questions.concept: Among atypical antipsychotics, ziprasidone (like aripiprazole) causes the least weight gain, dyslipidaemia and glucose intolerance, whereas olanzapine and clozapine cause the most; haloperidol is a typical (first-generation) antipsychotic and so is excluded by the stem.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: What is the diagnosis for a patient who believes their bodily sensations or movements are controlled or influenced by an external agency?
questions.concept: Somatic passivity - the delusion that one's bodily sensations or movements are imposed by an external agency - is a Schneiderian first-rank symptom of schizophrenia. Nihilistic delusion is belief that oneself/a body part does not exist; delusion of reference is that events refer to oneself; Othello syndrome is delusional jealousy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: Which among the following is most radiosensitive?
questions.concept: By the law of Bergonie-Tribondeau, radiosensitivity parallels mitotic activity; the rapidly dividing testicular germ cells are highly radiosensitive, whereas mature nerve and muscle are among the most radioresistant tissues.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: Radioisotope used in PET-CT scan?
questions.concept: PET-CT most commonly uses 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG), a positron-emitting glucose analogue that accumulates in metabolically active tissue such as malignant tumours.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents with a bulky scrotal swelling. On evaluation, malignancy is suspected, and an orchidectomy is performed. The gross section of the testicular mass is shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Seminoma is the commonest testicular germ-cell tumour in this age group and shows a classic homogeneous, lobulated, fleshy grey-white cut surface (no gross haemorrhage/necrosis). Options C and D are synonyms (yolk-sac tumour = endodermal sinus tumour), so neither can be the single answer, and age plus 'most common' point to seminoma even though the referenced gross image is not reproduced.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with gynecomastia. Ultrasound reveals a 1 cm solid mass within the body of the testis. Serum testosterone is 600 ng/dL, and estradiol is 35 pg/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A small solid testicular mass with gynaecomastia and raised oestradiol is a Leydig-cell tumour, a sex-cord/stromal tumour that secretes androgens and/or oestrogens; the excess oestrogen production causes the gynaecomastia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient with HIV presents with bouts of cough and fever. Which medium is most appropriate for diagnosis?
questions.concept: In an HIV patient with cough and fever, TB is the prime suspect; Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium is the classic solid culture medium for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Tinsdale and Loeffler serum slope grow Corynebacterium diphtheriae, and MacConkey grows gram-negative enterics.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 9-month-old child in ICU has recurrent sinusitis and otitis media due to Staphylococcus aureus. Blood tests show decreased serum IgA, IgG, IgM, IgE and absent plasma B cells. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Recurrent pyogenic infections after about 6 months of age with markedly low IgG/IgA/IgM/IgE and absent circulating B cells indicate Bruton X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (BTK gene defect blocking B-cell maturation). DiGeorge is a T-cell 22q11 defect and CGD is an NADPH-oxidase phagocyte defect.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has tingling of the lateral three digits with loss of sensation over the base of the thumb on the dorsal aspect of the hand. Which nerve is involved?
questions.concept: Sensory loss over the dorsal aspect of the base of the thumb and the first web space localises to the superficial branch of the radial nerve, which supplies the dorsum of the lateral hand. The median nerve supplies the palmar surface (and dorsal fingertips) of the lateral three-and-a-half digits, not the dorsal thumb base.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which segment of the nephron has the lowest osmolality under the influence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH)?
options: Descending limb of the loop of Henle
questions.concept: The early distal convoluted tubule is the most dilute point of the nephron (about 100 mOsm/kg) because the thick ascending limb and early DCT reabsorb NaCl while remaining impermeable to water; this stays hypotonic even when ADH concentrates the collecting duct downstream.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which of the following is the afferent limb of the corneal reflex?
questions.concept: The corneal (blink) reflex afferent limb is the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve; the efferent limb is the facial nerve (VII) driving orbicularis oculi. The optic nerve is the afferent for the pupillary light reflex, not the corneal reflex.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A firefighter is admitted with fever and cough. Sputum culture grows gram-negative, oxidase-positive bacilli whose colonies transilluminate (fluoresce) under UV light. Choose the correct agent.
questions.concept: A gram-negative, oxidase-positive bacillus whose colonies fluoresce under UV light is Pseudomonas aeruginosa (pyoverdin/pyocyanin pigments). Klebsiella and Serratia are oxidase-negative and do not fluoresce; Staphylococcus is gram-positive.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Chronic malnutrition is best measured by?
questions.concept: Chronic malnutrition (stunting) is best captured by low height (length)-for-age. Weight-for-height reflects acute malnutrition (wasting), and weight-for-age reflects underweight (a mix of both).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which of the following changes occurs during muscle contraction while exercising?
options: M-line length increases and I-band decreases
questions.concept: During contraction the sarcomere shortens: the I-band and H-band shorten while the A-band (myosin filament length) stays constant. The correct change is a decrease in I-band length.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which anti-epileptic drug is commonly associated with gum hypertrophy and dizziness as side effects?
questions.concept: Phenytoin classically causes gingival hyperplasia (gum hypertrophy) plus dose-related cerebellar toxicity (dizziness, nystagmus, ataxia); other effects include hirsutism, megaloblastic anaemia and fetal hydantoin syndrome. It acts via voltage-gated Na+ channel blockade.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The toughness of bacterial cell walls is due to:
questions.concept: The rigidity/toughness of the bacterial cell wall comes from peptidoglycan (murein), the cross-linked NAM-NAG mesh that resists osmotic lysis. Teichoic acid, LPS and the outer membrane serve other roles and are not the source of mechanical strength.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which anti-tubercular drug is associated with mutations in the katG gene (resistance)?
questions.concept: Isoniazid is a prodrug activated by the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase encoded by katG; katG mutations (e.g. Ser315Thr) abolish activation and cause INH resistance. Rifampicin resistance is via rpoB, fluoroquinolone via gyrA/gyrB, and ethambutol via embB.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following is excreted in the urine of patients with pentosuria?
questions.concept: Essential (benign) pentosuria is a deficiency of L-xylulose reductase, so L-xylulose is excreted in urine (and can be mistaken for a reducing sugar). It is asymptomatic and needs no treatment.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A group of students eat fried rice at a restaurant. Six hours later they start vomiting. What is the etiological agent?
questions.concept: Rapid-onset vomiting 1-6 hours after eating reheated/fried rice is the emetic form of Bacillus cereus food poisoning (preformed heat-stable toxin). C. botulinum gives descending paralysis at 12-36 h; ETEC and Shigella cause diarrhoeal illness with longer incubation.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A married female dies within 3 years of marriage. The inquest is done by?
questions.concept: Unnatural or suspicious death of a married woman within 7 years of marriage mandates a Magistrate's inquest (not police or coroner) because of the risk of a dowry-related death. The coroner system no longer operates in India.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A forensic expert receives a district-court summons to give evidence in a criminal case, but two days earlier had already received a summons for a civil case in the same district court on the same date. What should the doctor do?
options: Attend the court for which the summons came first
Attend the court for the criminal case
questions.concept: When summoned to both a criminal and a civil court for the same date, the doctor must attend the criminal court first, as criminal proceedings take precedence over civil; the civil court is informed and attended later.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A person is stabbed in the anterior thigh and dies. His body is brought for postmortem. What type of injury is this?
questions.concept: A knife stab is a penetrating (sharp-force) wound - its depth exceeds the surface length, unlike an incised wound (length greater than depth). Puncture usually denotes a wound from a fine pointed object; a knife stab is best classed as penetrating.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A villager assaulted by 4-5 people is brought to hospital in serious condition and his dying declaration is being taken. Which of the following is correct regarding this process?
options: A Magistrate can record the statement
A doctor can record the statement
Oath is compulsory before recording the statement
questions.concept: A dying declaration is ideally recorded by a Magistrate; no oath is administered and leading questions must be avoided. NOTE: option B (a doctor may record it, e.g. when a Magistrate is unavailable) is also true, so the item is ambiguous - the exam key is A.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: What type of skull fracture is caused by a hammer?
questions.concept: A hammer (a heavy object with a small striking surface) delivering a localised blow to the skull produces a depressed fracture (a signature fracture reflecting the weapon shape), rather than a linear/fissured fracture from diffuse force.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A married female dies in unnatural circumstances within 3 years of marriage. Her father files a report to police and inquiry will be done under which section?
questions.concept: Unnatural death of a married woman within 7 years of marriage triggers a Magistrate's inquiry into the cause of death under Section 176 CrPC, now Section 196 BNSS (option B). Section 174 CrPC / 194 BNSS is the ordinary police inquest.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with burns involving the entire head, neck and one upper limb. What is the percentage of burn?
questions.concept: By the paediatric Rule of Nines (Lund-Browder), a child's head and neck are about 18% TBSA and each upper limb about 9%, so burns of the whole head, neck and one upper limb total roughly 27% (25-30%).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: Leading questions can be asked in?
questions.concept: Leading questions are permitted during cross-examination; they are not allowed in examination-in-chief or re-examination except with the court's permission.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 6-year-old child has a refractive error of -2D in the right eye and +1D in the left eye. Fundus examination shows normal visual acuity and retinal findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A difference in refractive power between the two eyes (here -2D in one and +1D in the other) is anisometropia. Uncorrected anisometropia in a child can lead to amblyopia, but the primary diagnosis described is anisometropia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A patient with long-standing diabetes presents with cataracts. Which metabolic product is primarily responsible for cataract formation in this condition?
questions.concept: In chronic hyperglycaemia, aldose reductase converts excess glucose to sorbitol (polyol pathway); sorbitol accumulates osmotically in the lens, drawing in water and producing diabetic (osmotic) cataract. Galactitol causes the analogous cataract in galactosaemia.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: When is a blood sample taken to diagnose neonatal hypothyroidism?
questions.concept: Newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism (heel-prick dried blood spot for TSH/T4) is done at about 48-72 hours of life; sampling in the first 24-48 h is avoided because of the physiological neonatal TSH surge, and cord blood is used only for universal screening.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 70-year-old man is admitted with a murmur and blood culture positive for gram-positive cocci. Choose the common agent causing prosthetic valve infective endocarditis.
questions.concept: Coagulase-negative staphylococci, chiefly Staphylococcus epidermidis, are the commonest cause of prosthetic-valve endocarditis (especially early/nosocomial cases via device colonisation). Viridans streptococci typically cause native-valve or late prosthetic-valve endocarditis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct regarding indirect ophthalmoscopy?
options: The image is erect and real
The condenser lens needs to be kept close to the eye
questions.concept: Indirect ophthalmoscopy gives a wide field with low (about 3-5x) magnification and produces an inverted, real image, with the condensing lens held at arm's length. High (about 15x) magnification with an erect virtual image is the feature of direct ophthalmoscopy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A baby is born with microcephaly, intracerebral calcification and chorioretinitis. Which teratogenic infection is the mother suffering from?
questions.concept: The combination of chorioretinitis, diffuse intracranial calcification and hydrocephalus/microcephaly in a neonate suggests congenital toxoplasmosis (Toxoplasma gondii, a protozoan). NOTE: CMV overlaps but classically gives periventricular calcification with sensorineural deafness.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A newborn has a midline lesion over the back in which neural tissue is exposed on the surface without any covering skin or meninges. Identify the defect.
questions.concept: Exposed neural tissue on the back with no skin or meningeal covering is an open neural tube defect (rachischisis/myeloschisis) from failure of posterior neuropore closure. Meningocele/encephalocele are skin- or membrane-covered herniations, and spina bifida occulta is a closed vertebral-arch defect.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: During spermatogenesis, which of the following hormones inhibits Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) secretion?
questions.concept: Inhibin (inhibin B from Sertoli cells) selectively suppresses pituitary FSH secretion by negative feedback during spermatogenesis. Testosterone mainly feeds back to suppress LH.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with schizophrenia had been compliant with olanzapine for several months, then discontinued it. Which of the following is the most likely reason for discontinuation?
questions.concept: Olanzapine, an atypical antipsychotic, is strongly associated with weight gain and metabolic syndrome, the commonest reason patients stop it. Acute dystonia, akathisia and tardive dyskinesia are extrapyramidal effects seen more with typical/high-potency agents.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A young man presents with weakness of the entire right side of his face - drooping of the right angle of the mouth with inability to raise the right eyebrow or close the right eye. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
options: Infranuclear facial palsy on the right side
Supranuclear facial palsy on the left side
Infranuclear facial palsy on the left side
Supranuclear facial palsy on the right side
questions.concept: Involvement of the forehead (inability to raise the eyebrow and close the eye) along with the lower face on the same side indicates a lower-motor-neuron (infranuclear) facial nerve palsy on the right. An upper-motor-neuron lesion spares the forehead due to bilateral cortical input. NOTE: the recalled stem was garbled ('both sides'); the intended picture is unilateral right whole-face weakness.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A patient shows flat affect. What does it indicate?
questions.concept: Flat (blunted) affect is a negative symptom of schizophrenia, along with alogia, avolition and anhedonia. Positive symptoms are hallucinations and delusions.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is not reversed with the administration of atropine?
options: Muscle weakness due to neuromuscular blockade
questions.concept: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist, so it reverses muscarinic effects (bradycardia, salivation, bronchoconstriction) but has no action at nicotinic receptors of the neuromuscular junction - it cannot reverse muscle weakness from neuromuscular blockade (that needs an anticholinesterase/oxime).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A patient shows unilateral facial droop with inability to close the eye and loss of forehead wrinkling on the affected side. Which of the following is most likely involved?
questions.concept: Unilateral facial droop with inability to close the eye and loss of forehead wrinkling is a lower-motor-neuron facial (7th cranial nerve) palsy, i.e. Bell's palsy. A 3rd-nerve palsy causes ptosis/ophthalmoplegia, and Erb's palsy is a brachial-plexus (arm) injury.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A young man with a psychiatric disorder has become very aggressive. He speaks very rapidly, sleeps very little, and is hyperactive after discontinuing his prescribed medication. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Aggression with pressured/rapid speech, decreased need for sleep and hyperactivity after stopping medication describes a manic episode of bipolar disorder; discontinuing a mood stabiliser precipitates relapse into mania.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with respiratory difficulty and a history of chronic smoking. Pulmonary function testing shows a decreased FEV1%. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.concept: A chronic smoker with a reduced FEV1 and FEV1/FVC (<70%) has an obstructive pattern, most consistent with COPD. Fibrosis/ILD are restrictive (normal or high FEV1/FVC), and asthma is obstructive but reversible with bronchodilators.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A child with fused carpal bones comes to your clinic. What is the gene associated with hand-foot (hand-foot-genital) syndrome?
questions.concept: Hand-Foot-Genital syndrome (distal limb malformations - here fused/short carpals and short thumbs/great toes - with genitourinary anomalies) is caused by a mutation in the HOXA13 homeobox gene. BCL6 links to lymphoma, FGFR to skeletal dysplasias, and COL11 to hearing loss/Stickler syndrome.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient's labs are positive for malarial antigen, and the Widal test shows O antigen >1:300, H antigen >1:20, A >1:20, B >1:20. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A markedly raised Widal O-agglutinin titre (>1:300) with low H and paratyphoid titres indicates a recent Salmonella (enteric fever) infection; a rise in only H suggests convalescence/anamnestic response, and a rise in all H antigens suggests prior TAB vaccination.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A young female has episodes of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting. Which acid-base disturbance is she likely to have?
questions.concept: Recurrent self-induced vomiting (bulimia) loses gastric HCl, producing a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with a mid-upper-arm circumference of 105 mm eagerly completes all the therapeutic food provided. This patient is considered under?
questions.concept: A child with MUAC 10.5 cm (<11.5 cm) has severe acute malnutrition; because he passes the appetite test and has no oedema or medical complications, this is uncomplicated SAM, managed with home-based ready-to-use therapeutic food. Complicated SAM (failed appetite test, oedema, or danger signs) needs inpatient care.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient sample is positive for infectious Hepatitis B. Choose the correct marker for this condition.
questions.concept: High infectivity in hepatitis B is marked by HBsAg (active infection) together with HBeAg (active viral replication) - option B. Anti-HBe or anti-HBs indicate lower infectivity/recovery.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: In a renal biopsy, identify the cells located in the angle between the afferent and efferent arterioles, adjacent to the macula densa.
questions.concept: Cells lying in the angle between the afferent and efferent arterioles, adjacent to the macula densa, are the extraglomerular mesangial (lacis/Goormaghtigh) cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus, which relay signals between the macula densa and renin-secreting JG cells. Macula densa lies in the distal tubule and JG cells in the afferent arteriole wall.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Identify the lymphoid organ shown in histology: a lobulated structure with a darker outer cortex, a paler inner medulla, and concentric Hassall's corpuscles.
questions.concept: A lobulated organ with a darker T-cell-rich cortex, a paler medulla and Hassall's corpuscles is the thymus, the primary lymphoid organ for T-cell maturation and central tolerance. Lymph node/spleen/tonsil show germinal-centre follicles (and, for spleen, red and white pulp) rather than Hassall's corpuscles.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A person with a history of a long-term sexual relationship presents with painful ulcers on the genitals and tender lymphadenopathy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Painful genital ulcers with ragged edges plus tender, suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) indicate chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi). LGV ulcers are painless with later painful nodes; gonorrhoea/chlamydia cause discharge rather than ulcers.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Dehydration is more severe in infants than in adults. Which of the following is a true statement about infants?
options: Extracellular fluid (ECF) is more than intracellular fluid (ICF)
Intracellular fluid (ICF) is more than extracellular fluid (ECF)
Total body water in infants is more than in adults
questions.concept: Infants have a higher total body water fraction (about 75-80% of body weight vs about 60% in adults) and a higher water turnover, which is why they dehydrate faster. (ECF exceeds ICF at birth, but ICF comes to predominate after the first year.)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which drug is preferred for management of diabetes in a patient with cardiac and renal failure?
questions.concept: In a diabetic with heart failure and renal impairment, SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) are preferred for their proven cardio- and reno-protection. Metformin is contraindicated in advanced renal failure (lactic acidosis), pioglitazone worsens fluid overload/HF, and sulfonylureas risk hypoglycaemia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which adverse effect of bleomycin is exacerbated by radiation exposure?
questions.concept: Bleomycin's dose-limiting toxicity is pulmonary (interstitial pneumonitis progressing to fibrosis) from free-radical injury, and it is worsened by radiation (radiation-recall pneumonitis) and high FiO2. It has little GI, neural or hepatic toxicity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A child presents with telecanthus, hypertelorism, antimongoloid slant, and cardiac defects. What is the most likely chromosomal abnormality?
questions.concept: This picture (facial dysmorphism with hypertelorism plus conotruncal cardiac defects, and often hypocalcaemia/thymic aplasia) is DiGeorge / velocardiofacial syndrome, caused by a microdeletion at chromosome 22q11.2 - a defect of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient presents with gum bleeding, petechiae, poor wound healing, and other related symptoms. Which of the following vitamin deficiencies is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.concept: Bleeding gums, petechiae and poor wound healing are classic for scurvy (vitamin C deficiency); vitamin C is needed for collagen synthesis, so its lack gives fragile capillaries and defective connective-tissue repair.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient presents with arthritis, and arthroscopy reveals blackening of the joints. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.concept: Arthritis with blackening of joints (ochronosis) is alkaptonuria, due to deficiency of homogentisate oxidase; homogentisic acid accumulates and deposits in cartilage and joints, and the urine darkens on standing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient with a history of strenuous exercise skipped a meal and later consumed alcohol at a party. Alcohol inhibits which of the following biochemical processes, potentially leading to hypoglycemia?
questions.concept: Ethanol oxidation raises the hepatic NADH/NAD+ ratio, blocking the lactate-to-pyruvate and malate-to-oxaloacetate steps and thus inhibiting gluconeogenesis. After exercise and fasting (glycogen already depleted) this precipitates hypoglycaemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following is deficient in the mucopolysaccharidosis associated with Natowicz disease?
questions.concept: Natowicz disease is mucopolysaccharidosis type IX, caused by hyaluronidase deficiency, so hyaluronic acid (a non-sulfated GAG) accumulates. NOTE: the stem says 'deficient' but the intended answer is the GAG involved/accumulated (hyaluronic acid); the deficient enzyme is hyaluronidase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following enzymes is dependent on Vitamin C for its activity?
questions.concept: Prolyl (and lysyl) hydroxylase need vitamin C as a cofactor to hydroxylate proline/lysine residues, stabilising collagen; lysyl oxidase, in contrast, is copper-dependent, not vitamin C-dependent.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A disease with mitochondrial inheritance is inherited from which family member?
questions.concept: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited only from the mother (maternal/cytoplasmic inheritance) because sperm mitochondria are not transmitted to the zygote; every child of an affected mother inherits the trait.
