questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Which of the following drug dosages is incorrect for the treatment of leprosy in adults?
questions.concept: In WHO MDT for adult leprosy rifampicin is 600 mg once monthly (450 mg is the child dose), so 'rifampicin 450 mg' is the wrong adult dose. Dapsone 100 mg daily, clofazimine 300 mg monthly plus 50 mg daily are all correct.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 45-year-old male was admitted with respiratory distress. CT showed a nasal polyp with fluid collection in the sinus. Drainage of which of the following is obstructed?
questions.concept: The maxillary sinus drains through an ostium placed high on its medial wall into the middle meatus, so it drains poorly and readily retains fluid; antrochoanal polyps also classically arise from the maxillary antrum.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 49-year-old female from Nagaland presented with right-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. On examination, dull tympanic membrane with lymph nodes in the posterior triangle of the neck was seen. Which of the following is the management for the condition?
questions.concept: Unilateral serous otitis media (dull TM, conductive loss from Eustachian-tube blockage), tinnitus and posterior-triangle cervical nodes in a patient from north-east India point to nasopharyngeal carcinoma; it is radiosensitive, so radiotherapy is the mainstay.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A patient presents to the OPD with hearing loss. On examination: Rinne test- Positive in the left ear and negative in the right ear; Weber's test - lateralization towards the left; Bone conduction test - Reduced in the right ear and similar in the left ear. Interpret the findings.
options: Sensorineural hearing loss in left ear
Sensorineural hearing loss in right ear
Conductive hearing loss in left ear
Conductive hearing loss in right ear
questions.concept: Reduced bone conduction on the right and Weber lateralising to the left (better) ear indicate right sensorineural hearing loss; the right Rinne-negative result is a 'false-negative Rinne', seen in severe unilateral SNHL because the fork's bone-conducted sound is heard by the opposite normal cochlea.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A TB patient with HIV begins ART and experiences deterioration in health after 2 months. What is the likely cause?
options: Development of drug resistance to TB drugs
Drug-drug interactions between TB and ART medications
Development of drug resistance to ART
questions.concept: Deterioration a few weeks to months after starting ART in an HIV-TB patient is immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS): recovering CD4 function mounts an exaggerated inflammatory response against the existing TB. Both TB treatment and ART are continued, with NSAIDs/steroids if severe.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the culture media used for tuberculosis?
questions.concept: Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium is the standard egg-based solid medium for culturing Mycobacterium tuberculosis; MacConkey, blood and chocolate agar are used for other bacteria.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: What is the most common causative organism of prosthetic heart valve endocarditis?
questions.concept: Coagulase-negative staphylococci, chiefly Staphylococcus epidermidis, are the commonest cause of prosthetic-valve endocarditis (especially early PVE); S. aureus causes acute native-valve disease and viridans streptococci cause subacute native-valve endocarditis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, recurrent pregnancy loss
questions.stem: Edematous villi with chromosome XY was found. What will be the diagnosis?
questions.concept: A complete hydatidiform mole is diploid (46,XX or 46,XY, entirely paternal in origin) with diffusely oedematous/hydropic villi and no fetal parts; a partial mole is triploid (e.g., 69,XXY). A diploid XY karyotype with oedematous villi is therefore a complete mole.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: OCPs are not protective for?
questions.concept: Combined OCPs reduce the risk of ovarian, endometrial and colorectal cancers, but are not protective against breast cancer (slightly increased risk, as with cervical cancer).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, recurrent pregnancy loss
questions.stem: Which findings are suggestive of tubal pregnancy?
options: Ovarian mass with single layer of endometrium
Adnexal mass with empty uterus and fluid in pelvis
questions.concept: Tubal (ectopic) pregnancy shows an empty uterus (no intrauterine sac despite a positive test), an adnexal mass (tubal ring/sac), and free pelvic fluid suggesting haemoperitoneum from leakage or rupture.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A female presents with hirsutism, delayed periods, obesity. USG findings are given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Hyperandrogenism (hirsutism), oligomenorrhoea (delayed periods) and obesity are the classic triad of PCOS/PCOD; USG shows polycystic ovaries with multiple peripheral follicles (a 'string of pearls').

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: After how long is a patient advised to use alternative contraception following a vasectomy?
questions.concept: A man stays fertile until residual sperm clear from the vas after vasectomy, so alternative contraception is advised for about 3 months (or ~20 ejaculations) until azoospermia is confirmed on semen analysis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which of the following drugs were not given for hypertension in pregnancy?
questions.concept: ACE inhibitors such as enalapril (and ARBs) are contraindicated in pregnancy - they cause fetal renal damage, oligohydramnios and skull defects. Methyldopa, labetalol and nifedipine are the preferred antihypertensives.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which therapy is given for cervical cancer?
questions.concept: Locally advanced cervical cancer is treated with concurrent chemoradiation using cisplatin, a platinum-based drug, as the radiosensitiser; hormonal and targeted therapies are not the mainstay.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 23 year old male epileptic patient presented with pain in right shoulder region. Examination revealed that right upper limb was abducted and externally rotated and the movements could not be performed. Which of the following is most likely diagnosed?
questions.concept: An arm held abducted and externally rotated with loss of movement indicates an anterior shoulder dislocation, of which subglenoid is a variety. NOTE: the seizure history is a distractor pointing to posterior dislocation (which instead gives an adducted, internally rotated arm); the described position confirms an anterior/subglenoid dislocation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: Which of the following enzymes is typically elevated in prostate cancer?
questions.concept: Prostatic acid phosphatase rises in prostate cancer, especially with bone metastases (an older tumour marker now largely replaced by PSA). ALP rises in bone/liver disease, LDH is non-specific, and AFP marks hepatocellular and germ-cell tumours.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A child diagnosed with von Willebrand disease requires an understanding of the role of von Willebrand factor (vWF). What does von Willebrand factor primarily combine with?
questions.concept: von Willebrand factor binds platelet glycoprotein Ib, mediating platelet adhesion to subendothelial collagen, and also carries/stabilises factor VIII; its deficiency (von Willebrand disease) impairs adhesion and prolongs the bleeding time.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A male presents with a history of vestibular schwannoma and psammoma bodies in the brain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Psammoma bodies (laminated calcified concretions) in a brain tumour indicate meningioma; its association with vestibular schwannomas suggests neurofibromatosis type 2. GBM, pilocytic astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma do not characteristically show psammoma bodies.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the timing at which the triphenyl tetrazolium chloride can elicit findings post MI?
questions.concept: Triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC) stains viable myocardium (with intact dehydrogenases) brick-red and leaves infarcted tissue pale; it can demonstrate a myocardial infarct grossly by about 2-3 hours, earlier than routine light microscopy.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 7-year-old child was brought with bow legs and on x-ray of wrist following were the findings. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Bow legs (genu varum) with wrist X-ray changes of cupping, fraying and widening of the metaphysis in a child indicate rickets (vitamin D/calcium deficiency); scurvy instead causes bleeding and different subperiosteal/bone changes.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: What is the key difference between Cisplatin and Carboplatin?
options: Cisplatin is less neurotoxic than Carboplatin
Cisplatin causes fewer gastric issues compared to Carboplatin
Carboplatin is more neurotoxic than Cisplatin
Cisplatin has more nephrotoxic side effects compared to Carboplatin
questions.concept: Cisplatin is more nephrotoxic (causes acute tubular necrosis, needs aggressive hydration), and also more neuro/ototoxic and more emetogenic than carboplatin; carboplatin is instead more myelosuppressive (thrombocytopenia).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Scientists administered norepinephrine to guinea pigs, resulting in an increase in systolic and diastolic blood pressure and a decrease in heart rate. What mechanism explains this response?
questions.concept: Noradrenaline raises blood pressure by alpha-1 vasoconstriction; the rise stretches carotid/aortic baroreceptors, triggering a vagal reflex that slows the heart. This reflex bradycardia overrides noradrenaline's direct beta-1 cardiac stimulation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to the emergency department 6 hours after ingesting a large quantity of paracetamol tablets. What is the most likely progression of paracetamol poisoning in this case?
options: Increase in liver enzymes within 24 hours
Paracetamol achieves peak concentration within 4 hours
questions.concept: Paracetamol poisoning progresses in stages: nausea/vomiting first, then rising transaminases (AST/ALT), with peak hepatic damage and possible failure at 72-96 hours - not full failure within 24 hours. NOTE: option C (peak plasma level within ~4 hours) is itself true but is a pharmacokinetic fact, not the toxic 'progression' asked about; the transaminase rise is the intended progression answer.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is taking indomethacin and an ACE inhibitor for hypertension. What potential side effect is likely to be seen?
questions.concept: ACE inhibitors lower aldosterone (reducing potassium excretion) and NSAIDs like indomethacin reduce renal prostaglandins/perfusion; together they promote potassium retention, causing hyperkalaemia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with penicillin allergy presents with fever, burning micturition, and hearing problems accompanied by dizziness. Which drug is the most appropriate for the management?
questions.concept: For a UTI in a penicillin-allergic patient who already has hearing problems, ciprofloxacin is best: it covers common uropathogens and is safe in penicillin allergy, while amikacin (aminoglycoside) is ototoxic, azithromycin penetrates urine poorly, and amoxiclav is contraindicated by the allergy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: An elderly female undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer is experiencing significant hair loss. What is the most likely cause of her condition?
questions.concept: Cytotoxic chemotherapy abruptly injures the rapidly dividing matrix cells of anagen (growth-phase) follicles, causing anagen effluvium - rapid diffuse hair loss within days to weeks; telogen effluvium is instead delayed shedding after stress or illness.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A 35-year-old male experiences headache, nausea, and shortness of breath while trekking. The physician prescribes a drug to alleviate his symptoms. The drug administered primarily acts on which part of the nephron?
questions.concept: Acute mountain sickness is treated with acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor acting on the proximal convoluted tubule; it reduces bicarbonate reabsorption, causing a mild metabolic acidosis that stimulates ventilation and improves oxygenation.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following is the schedule of the OPV vaccine?
questions.concept: In India's National Immunization Schedule the primary OPV doses are given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks (in addition to a birth/zero dose and a booster at 16-24 months).

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a class of 100 students, 80% students were immunised with measles, 12 were affected. What is the secondary attack rate?
questions.concept: Secondary attack rate = new cases among susceptible contacts / total susceptible contacts x 100. With 80 of 100 immunised, only 20 are susceptible; 12 cases give SAR = 12/20 = 60%.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following is the population norm for an ASHA worker?
questions.concept: Under the National Health Mission the ASHA norm is about one per 1000 population in rural areas and one per 1000-2500 population (200-500 households) in urban areas (NUHM). NOTE: the keyed answer 1000-2500 reflects the urban norm; the rural norm is ~1 per 1000.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: A patient presents with a history of dysphagia, which is more pronounced for liquids than solids. Which radiological sign is most likely to be seen?
questions.concept: Dysphagia that is worse for liquids than solids suggests achalasia (a motility disorder); its barium-swallow hallmark is the 'rat-tail'/bird-beak sign - smooth tapering narrowing at the gastro-oesophageal junction from a non-relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the duration of abstinence (continued contraceptive precautions) recommended after vasectomy?
questions.concept: After vasectomy a man is not immediately sterile because viable sperm persist in the distal vas and seminal vesicles; alternate contraception must be continued for about 3 months (roughly 20 ejaculations) until azoospermia is confirmed on semen analysis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman who had a forceps delivery 24 hours ago presents with perineal pain. Her BP is 80/60 and examination shows a swelling with bluish discolouration. Which of the following is advised NOT to do?
options: Repair the wound in the ward
questions.concept: A post-forceps vulvovaginal (paravaginal) haematoma with hypotension is an obstetric emergency; correct management is resuscitation with blood transfusion, informing seniors and evacuating the haematoma in the OT under anaesthesia. Opening/repairing it on the ward is what should NOT be done.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Cell injury, adaptation, necrosis vs apoptosis
questions.stem: Which of the following is a change seen in irreversible cell injury?
questions.concept: Large amorphous (flocculent) densities within mitochondria are a morphological hallmark of irreversible cell injury, reflecting severe mitochondrial membrane damage; membrane blebbing, chromatin clumping and cellular (hydropic) swelling are features of reversible injury.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A patient presents to the OPD with greenish-black material in the nose associated with a foul (offensive) smell. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Atrophic rhinitis (ozaena) presents with greenish/greyish-black foul-smelling nasal crusts; the patient typically cannot smell the odour themselves (merciful anosmia). Rhinitis caseosa and sicca lack this classic foul-crust picture.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Fetal anaemia is monitored by which of the following?
questions.concept: Fetal anaemia (e.g. in Rh isoimmunisation) is monitored non-invasively by Doppler measurement of the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV); a rising MCA-PSV predicts significant anaemia and the need for intervention such as intrauterine transfusion.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following is the National Deworming Day in India?
questions.concept: In India, National Deworming Day is observed on 10th February each year (with a mop-up round, and a second round around August in many states), when albendazole is given to children and adolescents to control soil-transmitted helminths.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Histopathological examination shows follicular cells with pink eosinophilic cytoplasm. This is seen in which thyroid carcinoma?
questions.concept: Follicular (Hurthle-cell/oncocytic) thyroid carcinoma shows follicular cells with abundant granular pink eosinophilic cytoplasm; it is diagnosed by capsular/vascular invasion rather than nuclear features, unlike papillary carcinoma which shows Orphan-Annie-eye nuclei and psammoma bodies.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman had a difficult labour. She complains of dribbling of urine 7 days later. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Continuous painless dribbling of urine appearing about a week after obstructed/difficult labour indicates a vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) from pressure necrosis of the bladder wall; the delayed onset (day 7-14) fits ischaemic sloughing, whereas dribbling from day 1-2 would suggest direct surgical/ureteric injury.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A child presents with short stature, muscle weakness (hypotonia) and learning disability. Chromosome analysis reveals a deletion in the 15q11-q13 region on the paternal chromosome. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A paternally-derived deletion of chromosome 15q11-q13 causes Prader-Willi syndrome (hypotonia/muscle weakness, short stature, hyperphagia/obesity, intellectual disability); a maternal deletion of the same region instead causes Angelman syndrome (genomic imprinting). NOTE: the source wrote '15p' but the correct locus is 15q (long arm) - a likely extraction slip.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with lower-limb symmetric flaccidity and absent (lost) tendon reflexes, suggesting which condition?
questions.concept: Acute symmetrical ascending flaccid weakness with loss of deep tendon reflexes (areflexia) is characteristic of Guillain-Barre syndrome, an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy; CSF classically shows albuminocytological dissociation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with electrical burns and stable vitals is noted to have red-coloured urine. What is the most likely finding in this patient's blood?
questions.concept: Electrical burns cause deep muscle necrosis and rhabdomyolysis; released myoglobin turns the urine red and released intracellular potassium produces hyperkalaemia (with risk of myoglobinuric acute kidney injury). The red urine is myoglobinuria, not true haematuria.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Under IDSP (Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme), which diseases are covered under sentinel surveillance?
questions.concept: Under India's Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP), sentinel surveillance targets the bloodborne infections HIV and Hepatitis B (and C) through designated sentinel sites/blood banks, complementing regular and outbreak surveillance.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with melena containing gastric mucosa and acute intermittent pain in the right iliac region. On surgical exploration the structure shown was found. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Painless GI bleeding (melena) from ectopic gastric mucosa plus intermittent right-iliac-fossa pain in a young child is classic for Meckel's diverticulum (rule of 2s); a Tc-99m pertechnetate 'Meckel scan' detects the ectopic gastric mucosa, and symptomatic cases are resected.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman is brought to the ER after a fire incident. Her face and both lower limbs were spared. Calculate the approximate area of burn.
questions.concept: By the Wallace Rule of Nines in an adult, sparing the face and both lower limbs leaves the anterior trunk, posterior trunk, both upper limbs and perineum available to be burned - roughly 40-50% total body surface area. NOTE: the exact figure depends on which surfaces are actually involved (image), but the answer falls in the 40-50% bracket.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: After a fight, a boy is brought with severe chest pain, distended neck veins, dyspnoea and BP of 80/50 mmHg. Chest X-ray is shown. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Trauma followed by severe dyspnoea, distended neck veins (raised JVP), hypotension and mediastinal/tracheal shift indicates a tension pneumothorax causing obstructive shock; it is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate needle decompression (2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line) then chest-tube drainage.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT related to progression of a (basal cell) cancer?
questions.concept: In grading a cancer's aggressiveness, depth of invasion, anatomical site and stage all determine progression and prognosis, whereas the mere duration of the lesion does not directly indicate progression (as with slow-growing basal cell carcinoma). NOTE: the source stem omits the basal-cell-carcinoma context that appears only in the explanation.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A person living with HIV (PLHIV) presents with multiple dog bites with a punctured (deep) wound. Choose the correct management:
questions.concept: A category III rabies exposure (bleeding/deep bites), and any exposure in an immunocompromised person such as a PLHIV, requires the full regimen: thorough wound washing plus rabies immunoglobulin (RIG - human 20 IU/kg or equine 40 IU/kg, infiltrated around the wound) plus the anti-rabies vaccine series.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient is admitted with fever and nuchal rigidity. CSF analysis shows decreased glucose with increased protein and neutrophils. Choose the correct empirical treatment.
questions.concept: CSF showing low glucose, raised protein and neutrophilic pleocytosis indicates acute bacterial meningitis; the empirical first-line antibiotic in adults is a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone), adding vancomycin if resistant pneumococcus and ampicillin if Listeria is suspected.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 2-week-old neonate presents with non-bilious vomiting. On examination a lump is felt in the left epigastric region that becomes prominent while feeding. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A 2-6 week-old with non-bilious projectile vomiting and a palpable mobile 'olive' mass in the epigastrium has infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (gastric outlet obstruction); ultrasound (pyloric muscle >3 mm thick, channel >14 mm long) is the investigation of choice, and it classically causes a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has 5 days of left leg swelling and pain with a positive D-dimer. Duplex ultrasonography confirms extensive DVT involving the left popliteal and femoral veins. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: LMWH followed by an oral anticoagulant
questions.concept: For acute uncomplicated DVT, initial anticoagulation with LMWH bridged to/continued as an oral anticoagulant (a DOAC or warfarin) is the standard; catheter-directed thrombolysis is reserved for massive iliofemoral/limb-threatening DVT and IVC filters for when anticoagulation is contraindicated.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which of the following is the classical triad of acute cholangitis?
questions.concept: Charcot's triad of acute cholangitis is fever (with rigors), jaundice and right-upper-quadrant pain; adding hypotension/shock and altered mental status makes Reynolds' pentad, indicating acute obstructive suppurative cholangitis.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A 4-year-old unvaccinated child presents with fever, rash and Bitot's spots. What is the appropriate line of management?
questions.concept: Bitot's spots indicate vitamin A deficiency; in a child who already has measles, high-dose vitamin A supplementation is the priority as it reduces measles morbidity/mortality and treats the deficiency. The measles vaccine is for prevention and confers no benefit once infection has occurred.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: For the diagnosis of typhus, an antigen of Proteus is used (Weil-Felix test). What is this type of antigen called?
questions.concept: The Weil-Felix test diagnoses rickettsial infections such as typhus using Proteus OX strains, whose antigens are heterophile antigens - similar/shared antigens across unrelated species that cross-react with the patient's anti-rickettsial antibodies.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A 60-year-old presents with an ulcer on the medial canthus having rolled-out, beaded margins. Histopathology shows nests of cells with a peripheral palisading pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: An ulcer with rolled/beaded ('rodent ulcer') margins, classically at the medial canthus, showing islands/nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading on histology is basal cell carcinoma - the commonest skin cancer, locally invasive but rarely metastasising.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presents with a strong urge to urinate but inability to void. He has a history of perineal trauma, and blood is noted at the external urethral meatus. Which structure is most likely injured?
questions.concept: Perineal/straddle trauma with blood at the external urethral meatus and inability to void indicates an anterior (bulbar) urethral injury; posterior (membranous) urethral rupture instead accompanies pelvic fractures and gives a high-riding prostate on rectal examination.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Spread of prostate cancer to the lumbar vertebrae occurs via which route?
questions.concept: Prostate carcinoma metastasises to the lumbar vertebrae mainly via the valveless vertebral venous plexus of Batson (haematogenous/venous route), which allows retrograde spread and produces characteristic osteoblastic (sclerotic) bony deposits.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The ureter is safest (least at risk of injury) in which type of hysterectomy?
questions.concept: Vaginal hysterectomy carries the lowest risk of ureteric injury because there is minimal dissection near the ureter, whereas laparoscopic (thermal/traction), open and robotic approaches involve more ureteric handling and higher injury risk.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause of lower right abdominal pain with rebound tenderness in a patient who also has a Meckel's diverticulum?
questions.concept: Right-lower-quadrant pain with rebound tenderness (localised peritonism at McBurney's point) points to acute appendicitis; even when a Meckel's diverticulum is present, this classic localising sign indicates appendicitis rather than diverticular perforation or obstruction, which cause more diffuse or colicky pain.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with a painful, red, granular lesion on the vulva accompanied by bilateral lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A painful, soft, granular genital ulcer with painful (often suppurative) inguinal lymphadenopathy is characteristic of chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi; painless ulcers instead suggest syphilis (indurated) or granuloma inguinale (beefy-red, Donovan bodies, no nodes).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, recurrent pregnancy loss
questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding and 6 weeks of amenorrhea. Transvaginal ultrasound shows neither an intrauterine gestational sac nor features of ectopic pregnancy. Her serum beta-hCG is 1,200 IU/L, below the discriminatory zone. What is the next step in management?
questions.concept: In a haemodynamically stable woman with a pregnancy of unknown location - serum beta-hCG below the discriminatory zone (~1500-2000 IU/L) and non-diagnostic ultrasound - the next step is to repeat serum beta-hCG in 48 hours; appropriate doubling suggests an intrauterine pregnancy, while a suboptimal rise/plateau suggests ectopic or failing pregnancy.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following national health programmes is supported by DANIDA?
questions.concept: DANIDA (the Danish International Development Agency) is the external agency classically associated with India's National Programme for Control of Blindness; the TB, malaria and HIV programmes are supported by other agencies (e.g. World Bank, Global Fund).

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following is the use of Shakir's tape, and which principle of primary health care does it represent?
questions.concept: Shakir's tape is a colour-coded mid-upper-arm-circumference (MUAC) tape used to screen young children for protein-energy malnutrition; it is a classic example of 'appropriate technology', one of the principles of primary health care.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A mother brings her 5-month-old baby for a routine check-up. The baby actively looks at his mother's face and responds with interest as she talks, showing recognition and engagement. At what age is this milestone normally achieved?
questions.concept: Recognising the mother and responding socially with engagement/anticipation is a social developmental milestone attained around 3 months of age (the social smile appears by ~2 months); at 5 months this milestone should already be well established.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: A 35-year-old asthmatic patient is scheduled for a minor surgical procedure. Which induction agent and muscle relaxant combination is safest?
questions.concept: In an asthmatic, ketamine is a preferred IV induction agent because it causes bronchodilation, and vecuronium is a safe non-depolarising muscle relaxant that does not release histamine; succinylcholine and d-tubocurarine can provoke bronchospasm (via histamine release).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: All of the following are protected against by oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) EXCEPT?
questions.concept: Combined oral contraceptive pills reduce the risk of ovarian, endometrial and colorectal cancers, but do NOT protect against - and may slightly increase - breast cancer risk, so breast carcinoma is the exception.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT caused by food adulteration?
questions.concept: Epidemic dropsy (argemone oil in mustard oil), neurolathyrism (Lathyrus sativus/BOAA in pulses) and endemic ascites (pyrrolizidine alkaloids in cereals) are all food-adulteration/contamination diseases, whereas fluorosis is caused by excess fluoride in drinking water, not food adulteration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with fluctuating muscle weakness affecting speech and swallowing. Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a decremental response, and acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies are negative. Which antibody is most likely responsible?
questions.concept: Fatigable fluctuating weakness with prominent bulbar involvement, a decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation, and negative AChR antibodies points to anti-MuSK antibody-positive myasthenia gravis; MuSK is required for clustering of acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman who delivered a healthy term baby one week ago presents with a fishy-smelling, pale-brownish vaginal discharge. What is the nature of this discharge?
questions.concept: Lochia serosa is the normal puerperal discharge from about days 5-9, appearing yellowish/pink/pale-brownish (fewer RBCs, more leukocytes and wound exudate); lochia rubra (days 1-4) is red and lochia alba (days 10-15) is pale-white. The mild fishy odour is normal.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient undergoing surgery is administered succinylcholine for muscle relaxation. Shortly after administration, he develops hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, tremors, and tachycardia. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.concept: Succinylcholine (and volatile agents) can trigger malignant hyperthermia, a hypermetabolic crisis with hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, tachycardia and metabolic acidosis. The specific antidote is IV dantrolene, which blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; the triggering agents are stopped and the patient is actively cooled.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: A patient scheduled for elective hip surgery is currently taking aspirin, enalapril, a multivitamin, and metoprolol. The surgery is planned in 5 days. What is the appropriate perioperative management for this patient?
options: Stop aspirin to minimize perioperative bleeding risk
Stop metoprolol to increase cardiac output
Increase aspirin dosage for additional analgesic benefit
questions.concept: ACE inhibitors such as enalapril are stopped about 24 hours before elective surgery to avoid refractory intra-operative hypotension. Aspirin and beta-blockers are generally continued for most orthopaedic surgery, since abrupt beta-blocker withdrawal risks rebound ischaemia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: What is the most common defect in a ventricular septal defect?
options: Non-development of the perimembranous part of the septum
questions.concept: The interventricular septum has membranous and muscular parts; the perimembranous (membranous) region is the commonest site of a ventricular septal defect (about 80%). NOTE: option C describes maldevelopment of this same perimembranous septum, so B and C overlap, but 'membranous defect' is the standard intended answer.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A baby presents with the clinical features shown in the image, including characteristic perioral and perianal rash along with a history of diarrhea. Which of the following is the most likely deficiency responsible for this condition?
questions.concept: Perioral/perianal (periorificial) and acral dermatitis with diarrhoea, alopecia and poor growth is acrodermatitis enteropathica due to zinc deficiency (inherited SLC39A4/ZIP4 defect or acquired). Contrast pellagra (niacin), whose dermatitis is photosensitive and confined to sun-exposed skin.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A newborn child is brought to the emergency department with respiratory difficulty. The doctor evaluated, and the child was found to have a posterolateral defect, as shown in the x-ray given. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: A neonate with respiratory distress and a posterolateral diaphragmatic defect has a Bochdalek hernia, the commonest congenital diaphragmatic hernia (about 90%), usually left-sided and often complicated by pulmonary hypoplasia. Morgagni hernia is retrosternal/anterior.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which electrolyte abnormality will lead to cardiac arrhythmia in patients with severe vomiting?
questions.concept: Prolonged vomiting causes loss of gastric HCl and hypokalaemia (worsened by the accompanying metabolic alkalosis driving K+ into cells). Hypokalaemia flattens T waves, produces U waves and prolongs the QT interval, predisposing to ventricular arrhythmias/torsades.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A body brought for autopsy is cold and has developed rigor mortis in all 4 limbs and livor mortis at the back/fixed, but no signs of putrefaction. What will be the estimated time since death?
questions.concept: Combining the postmortem signs, a cold body with rigor fully established in all four limbs (about 12 h, persisting to 24-36 h), fixed livor (fixed by 6-12 h) and no putrefaction (begins about 24-36 h) places the time since death at roughly 12-24 hours.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 39-year-old patient with HIV and a CD4 count of 139 cells/µL presents with altered sensorium and impaired consciousness. CSF examination using an India ink preparation reveals a positive result. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.concept: In an HIV patient with a low CD4 count, meningoencephalitis with a capsulated budding yeast on India ink of CSF indicates Cryptococcus neoformans. Treatment is liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine, followed by fluconazole maintenance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient came to the hospital with muscle weakness, diarrhea, and bradycardia. He was diagnosed with organophosphate poisoning for which atropine was administered. After atropine administration, which of the following changes are not seen?
questions.concept: In organophosphate poisoning atropine antagonises the MUSCARINIC effects, so bradycardia is reversed (its cardinal action is to raise the heart rate) and is no longer seen. NOTE: sweating and rhinorrhoea (also muscarinic) improve too, but nicotinic muscle weakness persists because atropine has no action at the neuromuscular junction, so bradycardia is the single best 'not seen' answer despite the question being loosely worded.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A child was brought to the casualty with complaints of vomiting and loose stools with a history of laxative use. On examination, arrhythmia is present. What will be the abnormality present?
questions.concept: Vomiting, diarrhoea and laxative abuse all cause gastrointestinal potassium loss; the resulting hypokalaemia is the electrolyte disturbance that precipitates cardiac arrhythmias. Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT interval but is not the primary abnormality here.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient is positive for HBsAg and anti-HBc IgM. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: HBsAg positivity together with anti-HBc of the IgM class indicates acute hepatitis B (highly infectious). IgG anti-HBc with HBsAg denotes chronic infection; isolated anti-HBs indicates vaccination; and isolated IgM anti-HBc marks the window period.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A corneal wisp test was performed, and the corneal reflex was elicited. Which of the following nerves is responsible for the afferent limb of this reflex?
questions.concept: In the corneal (blink) reflex the afferent limb is the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V), and the efferent limb producing orbicularis oculi closure is the facial nerve (CN VII).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: A patient undergoing general anesthesia develops left lung collapse following intubation. On auscultation, breath sounds are heard only on the right side. What is the most likely cause of this condition?
options: Mucus secretions obstructing the endotracheal tube
Pneumothorax on the left side due to positive pressure ventilation
questions.concept: If the endotracheal tube is advanced too far it usually enters the more vertical right main bronchus, ventilating only the right lung, so breath sounds are heard on the right with left-lung collapse. Withdrawing the tube restores bilateral ventilation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with right-sided field defects in both eyes, but central vision remains unaffected. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A right homonymous hemianopia with preserved central (macular) vision localises to the contralateral (left) occipital visual cortex; the macula is spared because the occipital pole has a dual MCA/PCA blood supply, classically after a posterior cerebral artery stroke.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A neonate on examination has bilateral cataracts and, after investigations, is found to have a patent ductus arteriosus and salt & pepper retinopathy. What is the most likely congenital infection?
questions.concept: The triad of bilateral cataracts, patent ductus arteriosus and 'salt-and-pepper' retinopathy is classic congenital rubella syndrome (first-trimester infection); sensorineural deafness is the commonest defect. CMV instead causes periventricular calcification and chorioretinitis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A farmer presents with fever and subconjunctival hemorrhage. The microscopic agglutination test turns out to be positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: A farmer/water-exposed patient with fever and conjunctival suffusion or subconjunctival haemorrhage in whom the microscopic agglutination test (MAT, the gold standard) is positive has leptospirosis (Leptospira interrogans, a gram-negative spirochete). Brucella instead uses the standard serum tube agglutination test, not MAT.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cardiac cycle, ECG basis, BP regulation
questions.stem: A patient presents with high blood pressure accompanied by a decrease in heart rate. What is the most likely physiological mechanism responsible for this response?
questions.concept: A rise in blood pressure stretches carotid-sinus and aortic-arch baroreceptors, increasing afferent firing (via CN IX and X) to the medulla; the reflex withdraws sympathetic tone and raises vagal tone, lowering the heart rate. This baroreceptor reflex buffers acute changes in blood pressure.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A doctor asked the patient what her age is and she told him that she is married to an older man, and she has 2 kids of 15 and 18 years, and she is 39 years old. What is the disorder present?
questions.concept: When asked her age the patient supplies many unnecessary details but eventually reaches the correct answer; this over-inclusive yet goal-directed speech is circumstantiality. In tangentiality or derailment the patient never returns to the point.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A patient presents with vision problems and has a history of cataract surgery. OCT finding is shown below. What is the syndrome most likely associated with these findings?
questions.concept: Reduced vision weeks to months after cataract surgery due to cystoid macular oedema (petaloid pattern on OCT/fluorescein angiography) is Irvine-Gass syndrome (pseudophakic cystoid macular oedema). It is distinct from central serous retinopathy and from posterior capsule opacification (Elschnig pearls).

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: An unvaccinated 5-year-old child of a migrant worker family was brought to the casualty with fever and a characteristic skin rash. Upon eye examination, Bitot's spot was seen. What is the appropriate management?
options: Isolate and give nutritional supply with vitamin A supplement
Give measles vaccine and vitamin A supplement
Institutional Isolation, nutritional management with vitamin A supplement
questions.concept: A child with measles (fever, rash, coryza) plus a Bitot's spot (vitamin A deficiency) needs home isolation, supportive nutrition and age-based high-dose vitamin A supplementation. Institutional isolation is unnecessary without danger signs, and the measles vaccine has no role once the disease is established.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which of the following describes the chloride ion exchange in red blood cells, where bicarbonate ions are exchanged for chloride ions to maintain electrical neutrality?
questions.concept: In the tissues CO2 enters red cells and is converted by carbonic anhydrase to H+ and HCO3-; the HCO3- then leaves the cell in exchange for Cl- via the band-3 protein to preserve electrical neutrality, the chloride shift (Hamburger phenomenon). The process reverses in the lungs.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient presents with fever, neck rigidity, headache, vomiting, and petechial rashes on the lower limbs. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.concept: Fever, headache, vomiting and neck rigidity with a non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash indicate meningococcal meningitis/septicaemia caused by Neisseria meningitidis (a gram-negative diplococcus). Fulminant disease can progress to Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: According to the American Heart Association (AHA), what is the 6th link added to the chain of survival?
questions.concept: The AHA Chain of Survival gained a sixth link, Recovery (and rehabilitation), recognising that care continues beyond return of spontaneous circulation. Rapid defibrillation and high-quality CPR are earlier, pre-existing links.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A lady presents to the hospital after having a fight with her husband. She reports that she is unable to speak. However, all neurological and physical examinations are normal, and she does not seem concerned about her health status. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Acute loss of a function (here mutism) after emotional stress, with a normal neurological examination and a striking lack of concern about the deficit (la belle indifférence), points to a conversion (functional neurological) disorder rather than malingering, which has an external gain. NOTE: la belle indifférence is strictly the associated sign; the underlying diagnosis is conversion disorder, but it is the intended answer among these options.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A person came with a history of thorn prick a week ago. A few days later, he developed ulcers along lymphatic drainage. Choose the correct organism.
questions.concept: A thorn-prick followed by a nodule that ulcerates with further nodules tracking along the lymphatics (nodular lymphangitis) is sporotrichosis, caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii; treatment is itraconazole. This 'rose-gardener' pattern is classic.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the hospital with auditory hallucinations and inability to recognize his own family members. He reports his last alcohol intake was 48 hours ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Auditory hallucinations with disorientation (failure to recognise family) about 48 hours after the last drink indicate delirium tremens, whose hallmark is a clouded/altered sensorium with autonomic hyperactivity. NOTE: alcoholic hallucinosis is a close differential but classically occurs with a CLEAR sensorium, so the disorientation here favours delirium tremens.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which of the following factors causes a rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?
questions.concept: A rightward shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve means lower O2 affinity and easier tissue unloading. It is produced by increased CO2 and H+ (low pH, the Bohr effect), increased temperature and increased 2,3-BPG.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cardiac cycle, ECG basis, BP regulation
questions.stem: In the jugular venous pressure (JVP) waveform, the 'a' wave corresponds to:
options: Tricuspid valve bulging into Right atria
questions.concept: The 'a' wave of the jugular venous pulse is produced by right atrial contraction (just after the P wave, before S1). The 'c' wave reflects tricuspid bulging in early ventricular systole and the 'v' wave reflects atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A 3-month-old child has a respiratory rate of 56/min with no chest indrawing and no danger signs. As per IMNCI what is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.concept: Under IMNCI, in an infant aged 2-12 months a respiratory rate of 50/min or more is fast breathing; with no chest indrawing and no general danger sign this is classified simply as 'pneumonia' (treated with oral amoxicillin), not severe pneumonia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: What is the mechanism of action of botulinum toxin?
options: Inhibits acetylcholine release from the presynaptic terminal
questions.concept: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins (SNAP-25/synaptobrevin) in the presynaptic nerve terminal, preventing acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction and causing flaccid paralysis. It does not affect acetylcholine receptors or acetylcholinesterase.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A Tzanck smear prepared from a vesicle shows multinucleated giant cells. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: A Tzanck smear from a vesicle showing multinucleated giant cells indicates a herpesvirus infection, herpes simplex (or varicella-zoster). HPV instead produces koilocytes, and EBV shows atypical (Downey) lymphocytes on a blood film.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A patient reports difficulty switching between movements and experiences uncontrollable hand movements. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Impaired rapid alternating movements (for example pronation-supination), that is difficulty switching between movements, is dysdiadochokinesia, a sign of cerebellar dysfunction (along with ataxia, dysmetria and intention tremor). A resting tremor instead suggests Parkinsonism.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A neonate was born to a controlled gestational diabetes mother. At the time of birth, he was fine but 4 days later, he developed dyspnea with SpO2 80% at room air. What is the initial management?
questions.concept: A term neonate who becomes cyanotic on day 4 may have cyanotic congenital heart disease or lung disease; giving 100% oxygen (the hyperoxia test) distinguishes them, as PaO2 rises to at least 100 mmHg with lung disease but fails to rise with a cardiac right-to-left shunt. NOTE: 100% O2 here is a diagnostic first step, and oxygen must be used cautiously if a duct-dependent lesion is suspected.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: MOA of botulinum toxin is:
questions.concept: Botulinum toxin (from Clostridium botulinum) acts by inhibiting acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing flaccid paralysis. Contrast: diphtheria and Pseudomonas exotoxin A inhibit elongation factor-2; tetanus toxin blocks GABA/glycine release (spastic paralysis); cholera and pertussis toxins raise cAMP.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: In a child presenting with diarrhoea, the following finding is noted. What is the likely micronutrient deficiency?
questions.concept: A child with chronic diarrhoea and a periorificial/acral vesiculobullous, scaly rash (acrodermatitis enteropathica) has zinc deficiency. Copper deficiency instead causes anaemia and neutropenia rather than this rash.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A hypertensive patient's lab results reveal hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.concept: Hypertension with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis (and high-to-normal sodium) is primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome), from an adrenal adenoma or hyperplasia: aldosterone drives Na+ retention with renal K+ and H+ loss. Addison's disease is the mirror image (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, acidosis).

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: While evaluating a 3-year-old with short stature, height is measured at 90cm and the lower segment is 45 cm. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Height 90 cm with a lower segment of 45 cm gives an upper:lower segment ratio of 1:1, well below the roughly 1.3:1 expected at 3 years, indicating a short trunk. Short-trunk (reduced upper segment) dwarfism points to spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, whereas achondroplasia produces short limbs (a high US:LS ratio).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department with complaints of blurred vision, dizziness, and severe headache after ingesting an unknown quantity of homemade alcohol earlier in the day. On examination, he is disoriented. Laboratory tests reveal severe metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap. Which metabolite is primarily responsible for the toxicity in this case?
questions.concept: Home-brewed liquor causing visual blurring and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis is methanol poisoning. Methanol is oxidised to formaldehyde and then to formic acid (formate); formate inhibits cytochrome c oxidase and is the metabolite chiefly responsible for the acidosis and optic toxicity. Treatment is fomepizole/ethanol plus dialysis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following amino acids primarily acts as a buffer in blood due to its ability to accept and donate protons at physiological pH?
questions.concept: Histidine's imidazole side chain has a pKa near 6.0, close to physiological pH, so it readily accepts and donates protons, making histidine (and the histidine residues of haemoglobin) the main amino-acid buffer of blood. Arginine (pKa about 12.5) and tyrosine (pKa about 10) are poor buffers at pH 7.4.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: During starvation, which of the following hormones is primarily produced to maintain blood glucose levels?
questions.concept: During fasting/starvation, glucagon is the principal hormone maintaining blood glucose, driving hepatic glycogenolysis then gluconeogenesis and promoting lipolysis. Insulin falls, while the counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol, epinephrine and growth hormone) rise.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A child presents with micrognathia and low-set ears. These clinical features are commonly associated with which type of genetic abnormality?
questions.concept: Micrognathia with low-set ears is characteristic of chromosomal deletion syndromes (e.g. cri-du-chat 5p-, DiGeorge 22q11.2). Translocations classically drive malignancies (e.g. CML t(9;22)) and gene amplification drives oncogenes (HER2, N-myc) rather than these dysmorphic features.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A child presents with a right transverse palmar crease, a cardiac defect, survival into childhood, and mild intellectual impairment. What is the chromosomal abnormality most likely associated with these findings?
questions.concept: The single transverse palmar crease, congenital heart defect and mild intellectual impairment describe Down syndrome, and the emphasis on a mild phenotype with survival points to mosaic Down (mosaicism), which is milder than full trisomy 21. NOTE: classic Down is trisomy 21, but that is not offered; among these options mosaicism best explains the attenuated presentation (monosomy/haploidy are non-viable).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A girl presents with microcephaly and a high-pitched cry. Which of the following is the most likely chromosomal abnormality?
questions.concept: Microcephaly with a shrill, high-pitched 'cat-like' cry is cri-du-chat syndrome, caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A patient with CSOM presented to the OPD with seizures. On examination and evaluation, homonymous hemianopia and epilepsy were present. Identify the condition (CT scan provided).
questions.concept: In a chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) patient, contralateral homonymous hemianopia (optic-radiation involvement) plus seizures localises to a temporal-lobe brain abscess; a cerebellar abscess instead causes ataxia and nystagmus.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is associated with the Holman-Miller sign on CT?
questions.concept: The Holman-Miller sign (anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus) is characteristic of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, a highly vascular tumour of adolescent males presenting with recurrent epistaxis and nasal obstruction.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In paracetamol poisoning, N-acetylcysteine is administered as an antidote. How does it act to prevent toxicity?
questions.concept: In paracetamol overdose the toxic metabolite NAPQI accumulates once hepatic glutathione is depleted, causing hepatic necrosis. N-acetylcysteine acts as a glutathione (sulfhydryl) precursor, replenishing glutathione so NAPQI is detoxified; it does not directly inhibit or remove the toxin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: What is the primary mechanism behind tissue damage in long-standing diabetes?
questions.concept: Chronic hyperglycaemia is the fundamental driver of diabetic tissue injury, acting through advanced glycation end-products, the polyol (sorbitol) pathway, protein kinase C activation and the hexosamine pathway. Sorbitol accumulation is only one downstream arm, not the primary mechanism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with a history of I-131 ablation therapy presents with a neck mass. Which of the following is a likely long-term side effect of the treatment?
questions.concept: Hypothyroidism is the most common long-term complication of radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation because the therapy progressively destroys thyroid tissue. NOTE: the source stem also quoted high T4 / low TSH (a hyperthyroid picture), but the question asks for the expected side effect of I-131, which is hypothyroidism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with a history of vomiting. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals pH 7.5, pCO2 48 mm Hg and HCO3- 30 mmol/L. What is the most likely acid-base abnormality?
questions.concept: An alkalaemic pH (7.5) with a raised bicarbonate (30) is a primary metabolic alkalosis; here it results from loss of gastric HCl during vomiting, and the raised pCO2 (48) reflects appropriate respiratory compensation (hypoventilation).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: In the context of mitral stenosis, which clinical feature is typically observed?
questions.concept: Mitral stenosis classically produces a loud first heart sound (S1), from forceful closure of the thickened but still-mobile mitral leaflets, along with an opening snap and a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur. S1 softens only in late/calcific disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 9-month-old baby was admitted to the ICU with recurrent sinusitis and otitis media due to Staphylococcus aureus. Laboratory examination showed decreased serum IgA, IgG, IgM and IgE, and decreased plasma B cells. Which condition is described here?
questions.concept: Recurrent pyogenic infections beginning after about 6 months of age with panhypogammaglobulinaemia and absent B cells is X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinaemia, due to a BTK mutation that blocks B-cell maturation. DiGeorge is a T-cell defect and CGD is a neutrophil oxidative-burst defect.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A child presents with recurrent Staphylococcus infections. Laboratory examination shows very low levels of immunoglobulins (G, A, M, E) and a low quantity of B cells. There is a normal reaction to environmental antigens on the skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Very low levels of all immunoglobulin classes with absent/low B cells but preserved T-cell function (a normal delayed-hypersensitivity skin reaction) is Bruton X-linked agammaglobulinaemia. Hyper-IgM has normal/high IgM, and CVID usually presents later with normal B-cell numbers.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which of the following methods is used to measure fetal anemia?
options: Peak systolic velocity in the fetal middle cerebral artery (MCA)
questions.concept: Fetal anaemia is screened non-invasively by the peak systolic velocity in the middle cerebral artery (MCA-PSV); anaemia lowers blood viscosity and raises cerebral flow velocity. Cord blood sampling is diagnostic but invasive, and umbilical artery Doppler assesses placental resistance, not anaemia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Shoulder dystocia is diagnosed when the anterior shoulder is delivered after what interval from delivery of the head?
questions.concept: Shoulder dystocia is defined as a head-to-body delivery interval exceeding 60 seconds, or delivery requiring additional obstetric manoeuvres after routine gentle traction has failed.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: What is the hormone detected in a home pregnancy test?
questions.concept: Home urine pregnancy tests detect beta-hCG (the beta subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin), secreted by the trophoblast and rising rapidly in early pregnancy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: What is the earliest sign of pregnancy on transvaginal sonography (TVS)?
questions.concept: On transvaginal ultrasound the earliest visible sign of intrauterine pregnancy is the gestational sac (from about 4.5-5 weeks), appearing before the yolk sac, fetal pole and cardiac activity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with irregular periods, acne and excessive hair growth. What is the first-line management?
questions.concept: Oligomenorrhoea, acne and hirsutism describe PCOS, and first-line management is lifestyle modification (weight reduction, diet and exercise), which improves ovulation and hyperandrogenism before adding drugs such as OCPs, metformin or clomiphene.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: About 75% of iatrogenic ureteric injuries are due to gynaecological procedures. Which hysterectomy route has the least risk of ureteric injury?
questions.concept: The vaginal route carries the lowest risk of ureteric injury among hysterectomy approaches, whereas laparoscopic and abdominal hysterectomy carry higher rates because of dissection near the ureter at the pelvic brim and the cardinal ligament.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A postmenopausal woman presents with irregular bleeding; endometrial biopsy shows endometrial hyperplasia without atypia. What is the likely management?
questions.concept: Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia is treated with progestogens, and the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) is first-line because it delivers sustained local progestogen with the best regression rates. Unopposed estradiol would worsen the hyperplasia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: The development of cataracts in patients with diabetes mellitus is primarily due to the accumulation of which of the following substances in the lens?
questions.concept: In diabetes, excess glucose is reduced to sorbitol by aldose reductase (the polyol pathway); sorbitol is trapped in the lens, drawing in water (osmotic stress) and causing cataract. Dulcitol/galactitol accumulate in galactosaemia, not diabetes, and mannitol is an exogenous osmotic diuretic.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: An elderly man presents with an ulcerative lesion at the inner canthus of his eye with pearly margins. Microscopic examination shows a palisading arrangement of cells. Identify the lesion:
questions.concept: An ulcer with rolled pearly margins at the inner canthus (rodent ulcer) showing peripheral palisading of tumour cells is basal cell carcinoma, a slow-growing, locally invasive tumour that rarely metastasises. Squamous cell carcinoma instead shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which gene mutation is most commonly associated with Burkitt's lymphoma?
questions.concept: Burkitt lymphoma is characterised by translocation of the c-myc oncogene (chromosome 8) next to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus, classically t(8;14), driving unregulated proliferation and the 'starry-sky' histology.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A baby presents with chronic diarrhea and a rash resembling acrodermatitis on the skin. Based on the clinical picture, what is the most likely deficiency?
questions.concept: The combination of chronic diarrhoea and an acral/periorificial dermatitis (with later alopecia) is acrodermatitis enteropathica, caused by zinc deficiency. Niacin deficiency causes pellagra (photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia) with a different distribution.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antihypertensive drug is contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.concept: ACE inhibitors such as enalapril are contraindicated in pregnancy: blocking the fetal renin-angiotensin system causes renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia and growth restriction. Methyldopa, labetalol and nifedipine are the safe first-line agents.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A total of 60 patients were diagnosed with COVID-19, of which 12 deaths were reported. Calculate the case fatality rate.
questions.concept: Case fatality rate = (deaths from a disease / diagnosed cases of that disease) x 100 = 12/60 x 100 = 20%. It measures the lethality of a disease among diagnosed cases.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following is the formula for sensitivity?
questions.concept: Sensitivity = true positives / (true positives + false negatives) x 100, i.e. the proportion of truly diseased people the test correctly identifies. TP/(TP+FP) is positive predictive value and TN/(TN+FP) is specificity.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a normal distribution, the mean value is 82 and the SD is 1.5. Calculate the range covering two standard deviations from the mean.
questions.concept: Mean +/- 2 SD = 82 +/- (2 x 1.5) = 82 +/- 3, i.e. 79 to 85; in a normal distribution this interval contains about 95% of observations.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.concept: Varicella is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy because of a theoretical risk of fetal infection. Inactivated influenza, rabies (killed) and Tdap are safe and in fact recommended in pregnancy.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following vaccines is contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.concept: Live vaccines are avoided in pregnancy; among these options only varicella is a live attenuated vaccine and is therefore contraindicated, whereas inactivated influenza, rabies and Tdap are safe.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which is the nodal ministry for disaster management in India?
options: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Ministry of Human Resource and Development
questions.concept: In India the Ministry of Home Affairs is the nodal ministry for disaster management and houses the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), which is chaired by the Prime Minister.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with a history of breast cancer underwent Cobalt-60 radiotherapy. She now presents with respiratory distress, and imaging shows haziness in the left lung. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: New respiratory distress with lung haziness confined to a previously irradiated field after chest/breast radiotherapy is radiation pneumonitis, an inflammatory reaction of lung to ionising radiation that typically appears weeks to a few months after treatment.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 70-year-old patient presents with absolute constipation and abdominal distension; the abdominal X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: An elderly patient with gross abdominal distension and absolute constipation (obstipation) is the classic picture of sigmoid volvulus, which on plain film gives the coffee-bean / inverted-U sign arising from the pelvis. Caecal volvulus typically occurs in younger adults.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a study based in Delhi, doctors followed 100 people who did exercise for a year and later they checked who all had developed coronary heart disease. Which type of study is this?
questions.concept: Following a defined exposed group (exercisers) forward over time to see who develops the outcome (coronary heart disease) is a cohort study - it moves from exposure to outcome. Because follow-up runs forward it is also 'prospective', but the study TYPE being asked for is cohort.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which of the following is associated with a Graham-Steel murmur?
questions.concept: A Graham-Steell murmur is the early-diastolic murmur of pulmonary regurgitation, classically produced when pulmonary hypertension (e.g. from mitral stenosis) dilates the pulmonary valve ring.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following is the fIPV dose schedule under the National Immunization Schedule?
options: At birth, 6 weeks, 10 weeks, 14 weeks, 16-24 months, 5 years
questions.concept: Under India's current National Immunization Schedule, fractional IPV (fIPV) is given as three intradermal doses - at 6 weeks, 14 weeks and 9 months (the 9-month dose was added in the recent update). NOTE: immunization schedules change frequently, so re-verify against the latest NMC/MoHFW schedule before shipping.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with a history of throat infection presents with a water hammer pulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A collapsing 'water-hammer' (Corrigan) pulse signifies aortic regurgitation, and a preceding sore throat points to post-streptococcal rheumatic fever as the underlying cause - so rheumatic aortic regurgitation is the best fit.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following is the management of a HIV positive patient with multiple dog bites?
questions.concept: Multiple bites are Category III exposure, and an immunocompromised (HIV-positive) patient must receive full post-exposure prophylaxis: thorough wound washing PLUS rabies vaccine PLUS rabies immunoglobulin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The CSF findings in bacterial meningitis would include which of the following?
options: Elevated WBC count with normal glucose
questions.concept: Bacterial meningitis CSF shows raised protein, low glucose (organisms consume it) and a high neutrophilic cell count; the pairing of high protein with low glucose is the key marker.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: During laparoscopic surgery, where shouldn't the trocar be inserted?
questions.concept: Both the superior and inferior epigastric arteries run within the rectus sheath and are at risk during trocar insertion (upper and lower abdominal wall respectively), so trocars should be placed away from the rectus muscle at both levels. The aorta is a deep retroperitoneal structure, not a trocar-entry risk.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A patient with diffuse severely contaminated peritonitis underwent laparotomy and was left open after surgery. Which of the following might help?
questions.concept: For an open abdomen after laparotomy for severe contaminated peritonitis, negative-pressure (VAC) therapy is preferred: it removes infected exudate, reduces oedema, promotes granulation and helps avoid the abdominal compartment syndrome that forced primary closure would risk.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient diagnosed with Cryptococcal meningitis. What is the treatment?
questions.concept: Induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis is liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine (5-FC); fluconazole is used afterwards for consolidation/maintenance, not for initial induction.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: What is the usual method of collecting a sample of urine to detect UTI?
questions.concept: A clean-catch midstream sample is the usual, least-invasive way to collect urine for suspected UTI because it minimises contamination by peri-urethral commensals; early-morning samples are for proteinuria and initial-stream samples are contamination-prone.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: In a child presenting with a beaded appearance in the chest with the following X-ray, what is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: A 'rachitic rosary' (beading at the costochondral junctions) with metaphyseal cupping/fraying on X-ray is characteristic of rickets from vitamin D deficiency. Scurvy is vitamin C, beri-beri is thiamine (B1) and pellagra is niacin (B3) deficiency.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge?
questions.concept: Intraductal papilloma, a benign growth within a lactiferous duct, is the commonest cause of bloody (or serosanguineous) nipple discharge; carcinoma and duct ectasia can also bleed but are less common.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 23-year-old female visited the clinician with a solitary thyroid nodule and was advised for thyroid function tests where Tsh level is 27.3mU/L, T3 is 1.24 ng/ml, and T4 is 4.87 microgram/ml. Which of the following manifestations is true regarding the condition?
questions.concept: An elevated TSH with low/low-normal T4 indicates primary hypothyroidism, which slows metabolism and causes weight gain; heat intolerance, tachycardia and diarrhoea are hyperthyroid features.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 34-year-old male undergoes an open appendectomy for acute appendicitis. The choice of incision was McBurney's incision. Postoperatively, after a few days, he presents with pain and bulging in the right lower quadrant, which is diagnosed as an indirect inguinal hernia. Which nerve injury during the appendectomy is most likely responsible for this complication?
questions.concept: The ilioinguinal (and iliohypogastric) nerve is vulnerable in a McBurney grid-iron appendicectomy incision; losing its motor supply weakens the conjoint tendon and can lead to a later inguinal hernia. NOTE: classically this predisposes to a DIRECT inguinal hernia, though this recall labels it indirect - the nerve answer (ilioinguinal) is unchanged.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 60 y/o male suddenly experiences an intense headache, described as the worst headache of his life, followed by vomiting and photophobia. O/E he has neck stiffness and a dilated pupil on the right side. A CT scan reveals bleeding in the subarachnoid space. Which of the following is the most common cause of this condition?
questions.concept: A sudden 'worst headache of life' with neck stiffness and subarachnoid blood on CT is subarachnoid haemorrhage; rupture of a berry (intracranial) aneurysm is its commonest spontaneous cause (~50% of cases).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 45-year-old male patient was brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. O/E, he had multiple injuries all over his body and was found to be in class III hemorrhagic shock. The percentage of blood loss would be between:
questions.concept: In the ATLS haemorrhagic-shock classification, Class III corresponds to a blood loss of about 30-40%, accompanied by tachycardia, hypotension, reduced urine output and confusion.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: KAT G mutation associated with:
questions.concept: The katG gene encodes catalase-peroxidase, which activates the prodrug isoniazid; a katG mutation abolishes this activation and confers isoniazid resistance. Rifampicin resistance is via rpoB, fluoroquinolone via gyrA/gyrB, and ethambutol via embB.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 20-year-old male presents to the outpatient department with a swelling on his wrist. He reports fluctuation in size, mild numbness in the hand, and occasional pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A cystic wrist swelling that fluctuates in size (and may compress a nearby nerve, causing mild numbness) is most typically a ganglion cyst arising from a joint capsule or tendon sheath - the commonest soft-tissue swelling of the wrist.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A newborn male presents with urinary retention, lethargy and a distended bladder. Antenatal ultrasound showed a 'keyhole sign' with a thickened bladder wall. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A newborn boy with a distended, thick-walled bladder, urinary retention and an antenatal 'keyhole sign' (dilated bladder plus dilated posterior urethra) has posterior urethral valves, the commonest cause of lower urinary tract obstruction in male infants.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 30-year-old female presents to the OPD with a 3 cm breast lump in the upper medial quadrant. The lump has an uneven, bosselated surface, and the overlying skin is mildly ulcerated. Microscopic examination reveals the given findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A rapidly growing, bosselated (lobulated) breast lump with skin ulceration and stromal overgrowth in a leaf-like architecture on histology indicates a phyllodes tumour; fibroadenoma is smooth and mobile, while Paget's disease affects the nipple-areolar complex.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: In a follow-up case of prostate cancer, what do we need to check?
questions.concept: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is the marker of choice for monitoring treated prostate cancer - a rising PSA signals biochemical recurrence or progression. Alkaline phosphatase (bone metastases) and prostatic acid phosphatase (outdated) are not used for routine follow-up.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 38 Y/o woman presents with complaints of heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic discomfort, and frequent urination. On physical examination, her uterus is found to be irregularly enlarged. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Heavy menstrual bleeding with pressure symptoms (urinary frequency) and an irregularly, firmly enlarged uterus is classic for uterine leiomyoma (fibroids), benign myometrial smooth-muscle tumours.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
