questions.stem: A 25-year-old female presents with irregular menstrual cycles, acne, and excessive hair growth. An ultrasound reveals multiple ovarian cysts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Oligomenorrhoea with hyperandrogenism (acne, hirsutism) plus polycystic ovaries on ultrasound fits the Rotterdam picture of polycystic ovary syndrome (Stein-Leventhal syndrome).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 25-year-old female presents with complaints of a yellowish-green, foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She reports painful urination and pain during intercourse & no itching. On speculum examination, her vulva and vaginal walls appear inflamed. What is the causative agent?
questions.concept: A profuse, frothy, yellow-green, foul-smelling discharge with inflamed ('strawberry') vaginitis, dysuria and dyspareunia points to Trichomonas vaginalis, a flagellate protozoan. NOTE: the recall says 'no itching' (more typical of bacterial vaginosis), but the marked vaginal-wall INFLAMMATION favours trichomoniasis, since BV is a non-inflammatory vaginosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 35-year-old female patient presents to the clinic for evaluation of her fertility status. She has been trying to conceive for over a year without success. Which of the following is the single best test for assessing her ovarian reserve?
questions.concept: Anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH), produced by ovarian antral follicles, is the single best test of ovarian reserve because it mirrors the antral follicle pool and varies little across the menstrual cycle, unlike day-3 FSH/estradiol or inhibin B.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: During the active management of the third stage of labor, which intervention is recommended to prevent postpartum hemorrhage primarily due to uterine atony?
options: Immediate administration of 20 units of undiluted oxytocin intravenously
Vigorous fundal massage combined with a uterotonic agent
Controlled cord traction with immediate removal of the placenta
questions.concept: Active management of the third stage combines a uterotonic (oxytocin) with uterine (fundal) massage to prevent PPH from atony. Oxytocin must never be given as an undiluted IV bolus (hypotension/arrhythmia), and cord traction before placental separation risks uterine inversion. NOTE: prophylactic oxytocin is the single most important step; option B is wrong only because of its 'with crowning' timing (oxytocin is given after delivery of the baby).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most likely abnormality in a patient of recurrent vomiting with pH 7.5, pCO2 48mm Hg, and HCO3- 33?
questions.concept: A high pH (7.5) with a raised HCO3- (33) is a metabolic alkalosis, and the modestly raised pCO2 (48) is appropriate respiratory compensation. Recurrent vomiting causes it by loss of gastric H+ (with chloride, potassium and volume depletion).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with unilateral throbbing pain, photophobia, nausea, and vomiting. The symptoms improve after taking sumatriptan. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A unilateral throbbing headache with photophobia, nausea/vomiting that responds to a triptan (sumatriptan, a 5-HT1B/1D agonist) is characteristic of migraine.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following is not a food adulteration disease?
questions.concept: Lathyrism (Lathyrus sativus/kesari dal), epidemic dropsy (argemone oil adulterating mustard oil) and aflatoxicosis (Aspergillus toxin on stored grain/nuts) are food-adulteration/contamination diseases; fluorosis is caused by excess fluoride in drinking water, so it is NOT a food-adulteration disease.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 22-year-old male presents with pain and swelling over the distal radius. X-ray shows an expansile lytic lesion in the metaphysis. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) reveals a bloody aspirate with hemosiderin-laden macrophages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: An expansile, lytic metaphyseal lesion whose FNA yields a bloody aspirate with haemosiderin-laden macrophages (blood-filled cystic spaces, fluid-fluid levels on MRI) is an aneurysmal bone cyst; a giant cell tumour is epiphyseal and lacks haemosiderin on FNA.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with chronic stable angina presents with worsening chest pain during routine activities. His current medications include aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, and atorvastatin, but his symptoms persist. ECG shows ST-segment depression in V5-V6, and coronary angiography reveals 80% stenosis of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. What is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stent (DES)
Refer for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)
questions.concept: For chronic stable angina with limiting symptoms despite optimal medical therapy and a significant single-vessel stenosis (80% LAD), PCI with a drug-eluting stent is the best next step; CABG is reserved for left-main, multivessel, or LV-dysfunction/diabetic disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 72 y/o woman presents with severe chest pain and shortness of breath after a stressful argument. She is post-menopausal with no history of heart disease. O/E, she is slightly tachycardic with normal blood pressure. An echocardiogram shows left ventricular ballooning during systole, and cardiac enzymes are minimally elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Transient apical left-ventricular ballooning after acute emotional/physical stress in a post-menopausal woman, with chest pain but only minimal troponin rise and no obstructive coronary disease, is Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 68-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency department in acute distress. He is diaphoretic, tachycardic, and complains of severe chest pain. His ECG is given below. Given the patient's condition, what is the most appropriate immediate management for this patient?
questions.concept: A haemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmia (here atrial flutter with saw-tooth F-waves, causing distress, diaphoresis and chest pain) needs immediate synchronized DC cardioversion; antiarrhythmic drugs and ablation are for the stable or long-term setting. The instability alone dictates cardioversion regardless of the exact rhythm.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with increased breathlessness, cough, and sputum production over the last two days. She appears distressed and has a respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute. Her oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Which of the following management strategies is most appropriate for her immediate treatment?
options: Initiate high-flow oxygen therapy to maintain oxygen saturation above 95%
Start nebulised bronchodilator therapy with salbutamol and ipratropium
Order a chest X-ray before any treatment is provided
questions.concept: In an acute COPD exacerbation the immediate treatment is nebulised short-acting bronchodilators (salbutamol + ipratropium). Oxygen must be controlled to a target SpO2 of ~88-92% (not high-flow to >95%, which risks CO2 retention), and imaging must not delay treatment.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes presents for a routine follow-up. Her serum creatinine and potassium levels are normal, but she has microalbuminuria and an HbA1c of 8%. Her blood pressure and pulse are within normal limits, and she is currently on metformin for diabetes management. What should be the next step in her management?
options: Stop Metformin and start a different OHA
questions.concept: In type 2 diabetes with microalbuminuria, an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) is the next step - it slows progression of diabetic nephropathy and lowers cardiovascular risk even when blood pressure is normal (monitor potassium and creatinine).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 38-year-old male presents with a one-week history of fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, and myalgia. Skin examination reveals multiple purpura and petechiae on the left shoulder, trunk, and legs. Similar cases have been reported linked to increased incidence of mosquito breeding. What is the most common neurological complication associated with this condition?
questions.concept: The picture (fever, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, petechiae/purpura in a mosquito-breeding outbreak) is dengue; its commonest neurological complication is dengue encephalopathy (typically in DHF/DSS, with normal CSF), rather than true encephalitis, GBS or stroke.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cardiac cycle, ECG basis, BP regulation
questions.stem: An alcoholic patient presents with palpitations, dizziness and syncopal attacks. On examination the pulse is irregularly irregular. What will be seen on the JVP?
questions.concept: An irregularly irregular pulse in a chronic alcoholic points to atrial fibrillation ('holiday heart'). Because the atria fibrillate rather than contract in a coordinated way, the atrial-systole 'a' wave of the JVP disappears. A large a wave is seen in tricuspid stenosis/pulmonary hypertension, a cannon a wave in AV dissociation (complete heart block/VT), and a steep y descent in constrictive pericarditis.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: While testing drinking water from a village tank, which of the following parameters is NOT within the acceptable limits for safe drinking water?
questions.concept: The BIS acceptable limit for cadmium is 0.003 mg/L, so 0.03 mg/L is about ten times too high and unsafe. The other values are all within limits (fluoride up to 1.0, TDS up to 500 and nitrate up to 45 mg/L).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with a past history of rheumatic fever has a loud S1 and a mid-diastolic murmur. Which valvular lesion does she have?
questions.concept: Prior rheumatic fever with a loud S1 and a low-pitched apical mid-diastolic murmur is classic mitral stenosis: rheumatic disease fuses and thickens the leaflets, so the stiff valve shuts loudly and blood flows turbulently across the narrowed orifice in diastole. MR gives a pansystolic murmur and AR an early-diastolic murmur.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with a past history of heart disease presents with central chest pain. The ECG shows ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads (V2-V4) and lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6), with reciprocal ST depression in the inferior leads (III, aVF). What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: ST elevation spanning the anterior (V2-V4) and lateral (I, aVL, V5-V6) leads localises injury to the anterolateral wall (LAD +/- LCX/diagonal territory). The reciprocal inferior ST depression confirms acute MI and argues against pericarditis, which shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal changes.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A study analysed how much time nursing staff spend on different tasks (bed preparation, monitoring vitals, doctor's rounds, blood sampling, drug administration) by observing them at random intervals. Which management technique is most appropriate?
questions.concept: Sampling activities at random moments to estimate the proportion of time spent on each task is Work Sampling. A Time and Motion study instead times each step continuously, the Critical Path Method schedules dependent project tasks, and systems analysis studies whole processes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient develops a broad-QRS-complex tachycardia after an MI. His BP is 120/85 mmHg and he is haemodynamically stable. What is the best management?
questions.concept: A haemodynamically stable wide-QRS tachycardia after MI is monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, for which IV amiodarone is the appropriate pharmacologic choice. Nitroglycerin and beta-blockers (metoprolol/labetalol) do not terminate VT and could worsen the situation. (The source gave no explanation; the answer is confirmed on standard ACLS grounds.)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with weight gain, thinning of hair and dry skin and is diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Which antibody is characteristically seen?
questions.concept: Hashimoto's thyroiditis (autoimmune hypothyroidism) is marked by anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies, which drive autoimmune destruction of the gland. The long-acting thyroid stimulator (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin) belongs to Graves' disease, causing hyperthyroidism.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A road-traffic-accident patient has received 4 units of packed red cells within a few hours. Which of the following is most likely to be seen?
questions.concept: Stored blood is anticoagulated with citrate, which chelates ionised calcium, so rapid transfusion causes hypocalcaemia (citrate toxicity) with perioral tingling, tetany and QT prolongation. Hyperkalaemia from potassium leaking out of stored cells is the other classic change, but citrate-induced hypocalcaemia is the characteristic answer for rapid transfusion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A young woman presents with ptosis showing diurnal variation. CT chest reveals an anterior mediastinal thymic tumour. Which receptor is affected in this patient?
options: Voltage-gated calcium channels at the NMJ
questions.concept: Fatigable ptosis with diurnal variation plus a thymic (anterior mediastinal) mass indicates myasthenia gravis, caused by autoantibodies against the postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction. Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies instead define Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has 1 year of progressive limb weakness. Examination shows muscle fasciculations and hypertonia with an intact sensory system. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Combined upper motor neuron signs (hypertonia) and lower motor neuron signs (fasciculations) with completely spared sensation is the hallmark of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (motor neuron disease). SMA and multifocal motor neuropathy are pure LMN disorders, and Becker dystrophy is a myopathy without UMN signs or fasciculations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with symmetrical leg weakness and areflexia two weeks after an episode of diarrhoea and is diagnosed with GBS. What is the cause?
questions.concept: GBS is an acute immune-mediated demyelinating polyneuropathy (often post-Campylobacter diarrhoea) that strikes myelinated peripheral nerve fibres, producing ascending weakness and areflexia; it is a peripheral nerve/root process, not spinal-cord demyelination or cord inflammation. NOTE: the option wording ('A, B fibres') is imprecise since GBS predominantly hits myelinated somatic (A) fibres, but among the choices it is the only one describing peripheral demyelination, so it is the intended answer.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A patient with a 3-month history of cough and weight loss has a lung mass whose biopsy expresses chromogranin and synaptophysin. Which paraneoplastic syndrome is most likely?
questions.concept: Chromogranin and synaptophysin positivity identifies a neuroendocrine tumour, here small cell lung carcinoma, which classically secretes ectopic ADH producing SIADH and dilutional hyponatraemia. Ectopic ACTH/Cushing also occurs with small cell carcinoma but SIADH is the single best answer, while PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia belongs to squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with palpitations, headache and sweating and a BP of 180/100 mmHg. The 24-hour urinary metanephrines are elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations with hypertension and raised 24-hour urinary metanephrines is diagnostic of phaeochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting adrenal medullary tumour. Metanephrines (not urinary 5-HIAA of carcinoid or VMA/HVA of neuroblastoma) are the sensitive marker.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with osteoarthritis has taken ibuprofen for 3 months and develops occult GI bleeding. Which statement about the cause is correct?
options: PGE-2 and prostacyclin production were reduced
PGE-1 and prostacyclin production were reduced
Mucosal injury due to inhibition of COX-2
questions.concept: Ibuprofen inhibits cyclo-oxygenase, lowering gastric-protective PGE2 and prostacyclin (which normally increase mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow); loss of these prostaglandins, chiefly via COX-1, leaves the mucosa vulnerable to acid injury and bleeding. The key protective prostaglandin is PGE2, not PGE1 (option C).

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: What is the name of the technical platform developed under India's National Tele Mental Health Programme to deliver mental healthcare through telephone, digital platforms and online portals?
questions.concept: Tele-MANAS (Mental Health Assistance and Networking Across States) is the multi-tier tele-mental-health platform under the National Tele Mental Health Programme. NIKSHAY is the TB surveillance system, e-Sanjeevani is the general telemedicine OPD service, and quinidine is a drug (distractor).

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: After an ANM completes an immunization using a syringe with needle, a vaccine vial and a cotton swab, which statement about biomedical waste disposal is correct?
options: The syringe with the needle should be disposed of in a black translucent container
The used vaccine vial should be discarded in a blue bag
A used cotton swab should be discarded in a red bag
The needle should be bent and thrown in a red bag
questions.concept: A used (empty) glass vaccine vial is glassware and goes into the blue puncture-proof container. The other statements are wrong: sharps/needles go into white translucent puncture-proof containers (not black), blood/fluid-soaked cotton goes in the yellow bag (not red), and needles must never be bent before disposal.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Who is primarily responsible for registering eligible couples for family planning and maintaining their records under the national health system?
questions.concept: The Multipurpose Health Worker (Female)/ANM maintains the Eligible Couple Register and records contraceptive use at the sub-centre. ASHA and the Anganwadi worker help with mobilisation and education but do not keep the official register.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: An HIV-positive patient has chronic diarrhoea for 4 weeks. Stool microscopy shows oval/elliptical cysts measuring about 16 x 20 um. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Large oval/ellipsoidal acid-fast oocysts (roughly 16-20 um and larger) causing chronic diarrhoea in an HIV patient indicate Cystoisospora belli (formerly Isospora), treated with cotrimoxazole. Cryptosporidium oocysts are small (4-6 um) and round, Cyclospora are about 8-10 um, and Cryptococcus is a fungus causing meningitis, not diarrhoea.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: A known hyperthyroid patient not on medication is scheduled for total thyroidectomy, and the pre-anaesthetic check was not done properly. What is the leading complication that can occur during surgery?
questions.concept: An untreated hyperthyroid patient taken to surgery without proper preoperative optimisation has heightened catecholamine sensitivity and risks tachyarrhythmias (and thyroid storm) intraoperatively; arrhythmia is the leading immediate danger. Adequate preop control with antithyroid drugs and beta-blockers is essential.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents with a deep-seated retro-orbital pain of cluster headache. What is the best acute management?
questions.concept: High-flow 100% oxygen is the first-line abortive treatment for an acute cluster-headache attack, relieving pain within minutes. Verapamil, lithium and topiramate are prophylactic agents, not acute abortives.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient has hypertension with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. CT shows an adrenal mass and the aldosterone-renin ratio is elevated. What is the next best step in management?
questions.concept: Hypertension with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, a raised aldosterone-renin ratio and a unilateral adrenal mass is primary hyperaldosteronism from an aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn's); the definitive treatment for unilateral disease is laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Spironolactone is reserved for bilateral hyperplasia or non-surgical patients.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has chronic hypercalcemia for 1.5 years but a normal PTH level. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.concept: Chronic, stable hypercalcaemia with a normal PTH is PTH-independent; in a young man this fits sarcoidosis, where granuloma macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase and make excess calcitriol. Parathyroid hyperplasia would raise PTH and CKD tends to lower calcium. NOTE: malignancy is the commonest PTH-independent cause overall, but its hypercalcaemia is usually acute with weight loss, so the chronic stable course here favours sarcoidosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A patient has distended neck veins, absent breath sounds, hyperresonance and a shift of the trachea. What is the management?
options: Bedside CXR in casualty followed by chest tube insertion
questions.concept: Distended neck veins, absent breath sounds, hyperresonance and tracheal deviation away from the affected side are tension pneumothorax, a clinical diagnosis needing immediate needle decompression (wide-bore cannula in the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line) before any imaging, followed by a chest tube. Waiting for a CXR can be fatal.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman presents with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. Serum prolactin is elevated and MRI shows a pituitary adenoma. What is the best management?
questions.concept: Amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea with a high prolactin and a pituitary adenoma is a prolactinoma; first-line therapy is a dopamine agonist (bromocriptine or cabergoline), which lowers prolactin and shrinks the tumour. Surgery is reserved for drug resistance or compressive symptoms.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A child presents with progressive pallor and bone pain, and HPLC shows elevated HbS. Which is the best treatment to manage haemolysis in this patient?
questions.concept: Elevated HbS on HPLC confirms sickle cell disease. Voxelotor, an HbS-polymerisation inhibitor that raises haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, directly reduces sickling and haemolysis, which is what this question specifically asks about. NOTE: hydroxyurea remains the traditional mainstay for the disease overall (it raises HbF and cuts vaso-occlusive crises) but acts less directly on haemolysis, which is why voxelotor is the keyed answer for haemolysis control.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: What is the probable diagnosis in a patient with miosis, anhidrosis, mild ptosis and a persistently small pupil even in low light?
questions.concept: Miosis, mild ptosis (weak Muller muscle) and ipsilateral facial anhidrosis with a pupil that stays small in dim light is Horner syndrome, due to interruption of the ocular sympathetic pathway. Argyll Robertson pupils (neurosyphilis) are small but light-near dissociated, Adie's is a large tonic pupil, and Marcus Gunn is a relative afferent defect.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with weakness, back pain and repeated infections, and workup shows an M-spike on serum electrophoresis. Prognosis is determined by which of the following?
questions.concept: An older patient with bone pain, recurrent infections and a serum M-spike has multiple myeloma; its International Staging System uses serum albumin and beta-2-microglobulin (a marker of tumour burden and renal function) to determine prognosis. The IgG level and LDH are not part of the classic ISS.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A young man has the following serology: HBsAg positive, IgM anti-HBc negative, IgG anti-HBc positive, HBeAg positive. What is the best treatment?
questions.concept: HBsAg positive with IgM anti-HBc negative but IgG anti-HBc positive and HBeAg positive indicates chronic active hepatitis B with high replication, warranting antiviral therapy; of the options only lamivudine (an HBV DNA-polymerase inhibitor) treats HBV. Ombitasvir is for HCV, and ritonavir and abacavir are HIV drugs. (Tenofovir/entecavir are preferred first-line but were not offered.)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient after a road traffic accident is passing red-coloured urine due to myoglobinuria. Which of the following is most likely to be seen?
questions.concept: Myoglobinuria after trauma reflects rhabdomyolysis, which releases intracellular potassium and causes pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis that impairs potassium excretion, so hyperkalaemia results.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient develops renal shutdown after a road traffic accident. Workup shows FeNa < 1%, urine osmolality 300 mOsm/kg and urinary sodium 40 mEq/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A urine sodium of about 40 mEq/L with isosthenuric urine (osmolality ~300, similar to plasma) reflects failed tubular sodium reabsorption and concentration, i.e. acute tubular necrosis rather than pre-renal AKI (which shows urine Na <20 and osmolality >500). NOTE: the quoted FeNa <1% is atypical for ATN and would fit pre-renal, but a low FeNa is a recognised exception in early/pigment-induced ATN, and the high urine Na plus isosthenuria point to ATN.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: In the ICU there is a failed attempt at subclavian vein catheterization, and shortly afterwards the BP drops and the pulse rises. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: The subclavian vein lies against the pleural dome, so a failed subclavian cannulation commonly causes pneumothorax; air in the pleural space reduces venous return, giving hypotension with reflex tachycardia and threatening a tension pneumothorax. Air embolism is possible but pneumothorax is the classic complication of this attempt.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: After a road traffic accident, NCCT head was normal on admission. The patient later died in the ICU following coma, and brain biopsy revealed multiple punctate haemorrhages. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: A high-speed head injury with a normal initial CT but prolonged coma and multiple deep punctate white-matter haemorrhages is diffuse axonal injury, caused by shearing/rotational forces tearing axons in the white matter, corpus callosum and brainstem. Subdural bleeds are crescentic on CT and ischaemic infarcts give territorial hypodensity, not scattered petechiae.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with fever and altered sensorium, and the peripheral smear shows multiple ring stages. What is the best treatment?
questions.concept: Fever with altered sensorium and numerous ring forms indicates severe/cerebral falciparum malaria; per WHO, IV artesunate is the drug of choice for severe malaria, giving faster parasite clearance and lower mortality than quinine. Primaquine only clears vivax/ovale hypnozoites, and chloroquine fails against resistant falciparum.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: Which is the best confirmatory method to check that a central line is correctly placed via the internal jugular vein?
questions.concept: After central-line insertion a chest X-ray is the standard confirmatory investigation for catheter tip position and to exclude pneumothorax; blood pH, colour and ETCO2 are unreliable for this. NOTE: distinguishing venous from arterial placement is strictly better done by pressure-waveform/blood-gas or ultrasound, but among the given options CXR is clearly the best confirmatory method.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: What defect is seen in Bernard-Soulier syndrome?
questions.concept: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is a defect of platelet glycoprotein Ib (the receptor for von Willebrand factor), impairing platelet adhesion and producing giant platelets, thrombocytopenia and a prolonged bleeding time. GpIIb/IIIa deficiency is Glanzmann thrombasthenia (defective aggregation), and vWF deficiency is von Willebrand disease.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: A patient presents with shortness of breath and fatigue. The chest X-ray shows bilateral calcified pleural plaques (along the parietal pleura and diaphragm) with lower-zone interstitial fibrosis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Calcified pleural plaques along the parietal pleura and diaphragm with lower-zone fibrosis are the hallmark of asbestosis. Silicosis favours upper-zone nodules with eggshell hilar-node calcification, TB is typically apical with cavitation, and pleural calcification is not a feature of byssinosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with 6 months of progressive shortness of breath and dry cough. Auscultation reveals bilateral basal end-inspiratory crepitations. There is no history of fever, joint pain or occupational exposure. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Months of progressive exertional dyspnoea and dry cough with bilateral basal end-inspiratory (Velcro) crackles, and no fever, arthralgia or exposure history, indicate idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The absence of antigen exposure argues against hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and there are no systemic or hilar features of sarcoidosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient has a long arm span, hypermobile joints and a subluxated (hypermobile) lens. What is the defective protein?
questions.concept: A tall arm span, joint hypermobility and ectopic lens describe Marfan syndrome, caused by FBN1 mutations producing defective fibrillin-1, the microfibril protein that also regulates TGF-beta signalling. Collagen defects cause Ehlers-Danlos/osteogenesis imperfecta and elastin defects relate to Williams syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A child with Kawasaki disease develops multiple small coronary artery aneurysms. What is the treatment?
questions.concept: In Kawasaki disease with small coronary artery aneurysms, low-dose aspirin is continued for roughly 6-8 weeks (covering the high-thrombosis remodelling period) as small aneurysms often regress, alongside acute-phase IVIG. Lifelong aspirin is for giant/persistent aneurysms and about 4 weeks applies when there is no coronary involvement. NOTE: exact duration guidance varies (some continue antiplatelet until aneurysm regression), but among the options 6 weeks best fits small aneurysms.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: An infant is being evaluated for recurrent seizures, and the EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. Which drug is preferred for management?
questions.concept: Infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia on EEG (West syndrome) are treated first-line with ACTH (hormonal therapy), which reduces spasms and improves developmental outcomes. Vigabatrin is preferred when spasms are due to tuberous sclerosis, and carbamazepine can worsen them.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with contralateral weakness of the face, arm and leg, and NCCT shows an intracerebral haemorrhage. What is the most likely location of the bleed?
questions.concept: A hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage causing dense contralateral face-arm-leg weakness most often arises in the basal ganglia (putamen), where the bleed compresses the corticospinal fibres of the adjacent internal capsule. Brainstem bleeds typically add cranial-nerve signs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: What is the management of undulant fever?
questions.concept: Undulant fever is brucellosis, and the standard regimen is combination doxycycline plus rifampicin for about 6 weeks, since monotherapy has a high relapse rate. Ceftriaxone is added for neurobrucellosis, not routine disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient has cheilosis with koilonychia and anaemia. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Angular cheilosis and koilonychia with anaemia are signs of iron deficiency; the associated triad (with esophageal webs and glossitis) is Plummer-Vinson syndrome, which carries an increased risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Achalasia and tylosis do not produce this iron-deficiency picture.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which classification is used for Barrett esophagus?
questions.concept: Barrett esophagus is graded endoscopically by the Prague C&M classification (C = circumferential extent, M = maximal extent above the gastroesophageal junction). Savary-Miller grades reflux esophagitis and Forrest grades bleeding peptic ulcers.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A woman complains of chest pain on waking in the morning, more marked in the winter months. Which of the following best describes the mechanism?
options: Subendocardial ischemia due to increased demand of myocardium
Increased sympathomimetic drive in morning hours
questions.concept: Rest chest pain on waking, worse in cold weather, describes Prinzmetal (variant) angina from coronary vasospasm; acetylcholine and other vasoconstrictors can provoke the spasm (with transient ST elevation during pain). Fixed plaque obstruction and demand ischaemia cause exertional stable angina, not rest vasospasm.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: CSF shows abundant PMNs with low sugar and elevated protein. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: CSF with neutrophil (PMN) predominance, low glucose and high protein is typical of acute bacterial meningitis. Tubercular and fungal meningitis show lymphocytic predominance with low glucose, while viral meningitis has lymphocytes with normal glucose.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with haematemesis and is found to have splenomegaly. There is a past history of exchange transfusion for neonatal jaundice. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.concept: Haematemesis with splenomegaly in a child who had neonatal umbilical vein catheterisation (during exchange transfusion) points to extrahepatic portal vein thrombosis, a leading cause of pre-hepatic portal hypertension and variceal bleeding in children, typically with a normal liver. Cirrhosis is unlikely at this age without chronic liver disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A skin graft was performed on an immunocompromised patient using tissue from another immunocompromised individual. Weeks later the patient developed contractures and systemic symptoms. What is the most likely cause?
options: Rejection due to recipient T8 cells
questions.concept: When immunocompetent donor lymphocytes are transferred into a recipient who cannot reject them (immunocompromised host), the donor T cells attack host tissues: graft-versus-host disease, giving systemic features (fever, rash, hepatitis, diarrhoea) plus sclerodermatous skin contractures. Host-versus-graft rejection requires an immunocompetent recipient, and graft failure/necrosis occurs early without systemic immune features.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A patient with a pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasm presents with loss of visual field. What visual field defect will be seen?
questions.concept: A pituitary adenoma compresses the central optic chiasm, damaging the decussating nasal-retinal fibres from both eyes, which carry the temporal visual fields, producing bitemporal hemianopia. Optic tract lesions instead cause homonymous hemianopia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A patient with eye strain is shown an optical diagram in which parallel light rays in different meridians focus at two separate focal lines rather than a single point (Sturm's conoid). Which refractive error is present?
questions.concept: Unequal refractive power in different corneal/lenticular meridians produces two focal lines (Sturm's conoid) instead of a single focus - this is astigmatism, which causes blurring and asthenopia (eye strain). Hypermetropia and presbyopia give a single defocused image, and amblyopia is a developmental visual deficit, not an optical focusing error.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A myopic patient presents with flashes and floaters. On examination the anterior chamber is deep. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: High myopia causes axial elongation with retinal thinning and lattice degeneration, predisposing to retinal breaks; liquefied vitreous then passes through a break into the subretinal space, producing a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment that classically presents with photopsia and floaters. Tractional and exudative detachments lack retinal breaks, and central serous retinopathy causes central blurring without flashes/floaters.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: An elderly woman presents with sudden pain, redness and decreased vision. Examination shows a hazy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and a shallow anterior chamber. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: NOTE: the scraped key said A (acute uveitis) but that is wrong. A fixed mid-dilated pupil, a shallow anterior chamber and a hazy (oedematous) cornea with sudden pain in an elderly patient are the hallmark of acute angle-closure (congestive) glaucoma. Anterior uveitis instead gives a small/miotic or irregular pupil with a normal-depth chamber and keratic precipitates, so C is the correct answer.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient has a deep anterior chamber and a jet-black pupil and is corrected with +12 D spectacles. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Absence of the crystalline lens (aphakia, usually after cataract extraction without an IOL) removes about +15 D of refractive power, so a high-plus correction (roughly +10 to +12 D) is needed; the eye also shows a deep anterior chamber, iridodonesis and a jet-black pupil. A pseudophakic eye (with an IOL) needs little correction, and simple hypermetropia rarely needs more than +4 to +5 D.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A man is brought in with bizarre behaviour, unable to recall his personal identity or how he travelled 100 km to the hospital. He had lived through a severe earthquake a few months earlier. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Loss of autobiographical memory (personal identity) triggered by a severe psychological stressor, together with purposeful travel away from home with amnesia for the journey (dissociative fugue), is classic dissociative amnesia. Dissociative identity disorder requires distinct alternate personalities, and 'global amnesia' implies an organic cause, which is absent here.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which Government of India online/tele service is used to provide mental health support (for example, for a patient with schizophrenia presenting at a PHC)?
questions.concept: Tele MANAS (Tele Mental Health Assistance and Networking Across States) is the GOI's 24x7 toll-free (14416) tele-mental-health service under the National Mental Health Programme. U-WIN is for immunization tracking, NIKUSHT for sickle-cell disease, and NIKSHAY is the national TB reporting system.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has had sleep disturbance, low mood and stress for 3 months, which he attributes to ongoing problems at work. He has no prior psychiatric history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Emotional symptoms arising within 3 months of an identifiable, non-traumatic stressor (work pressure) and not meeting criteria for another disorder define adjustment disorder. GAD requires excessive worry for at least 6 months, whereas acute stress disorder and PTSD both require exposure to a genuinely traumatic event.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A woman is excessively talkative and hyperactive, sleeps very little, spends large amounts on shopping sprees, and becomes irritable when confronted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Elevated/irritable mood with pressured speech, decreased need for sleep and reckless spending, causing marked functional/financial impairment, is a full manic episode - the defining feature of bipolar I disorder. Hypomania (bipolar II) is milder and does not cause marked impairment or psychosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient has an absent pupillary light reflex but a preserved near (accommodation) reflex. Where is the lesion most likely located?
questions.concept: Loss of the light reflex with a preserved near reflex (light-near dissociation) localizes to the pretectal area, where the afferent light pathway reaches the Edinger-Westphal nuclei before the near-reflex (cortical) fibres join - the basis of the Argyll Robertson pupil and Parinaud syndrome. An optic-nerve or oculomotor-nerve lesion abolishes both reflexes, as would destruction of the Edinger-Westphal nucleus itself.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A person has a false belief that he owns a great deal of property and that someone he knows is trying to take it from him. Which delusions is he experiencing?
questions.concept: An exaggerated false belief about one's wealth/importance is a grandiose delusion, while the belief that someone is conspiring to harm or rob him is a persecutory delusion. A delusion of reference (neutral events aimed at oneself) and a nihilistic delusion (self/world does not exist) are not described here.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A girl develops painful eyes after a picnic; she had not maintained proper hygiene of her contact lenses. What is the most likely cause?
questions.concept: Contact-lens wear with poor hygiene and likely contaminated-water exposure points to Acanthamoeba, a free-living protozoan that causes keratitis with pain out of proportion to signs and radial keratoneuritis. Pseudomonas is the commonest bacterial contact-lens keratitis, but the water-exposure clue favours the protozoan; Plasmodium does not cause keratitis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient on antipsychotics developed acute muscular dystonia and was treated for it; he now has dry mouth, dizziness and hypotension. Which drug is most likely responsible for these new effects?
questions.concept: Acute drug-induced dystonia is treated with a central anticholinergic such as benztropine, whose antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, dizziness/orthostatic symptoms) explain the new complaints. Haloperidol and risperidone cause dystonia rather than treat it, and propranolol is used for akathisia.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A child has persistently below-average mathematical skills despite a normal IQ, age-appropriate learning in other areas, and no improvement after a year of private maths tutoring. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Persistent difficulty in one academic domain (here mathematics/dyscalculia) despite normal intelligence and adequate instruction is a specific learning disorder; 'mathematics learning disorder' is not a stand-alone DSM-5 label but a specifier of SLD. ADHD causes global inattention rather than an isolated skill deficit, and Asperger's involves social-communication impairment.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A patient has a 'down and out' right eye with ptosis, present since birth. Which nerve palsy is this?
questions.concept: An eye that is depressed and abducted ('down and out') with ptosis reflects loss of the oculomotor (CN III) supply to the medial/superior/inferior recti, inferior oblique and levator palpebrae superioris, leaving the intact lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) unopposed. CN IV and CN VI palsies do not cause ptosis or this position, and CN VII affects facial muscles.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A posterior staphyloma is observed on fundus examination. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A posterior staphyloma is an ectasia of the weakened, stretched posterior sclera at the posterior pole and is characteristic of pathological (degenerative) high myopia, in which progressive axial elongation thins the sclera, choroid and retina. Hypermetropia has a short axial length, and glaucoma and retinitis pigmentosa do not cause scleral ectasia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman develops menstrual disturbance after a dilation and curettage (D&C). All hormone levels, including oestrogen and progesterone, are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Secondary amenorrhoea after uterine instrumentation (D&C) with entirely normal ovarian and pituitary hormones indicates an outflow-tract cause - intrauterine adhesions/fibrosis, i.e. Asherman syndrome (diagnosed by hysteroscopy). PCOS shows hyperandrogenism and an altered LH:FSH ratio, and POI shows low oestrogen with high FSH/LH.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient has multiple small, pink, umbilicated papules on the face. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Small, dome-shaped, flesh-coloured/pink papules with a central umbilication are pathognomonic of molluscum contagiosum, a poxvirus infection. Herpes simplex causes grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, HPV causes hyperkeratotic warts, and acne produces comedones, papules and pustules - none of which are umbilicated.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the characteristic lesion of Kaposi sarcoma?
options: A white, striated lesion that cannot be scraped off
questions.concept: Kaposi sarcoma (caused by HHV-8, an AIDS-defining malignancy) presents as violaceous, raised purple-red macules, plaques and nodules, the colour reflecting proliferating vessels with extravasated red cells and haemosiderin. A pus-filled yellow lesion is bacterial, and a white non-scrapable striated plaque describes leukoplakia/lichen planus.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A child has accidentally swallowed a bottle of iron tablets. Which drug is the antidote for acute iron poisoning?
questions.concept: Acute iron poisoning is treated with parenteral deferoxamine, a chelator that binds free iron for urinary excretion. Deferiprone is an oral chelator for chronic iron overload (e.g., thalassaemia), DMSA (succimer) chelates lead/arsenic, and luspatercept treats anaemia - none is the antidote for acute iron toxicity.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient with borderline tuberculoid leprosy develops a reaction with a visibly thickened nerve in the neck. Which hypersensitivity type and which enlarged nerve are involved?
questions.concept: A type 1 (reversal) leprosy reaction is a delayed, cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction, and the greater auricular nerve is the classic thickened nerve palpable in the neck. (The type 2 reaction / erythema nodosum leprosum is instead an immune-complex, type III phenomenon.) Hence type IV plus the greater auricular nerve.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A child has multiple vesicular lesions on the palms, soles and oral mucosa. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.concept: Vesicles on the hands, feet and mouth are hand-foot-and-mouth disease, whose prototypical cause is Coxsackievirus A16, making 'Coxsackie virus' the single best answer. Enterovirus 71 (genus Enterovirus, option C) can also cause it, so C is a close distractor; varicella gives a truncal rash and HHV-6 causes roseola.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Oral contraceptive pills protect against all of the following cancers EXCEPT:
questions.concept: Combined OCPs reduce the risk of epithelial ovarian and endometrial cancer (and modestly colorectal cancer) via ovulation suppression and a progestin-dominant endometrium. Prolonged OCP use is instead associated with a slightly increased risk of cervical cancer (facilitating HPV persistence), so cervical cancer is the exception.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient reports recurrent skin lesions that appear within hours each time he takes an NSAID, recurring at the same site. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques that recur at the same site within hours of a specific drug (classically NSAIDs or sulfonamides) and heal with residual hyperpigmentation define a fixed drug eruption. Erythema multiforme shows target lesions without same-site recurrence, and drug-induced pigmentation is persistent rather than acute and recurrent.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient has a severe headache; brain CT shows an abnormality in the basal cisterns (marked 'X'). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A sudden severe ('thunderclap') headache with blood filling the basal cisterns (a star-shaped pattern) on non-contrast CT is a subarachnoid haemorrhage, usually from a ruptured berry aneurysm. NOTE: the source stem describes the lesion as 'hypodense', which is inconsistent - acute subarachnoid blood is HYPERdense (bright); this is almost certainly a PDF/transcription error, so the item is flagged pending review even though SAH is the intended answer. A brain abscess is ring-enhancing and pneumocephalus shows air (very dark) density.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: A sand-mine (silica-exposed) worker has a chest X-ray showing eggshell calcification of the hilar lymph nodes with upper-zone nodular opacities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Chronic inhalation of crystalline silica (sand mining, stone cutting, quarrying) causes silicosis, whose hallmark radiographic sign is eggshell calcification of enlarged hilar nodes with upper-zone nodular fibrosis. Sarcoidosis gives bilateral hilar adenopathy without eggshell calcification, and asbestos causes lower-zone fibrosis with pleural plaques.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: What does a linear accelerator (LINAC) produce for radiation therapy?
questions.concept: A LINAC accelerates electrons to high energy; these electrons can treat superficial tumours directly or strike a target to generate high-energy X-rays (photons) for deep tumours - so it produces X-rays and electrons. Gamma rays come from radioactive isotopes (e.g., cobalt-60), not from a LINAC.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Fetal anaemia is primarily assessed by Doppler of which artery?
questions.concept: Fetal anaemia lowers blood viscosity and raises cardiac output, increasing the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity; an MCA-PSV above 1.5 multiples of the median indicates moderate-to-severe anaemia. Umbilical artery Doppler assesses placental resistance, ductus venosus reflects cardiac compromise (a late sign), and uterine artery Doppler reflects maternal placental perfusion.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, recurrent pregnancy loss
questions.stem: A primigravida has first-trimester vaginal bleeding; ultrasound shows a well-formed gestational sac with an embryo and present fetal cardiac activity. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.concept: First-trimester bleeding with a viable intrauterine pregnancy (sac, embryo and fetal cardiac activity) and a closed cervix is a threatened abortion, which may still continue. Inevitable/incomplete abortion have an open cervix (with a low sac or retained products), and complete abortion shows an empty uterus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: On ultrasound a placental mass is seen invading through the uterine wall into the urinary bladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Placenta percreta is the most severe placenta-accreta-spectrum disorder, in which chorionic villi penetrate through the myometrium and serosa into an adjacent organ - here bladder invasion confirms percreta. Accreta is villi adherent to the myometrium and increta is invasion into (but not through) the myometrium; placenta previa is implantation over the cervical os and does not invade the bladder. (NOTE: the source listed 'placenta previa' twice; the duplicated 4th option has been corrected to the spectrum's missing 'placenta increta', which the source explanation itself defines.)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman has profuse uterine bleeding after a lower-segment caesarean section; oxytocin has been given but bleeding continues. What is the next (first) step of management?
questions.concept: In atonic PPH the stepwise approach is uterotonics, then mechanical uterine balloon tamponade (e.g., Bakri balloon), then surgical vessel ligation, and finally hysterectomy. After oxytocin fails, balloon tamponade is the least invasive, fertility-preserving next step, ahead of embolization, iliac ligation or hysterectomy.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: An investigator compares the mean blood pressure (with standard deviations) between two independent groups. Which statistical test is most appropriate?
questions.concept: Comparing the means of two independent groups of continuous, approximately normal data uses the unpaired (independent-samples) t-test. The paired t-test is for matched/before-after data, chi-square is for categorical associations, and ANOVA compares means of more than two groups.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A CTG shows variable decelerations. What do these indicate?
questions.concept: Variable decelerations are abrupt, variably shaped falls in fetal heart rate caused by transient umbilical cord compression (vagally mediated). Early decelerations mirror contractions and reflect head compression, while late decelerations follow the contraction peak and indicate uteroplacental insufficiency.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: In a face presentation during labour, which fetal head diameter engages?
questions.concept: In a fully extended (face) presentation the engaging diameter is the submentobregmatic (9.5 cm), which allows vaginal delivery when the mentum is anterior. The mentobregmatic (13.5 cm) belongs to a brow presentation, the suboccipitobregmatic to a well-flexed vertex, and the occipitofrontal to a deflexed vertex.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Secondary prevention (early detection and treatment) is most useful for which of the following cancers?
questions.concept: Secondary prevention works best when there is a long detectable preclinical phase and a reliable screening test; cervical cancer fits, with a well-defined precancerous (CIN) stage detectable by Pap smear/HPV testing/VIA. Pancreatic, ovarian and glioblastoma lack effective population screening and have short asymptomatic phases.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: What is the best diagnostic test for evaluating endometrial pathology?
questions.concept: Hysteroscopy-guided biopsy allows direct visualization of the cavity and targeted sampling, giving the highest diagnostic accuracy for both focal and diffuse endometrial lesions. Pipelle and blind D&C can miss focal lesions, and transvaginal sonography measures endometrial thickness but cannot provide histology. (Some sources still favour Pipelle/D&C for diffuse disease, so confidence is moderate.)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: In which of the following is an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) an absolute contraindication?
questions.concept: Among these options only HIV/AIDS can contraindicate an IUCD - active, symptomatic AIDS with immunosuppression raises the risk of ascending pelvic infection (WHO MEC category 3-4). Hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and diabetes are not contraindications to a copper IUCD. (NOTE: under current WHO MEC, HIV that is well controlled on ART is only category 2, so 'HIV' is the intended best answer among these choices rather than an absolute rule - hence moderate confidence.)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: Which occupational exposure is most strongly associated with mesothelioma?
questions.concept: Asbestos fibres (especially crocidolite) lodge in the pleura and, after a long latency (20-40 years), cause malignant mesothelioma - the tumour most specifically linked to asbestos. Silica causes silicosis, cotton dust byssinosis and coal dust coal-workers' pneumoconiosis, none of which is strongly linked to mesothelioma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl has Tanner stage II breast development and a white, odourless vaginal discharge. This discharge is most likely due to which hormone?
questions.concept: Rising oestrogen in early puberty makes the vaginal epithelium proliferate and produce glycogen, which lactobacilli convert to lactic acid, giving a normal white, odourless physiological leukorrhoea. GnRH and inhibin B act on the pituitary/gonadal axis without directly producing this discharge (and 'B-Lynch suture' is a surgical technique - an erroneous distractor).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 36-year-old P2L2 woman with severe recurrent endometriosis and pelvic adhesions (prior tubal ligation and adhesiolysis) is undergoing laparoscopy. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.concept: As the patient has completed childbearing and has severe recurrent disease, the definitive treatment is total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, removing both the disease and the ovarian oestrogen that drives recurrence. Observation ignores symptomatic disease, hysterectomy alone leaves oestrogen-producing ovaries, and oophorectomy alone leaves uterine disease untreated.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A woman has a breast lump with skin dimpling and nipple retraction. Which structure is most responsible for the skin dimpling?
questions.concept: Malignant infiltration and fibrosis shorten the suspensory (Cooper's) ligaments, which run from the dermis to the pectoral fascia, tethering and puckering the overlying skin (dimpling). Lactiferous duct involvement causes nipple retraction, and pectoral fascia involvement fixes the breast to the chest wall rather than dimpling the skin.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A long-term study found that individuals who had high blood pressure (BP) during childhood continued to have high BP in adulthood, and those with low BP in childhood tended to maintain lower levels later in life. Which epidemiological concept does this pattern best represent?
questions.concept: Tracking describes the tendency of an individual to keep their relative rank within a population distribution over time, so a child at the high end of BP stays high as an adult. It differs from regression to the mean (extreme values drifting toward the average on re-measurement) and the cohort effect (differences between people born in different periods).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: In the image shown, identify the function of the marked structure on the endotracheal tube.
options: Prevention of air leakage and aspiration
Suctioning of lower respiratory tract secretions
questions.concept: The marked structure is the inflatable cuff of the endotracheal tube; when inflated it seals the tube against the tracheal wall, preventing air leak during positive-pressure ventilation and reducing aspiration of upper-airway secretions. Cuff pressure is kept around 20-30 cm H2O to avoid tracheal mucosal ischaemia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, recurrent pregnancy loss
questions.stem: After an initial serum β-hCG test in a patient with suspected pregnancy, when should the repeat β-hCG level ideally be checked to assess viability or progression?
questions.concept: Serum β-hCG is repeated at 48 hours because a normal early intrauterine pregnancy shows a rise of at least about 66% over that interval; a sub-optimal rise or plateau suggests an ectopic or failing pregnancy. The discriminatory zone (level above which a sac should be seen on TVS) is roughly 1500 IU/L.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, recurrent pregnancy loss
questions.stem: A pregnant woman with a short cervix undergoes a cervical cerclage procedure. What is the most likely procedure performed?
questions.concept: The McDonald cerclage, a purse-string non-absorbable suture at the cervicovaginal junction, is by far the most commonly performed cerclage for cervical insufficiency. NOTE: the scraped key said D (Modified Shirodkar), but the question asks for the 'most likely/most commonly performed' technique, which is McDonald's; the Shirodkar variants (higher placement after bladder dissection) are reserved for when a higher, stronger cerclage is needed, so this recall/key appears unreliable.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman comes for emergency contraception within 8 hours after sexual intercourse. She prefers a single pill rather than multiple pills. What would you recommend?
questions.concept: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg as a single dose is the preferred progestin-only emergency contraceptive within 72 hours of unprotected sex; being estrogen-free it avoids the nausea and vomiting of the estrogen-containing Yuzpe regimen and suits her wish for a single pill, whereas levonorgestrel 0.75 mg needs two doses.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A patient presents with obstructed labor, and on abdominal examination a groove or band is palpable across the uterus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A palpable transverse groove across the uterus in obstructed labour is Bandl's ring, a pathological retraction ring rising between the actively contracting upper segment and the thinned, over-stretched lower segment; it signals impending uterine rupture and mandates urgent delivery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 2-month-old male infant has a scrotal swelling present since birth that has suddenly become painful, red, and irreducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A congenital (since-birth) inguinoscrotal swelling that turns irreducible, red and painful indicates a strangulated inguinal hernia, where trapped bowel has lost its blood supply - a surgical emergency. An incarcerated hernia is irreducible but still viable, without redness or severe tenderness.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A patient underwent split-thickness skin grafting for a burn injury on the arm. On post-operative day 6 he develops stiffness of the arm during physiotherapy. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Passive extension of the joint under direct visualization of the graft
Remove the graft and regraft the area
questions.concept: On post-op day 6 a split-thickness graft is still only loosely adherent during early revascularisation, so joint stiffness should be addressed by gentle passive extension under direct visualisation of the graft to avoid shearing it off. Contracture excision or regrafting are not indicated this early.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman is being assessed for induction of labor. On vaginal examination: dilation 2 cm, effacement 20%, consistency soft, position midline, station -2. What is the modified Bishop Score?
questions.concept: Modified Bishop score here = dilation 2 cm (1) + effacement 20% (0) + station -2 (1) + soft consistency (2) + mid position (1) = 5, which is unfavourable, so cervical ripening is needed before oxytocin induction. (The source's per-line breakdown was garbled, but the total of 5 is correct.)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which of the following is a recommended treatment for esophageal varices?
questions.concept: Endoscopic variceal band ligation is first-line for both acute bleeding oesophageal varices and secondary prophylaxis, obliterating varices with fewer complications than sclerotherapy. TIPS is salvage therapy for uncontrolled bleeding, and prophylaxis uses non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol/nadolol), not labetalol.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: During the management of shoulder dystocia in childbirth, which of the following is the earliest/first maneuver typically attempted?
questions.concept: The McRoberts manoeuvre (hyperflexion of the maternal thighs onto the abdomen) is the first step in shoulder dystocia; it flattens the lumbosacral angle and rotates the symphysis to free the impacted anterior shoulder, followed if needed by suprapubic pressure and rotational manoeuvres.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: OCPs can be given in which of the following conditions?
questions.concept: HIV infection is not a contraindication to combined OCPs (though interactions with some antiretrovirals may reduce efficacy). Uncontrolled hypertension, diabetes with vascular complications, and hyperlipidaemia are the estrogen-related contraindications because of increased thromboembolic and cardiovascular risk.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman sustains a perineal tear during delivery. Examination reveals that less than 50% of the external anal sphincter is involved. What is the most appropriate description of this injury?
questions.concept: A third-degree perineal tear involves the anal sphincter complex; grade 3a means less than 50% of external anal sphincter thickness is torn, 3b more than 50%, and 3c both external and internal sphincters. Second degree spares the sphincter and fourth degree also breaches the anal epithelium.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 46-year-old man has a tumor in the left lobe of the liver, so a left hemihepatectomy is planned. Which of the following segments will be resected?
questions.concept: By Couinaud's functional anatomy the left hemiliver comprises segments II, III and IV, so a left hemihepatectomy resects segments II-IV. Segments V-VIII form the right hemiliver, and segment I (caudate lobe) is functionally separate and not routinely removed.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: What is the correct sequence of damage control surgery? 1. Patient selection 2. Primary exploration 3. ICU care 4. Secondary exploration
questions.concept: Damage-control surgery runs in order: patient selection (identify the unstable, acidotic, coagulopathic, hypothermic patient), abbreviated primary exploration to control haemorrhage and contamination, ICU resuscitation to reverse the lethal triad, then definitive secondary exploration once stable - sequence 1-2-3-4.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl has developed breast and pubic hair. The mother wants to know which sign of puberty will typically occur next.
questions.concept: In the female pubertal sequence (thelarche then pubarche then peak height velocity then menarche), a girl who already has breasts and pubic hair will next reach her peak height velocity, which precedes menarche by roughly a year.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 12-year-old raised as a girl presents with primary amenorrhea. She has not developed breast tissue, ultrasound shows absence of the uterus, and karyotyping shows a 46,XY pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A 46,XY phenotypic girl with primary amenorrhoea, an absent uterus AND absent breast development points to 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency: functioning testes make AMH (no uterus) but the enzyme block halts both androgen and estrogen synthesis (no breasts), typically with hypertension and hypokalaemia. AIS would have breasts (androgens aromatized to estrogen) and Swyer's would have a uterus (streak gonads, no AMH).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate treatment for an 8 cm chylolymphatic mesenteric cyst?
options: Resection of the cyst along with the adjacent bowel
questions.concept: A chylolymphatic mesenteric cyst has its own blood supply independent of the bowel, so complete enucleation with bowel preservation is the treatment of choice. Bowel resection with anastomosis is needed only for enterogenous cysts that share the bowel's vasculature; aspiration or observation risk recurrence, infection, torsion or rupture.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: During assisted vaginal delivery, where is the vacuum device typically applied?
options: At 3 cm behind the anterior fontanelle
3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle
Between the anterior and posterior fontanelle
questions.concept: The vacuum cup is placed over the flexion point, about 3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle along the sagittal suture, so that traction flexes the fetal head and presents the smallest (suboccipitobregmatic) diameter, improving success and minimizing trauma.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for laparoscopic surgery under general anesthesia in a day-care setting. Which of the following factors makes him unsuitable for day-care surgery?
options: Home is 45 minutes away from the hospital
The surgical procedure is expected to last slightly over 1 hour
No attendant is available at home to care for the patient postoperatively
The patient has had general anesthesia in the past without complications
questions.concept: Day-care surgery under general anaesthesia requires a responsible adult to escort the patient home and supervise them for about 24 hours, since residual sedation impairs judgement and coordination. Lack of an attendant makes discharge unsafe; a 45-minute distance, a procedure just over an hour, and prior uneventful GA are all acceptable.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: What is the co-test in cervical cancer screening?
questions.concept: Co-testing in cervical cancer screening combines HPV DNA testing with the Pap smear (cytology); together they raise sensitivity, allowing 5-yearly screening in women aged 30-65 when negative. VIA is a low-resource alternative and colposcopy is a diagnostic follow-up, not a primary screening test.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which of the following is a contraindication to a subcutaneous contraceptive implant?
questions.concept: Undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding is a WHO MEC Category 4 (unacceptable risk) contraindication to a progestin implant because inserting it could mask endometrial or cervical pathology; the cause must be worked up first. Controlled hypertension, diabetes and PID are not contraindications to a progestin-only implant.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant pain 4 days after cholecystectomy. USG shows a significant collection in the RUQ. What will you do next?
questions.concept: A symptomatic RUQ collection a few days after cholecystectomy is first managed by ultrasound-guided aspiration, which both drains it and characterizes the fluid (bile, pus or blood); if bile is found, MRCP/ERCP is then used to map and treat the leak. Aspiration is preferred over blind antibiotics or re-exploration in a stable patient.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: During general anesthesia, which nerve is commonly monitored using a nerve stimulator to assess neuromuscular blockade?
questions.concept: Neuromuscular blockade is monitored by stimulating the ulnar nerve at the wrist and observing adductor pollicis twitches; the nerve is superficial and gives a clear, reproducible response, making it the standard site to gauge depth of block and adequacy of reversal.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A patient with a previous cesarean section is in labor with contractions 3/10, no fetal distress and intact membranes. What is the next step in management?
options: Perform artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) and monitor
questions.concept: In a woman attempting VBAC/TOLAC who is progressing with intact membranes and no fetal distress, artificial rupture of membranes with continued monitoring is the safer way to augment labour; oxytocin raises the risk of scar rupture, and instrumental or repeat caesarean delivery are not yet indicated in a stable second-trimester-of-labour picture.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: A patient under anesthesia is found to be in a cannot-intubate-cannot-ventilate (CICV) scenario. What is the next best step in management?
questions.concept: In a cannot-intubate-cannot-ventilate emergency an immediate surgical airway is required; cricothyroidotomy is the fastest and most accessible option (incision through the cricothyroid membrane) and is preferred over the slower tracheostomy. An NPA is only an adjunct and an LMA has already failed by this point.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A follow-up patient with GERD is found on endoscopy to have a nodule in the 2nd part of the duodenum. Which hormone do you suspect to be raised?
questions.concept: A duodenal (second-part) nodule with refractory acid-peptic/GERD symptoms suggests a gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) secreting gastrin, which drives marked acid hypersecretion. VIP (VIPoma) and glucagon (glucagonoma) cause different syndromes, and inulin is not a hormone (it is a GFR marker).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A patient undergoing surgery develops sudden deranged vitals following a failed attempt at subclavian vein catheterization. The trachea is shifted to one side and breath sounds are absent on the same side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Sudden deterioration with tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds after a failed subclavian puncture is a tension pneumothorax; a one-way air leak collapses the lung and shifts the mediastinum, dropping venous return and causing hypotension. It is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate decompression.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A neonate has intestines protruding from the abdomen without any external covering. What is the next line of management?
options: Cover the content with a Silo bag and wait
questions.concept: Bowel protruding with no covering membrane is gastroschisis; when the abdominal cavity is too small for the oedematous bowel, the viscera are placed in a sterile silo and reduced in stages over several days before closure, avoiding abdominal compartment syndrome. (Omphalocele differs by having a peritoneal-amniotic sac.)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the ER 6 hours after a burn, with 22% BSA burns. On examination: cool extremities, BP 92/50 mmHg, PR 56 bpm, urine output since the burn 30 mL. What is the next step in management?
questions.concept: This child with over 15% BSA burns and shock (hypotension, cool peripheries, low urine output and ominous bradycardia) needs an urgent crystalloid (Ringer's lactate) bolus, about 10 mL/kg, before calculated Parkland resuscitation; colloids are avoided in the first 24 hours because of capillary leak, and a 30 mL/kg bolus risks fluid overload. (The bolus wording in the recall is imprecise.)

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: After a road traffic accident, a patient has severe maxillofacial trauma with SpO2 80% on room air and cannot be intubated or ventilated. What is your immediate step?
options: Do suction and again try intubation
questions.concept: Severe maxillofacial trauma with a cannot-intubate-cannot-ventilate state and desaturation is an indication for an emergency surgical airway; cricothyrotomy provides oxygenation within seconds and is preferred over the slower tracheostomy or re-attempting intubation in a rapidly desaturating patient.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy presents with right testicular pain 2 hours after being hit by a cricket ball. On examination there is severe testicular pain and an absent cremasteric reflex. What is the next step?
questions.concept: Acute severe testicular pain with an absent cremasteric reflex is testicular torsion until excluded. Colour Doppler US (arterial flow) is the first-line investigation when the diagnosis is uncertain, showing reduced/absent intratesticular flow. NOTE: the scraped key A (arterial Doppler) is defensible here given the trauma history, but with classic torsion signs many guidelines advise immediate surgical exploration (option D) without delaying for imaging - hence flagged as genuinely ambiguous.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with recurrent abdominal pain and blood in his stools. He has darkly pigmented spots on his lips and oral mucosa, and endoscopy reveals multiple hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Mucocutaneous pigmentation of the lips and oral mucosa with GI bleeding and hamartomatous small-bowel polyps is Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (autosomal dominant, STK11/LKB1 mutation), which raises the risk of GI, breast and gonadal cancers and commonly presents with intussusception. FAP instead has numerous adenomatous polyps without pigmentation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the ER with penetrating chest trauma. On examination there is severe tracheal deviation. What is the immediate step of management?
questions.concept: Penetrating chest trauma with marked tracheal deviation is a tension pneumothorax; treatment is immediate needle decompression with a large-bore cannula (classically 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line, or 5th ICS mid-axillary line) followed by chest-drain insertion - never delayed for a chest X-ray or E-FAST.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A young adult presents with a fracture of the neck of the femur. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.concept: In a young adult a femoral neck fracture is managed by urgent anatomical reduction and internal fixation to preserve the native femoral head and reduce avascular necrosis and non-union; arthroplasty (hemi or total) is reserved for elderly or low-demand patients with displaced fractures.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A patient presents with a ring-shaped (lytic) lesion in the bone. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A well-defined lytic lesion surrounded by a thick sclerotic rim (ring-like) in a long-bone metaphysis is a Brodie's abscess, a walled-off subacute osteomyelitis that classically causes night pain relieved by NSAIDs. Simple and aneurysmal bone cysts lack that dense reactive sclerotic rim.

questions.subject: Surgery
