questions.stem: A child comes in after a train accident with stable vitals but a large laceration on the leg. Which triage category does the patient fall under?
questions.concept: In mass-casualty triage a patient with a serious but non-life-threatening injury and stable vitals (here a large but stable leg laceration) is tagged Yellow (delayed), treated after Red/immediate cases. Red is for immediate life threats, Green for minor/walking wounded, and Black for expectant/deceased.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A 2-week-old infant is brought to hospital. The parents report a single fall, but X-ray reveals multiple fractures at different stages of healing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Multiple fractures at different stages of healing with a history that does not fit the injuries is the hallmark of non-accidental injury (battered baby syndrome); metaphyseal corner (bucket-handle) and posterior rib fractures are especially suggestive. Osteogenesis imperfecta would show blue sclerae and a consistent minimal-trauma history.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which of the following veins is involved in the formation of esophageal varices?
questions.concept: Oesophageal varices form at the porto-systemic anastomosis where the left gastric (coronary) vein of the portal system meets the oesophageal veins draining to the azygos/SVC; portal hypertension engorges this channel. The right gastric and gastroepiploic veins drain elsewhere and are not the key contributors.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: An elderly woman involved in a road traffic accident presents with difficulty breathing and altered mental status. D-dimer is elevated and X-ray findings are suggestive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Respiratory distress with altered mental status developing after a road-traffic long-bone injury is fat embolism syndrome - marrow fat reaches the lungs and brain, producing hypoxia, neurological signs and often petechiae, with ARDS-like patchy infiltrates on chest X-ray. D-dimer is non-specific; the neurological features and fracture context favour fat embolism over pulmonary embolism.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant is brought for a routine check-up. Which of the following developmental milestones is most likely to be present at this age?
options: Creeps well on hands and knees
questions.concept: By around 9 months an infant is creeping/crawling on hands and knees (and pulling to stand), so this is the expected milestone here. A mature pincer grasp (about 12 months), hopping on one foot (about 4 years) and running steadily (about 2 years) all appear later.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A doctor receives two summons, one to appear in court in a murder case and another to provide expert medical opinion. Which of the following should the doctor prioritise?
options: Appearance for providing medical expert opinion
questions.concept: When a doctor holds two summonses at once, the one from the higher/criminal court takes precedence; a Sessions Court summons in a murder trial therefore outranks a request merely to furnish an expert opinion. Timing of receipt does not override the legal gravity of the criminal-case summons.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 30-year-old man came with choking episodes after ingestion of fish bone while eating. The fishbone got impacted at the level of T4 in the esophagus. Which is the most likely site of obstruction?
questions.concept: The oesophagus has four normal constrictions; at the T4 vertebral level it is indented by the arch of the aorta (~22.5 cm from the incisors), the most likely site for an impacted foreign body here. Cricopharyngeus lies at C6, the left main bronchus at T4/T6 and the diaphragmatic hiatus at T10.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A man fell on his shoulder with his head pushed to the opposite side and presented with the affected upper limb hanging adducted and medially rotated, the forearm pronated (waiter's tip posture). Which nerve root values are most likely affected?
questions.concept: A fall driving the shoulder down while the head is forced to the opposite side stretches the upper trunk (C5-C6) of the brachial plexus, producing Erb-Duchenne palsy with the classic 'waiter's tip' posture. C8-T1 (lower trunk) injury instead gives Klumpke's palsy with hand-muscle weakness.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: In an embryo, an arrow points to the notochord (the rod-like midline structure lying ventral to the neural tube). Which adult structure is formed from it?
questions.concept: The notochord is the midline embryonic axial rod that induces neural-tube formation and persists in the adult only as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc. The annulus fibrosus arises from sclerotome (mesoderm), and the neural tube forms from ectoderm induced by the notochord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A diabetic worker sustains a stab injury to the central region of his palm. After 3 days, he develops swelling, severe pain, and inability to extend his middle and ring fingers. Pus accumulation is suspected in one of the palmar spaces. Which of the following spaces is most likely involved?
questions.concept: A deep central-palm injury tracking to the midpalmar space involves the medial (3rd-4th) digital compartment, causing swelling and loss of extension of the middle and ring fingers. The thenar space instead relates to the index finger and thumb. (Options relabelled from the original figure using the source key.)

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: Which is the narrowest part of the adult laryngeal airway?
questions.concept: In the adult larynx the narrowest part is the glottis (rima glottidis, between the true vocal cords); in children the narrowest part is instead the subglottis at the cricoid cartilage.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Lower limb: femoral/sciatic nerve, foot drop
questions.stem: A man sustained trauma on the lateral side of his right knee. Two days later, he complains of difficulty in walking, as his toes keep dragging on the ground. He also notices numbness over the upper lateral aspect of the leg and dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.concept: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve is superficial at the neck of the fibula on the lateral knee, so trauma there causes foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion/eversion) with sensory loss over the upper lateral leg and dorsum of the foot. The deep peroneal branch alone would not explain the wider lateral-leg sensory loss.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A young patient experiences shortness of breath specifically during exercise in winter, which subsides after using salbutamol. What is the most likely explanation for this condition?
options: Vagal stimulation due to cold air exposure
Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction triggered by cold air
Airway hyperreactivity due to cold-induced asthma exacerbation
questions.concept: Exercise in cold, dry air causes airway heat/water loss and hyper-reactivity, triggering exercise-induced bronchoconstriction that reverses with an inhaled beta-2 agonist such as salbutamol. Exercise is the specific trigger here, distinguishing it from a general asthma exacerbation (option D is close but not exercise-specific).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: During an explosion, a patient sustains a crushed lower limb injury by collapse of a building. What type of blast injury does this represent?
questions.concept: Blast injuries: primary = pressure-wave barotrauma (ear, lung, gut); secondary = penetrating trauma from flying debris; tertiary = victim thrown by the blast wind; quaternary = miscellaneous effects including crush injury from structural/building collapse (as here), burns and toxic inhalation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: The upper part of the uncinate process commonly attaches to?
questions.concept: The uncinate process is a hook-shaped ethmoid bony leaflet of the lateral nasal wall whose upper end most commonly attaches to the middle turbinate; with the ethmoid bulla it bounds the hiatus semilunaris of the middle meatus. (Its superior attachment is variable, but the middle turbinate is the textbook answer.)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: In a diagram of a neuronal action potential, step 3 is the falling phase in which the membrane potential returns from its peak back toward the resting level. What best describes step 3?
options: Resting membrane potential is maintained by the Na-K pump
questions.concept: Repolarisation (the falling phase of the action potential) is produced by opening of voltage-gated K+ channels causing K+ efflux, which returns the membrane potential toward rest after the Na+ channels have inactivated. Na+ influx drives depolarisation, not this phase.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A child is brought to the hospital with pinpoint pupils and difficulty breathing after playing at home. What is the most likely substance the child accidentally ingested?
questions.concept: Miosis (pinpoint pupils) with respiratory depression and no muscarinic secretions is the classic opioid toxidrome, reversed by naloxone. NOTE: organophosphate poisoning is the key differential (also causes miosis plus respiratory distress) but is distinguished by prominent SLUDGE secretions, sweating and fasciculations, which are not described here.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Lower limb: femoral/sciatic nerve, foot drop
questions.stem: A patient presents with dilated, tortuous superficial veins running up the medial side of the leg and thigh. Which vein is mainly affected?
questions.concept: Varicose veins tracking up the medial leg and thigh follow the great saphenous vein, the long superficial vein running anterior to the medial malleolus and draining into the femoral vein; valve incompetence here is the commonest cause of varicosities. The short saphenous vein runs posteriorly and the femoral vein is deep.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: An alcoholic patient is admitted to the hospital 48 hours after his last drink. He presents with altered consciousness, disorientation, and severe agitation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Delirium tremens is the most severe alcohol-withdrawal state, appearing 48-72 h after the last drink with clouded consciousness, disorientation, severe agitation and autonomic instability; it is a medical emergency treated with benzodiazepines and thiamine. Korsakoff psychosis is a chronic amnestic syndrome, not this acute picture.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which among the following hormones, in a lactating mother, is responsible for the growth of breast tissue?
questions.concept: In a lactating mother prolactin drives lobuloalveolar growth of breast tissue and milk synthesis, while oxytocin causes milk ejection. NOTE: estrogen (ductal growth) and progesterone (alveolar growth) also enlarge the breast, but the lactation-specific answer intended here is prolactin.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A patient presented to OPD with ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. Diagnosis of superior orbital fissure syndrome was confirmed after examination. Which nerves are compressed in this case?
questions.concept: The superior orbital fissure transmits cranial nerves III, IV, V1 (ophthalmic) and VI plus the ophthalmic veins; a lesion here gives ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. The optic nerve (II) passes the optic canal and the maxillary nerve (V2) the foramen rotundum, so neither traverses the fissure.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A deceased woman was sent for an autopsy. She was found dead in a locked room with a heat stove still running. What is the most likely cause of death?
questions.concept: A body found in a closed room with a running fuel stove points to carbon monoxide poisoning from incomplete combustion; CO binds haemoglobin ~200-250x more avidly than oxygen, causing tissue hypoxia despite a normal PaO2 and the classic cherry-red post-mortem lividity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A 35-year-old man wakes up after sleeping with his arm draped over a chair and complains of pain. Which of the following accurately describes the order of susceptibility of nerve fibers in the given condition?
questions.concept: This is a pressure (compression) palsy. Nerve fibres are affected by pressure in the order A > B > C, because large myelinated (A) fibres are most vulnerable to pressure and hypoxia; local anaesthetics, by contrast, block the small fibres (C, B) first.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Lower limb: femoral/sciatic nerve, foot drop
questions.stem: The artery that is palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon is?
questions.concept: The posterior tibial artery is palpated behind and below the medial malleolus, between it and the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon, where it runs deep to the flexor retinaculum (mnemonic Tom-Dick-ANd-Harry). The dorsalis pedis is felt on the dorsum of the foot.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A woman from Delhi travels to Ladakh, a high-altitude region. Soon after arrival, she develops symptoms such as breathlessness, headache, and lightheadedness. What is the primary underlying mechanism responsible for her symptoms?
questions.concept: At high altitude the low ambient oxygen stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors to hyperventilate, washing out CO2 and raising blood pH, so the initial acid-base disturbance of acute mountain sickness is respiratory alkalosis (later compensated by renal bicarbonate excretion).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: After the parotidectomy operation, a patient presents with excessive sweating and redness over the parotid region. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating and facial flushing over the parotid region on eating) follows parotidectomy when the injured auriculotemporal nerve regenerates aberrantly, wiring parasympathetic salivary fibres to the skin's sweat glands. Horner's syndrome instead causes loss (not excess) of sweating.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A patient with colorectal carcinoma has a strong family history of Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC). Which DNA repair mechanism is most likely defective in this condition?
questions.concept: HNPCC (Lynch syndrome) is caused by defective DNA mismatch repair (commonly MLH1/MSH2 mutations), producing microsatellite instability and colorectal cancer. Nucleotide-excision-repair defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum, and double-strand-break repair defects link to BRCA-associated cancers.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: In malignant hyperthermia, a genetic mutation in the ryanodine receptor (RYR1) leads to a life-threatening reaction to certain anesthetic agents. What is the primary ionic abnormality caused by this receptor defect?
options: Increased sodium influx into the muscle cell
Increased potassium uptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Increased chloride efflux from the muscle cell
Increased calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.concept: In malignant hyperthermia a mutated RYR1 ryanodine receptor, triggered by volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine, causes massive Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, producing sustained muscle contraction, rigidity and a hypermetabolic crisis (hyperthermia, hypercapnia, rhabdomyolysis).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A man presents with high VLDL and chylomicrons, with eruptive xanthomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Markedly raised VLDL and chylomicrons with eruptive xanthomas indicate severe hypertriglyceridaemia (familial hypertriglyceridaemia), which carries a pancreatitis risk. Familial hypercholesterolaemia instead raises LDL with tendon xanthomas, and dysbetalipoproteinaemia raises IDL/remnants.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: What is the primary protein that binds to thyroxine?
questions.concept: Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) is the principal, highest-affinity plasma carrier of thyroid hormones and transports the majority of circulating T4/T3; transthyretin (prealbumin) and albumin carry smaller fractions.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which opportunistic pathogen demonstrates a "crushed ping pong ball appearance" on Gomori methenamine stain?
questions.concept: Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts show a 'crushed ping-pong ball' (also cup-and-saucer/helmet) appearance on Gomori methenamine silver stain and cause pneumonia in the immunocompromised (e.g. HIV with CD4 <200); treatment is co-trimoxazole.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which antibody is the first to appear and acts fastest during a primary (first) immune response to an infection?
questions.concept: IgM is the first antibody produced in the primary immune response; as a pentamer with 10 binding sites it has high avidity and activates the classical complement pathway efficiently, even before affinity maturation. IgG dominates the secondary response.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A breastfed infant presents with lethargy, hepatomegaly, and cataracts. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.concept: Classic galactosemia is deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT); toxic galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol accumulate after milk feeds, so a breastfed infant develops lethargy, hepatomegaly, jaundice and cataracts. Galactokinase deficiency gives isolated cataracts without severe liver disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which vitamin deficiency can lead to lactic acidosis?
questions.concept: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is the cofactor of pyruvate dehydrogenase; in deficiency pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle and is diverted to lactate, producing lactic acidosis (seen with beriberi and Wernicke's encephalopathy).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which among the following best describes 'Neuropraxia'?
questions.concept: Neurapraxia is the mildest (Seddon grade I) nerve injury: a temporary conduction block from focal myelin/sheath damage with the axon intact and no Wallerian degeneration, so recovery is complete. Axonotmesis damages the axon, and neurotmesis disrupts the whole nerve.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the immortality of cancer cells?
questions.concept: Telomerase rebuilds the telomeres that normally shorten with each division; its reactivation/over-expression in cancer cells lets them bypass replicative senescence and divide indefinitely ('immortality').

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A subject was brought to the Casualty with a history of RTA and head injury. On examination, he was conscious. When the doctor asked questions about the incident, his answers were irrelevant to the questions, but his speech was fluent. What could be the possible site of injury?
questions.concept: Fluent but meaningless (irrelevant) speech with impaired comprehension in a conscious patient is receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia, localising to the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. The inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area) instead gives non-fluent aphasia with preserved comprehension.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient presents with fatigue, anemia, and hepatomegaly. Hemoglobin electrophoresis reveals the presence of HbS. What will be the appropriate treatment?
questions.concept: HbS on electrophoresis indicates sickle cell anaemia; hydroxyurea is the mainstay disease-modifying therapy because it raises fetal haemoglobin (HbF), reducing sickling and vaso-occlusive crises. Transfusion is reserved for severe crises, and iron/B12 are not specific treatments.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Tau protein inclusions are involved in:
questions.concept: Alzheimer's disease is characterised by intraneuronal neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau protein together with extracellular amyloid-beta plaques. Huntington's involves mutant huntingtin, and ALS involves SOD1/TDP-43, not tau.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: As a neuron's diameter increases, what effect manifests?
questions.concept: Increasing axon diameter lowers internal (axial) resistance, letting local currents spread faster along the fibre, so conduction velocity increases. Action-potential amplitude is set by ion-channel and equilibrium-potential properties, not diameter.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Cell injury, adaptation, necrosis vs apoptosis
questions.stem: Which of the following acts as a major intracellular antioxidant and helps in detoxifying reactive oxygen species?
questions.concept: Glutathione is the major intracellular antioxidant (a glutamate-cysteine-glycine tripeptide) that neutralises reactive oxygen species by donating electrons and helps regenerate vitamins C and E. SOD, catalase and peroxidases are the antioxidant enzymes that act on specific radicals.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which of the following genetic mutations is most commonly associated with familial cases of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)?
questions.concept: Familial (inherited) ALS is most often caused by an autosomal-dominant SOD1 (superoxide dismutase 1) mutation acting through a toxic gain of function that kills motor neurons. CFTR causes cystic fibrosis, HTT Huntington's disease and FMR1 fragile X syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 7-year-old child is brought to the clinic with complaints of fatigue and poor concentration. The mother reports that the child has been eating non-food items such as chalk and soil for the past few months. A peripheral blood smear shows microcytic, hypochromic red blood cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Pica (craving non-food items such as chalk and soil) with a microcytic, hypochromic blood picture in a child indicates iron deficiency anaemia; it is confirmed by low ferritin and raised TIBC and treated with oral iron. B12 deficiency causes macrocytic (not microcytic) anaemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is brought to the clinic with abdominal pain, irritability, and developmental delay. On examination, the child has pallor and a bluish line on the gums. Laboratory tests reveal microcytic anemia, and a peripheral blood smear shows red blood cells with basophilic stippling. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Abdominal pain, developmental delay, a bluish gingival (Burton) line and microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling indicate lead poisoning; manage by removing exposure and chelation (e.g. EDTA). Iron deficiency lacks stippling and the Burton line.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: For testing blood clotting/coagulation parameters, blood is collected in which color-coded vacutainer tube?
questions.concept: Coagulation studies (PT, aPTT) use the light-blue-topped vacutainer containing sodium citrate, which reversibly chelates calcium and preserves the clotting factors. Lavender/EDTA is for CBC and grey/fluoride for glucose.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a village of Assam, a man is observed walking with the help of a stick and has genu valgum. Many people in the same village present with similar symptoms. What is the most probable cause of this condition?
questions.concept: Genu valgum and skeletal deformity clustering in many villagers of a high-fluoride region (e.g. Assam) indicate endemic skeletal fluorosis from chronic fluoride in drinking water (osteosclerosis on X-ray, seen at 3-6 mg/L); it is prevented by defluoridation/safe water. Community clustering argues against isolated nutritional deficiency.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Cell injury, adaptation, necrosis vs apoptosis
questions.stem: Which of the following is pro-apoptotic?
questions.concept: In the Bcl-2 family, Bax (with Bak) is pro-apoptotic, permeabilising the mitochondrial outer membrane to release cytochrome c, whereas Bcl-2, Bcl-xL and Mcl-1 are anti-apoptotic and preserve mitochondrial membrane integrity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A young boy presents with joint swelling after a fall. Lab investigations show normal PT and raised aPTT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Haemarthrosis after minor trauma with a normal PT but prolonged aPTT points to haemophilia (intrinsic-pathway factor VIII or IX deficiency). Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding, and platelet disorders cause petechiae with usually normal PT/aPTT.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with tremors, difficulty in speech, and behavioral changes. On examination, he has hepatomegaly and a golden-brown ring at the limbus of the cornea (Kayser-Fleischer ring). Wilson's disease is suspected. Which of the following is the best investigation to support the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Wilson's disease is confirmed most specifically by quantitative hepatic copper on liver biopsy (the gold standard, >250 ug/g dry weight). NOTE: low serum ceruloplasmin is the best initial screening test and 24-h urinary copper is raised, but liver-biopsy copper is the definitive confirmatory investigation.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A family that consumes a diet predominantly of rice and pulses developed signs of muscle weakness and impaired movement. Which of the following should be given for prophylaxis?
questions.concept: A diet of only polished rice and pulses lacks thiamine (removed with the aleurone layer on polishing), causing dry beriberi with peripheral neuropathy and muscle weakness; prophylaxis and treatment is thiamine (vitamin B1).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with lethargy, vomiting, and poor feeding. The episode occurred after prolonged fasting. Laboratory results reveal hypoglycemia, low ketone levels (hypoketosis), and mild hepatomegaly. These findings suggest a defect in fat metabolism. Which of the following is the most likely underlying disorder?
options: Glycogen storage disease type I (Von Gierke disease)
questions.concept: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with hepatomegaly precipitated by prolonged fasting in an infant indicates a fatty-acid beta-oxidation defect, most commonly medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency; ketones are low because fat cannot be used for energy. Von Gierke disease instead shows lactic acidosis with normal/high ketones.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant presents with poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy. Laboratory studies show hyperammonemia and elevated levels of orotic acid in the urine. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme deficiency?
questions.concept: Hyperammonemia with elevated urinary orotic acid (and normal citrulline) indicates X-linked ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency; the blocked urea cycle diverts accumulated carbamoyl phosphate into pyrimidine synthesis, raising orotic acid. CPS-I deficiency has normal orotic acid; argininosuccinate lyase deficiency raises citrulline.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which CD markers are typically positive in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL)?
questions.concept: CLL is a mature B-cell neoplasm expressing B-cell markers CD19, CD20 and CD23 with aberrant co-expression of the T-cell marker CD5, the key diagnostic immunophenotype. CD10/CD19/CD22 suggests precursor B-ALL, and CD13/CD33/CD117 are myeloid (AML) markers.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 2-year-old with fever, lymphadenopathy and biopsy showing hallmark cells is diagnosed with anaplastic large cell lymphoma. Most likely translocation?
questions.concept: Anaplastic large cell lymphoma characteristically carries the t(2;5) translocation creating the NPM-ALK fusion, which constitutively activates ALK tyrosine kinase; biopsy shows hallmark cells with horseshoe/kidney-shaped nuclei. t(8;14) is Burkitt, t(14;18) follicular lymphoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Cell injury, adaptation, necrosis vs apoptosis
questions.stem: In Barrett's oesophagus, which of the following epithelial transformations occurs?
questions.concept: Barrett's oesophagus is a complication of chronic GERD in which the distal oesophageal stratified squamous epithelium undergoes intestinal-type metaplasia (columnar epithelium with goblet cells). This adaptive metaplasia raises the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A child presents with abdominal distension and an enlarged liver 8 cm below the costal margin. The liver is smooth on palpation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Massive but smooth (non-nodular) hepatomegaly in a young child without splenomegaly points to glycogen storage disease (e.g., Von Gierke), where glycogen accumulates in hepatocytes. Lysosomal storage diseases typically add splenomegaly, coarse facial features and neuroregression; HCC gives a firm nodular liver.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is caused by a defect in which of the following platelet glycoproteins?
questions.concept: Bernard-Soulier syndrome results from a defect in the platelet GpIb/IX complex, the receptor for von Willebrand factor, so platelet adhesion fails; it shows giant platelets and absent ristocetin aggregation (not corrected by normal plasma). The GpIIb/IIIa defect instead causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following substances, at the given concentration, makes water unsuitable for human consumption according to safety standards?
questions.concept: Cadmium 0.3 mg/L is unsafe because the permissible limit is only about 0.003 mg/L; the other values are within limits (fluoride <1.5, chloride <250, calcium <75-200 mg/L). Chronic cadmium exposure causes proximal renal tubular damage and Itai-Itai disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient with renal disease undergoes a biopsy. On Congo red staining, the deposits show apple-green birefringence under polarised light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Apple-green birefringence under polarised light after Congo red staining is the hallmark of amyloidosis; the deposits are salmon-pink on light microscopy and have a cross-beta-pleated-sheet structure. The other glomerular diseases are Congo red negative.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 12-year-old child presents with palpitations, tremors, dry mouth, heart rate 130 bpm and respiratory rate 34/min. Which of the following substances is most likely responsible?
questions.concept: Tachycardia, tremor and anticholinergic signs (dry mouth) form the tricyclic antidepressant toxidrome; TCA overdose also causes CNS excitation/convulsions, hypotension and cardiac conduction defects. Lithium lacks the anticholinergic picture, opioids cause miosis and respiratory depression, and propranolol causes bradycardia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 39-year-old male presents with stress and inability to manage work-life balance. On evaluation his blood pressure is 150/95 mmHg with elevated blood sugar. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Advise rest only, no pharmacological treatment
questions.concept: For stage 2 hypertension with hyperglycaemia, an ARB such as telmisartan is preferred because it lowers BP, is renoprotective and metabolically neutral (may even improve insulin sensitivity), unlike thiazides which can worsen glycaemia. Glucocorticoids would raise both BP and sugar, and lifestyle change alone is inadequate for stage 2 HTN.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease presents with severe anemia. Laboratory tests reveal a normocytic, normochromic anemia. What is the most appropriate treatment to manage this patient's anemia?
questions.concept: The normocytic normochromic anaemia of chronic kidney disease is mainly due to erythropoietin deficiency, so the core therapy is an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent such as darbepoetin alfa (with iron repletion as needed). Folate/B12 treat megaloblastic anaemia and chelation is for iron overload.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 75 kg person is administered a drug with a half-life of 3 hours. What is the approximate clearance of the drug?
questions.concept: Clearance = 0.693 x Vd / t-half; taking the standard Vd of about 100 mL/kg (Vd ~7000 mL) and t-half = 3 h gives roughly 1600 mL/h, i.e. about 23 mL/min, the only per-minute option. NOTE: the recalled stem omits the volume of distribution, which must be assumed (~100 mL/kg) to solve it; option B (1670) is the mL/h value mislabelled as mL/min.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which medication is used to reduce the frequency of future headache episodes in a 26-year-old woman with one-sided pulsating headaches accompanied by nausea, vomiting and photophobia, who finds relief in a dimly lit environment?
questions.concept: Unilateral pulsatile headache with nausea, photophobia and relief in a dark room is migraine; the beta-blocker propranolol is a drug of choice for migraine prophylaxis (reducing attack frequency). Triptans and ergots are for acute attacks, not prophylaxis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A man was abducted from his home, and his son subsequently claimed rights to his father's property. As per Section 111 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), until when is the son not entitled to claim inheritance?
questions.concept: Under Section 111 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (formerly Sec 108 of the Indian Evidence Act), a person unheard of for 7 years by those who would naturally have heard from them is presumed dead; until 7 years elapse the heirs cannot claim the inheritance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient presents with excessive thirst and increased urination of around 6-7 litres per day. He had a history of cerebral trauma one month ago. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.concept: Polyuria and polydipsia (6-7 L/day) after head trauma indicate central diabetes insipidus from deficient ADH; desmopressin (a V2-selective vasopressin analogue) is first-line, restoring water reabsorption in the collecting ducts. Thiazides help nephrogenic DI, and tolvaptan (a V2 antagonist) is for SIADH.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with a history of peptic ulcer disease presents with arthritis and develops carditis. Which of the following is the most appropriate anti-inflammatory drug?
questions.concept: When an anti-inflammatory is needed in a patient with peptic ulcer disease, the COX-2 selective agent celecoxib is preferred because it spares COX-1-mediated gastric mucosal protection, lowering GI ulcer/bleed risk compared with non-selective NSAIDs like ibuprofen or diclofenac. Naloxone is an opioid antagonist, not an anti-inflammatory.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with known rheumatic heart disease is found to have a 1-2 cm aneurysm on imaging. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.concept: A large (10-20 mm) coronary artery aneurysm carries a high risk of thrombosis, embolisation and MI, so long-term (lifelong) low-dose aspirin is the mainstay of antithrombotic prophylaxis; dual antiplatelets are reserved for giant aneurysms or acute events. NOTE: the recalled stem says 'rheumatic heart disease' but the explanation clearly concerns a coronary artery aneurysm (Kawasaki-type management), which appears to be a recall/extraction artifact; answer A holds for a large coronary aneurysm.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct triple drug regimen for the treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection?
questions.concept: A standard first-line H. pylori triple regimen combines a PPI with two antibiotics; omeprazole + clarithromycin + metronidazole is a valid clarithromycin-based triple therapy. Combinations lacking a macrolide (or built on ciprofloxacin) are not standard triple therapy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with asthma on inhaled corticosteroids and a LABA continues to have exacerbations. FEV1 is normal, there is no improvement with a salbutamol challenge, and symptoms worsen seasonally. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.concept: In a patient still uncontrolled on ICS + LABA, the GINA approach is to first check adherence/technique/triggers and optimise anti-inflammatory control by stepping up the ICS dose before adding LAMA or biologics; omalizumab is reserved for severe allergic asthma failing maximal inhaled therapy. NOTE: management-step questions are guideline-dependent, but increasing ICS is the conventional next step here.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient developed Achilles tendonitis and leg swelling after taking a certain antibiotic. This adverse effect is commonly associated with fluoroquinolones. What is the most likely mechanism of action of the drug involved?
options: Inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
Inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis at 50S subunit
Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis
Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis
questions.concept: Achilles tendinopathy/rupture is a classic adverse effect of fluoroquinolones, which act by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication. 50S inhibition is macrolides, folate-synthesis inhibition is sulfonamides, and cell-wall inhibition is beta-lactams.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A person was found dead in a swimming pool. On autopsy, the stomach and lungs were filled with water, and there was mucoid froth at the nose and mouth. What is the most likely mode of death?
questions.concept: Water in the lungs and stomach with copious, persistent fine froth at the mouth and nose indicates wet drowning, where aspirated water washes out surfactant causing alveolar collapse and hypoxaemia. Dry drowning is death from laryngospasm with essentially dry lungs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient took a drug for migraine treatment, following which there was numbness and the hand appeared discoloured (as shown). What is the possible drug that was taken?
questions.concept: Numbness and colour change of the fingers (Raynaud-like peripheral vasoconstriction that can progress to gangrene) after a migraine drug points to an ergot alkaloid such as dihydroergotamine; sumatriptan, butorphanol and aspirin do not cause this ergotism.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A 30-year-old apparently healthy man carrying laxatives and enema apparatus developed abdominal pain at the airport; an abdominal X-ray (shown) reveals radio-opaque cylindrical objects. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A traveller carrying laxatives/enema equipment who develops abdominal pain, with radio-opaque cylindrical packets on abdominal X-ray, is a body packer ('mule') who has swallowed or inserted drug-filled wrappings to smuggle drugs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with hypertension, tachycardia and early renal involvement is prescribed an ARB (telmisartan). What is the most likely mechanism by which the drug helps improve heart rate and blood pressure?
options: By increasing sodium excretion via loop diuretics
questions.concept: ARBs such as telmisartan lower blood pressure chiefly by blocking angiotensin II at AT1 receptors, causing vasodilation and a fall in peripheral vascular resistance; the resulting BP drop can secondarily blunt reflex tachycardia. They neither block beta-1 receptors nor act as diuretics.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: What is the preferred preoperative drug for managing blood pressure in a patient with pheochromocytoma?
questions.concept: Phenoxybenzamine, a long-acting irreversible non-selective alpha-blocker, is the classic preoperative agent for phaeochromocytoma to control BP and prevent intraoperative catecholamine surges; alpha blockade must precede any beta blockade to avoid unopposed alpha vasoconstriction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A woman taking cetirizine for allergic rhinitis complains of excessive sleepiness. Which of the following is the best alternative with minimal sedative effect?
questions.concept: Fexofenadine is a second-generation H1 antihistamine with minimal CNS penetration, so it is the best low-sedation alternative when cetirizine causes drowsiness; hydroxyzine, diphenhydramine and promethazine are all sedating first-generation agents.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which of the following drugs acts by inhibiting the catechol-O-methyltransferase enzyme?
questions.concept: Tolcapone inhibits catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), prolonging the action of levodopa/dopamine as adjunct therapy in Parkinson's disease (risk of hepatotoxicity). Amantadine boosts dopamine release, rotigotine is a dopamine agonist, and selegiline inhibits MAO-B.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient presents with blackish discoloration of the nasal cavity and posterior buccal mucosa. He has a history of high-dose steroid use. What is the most appropriate drug for treatment?
questions.concept: Black necrotic nasal/oral mucosa in an immunosuppressed patient (high-dose steroids) suggests mucormycosis, treated with lipid/liposomal amphotericin B plus urgent surgical debridement; azoles like fluconazole and itraconazole are ineffective against Mucorales, and griseofulvin only treats dermatophytes.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient is brought to the emergency department with signs suggestive of opioid poisoning. What is the antidote of choice?
questions.concept: Naloxone is the opioid-receptor antagonist of choice for opioid overdose, rapidly reversing respiratory depression and miosis; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and physostigmine treats anticholinergic toxicity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: What is Zileuton's mechanism of action?
questions.concept: Zileuton is a 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor that blocks synthesis of leukotrienes from arachidonic acid, used to control asthma. COX inhibition describes NSAIDs, PDE-5 inhibition describes sildenafil, and mast-cell stabilisation describes cromolyn.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with hypertension on antihypertensive drugs has uncontrolled BP even after adding diuretics. The serum electrolytes show hypokalemia. What is the next step in the treatment of this patient?
questions.concept: Resistant hypertension with spontaneous hypokalaemia despite diuretics suggests primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome); the aldosterone antagonist spironolactone is both diagnostic and therapeutic, correcting the hypokalaemia and lowering BP. KCl only masks the hypokalaemia, and loop/thiazide diuretics worsen it.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A patient presents with lung injury and tympanic membrane rupture following a blast exposure. These injuries are characteristic of which level of blast wave effect?
questions.concept: Injury to air-filled organs (blast lung and tympanic membrane rupture) caused by the overpressure wave alone is a primary (Level I) blast injury. Secondary injuries are from flying debris, tertiary from being thrown against objects, and quaternary from burns/toxic exposure.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A patient presents with a fish bone stuck in the pyriform sinus. During the removal procedure there is accidental nerve injury. Which nerve is most likely to be damaged?
options: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
questions.concept: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and gives sensory supply to the pyriform fossa and supraglottic larynx, so it is at risk during fish-bone removal there; its injury causes supraglottic anaesthesia and a lost cough reflex, predisposing to aspiration.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is most strongly associated with which of the following head and neck cancers?
questions.concept: HPV (especially type 16) is most strongly linked to oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (tonsil, base of tongue) via the E6/E7 oncoproteins, and these HPV-positive tumours have a better prognosis. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is EBV-associated, while hypopharyngeal and laryngeal cancers are chiefly tobacco/alcohol-related.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A professional singer presents with difficulty raising the pitch of her voice following thyroid surgery. There is no hoarseness, but high-pitched voice production is impaired. Which nerve is most likely injured?
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN)
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (IBSLN)
questions.concept: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle that tenses the vocal cords for high-pitched phonation; its injury during thyroid surgery causes loss of vocal pitch/range (noticed especially by singers) without hoarseness, since cord mobility is preserved. RLN injury instead causes hoarseness.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A patient presents with enophthalmos and periorbital ecchymosis after being hit by a ball. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Blunt periocular trauma (e.g., a ball) that suddenly raises orbital pressure fractures the thin orbital floor, herniating contents into the maxillary sinus; enophthalmos with periorbital ecchymosis (often with diplopia and infraorbital nerve numbness) is the classic orbital blow-out fracture.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: A patient presents with a history of a fall and is found to have bleeding from the ear on examination. What is the investigation of choice?
questions.concept: Bleeding from the ear after head trauma suggests a temporal bone fracture; high-resolution CT of the temporal bone is the investigation of choice to demonstrate fracture lines, ossicular injury and complications. MRI is for soft-tissue/brain injury, and plain skull X-ray lacks the needed bony detail.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man complains of gradual hearing loss over several years, with difficulty hearing conversations especially in noisy environments and trouble perceiving high-pitched sounds. There are no episodes of vertigo, tinnitus, or ear fullness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Gradual, bilateral, symmetric high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with poor speech discrimination in noise, without vertigo or tinnitus, is presbycusis (age-related cochlear hair-cell degeneration starting at the basal turn). Meniere's has vertigo/fullness, otosclerosis is conductive, and acoustic neuroma is unilateral.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A diabetic male presents with facial pain and blackish discoloration in the nose. The CT shows bone erosion and sinus involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A diabetic with facial pain, black necrotic nasal mucosa and CT showing bone erosion/sinus involvement has rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, an angioinvasive fungal infection (Rhizopus/Mucor) causing vascular thrombosis and tissue necrosis. Bacterial or allergic fungal sinusitis and polyposis do not cause invasive bone destruction with eschar.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A tympanometry graph shows a shallow peak at pressure = 0 daPa. What is the most likely diagnosis based on this tympanometry result?
questions.concept: A tympanogram with the peak at normal (0 daPa) pressure but reduced (shallow) compliance is Type As, indicating a stiffened/fixed ossicular system such as otosclerosis or tympanosclerosis. Type A is normal, Type B is flat (effusion), and Type Ad is a very tall peak (ossicular discontinuity).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: Which of the following is not seen in Meniere's disease?
questions.concept: Meniere's disease (endolymphatic hydrops) presents with episodic vertigo, low-frequency roaring tinnitus, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss and aural fullness; ear pain (otalgia) is not a feature unless there is a secondary complication.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A farmer presents with fever, malaise and diarrhea, with a history of exposure to livestock. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible for the illness?
questions.concept: An acute febrile illness (fever, malaise, diarrhoea, sometimes pneumonia/hepatitis) in a farmer with livestock contact suggests Q fever from Coxiella burnetii, acquired by inhaling aerosols from animal birth products and excreta; notably there is no rash, unlike other rickettsial infections.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with fever after returning from a forest trip. On examination, a black eschar is noted on the abdomen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and its drug of choice?
questions.concept: Fever with an eschar after a forest/scrub exposure is scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi, transmitted by trombiculid chigger mites), and doxycycline is the drug of choice. Penicillin and ceftriaxone are ineffective for rickettsial disease, and artesunate is antimalarial.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A diabetic patient presents with whitish plaques in the oral cavity. A KOH mount confirms budding yeast with pseudohyphae. Which of the following is the most appropriate culture medium for isolation of this organism?
questions.concept: White oral plaques in a diabetic with KOH showing budding yeast plus pseudohyphae indicate oral candidiasis (Candida albicans), which is cultured on Sabouraud dextrose agar. Chocolate agar is for fastidious bacteria, Thayer-Martin for Neisseria, and Loeffler's serum for Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: What is the vector responsible for transmitting the Zika virus among the options listed?
questions.concept: Zika virus (a flavivirus) is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes; among the options Aedes albopictus (the Asian tiger mosquito) is the recognised vector, along with Aedes aegypti (not listed) - the same vectors as dengue and chikungunya.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old man develops profuse vomiting and diarrhea within 3 hours of consuming pre-packaged salad and milk at a picnic. There is no fever. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.concept: Sudden vomiting and diarrhoea within 1-6 hours of eating dairy/salad foods, without fever, is caused by the preformed heat-stable enterotoxins of Staphylococcus aureus; because it is toxin-mediated, onset is rapid and the illness is self-limited. Clostridium perfringens and Salmonella have longer incubation periods.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A woman presents with sudden-onset high-grade fever, hypotension, a diffuse rash, and a history of using a tampon for an extended period. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Sudden high fever, hypotension and a diffuse erythrodermic rash (with later desquamation) after prolonged tampon use is toxic shock syndrome, mediated by the Staphylococcus aureus superantigen TSST-1 (occasionally group A streptococcus), which triggers massive T-cell activation and cytokine release.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The receptor used for the entry of HIV into the host cell is?
questions.concept: HIV enters host CD4+ cells by binding gp120 to CD4 plus a chemokine co-receptor; among the options CCR5 (used by macrophage-tropic strains) is correct, and the CCR5-delta32 mutation confers resistance. CD4, the main receptor, is not among the options.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: What is the most likely causative agent for a Tzanck smear showing multinucleated cells?
questions.concept: Multinucleated giant epithelial cells on a Tzanck smear indicate a herpesvirus infection, and herpes simplex virus is the usual single best answer for localised herpetic lesions. NOTE: varicella-zoster virus also produces multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck, so this 'most likely' item is somewhat ambiguous; HSV is the conventional answer.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: An AIDS-positive patient presents with fever, vomiting and meningismus. Which of the following tests helps in the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis?
options: Urine lateral flow assay for cryptococcal antigen
questions.concept: For rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis in an AIDS patient, the urine/serum cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay is the best test - highly sensitive, specific and point-of-care. India ink has low sensitivity, and blood/CSF culture take several days.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which organism is most commonly responsible for gas gangrene?
questions.concept: Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) is most often caused by Clostridium perfringens (type A), whose alpha-toxin (a lecithinase) destroys cell membranes and produces crepitant, gas-filled necrotic muscle. C. difficile causes pseudomembranous colitis, C. tetani spastic paralysis, and C. botulinum flaccid paralysis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A woman was bitten by a rabid dog. The dog developed symptoms and died within a week. What is the best method for antemortem diagnosis of rabies?
questions.concept: The direct fluorescent antibody test (DFAT) is the standard antemortem test for rabies, detecting viral antigen in corneal smears, nuchal skin biopsy (hair follicles), or saliva. Negri bodies and Seller's stain are histologic (postmortem) findings; brain biopsy is invasive and not used antemortem.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 20-year-old male was admitted with fever, headache and retro-orbital pain with rash. The tourniquet test is positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Fever with retro-orbital pain, rash, and a positive tourniquet (Hess) test indicating capillary fragility is classic for dengue haemorrhagic fever. Secondary infection with a different serotype triggers antibody-dependent enhancement, plasma leakage, thrombocytopenia and bleeding.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with headaches, visual disturbances and hypertension. MRI shows a cerebellar hemangioblastoma, and abdominal imaging reveals renal cysts with a solid mass suggestive of renal cell carcinoma. His father died of a brain tumor in his 40s. Which chromosomal abnormality is most likely associated?
questions.concept: Cerebellar/retinal hemangioblastomas plus clear-cell RCC and a dominant family history point to Von Hippel-Lindau disease, caused by loss of the VHL tumour suppressor at 3p25-26. Loss of function stabilises HIF, raising VEGF and driving angiogenic tumours. 13q loss = retinoblastoma, 17p = Li-Fraumeni, trisomy 12 = CLL.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: Mutation in which of the following genes is most commonly associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma?
questions.concept: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from calcitonin-secreting parafollicular C cells and is driven by RET proto-oncogene mutations (sporadic or MEN 2). By contrast, papillary carcinoma links to BRAF V600E/RET-PTC, follicular to RAS/PAX8-PPARgamma, and anaplastic to TP53.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC), also known as Lynch syndrome, is caused by mutations in which type of genes?
questions.concept: Lynch syndrome results from germline mutations in DNA mismatch-repair (MMR) genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2), causing microsatellite instability and increased colorectal (often right-sided) and endometrial/ovarian cancers. APC underlies FAP, not Lynch.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with irritability, poor school performance and recurrent ear infections. Otoscopy shows a dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid behind it and no blood clot. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A dull, retracted drum with non-purulent middle-ear effusion and no acute signs is otitis media with effusion (glue ear), driven by eustachian tube dysfunction - most commonly from adenoid hyperplasia in children. Acute otitis media gives a red bulging drum; cholesteatoma gives foul discharge and a retraction pocket.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A chronic smoker who worked in a cement factory for 20 years developed mesothelioma. This association is most likely due to?
questions.concept: Malignant mesothelioma of the pleura is strongly linked to asbestos exposure (asbestosis), encountered in cement manufacture, insulation and shipbuilding. Smoking dramatically multiplies the risk of bronchogenic carcinoma but not mesothelioma itself. The other pneumoconioses are not causally tied to mesothelioma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The stapedial (acoustic) reflex depends on the integrity of which cranial nerve for its motor response?
questions.concept: The stapedial reflex protects the inner ear from loud sound. Its afferent limb is the cochlear nerve (CN VIII); its efferent (motor) limb is the facial nerve (CN VII) via the nerve to stapedius. A proximal facial nerve lesion abolishes the reflex and can cause hyperacusis. The tensor tympani reflex uses CN V.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: Obstruction at which laryngeal subunit is most characteristically associated with inspiratory stridor?
questions.concept: Supraglottic (extrathoracic) obstruction produces inspiratory stridor because negative airway pressure on inspiration collapses the floppy tissue inward (e.g. laryngomalacia, epiglottitis). Fixed glottic/subglottic narrowing gives biphasic stridor, and intrathoracic tracheal lesions give expiratory sounds.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Basophilic stippling of red blood cells is most characteristically seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.concept: Coarse basophilic stippling (punctate basophilia) reflects aggregated ribosomes and is classic for lead poisoning, where lead inhibits pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase and haem-synthesis enzymes. It is also seen in thalassaemia and sideroblastic anaemia, but not typically in iron deficiency, megaloblastic anaemia or spherocytosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: In conventional Pap smear cytology, which fixative is most appropriate to preserve cellular detail immediately after smearing?
questions.concept: For a conventional cervical (Pap) smear, the slide is fixed immediately in 95% ethanol (or a spray fixative) to preserve nuclear detail before it air-dries. Formalin is the routine histology fixative, not the cytology smear fixative.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 12-year-old presents with short stature. Bone age is less than chronological age, there are no dysmorphic features, and the child is otherwise healthy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
questions.concept: A healthy child with delayed bone age relative to chronological age and no dysmorphism is a constitutional 'late bloomer' (CDGP) who ultimately reaches normal adult height. In familial short stature the bone age equals chronological age; achondroplasia/chondrodysplasia cause disproportionate short stature with deformity.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A newborn of a diabetic mother is symptomatic at 24 hours of life with a blood glucose <35 mg/dL. What is the next best step in management?
options: Administer IV bolus of Hartmann solution
Administer IV glucose and recheck blood glucose after 20 minutes
questions.concept: A symptomatic neonate with glucose <35-40 mg/dL needs immediate IV 10% dextrose (about 2 mL/kg bolus) followed by a glucose infusion, with a recheck in 20-30 minutes. Infants of diabetic mothers are prone to hypoglycaemia from fetal hyperinsulinism. Oral feeds/observation suit only mild asymptomatic cases; Hartmann's has no glucose.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which genetic syndrome is caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p deletion)?
questions.concept: Cri-du-chat syndrome results from a 5p deletion, producing the characteristic high-pitched cat-like cry (laryngeal hypoplasia), microcephaly, hypertelorism and intellectual disability. Edward = trisomy 18, Patau = trisomy 13, Turner = 45,X.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A young boy is brought for developmental assessment. He has a prominent epicanthal fold, a single transverse palmar crease, hypotonia, intellectual disability and a flat facial profile with upslanting palpebral fissures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Flat facies with upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, a single (simian) palmar crease and hypotonia with intellectual disability is Down syndrome (trisomy 21). Patau (trisomy 13) has cleft lip/polydactyly, Edward (trisomy 18) has clenched overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet, and Fragile X has macro-orchidism with a long face.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 10-year-old child weighs 40 kg and has intellectual disability. The upper segment to lower segment (US:LS) ratio is 1.1:1. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: The source keys rickets, arguing that an elevated US:LS ratio (1.1:1 vs the normal ~1.0 at age 10) reflects a shortened lower segment from long-bone disease. NOTE: this is disputed - rickets does not cause intellectual disability, whereas cretinism/congenital hypothyroidism classically gives BOTH an increased US:LS ratio AND mental retardation, so options A (cretinism) and D (hypothyroidism) are the stronger clinical fit and overlap with each other. Flagged for review.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: FBN1 gene mutation is seen in which of the following genetic disorders?
questions.concept: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder from FBN1 (fibrillin-1) mutations on chromosome 15, giving defective microfibrils, excess TGF-beta signalling, tall arachnodactylic habitus, aortic root dilatation and upward ectopia lentis. Ehlers-Danlos involves collagen genes; homocystinuria is cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A mutation in the SOD1 gene is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.concept: SOD1 (superoxide dismutase 1) mutations account for about 20% of familial ALS. Misfolded SOD1 gains a toxic function causing oxidative stress and degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons, with sensation and cognition typically preserved. Huntington = CAG repeats in HTT; Parkinson = SNCA/LRRK2.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Blood transfusion reactions are mediated by which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.concept: Acute haemolytic transfusion reactions are Type II (antibody-mediated cytotoxic) hypersensitivity: preformed recipient IgM anti-A/anti-B bind donor RBC antigens and activate complement, causing intravascular haemolysis. Type I is IgE, Type III immune-complex, Type IV T-cell mediated.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 58-year-old male with a history of multiple sexual partners presents with anorexia and jaundice. Liver biopsy shows hepatocytes with ground-glass cytoplasm. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.concept: Ground-glass hepatocytes (finely granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm from HBsAg accumulating in the endoplasmic reticulum) are the hallmark of chronic hepatitis B, which fits the sexual-transmission risk factor here. (Source explanation was missing; answer confirmed from standard pathology.)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Cell injury, adaptation, necrosis vs apoptosis
questions.stem: A diabetic male presents with seizures. Imaging shows a brain lesion and histopathology reveals liquefactive necrosis. What is the most important mechanism responsible?
questions.concept: Liquefactive necrosis (typical of brain and abscesses) is driven by hydrolytic/lysosomal enzyme digestion released by microglia and neutrophils; the lipid-rich, stroma-poor brain rapidly liquefies. Even when the trigger is ischaemia or infection, the necrosis type in the CNS is liquefactive and the mechanism is enzymatic breakdown.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: What is the eye manifestation seen in HLA-B27-positive patients with ulcerative colitis?
questions.concept: The HLA-B27-associated ocular lesion in inflammatory bowel disease and the spondyloarthropathies is acute anterior uveitis. NOTE: option D 'iridocyclitis' is a synonym for anterior uveitis, so A and D describe the same entity and the item effectively has two correct options. Keyed answer A ('uveitis', the broader conventional term) retained but flagged. (Source explanation was missing.)

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: An 8-year-old presents with bedwetting (enuresis). There is no urinary tract infection, no neurological deficit and no daytime symptoms. What is the best next step in management?
questions.concept: First-line treatment of primary nocturnal enuresis is behavioural: evening fluid restriction, timed voiding, positive reinforcement and enuresis alarms. Pharmacotherapy (desmopressin, or anticholinergics for detrusor overactivity) is reserved for when behavioural measures fail or when rapid short-term control is needed.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: On 1 January 2024, an area of 10,000 people had 100 TB cases. During the year 30 were cured, 10 died, 20 new cases occurred, and 5 of the new cases were cured by 31 December. What are the incidence and prevalence of TB (per 1,000 and %, respectively)?
questions.concept: Incidence counts only new cases among those at risk: 20/(10,000-100) x 1,000 = about 2 per 1,000. Period prevalence counts all cases during the interval: (100 existing + 20 new)/10,000 = 1.2%. NOTE: the source's route (75/10,000 = 0.75% ~ 1.2%) is arithmetically wrong; 1.2% is correctly the period prevalence, and the option mixes units (per-1,000 for incidence, % for prevalence).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 5-year-old presents with exertional dyspnea, a history of cyanotic spells and clubbing, and a harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border. Chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Cyanotic (tet) spells, clubbing and a harsh systolic murmur from right ventricular outflow obstruction, with a boot-shaped heart, is Tetralogy of Fallot (PS, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH). TAPVC gives a 'snowman' shadow, TGA an 'egg-on-string' with neonatal cyanosis, and ASD is acyanotic. Image referenced but the clinical picture is diagnostic.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which of the following is considered harmful to a newborn baby in the immediate postnatal period?
options: Cleaning the eyes with a wet sterile swab
Giving a bath immediately after birth
Placing the baby on the mother's chest
questions.concept: Bathing a newborn immediately after birth causes hypothermia, removes the protective vernix caseosa and delays skin-to-skin contact and early breastfeeding; WHO advises delaying the first bath at least 24 hours. Eye care, early breastfeeding and skin-to-skin contact are all beneficial.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In which of the following should a cotton swab soaked with pus be discarded?
questions.concept: A pus-soaked cotton swab is soiled (infectious) waste, discarded in the yellow category for incineration/deep burial. Chlorination is not used for these biodegradable items (it is for the red-category recyclable plastics). Hence a yellow, non-chlorinated bag.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant has a respiratory rate of 66/min with chest indrawing and nasal flaring, and no other danger signs. Per WHO IMNCI, what is the most likely classification?
questions.concept: By revised WHO IMNCI (2-59 months), fast breathing (>=50/min; here 66) and/or chest indrawing WITHOUT a general danger sign is classified as 'pneumonia', treated with oral amoxicillin; danger signs, hypoxia or stridor make it 'severe pneumonia'. NOTE: older IMCI classified any chest indrawing as severe pneumonia, so the answer depends on the guideline version.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A newborn presents with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, intrahepatic cholestasis, high alkaline phosphatase and eosinophilic PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules on liver biopsy (suggestive of alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency). What is the most common cause of jaundice in this setting?
questions.concept: Idiopathic neonatal hepatitis is the classic most common cause of neonatal conjugated hyperbilirubinemia/cholestasis (intrahepatic cholestasis, giant-cell change), and the PAS-positive globules point to alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency as the specific etiology. NOTE: biliary atresia is the main competing answer (commonest surgical cause) and physiological jaundice is unconjugated - hence moderate confidence.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: An elderly man presents with bowing of the legs and skeletal deformity, and several other villagers show similar features. Given the geographic clustering, what is the most appropriate next step in investigation?
options: Collect and analyze water samples for fluoride content
questions.concept: A cluster of skeletal deformities in one village points to an environmental cause - endemic skeletal fluorosis from drinking water fluoride >1.5 mg/L. The logical next step is testing the local water for fluoride, rather than individual serum vitamin D/calcium/PTH testing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A teenager, previously raised as a girl, presents with primary amenorrhea and lack of secondary sexual characteristics. Examination shows tall stature, small testes and gynecomastia, with a normal testosterone level. What is the most likely genotype?
questions.concept: Tall stature with small firm testes, gynaecomastia and hypogonadism is Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY): primary testicular failure gives low-to-normal testosterone with elevated gonadotropins (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism). 45,X is Turner, 46,XX normal female, 47,XYY tall fertile males.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A patient with increased consumption of Bajra (pearl millet) roti now complains of drowsiness and giddiness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Bajra contaminated with Claviceps purpurea (ergot fungus) produces ergot alkaloids causing vasoconstriction, giddiness, drowsiness and tingling - ergotism. Epidemic dropsy comes from argemone-adulterated mustard oil; botulism from canned food; fusarium toxicity from mouldy grain causing alimentary toxic aleukia.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A mother brings her 9-month-old baby concerned that no BCG scar has appeared, though the baby received BCG at birth. What is the next best step?
options: Do the Mantoux test and wait for the result
Refer the baby for a chest X-ray and further evaluation
questions.concept: Absence of a BCG scar in an otherwise healthy vaccinated child does not indicate lack of immunity and is not an indication for revaccination, Mantoux testing or imaging - the caregiver should simply be reassured.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Between the MR and Pentavalent vaccines, which can be reused and which must be discarded once the vial is opened, per the open vial policy?
questions.concept: The Pentavalent vaccine is a preserved liquid multi-dose vial eligible for the open vial policy (reusable up to 28 days if the cold chain and VVM are intact). The MR vaccine is a reconstituted lyophilised vaccine without preservative and must be discarded within a few hours of reconstitution. So: discard MR, reuse Pentavalent.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a group the mean blood glucose is 105 mg/dL with a standard deviation of 10 mg/dL. Assuming a normal distribution, what range covers approximately 95% of the population?
questions.concept: By the empirical rule, about 95% of a normal distribution lies within mean +/- 2 SD. Here 105 +/- (2 x 10) = 85 to 125 mg/dL. (+/-1 SD covers ~68%, +/-3 SD ~99.7%.)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a family with three siblings, the eldest sibling moves out of the household and a new (third) child is born. What is this change in the family structure called?
questions.concept: In the family life cycle, extension is the phase of adding members (births) while contraction is losing them (children leaving). NOTE: this scenario mixes both (the eldest leaves while a new child is born) and the source's definition of 'complete extension' (multi-generational overlap) is non-standard, so the mapping is genuinely ambiguous. Keyed answer C retained but flagged for review.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A person is travelling from Nigeria to the United States. Which vaccine is required for this international travel?
questions.concept: Under the International Health Regulations, travellers from yellow-fever-endemic countries such as Nigeria must present a valid yellow fever (17D live-attenuated) vaccination certificate, given at least 10 days before travel, to prevent international spread. JE, measles and rabies are not certificate requirements for this route.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A study used office records over the past 20 years to compare the incidence of disease among factory workers exposed to aniline dye versus unexposed clerical staff. What type of epidemiological study is this?
questions.concept: Grouping subjects by exposure (aniline dye vs clerical) and tracing disease incidence through already-existing past records is a retrospective (historical) cohort study - both exposure and outcome had occurred before the study began. Case-control starts from disease status, not exposure; ecological uses population-level not individual data.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient whose diet mainly consists of pulses and rice presents with bowed legs (stick deformity). Which vitamin could have prevented this condition?
questions.concept: Bowed legs from defective bone mineralisation is rickets, caused by vitamin D deficiency (a rice-and-pulses diet is low in vitamin D and calcium). Vitamin D drives intestinal calcium/phosphate absorption and bone mineralisation. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, C scurvy, and B12 megaloblastic anaemia.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: What does the Langelier Saturation Index (LSI) primarily indicate in water quality management?
questions.concept: The Langelier Saturation Index indicates whether water tends to deposit calcium carbonate scale (positive LSI) or dissolve it and corrode pipes (negative LSI), with zero being balanced; it is derived from pH, alkalinity, hardness and temperature. It does not measure TDS or biological contamination.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A factory worker sustained burns over 25% of his body on duty and later developed infections and complications. Under the ESI Act, which benefit is he eligible for?
questions.concept: Under the ESI Act, Extended Sickness Benefit covers insured workers with specified long-term diseases needing prolonged treatment, payable up to 2 years at about 140% of the standard rate. NOTE: eligibility requires the condition to be on the list of specified diseases, so the burns-complication link is a somewhat niche interpretation. Ordinary Sickness Benefit runs only ~91 days; Enhanced is for sterilisation; Dependants' is for death from employment injury.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A middle-aged man has progressive effort intolerance and visible bounding carotid pulsations. Nail beds show rhythmic flushing with each heartbeat. Which auscultatory finding best explains this condition?
questions.concept: The signs (wide pulse pressure with a bounding water-hammer carotid pulse and Quincke's capillary nail-bed pulsations) indicate chronic aortic regurgitation, which produces a high-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border as blood leaks back into the left ventricle during diastole.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A young patient has persistent hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Renal parameters are normal and there is no diuretic use. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Hypertension with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis, normal renal function and no diuretics is the classic triad of primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome): excess aldosterone drives renal Na+ retention (hypertension) with K+/H+ loss. Liddle syndrome mimics it but has LOW aldosterone and renin and is the far rarer answer, usually signposted by family history.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A woman complains of dryness of eyes and mouth, joint pain, and pruritus. There is no Raynaud phenomenon or skin tightening. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Dry eyes and dry mouth (sicca) with arthralgia and no skin tightening or Raynaud is Sjogren syndrome, an autoimmune exocrinopathy with lymphocytic destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands (anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB positive). Absence of skin changes and Raynaud argues against scleroderma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A patient has vague abdominal pain and weight loss. Imaging shows a diffusely enlarged 'sausage-shaped' pancreas with high IgG4 levels. Best treatment?
questions.concept: A diffusely enlarged 'sausage-shaped' pancreas with raised serum IgG4 is type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis, which characteristically responds dramatically to corticosteroids; recognising it avoids unnecessary surgery for suspected malignancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient in circulatory failure has ABG values: pH 7.3, HCO3- 10 mEq/L, pCO2 25 mmHg. What is the acid-base status?
options: Mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis
