questions.concept: Kwashiorkor is oedematous protein-energy malnutrition: bilateral pitting oedema, hepatomegaly (fatty liver), hair and skin changes and hypoalbuminaemia, with relatively preserved subcutaneous fat. Marasmus is severe wasting WITHOUT oedema ('old man' facies).

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 3-year-old from a poor community has difficulty seeing in dim light, dry conjunctivae and triangular foamy grey spots on the bulbar conjunctiva. Which deficiency is responsible?
questions.concept: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness (earliest symptom), conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots (the foamy grey triangular spots), keratomalacia and eventually blindness. It is a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness and is treated with high-dose vitamin A.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Under India's National Immunization Schedule, which vaccines are given at BIRTH?
options: BCG, OPV-0 and the Hepatitis B birth dose
questions.concept: At birth the National Immunization Schedule gives BCG, the zero dose of oral polio vaccine (OPV-0) and the Hepatitis B birth dose. Pentavalent, OPV, rotavirus and PCV start at 6 weeks; measles-rubella is given at 9 months.
questions.reference: MoHFW / UIP National Immunization Schedule - web-verified 2026-07-04

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: An unimmunized 4-year-old has high fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, with tiny bluish-white spots on an erythematous buccal mucosa, followed by a maculopapular rash that spreads from the face downward. Which statement is correct?
options: The buccal spots are Koplik spots (pathognomonic of measles); the first measles-rubella dose is due at 9 months
These are Forchheimer spots of rubella; the vaccine is given at birth
This is scarlet fever and no vaccine exists
This is roseola and measles vaccine is given only at 5 years
questions.concept: Koplik spots (grey-white spots on a red buccal mucosa) are pathognomonic of measles and precede the cephalocaudal maculopapular rash. In the Indian schedule the first measles-rubella (MR) dose is given at 9 completed months (second at 16-24 months). Pneumonia is the commonest cause of measles death.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e / UIP schedule - web-verified 2026-07-04

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 30% remains breathless (NYHA class II-III) despite an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker at target doses, with potassium 4.4 mmol/L and normal renal function. Which additional class has the best evidence for reducing MORTALITY in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
questions.concept: In HFrEF, mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists (spironolactone/eplerenone) reduce mortality when added to an ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker (RALES/EMPHASIS-HF). Loop diuretics relieve congestion but have no proven mortality benefit; digoxin reduces hospitalisation but not mortality.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21e - Heart Failure: Management

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 70-year-old man reports exertional chest pain, breathlessness and two episodes of exertional syncope. There is a harsh ejection systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space radiating to the carotids, a slow-rising low-volume pulse and a soft second heart sound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: The triad of angina, syncope and dyspnoea with an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, a slow-rising (parvus et tardus) pulse and a soft A2 is severe aortic stenosis; symptom onset signals poor prognosis and need for valve replacement. The murmur of HOCM instead INCREASES with Valsalva and decreases on squatting.
questions.reference: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine 24e - Valvular Heart Disease

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: An ECG in a 58-year-old with 40 minutes of crushing chest pain shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. He becomes profoundly hypotensive shortly after a dose of sublingual nitrate. Which vessel is most likely occluded, and why did the nitrate cause hypotension?
options: Left anterior descending artery; extensive anterior infarct
Left circumflex artery; lateral wall infarct
Right coronary artery; associated right-ventricular infarction is preload-dependent
questions.concept: Inferior STEMI (ST elevation in II, III, aVF) is usually right coronary artery occlusion. It may extend to the preload-dependent right ventricle, so nitrates (venodilators that cut preload) can precipitate profound hypotension - RV infarcts need fluids, not nitrates. LAD occlusion instead produces anterior (V1-V4) changes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Three days after an anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI, a patient suddenly becomes hypotensive with a new harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border. Catheter sampling shows an oxygen saturation step-up from the right atrium to the right ventricle. What is the most likely mechanical complication?
options: Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture
Free wall rupture with cardiac tamponade
questions.concept: A new pansystolic murmur with an oxygen 'step-up' from right atrium to right ventricle indicates a post-infarction ventricular septal rupture (a left-to-right shunt), typically a few days after MI. Papillary muscle rupture also causes acute MR but produces NO oxygen step-up; free-wall rupture causes tamponade/PEA; Dressler pericarditis appears weeks later.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 55-year-old diabetic man gets central chest tightness on climbing two flights of stairs that is relieved within minutes by rest; resting ECG and troponin are normal. He is started on aspirin and a high-intensity statin. Which additional drug class is first-line to RELIEVE his anginal symptoms?
options: A continuous long-acting nitrate patch worn 24 hours a day
questions.concept: This is stable angina; a beta-blocker (or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker) is first-line anti-anginal therapy, reducing myocardial oxygen demand. Continuous long-acting nitrate use causes tolerance (a nitrate-free interval is needed); anticoagulation and digoxin have no role in relieving stable angina.
questions.reference: Davidson's 24e - Stable Angina / Harrison's 21e - Ischaemic Heart Disease

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 44-year-old man has resistant hypertension (168/104 mmHg on three agents) and persistent hypokalaemia (K 2.9 mmol/L) despite taking no diuretics, plus a mild metabolic alkalosis. Plasma aldosterone is high, plasma renin activity is suppressed, and the aldosterone-to-renin ratio is markedly raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Hypertension with hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, HIGH aldosterone and SUPPRESSED renin (a high aldosterone:renin ratio) is classic primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), from an adrenal adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia. Renal artery stenosis causes SECONDARY hyperaldosteronism in which renin is HIGH, not suppressed.
questions.reference: Harrison's 21e - Disorders of the Adrenal Cortex

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has months of fatigue, weight loss, salt craving and dizziness on standing. She shows postural hypotension, hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and buccal mucosa, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia; a short Synacthen (ACTH stimulation) test gives a subnormal cortisol response. If she deteriorates into crisis, what is the definitive immediate treatment?
options: IV hydrocortisone together with IV normal saline
questions.concept: The picture is primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease): hyperpigmentation (high ACTH/POMC), hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and a failed Synacthen response. Adrenal (Addisonian) crisis is treated with immediate IV hydrocortisone plus aggressive IV saline; oral fludrocortisone alone is inadequate in a crisis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has central obesity, purple abdominal striae wider than 1 cm, proximal muscle weakness, new hypertension and new diabetes, and you suspect Cushing syndrome. Which is the most appropriate FIRST-LINE screening test to confirm cortisol excess?
questions.concept: Screening for Cushing syndrome uses tests of cortisol excess: the overnight low-dose (1 mg) dexamethasone suppression test, late-night salivary cortisol, or 24-hour urinary free cortisol. A random plasma cortisol is unreliable (diurnal variation). Plasma ACTH and imaging are used to LOCALISE the cause only AFTER excess is confirmed.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, deep sighing breathing and drowsiness. Glucose 28 mmol/L, pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L, ketones ++++, serum K 5.6 mmol/L. After starting a rapid IV isotonic fluid bolus, what is the correct next priority regarding insulin and potassium?
options: Start a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion and monitor/replace potassium as it falls
Give IV sodium bicarbonate to correct the pH first
Give IV potassium immediately regardless of the level
Withhold all insulin until the ketones have cleared
questions.concept: DKA management is fluids first, then a fixed-rate insulin infusion; insulin drives potassium intracellularly, so serum K (even if initially high from acidosis) falls quickly and must be monitored and replaced once it is below ~5.0-5.5 mmol/L. Routine bicarbonate is not recommended, and insulin must not be withheld as it is needed to switch off ketogenesis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 52-year-old with type 2 diabetes for 8 years is found on repeat testing to have persistent moderately increased albuminuria (urine albumin 60 mg/g) with a normal creatinine and BP 138/86 mmHg. Which drug class should be started to slow progression of his diabetic kidney disease?
options: An ACE inhibitor or angiotensin-receptor blocker
A calcium-channel blocker only if oedema develops
questions.concept: Moderately increased albuminuria (formerly 'microalbuminuria') is the earliest clinical marker of diabetic nephropathy. ACE inhibitors or ARBs reduce intraglomerular pressure (efferent arteriolar dilatation) and slow progression of albuminuria and nephropathy, so they are the renoprotective agents of choice even with only modestly raised BP. A loop diuretic offers no such renoprotection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with untreated Graves' disease develops fever 39.5 C, marked agitation, atrial fibrillation at 150/min and vomiting after an infection - a thyroid storm. In sequencing therapy, why must Lugol's iodine be given only AFTER an antithyroid drug such as propylthiouracil?
options: Iodine must be delayed to avoid hypocalcaemia
Giving iodine first supplies substrate that can transiently increase hormone synthesis (Jod-Basedow effect)
questions.concept: In thyroid storm a thionamide (propylthiouracil, which also blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion) is given first to block new hormone synthesis; iodine is added at least an hour later to inhibit hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff effect). Giving iodine first supplies extra substrate and can transiently worsen thyrotoxicosis (Jod-Basedow phenomenon). Beta-blockers control the adrenergic symptoms.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has a painful, tender thyroid, fever and thyrotoxic symptoms three weeks after a viral upper-respiratory infection. ESR is very high, and a radioactive iodine uptake scan shows markedly REDUCED uptake. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A painful, tender thyroid after a viral illness, with a high ESR and LOW radioiodine uptake, is subacute (de Quervain's) thyroiditis; the thyrotoxicosis comes from leakage of preformed hormone, so uptake is suppressed and the illness is self-limiting (NSAIDs, sometimes steroids). Graves' disease is painless with HIGH diffuse uptake.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A man with alcoholic cirrhosis and tense ascites develops fever, diffuse abdominal pain and worsening encephalopathy. A diagnostic ascitic tap shows 480 polymorphonuclear cells/mm3 with no surgical source on imaging. Besides IV cefotaxime, which intervention reduces the risk of hepatorenal syndrome and improves survival?
options: Immediate large-volume paracentesis of all the ascites
questions.concept: An ascitic PMN count of 250/mm3 or more diagnoses spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; treatment is a third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime) PLUS IV albumin (typically on day 1 and day 3), which reduces hepatorenal syndrome and mortality. Rifaximin/lactulose treat encephalopathy, not SBP; FFP is not indicated without active bleeding.
questions.reference: Harrison's 21e - Cirrhosis and its Complications (Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with known cirrhosis presents with a large haematemesis and melaena. After airway protection and resuscitation, he is started on a splanchnic vasoconstrictor and prophylactic antibiotics. Which is the DEFINITIVE procedure of choice to control the likely bleeding oesophageal varices?
questions.concept: Endoscopic variceal band ligation is the definitive first-line treatment for bleeding oesophageal varices, combined with a vasoconstrictor (terlipressin/octreotide) and prophylactic antibiotics. Balloon tamponade is only a temporary bridge; TIPS is reserved for refractory bleeding; PPIs treat peptic ulcers, not varices.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A traveller returning from sub-Saharan Africa has high fever, jaundice, confusion and dark urine. A Giemsa-stained blood film shows numerous small ring forms, some red cells with multiple rings, and banana (crescent)-shaped gametocytes; parasitaemia is 6%. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.concept: Crescentic (banana-shaped) gametocytes, multiply-infected red cells and high parasitaemia indicate Plasmodium falciparum, and cerebral involvement with jaundice and haemoglobinuria defines SEVERE malaria - the treatment of choice is IV artesunate. Chloroquine is inadequate (widespread resistance); primaquine only clears hypnozoites/gametocytes, not the acute severe infection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: On day 5 of a febrile illness a teenager's fever settles but he develops severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, restlessness and cool peripheries. His haematocrit has risen 22% while the platelet count has fallen to 40,000/mm3. These 'warning signs' at defervescence most likely indicate:
options: Onset of bacterial sepsis needing immediate blood transfusion
The simple recovery phase needing only reassurance
Plasma leakage of the dengue critical phase requiring careful fluid therapy
questions.concept: In dengue the critical phase begins around defervescence (day 4-6): a rising haematocrit with a falling platelet count plus warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, restlessness) signals plasma leakage and impending shock, needing judicious isotonic fluid therapy and close monitoring. Aspirin/NSAIDs are avoided (bleeding risk) and routine transfusion is not the first response.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 24-year-old in diabetic ketoacidosis has ABG pH 7.22, HCO3 10 mmol/L and PaCO2 24 mmHg, with serum Na 138 and Cl 100 mmol/L. Using Winter's formula (expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8, plus or minus 2), how is the acid-base disturbance best classified?
options: High anion-gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Metabolic acidosis with a superimposed respiratory acidosis
questions.concept: Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3) = 138 - (100 + 10) = 28, i.e. raised, so this is a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis (ketoacids). Winter's formula predicts PaCO2 = 1.5 x 10 + 8 = 23, plus or minus 2 (range 21-25); the measured 24 lies within range, so respiratory compensation is appropriate rather than a separate respiratory disorder.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: An ECG from a patient with acute kidney injury and serum potassium 7.4 mmol/L shows tall, tented (peaked) T waves, flattened P waves and a progressively widening QRS approaching a sine-wave pattern. Which is the most appropriate IMMEDIATE first drug to give?
options: An oral or rectal potassium-binding resin
questions.concept: In severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, IV calcium gluconate is given FIRST to stabilise the myocardial membrane and prevent arrhythmia (it does not lower the potassium itself). Insulin-dextrose and salbutamol then shift potassium into cells, and resins or dialysis actually remove it from the body.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 70-year-old with small-cell lung cancer has confusion, serum Na 112 mmol/L, low serum osmolality, high urine osmolality and high urine sodium, and is clinically euvolaemic. While correcting the sodium, which complication must you prevent by limiting the rate of rise to roughly 8 mmol/L per 24 hours?
questions.concept: This is SIADH (euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and high urine Na). Over-rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia causes osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis), so correction is limited to about 6-8 mmol/L in 24 hours. Cerebral oedema instead results from OVER-fast lowering of sodium or from acute hyponatraemia.
questions.reference: Harrison's 21e - Hyponatraemia and Disorders of Sodium Balance

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy reports difficulty climbing stairs and cramps after exertion but still walks independently. He has calf pseudohypertrophy and a markedly raised serum creatine kinase; a maternal uncle had similar but milder weakness and lived into his 40s. Muscle biopsy shows reduced, patchy dystrophin staining rather than its complete absence. The diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Becker muscular dystrophy is an X-linked dystrophinopathy in which in-frame DMD gene mutations yield reduced or abnormal (but present) dystrophin, giving a LATER-onset, MILDER course with ambulation preserved into adulthood and a high CK. Duchenne has out-of-frame mutations with ABSENT dystrophin, onset at 3-5 years, and loss of walking by about 12.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A video shows a 4-year-old boy asked to stand up from the floor: he rolls prone, pushes onto his hands and feet, then 'walks' his hands up his own thighs to reach standing. He has bulky calves and a waddling gait. This manoeuvre and the most likely inheritance pattern are:
questions.concept: Using the hands to 'climb up' the legs when rising is Gower's sign, indicating proximal (pelvic-girdle) weakness - classically Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive dystrophinopathy with absent dystrophin and calf pseudohypertrophy. A Trendelenburg sign reflects hip-abductor weakness; a Romberg sign reflects proprioceptive/dorsal-column loss.
questions.reference: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics 21e / Harrison's 21e - Muscular Dystrophies

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has fluctuating drooping eyelids and double vision that worsen through the day and after sustained upgaze, plus fatigable proximal limb weakness that improves with rest. Reflexes and sensation are normal. Which antibody is most likely responsible?
questions.concept: Fatigable, fluctuating weakness with ptosis and diplopia that worsen with activity and improve with rest is myasthenia gravis, caused by anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibodies at the postsynaptic neuromuscular junction. Anti-VGCC antibodies instead cause Lambert-Eaton syndrome, in which power briefly IMPROVES with repeated effort and which is linked to small-cell lung cancer.
questions.reference: Harrison's 21e - Myasthenia Gravis and Other Diseases of the Neuromuscular Junction

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A video of a 60-year-old with acute onset shows vertigo and nystagmus, hoarseness, loss of pain and temperature on the LEFT side of the face and the RIGHT side of the body, ataxia of the left arm, a left partial ptosis with a small pupil, and difficulty swallowing - but no limb weakness. Which artery is most likely occluded?
options: Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (lateral medullary / Wallenberg syndrome)
questions.concept: Crossed sensory loss (ipsilateral face, contralateral body), ipsilateral Horner syndrome, ataxia, vertigo/nystagmus and bulbar signs (dysphagia, hoarseness) with NO limb weakness define the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, from posterior inferior cerebellar / vertebral artery occlusion. An MCA stroke instead causes contralateral face-and-arm weakness and, on the dominant side, aphasia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 68-year-old hypertensive man has sudden right-sided limb weakness. On examination the LEFT eye is deviated 'down and out' with ptosis and a dilated pupil, and there is a RIGHT-sided upper-motor-neuron facial and limb weakness. Where is the lesion?
questions.concept: An ipsilateral oculomotor (CN III) palsy - eye 'down and out', ptosis, dilated pupil - with contralateral hemiparesis localises to the midbrain (Weber syndrome), where the CN III fascicles and the descending corticospinal fibres lie together. A pure internal-capsule lacunar stroke causes contralateral hemiparesis WITHOUT a third-nerve palsy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 68-year-old with a COPD exacerbation is drowsy; ABG on 40% oxygen shows pH 7.28, PaCO2 68 mmHg, PaO2 60 mmHg and HCO3 34 mmol/L. Besides nebulised bronchodilators and steroids, what is the most appropriate next step for his type-2 respiratory failure?
options: Increase FiO2 to 100% via a non-rebreathe mask
Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) with controlled oxygen targeting SpO2 88-92%
questions.concept: This is acute-on-chronic hypercapnic (type-2) respiratory failure with a respiratory acidosis; non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) is indicated when pH is below 7.35 with hypercapnia despite medical therapy, and oxygen must be controlled (target SpO2 88-92%) to avoid worsening CO2 retention. Uncontrolled high-flow oxygen can precipitate CO2 narcosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 60-year-old lifelong smoker has a chronic productive cough and progressive exertional breathlessness. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC of 0.58, with the FEV1 improving only 6% after salbutamol. What does this spirometry best confirm?
options: Persistent (largely irreversible) airflow obstruction consistent with COPD
Reversible airflow obstruction typical of asthma
questions.concept: A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 that shows little reversibility (here only 6%) defines the fixed airflow obstruction of COPD. Asthma typically shows significant reversibility (a rise of 12% and at least 200 mL); a restrictive defect shows a reduced FVC with a preserved or raised FEV1/FVC ratio.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient two months into standard four-drug anti-tubercular therapy develops reduced visual acuity with impaired red-green colour discrimination, and separately reports tingling numbness of both feet. Which two drugs are most likely responsible, respectively?
questions.concept: Ethambutol classically causes dose-dependent retrobulbar (optic) neuritis with loss of visual acuity and red-green colour vision. Isoniazid causes a pyridoxine (B6)-responsive peripheral neuropathy, prevented or treated with vitamin B6. Option B simply swaps the two culprits; rifampicin causes orange secretions and hepatotoxicity, pyrazinamide hyperuricaemia and hepatotoxicity.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e - Antitubercular Drugs

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 25-year-old has three weeks of fever, weight loss and left-sided pleuritic chest pain with a unilateral pleural effusion. The aspirated pleural fluid is straw-coloured, an exudate, with lymphocyte predominance and a markedly raised adenosine deaminase (ADA). What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A transudative effusion from heart failure
questions.concept: A lymphocyte-predominant exudative pleural effusion with a high ADA in a young patient with constitutional symptoms strongly suggests tuberculous pleuritis. A bacterial parapneumonic effusion is neutrophil-predominant, while a heart-failure effusion is a transudate with low protein and LDH. Lymphocytosis plus high ADA are the key discriminators.
questions.reference: Harrison's 21e - Tuberculosis / Disorders of the Pleura

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A researcher compares the mean fasting blood glucose across THREE independent groups (drug A, drug B, placebo); within each group the values are approximately normally distributed with similar variances. Which statistical test is most appropriate to test whether the three group means differ?
questions.concept: Comparing the means of THREE or more independent, normally distributed groups uses one-way ANOVA; running multiple t-tests instead inflates the type-I error rate. The chi-square test is for categorical/proportional data, and a paired t-test is for two related (before-after) measurements on the same subjects.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a large sample, serum cholesterol follows a symmetrical bell-shaped (normal) distribution. Approximately what proportion of observations lies within the mean plus or minus 2 standard deviations, and how do the mean, median and mode compare in this distribution?
options: About 68%; mean is greater than median which is greater than mode
About 95%; mean equals median equals mode
About 99.7%; mean is less than median which is less than mode
About 50%; only the mean and median are equal
questions.concept: For a normal distribution about 68% of values lie within 1 SD, about 95% within 2 SD and about 99.7% within 3 SD of the mean; because it is symmetrical, the mean, median and mode coincide. Inequalities among the mean, median and mode instead indicate a skewed (non-normal) distribution.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e - Normal Distribution

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: During measles-control planning, the basic reproduction number (R0) of measles is taken as 15. Using the herd-immunity-threshold formula (1 minus 1/R0), what approximate proportion of the population must be immune to interrupt sustained transmission?
questions.concept: The herd immunity threshold equals 1 minus 1/R0. For measles with an R0 of about 15 that is 1 minus 1/15 = 0.933, i.e. roughly 93% of the population must be immune to stop sustained transmission - which is why measles needs very high vaccination coverage. Diseases with a lower R0 need a lower threshold.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e - Principles of Epidemiology / Immunising Agents

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A college student is admitted with meningococcal meningitis. His roommate, who shared the dormitory, asks what he should take to reduce his own risk of the disease. Which is the most appropriate chemoprophylaxis for close household or dormitory contacts?
options: Rifampicin (or a single dose of ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone)
No prophylaxis; only observe the contact
questions.concept: Close contacts of meningococcal disease receive chemoprophylaxis to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage - rifampicin, or a single dose of ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone. Amoxicillin and isoniazid are not used for meningococcal prophylaxis, and simple observation misses the narrow window to prevent secondary cases.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e - Meningococcal Meningitis

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a demographic report a country has a Net Reproduction Rate (NRR) of exactly 1.0. What does this value indicate about the population's long-term replacement?
options: The population will double within one generation
Each generation of mothers is exactly replaced by one surviving daughter (replacement level)
The crude birth rate equals the crude death rate this year
The total fertility rate must be zero
questions.concept: The NRR is the average number of daughters a woman would bear who survive to reproductive age, allowing for mortality. An NRR of 1 is exactly replacement level (each mother replaced by one surviving daughter); above 1 means growth and below 1 means eventual decline. It is not the same as equal crude birth and death rates in a single year.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e - Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A new contraceptive method is evaluated in a trial and reported to have a Pearl Index of 0.3. What does this figure represent, and how effective is the method?
options: 0.3 pregnancies (failures) per 100 woman-years of use - a highly effective method
30 failures per 100 users in the first month
A relative risk of 0.3 for side-effects
questions.concept: The Pearl Index expresses contraceptive failure as the number of unintended pregnancies per 100 woman-years of exposure; a LOWER value means HIGHER efficacy. A Pearl Index of 0.3 therefore indicates a very effective method (comparable to an IUD or implant). It is a failure rate, not a measure of preference or of side-effects.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e - Contraceptive Methods

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A photograph shows colour-coded biomedical-waste bins in a hospital operating under India's Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016. Used needles, syringes with fixed needles and scalpel blades (sharps) should be discarded into which colour-coded, puncture-proof container?
questions.concept: VERIFY: confirm against the CURRENT Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules 2016 (as amended) colour code before trusting this key, as categories are policy-set and periodically revised. As authored: sharps (needles, blades) go to a WHITE translucent puncture-proof container; yellow = anatomical/soiled/pathological waste; red = contaminated recyclable plastics (tubing, IV sets); blue = discarded glassware and metallic implants.
questions.reference: Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 (India) - CONFIRM current amended schedule

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A field medical officer chlorinates a village well after a diarrhoeal outbreak. To ensure adequate disinfection, what minimum free residual chlorine should remain after the recommended contact period, and how long is that contact period?
options: 0.5 mg/L free residual chlorine after a contact period of about 1 hour
5 mg/L free residual chlorine after just 5 minutes
No residual is required if the water looks clear
questions.concept: For effective chlorination the classic standard is a free residual chlorine of about 0.5 mg/L after a minimum contact period of roughly 1 hour, which kills most pathogens including Vibrio cholerae. The measurable residual is what confirms adequate disinfection; the clarity of the water does not guarantee microbiological safety.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e - Water Purification (Chlorination)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: An epidemic-curve histogram of an acute gastroenteritis outbreak shows a single sharp peak: cases rise abruptly, peak within the span of one incubation period of the pathogen, and fall rapidly, with no secondary waves. Which type of epidemic does this pattern most suggest?
options: A continuous common-source epidemic over months
questions.concept: A single sharp peak with all cases occurring within one incubation period indicates a point-source (common-source, single-exposure) epidemic - for example a contaminated meal at one event. A propagated epidemic instead shows successive rising peaks about one incubation period apart from person-to-person spread, and a continuous common source produces a prolonged plateau.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e - Epidemiology (Types of Epidemic)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Investigators studying a rare cancer enrol 100 patients who already have the cancer and 200 matched people without it, then compare their past exposure to a suspected chemical. Which study design is this, and which measure of association can it directly yield?
options: A case-control study; the odds ratio
A cohort study; the relative risk
A randomised controlled trial; the absolute risk reduction
A cross-sectional study; the prevalence ratio
questions.concept: Selecting subjects by disease status (cases versus controls) and looking BACK at exposure is a case-control study - efficient for rare diseases and yielding an odds ratio. Incidence and relative risk require a cohort design (subjects selected by exposure and followed forward); a case-control study cannot directly measure incidence.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e - Epidemiological Study Designs

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A screening test with a fixed sensitivity of 95% and specificity of 90% is applied first in a high-prevalence clinic population and then in a low-prevalence general population. As the disease prevalence falls, what happens to the test's positive predictive value (PPV), and why?
options: PPV rises, because specificity increases when prevalence is low
PPV is unchanged, because it depends only on sensitivity and specificity
PPV falls, because a larger share of the positives are false positives when prevalence is low
questions.concept: Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic to the test and do not change with prevalence, but the PPV DOES depend on prevalence: as prevalence falls, a larger fraction of positive results are false positives, so the PPV declines. This is why screening a low-prevalence population produces many false-positive results.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e - Screening for Disease (Predictive Values)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: During cold-chain planning for the immunization programme, a health officer must classify vaccines by their heat and freeze sensitivity. Which of the following statements about vaccine thermostability is correct?
options: All vaccines are equally stable at room temperature
OPV is freeze-sensitive and must never be frozen
BCG is the most heat-stable vaccine and can be kept at room temperature
Oral polio vaccine is the most heat-sensitive, whereas DPT, hepatitis B and TT are damaged by freezing
questions.concept: OPV is the MOST heat-sensitive vaccine and is kept at the coldest point/frozen, whereas the adsorbed vaccines - DPT, DT, TT and hepatitis B - are damaged by FREEZING and must be held at 2-8 C. Cold-chain failure destroys potency, and the shake test detects freeze-damaged adsorbed vaccines. These thermostability properties are intrinsic to each vaccine (not schedule-dependent).
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e - Cold Chain and Immunization

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Under India's Universal Immunization Programme, a mother brings her newborn on the day of birth after an institutional delivery. Which set of vaccines is scheduled to be given at birth?
options: BCG, oral polio vaccine (OPV-0) and the hepatitis B birth dose
questions.concept: VERIFY: confirm against the CURRENT National Immunization Schedule (MoHFW / UIP) before trusting this key, as the birth-dose composition and timing are periodically revised. As authored, the institutional-delivery birth dose comprises BCG, OPV-0 and the hepatitis B birth dose; DPT/pentavalent and measles-containing doses are given later in infancy.
questions.reference: National Immunization Schedule, UIP (MoHFW, India) - CONFIRM current schedule

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A photograph shows a 2-year-old with bilateral pitting pedal oedema, a distended abdomen, sparse depigmented 'flag-sign' hair, a moon face and marked apathy; weight is about 65% of that expected for age with relatively preserved subcutaneous fat. Which form of severe acute malnutrition does this best represent?
questions.concept: Oedema (the defining feature), skin and hair depigmentation (flag sign), a moon face, hepatomegaly with a distended abdomen and apathy - with relatively preserved subcutaneous fat - characterise kwashiorkor (predominantly protein deficiency). Marasmus instead shows gross wasting, a wizened 'old-man' face and NO oedema, usually with weight below 60% of expected.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e - Protein-Energy Malnutrition

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A poor patient whose staple diet is maize develops a photosensitive pigmented dermatitis over sun-exposed skin (including a 'Casal's necklace'), chronic diarrhoea and progressive dementia. Deficiency of which vitamin is responsible, and why is a maize-based diet a particular risk?
options: Vitamin C; maize is devoid of ascorbate
Niacin (vitamin B3); maize niacin is bound and poorly bioavailable and maize is low in tryptophan
Vitamin D; maize blocks its cutaneous synthesis
questions.concept: The triad of dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia (the 3 D's) with a 'Casal's necklace' is pellagra, due to niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency. Maize-based diets predispose because their niacin is bound (as niacytin) and poorly available and maize is low in tryptophan, a niacin precursor. Untreated pellagra can progress to death (the fourth D).

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Under India's national tuberculosis programme, a newly diagnosed pulmonary TB patient is to begin supervised treatment. Which statement about the current programme's diagnostic and treatment strategy is authored here for confirmation against the latest guidelines?
options: It relies only on sputum microscopy and thrice-weekly therapy, with no molecular testing
It uses chest X-ray alone to confirm every case
The programme (now NTEP) uses rapid molecular tests such as CBNAAT/Truenat for diagnosis and daily fixed-dose-combination therapy under supervised DOTS
questions.concept: VERIFY: confirm the CURRENT programme name, diagnostic algorithm and drug regimen (NTEP, formerly RNTCP) against the latest MoHFW/NTEP guidelines before trusting this key, as programme names, schedules and targets are revised periodically. As authored, NTEP emphasises rapid molecular diagnostics (CBNAAT/Truenat) and daily fixed-dose-combination therapy under supervised DOTS.
questions.reference: National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP), MoHFW, India - CONFIRM current guidelines

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A newly posted medical officer is briefed on the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme delivered through the Anganwadi centre. Which package of services is authored here as ICDS's core offering, for confirmation against current guidelines?
options: Supplementary nutrition, immunization, health check-up, referral services, nutrition and health education, and pre-school non-formal education
Only supplementary nutrition to pregnant women
Only hospital treatment of severe acute malnutrition
questions.concept: VERIFY: confirm the current ICDS service package and beneficiary definitions against the latest Ministry of Women & Child Development guidelines, as scheme details are periodically revised. As authored, ICDS delivers six services via the Anganwadi - supplementary nutrition, immunization, health check-up, referral, nutrition and health education, and pre-school non-formal education - targeting under-6 children plus pregnant and lactating women.
questions.reference: ICDS scheme, Ministry of Women & Child Development, India - CONFIRM current package

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, recurrent pregnancy loss
questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with 7 weeks of amenorrhoea and prior pelvic inflammatory disease presents with sudden severe left iliac fossa pain, one episode of syncope and right shoulder-tip pain. BP is 80/50 mmHg with tachycardia; there is cervical motion tenderness and fullness in the pouch of Douglas. Serum beta-hCG is 2600 and transvaginal scan shows an empty uterus with a left adnexal mass and free fluid. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Repeat serum beta-hCG in 48 hours and observe
questions.concept: Shoulder-tip pain, shock and free fluid indicate a RUPTURED ectopic pregnancy; the priority is resuscitation and immediate surgery (salpingectomy for the unstable patient). Methotrexate is only for a stable, unruptured ectopic meeting strict criteria and is unsafe here.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, recurrent pregnancy loss
questions.stem: A haemodynamically stable 28-year-old woman has an unruptured right tubal ectopic pregnancy: serum beta-hCG 1800, adnexal mass 2.5 cm with no fetal cardiac activity, no free fluid, and normal CBC, liver and renal function, with reliable follow-up assured. Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Emergency laparotomy with total abdominal hysterectomy
Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate with serial beta-hCG monitoring
questions.concept: Medical management with single-dose methotrexate is appropriate for a stable, unruptured ectopic when beta-hCG is low (roughly <5000, ideally <3500), the mass is small (<3.5-4 cm), there is no fetal cardiac activity or significant free fluid, and organ function and follow-up are adequate. Hysterectomy is never indicated for a tubal ectopic.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Obstetrics 9e (Ectopic pregnancy - medical management)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, recurrent pregnancy loss
questions.stem: A transvaginal ultrasound in an asymptomatic woman at 8 weeks by dates shows a single intrauterine gestational sac with a mean sac diameter of 26 mm containing no yolk sac and no fetal pole; a repeat scan confirms the same findings. The most appropriate diagnosis is:
options: Anembryonic pregnancy (missed miscarriage) - offer expectant, medical or surgical evacuation
Viable early intrauterine pregnancy - rescan in one week
questions.concept: A gestational sac with mean diameter >=25 mm and no embryo (or a fetal pole >=7 mm with no cardiac activity) is diagnostic of early pregnancy failure - here anembryonic pregnancy. It is confirmed and management options (expectant, medical with misoprostol, or suction evacuation) can be offered; it is not viable, so rescanning is not required for the diagnosis.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Obstetrics 9e (Abortion) / Society of Radiologists in Ultrasound criteria

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, recurrent pregnancy loss
questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has had three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages and one second-trimester fetal loss, plus a past deep vein thrombosis. Investigations show a prolonged aPTT that fails to correct on mixing, with lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies positive on two occasions 12 weeks apart. What is the most appropriate treatment in her next pregnancy?
questions.concept: This is antiphospholipid syndrome causing recurrent pregnancy loss; the evidence-based treatment is low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic heparin (LMWH) started in early pregnancy. Warfarin is teratogenic (warfarin embryopathy) and is avoided; steroids and IVIG are not first-line for obstetric APS.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Obstetrics 9e (Recurrent pregnancy loss / antiphospholipid syndrome)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, recurrent pregnancy loss
questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman at 10 weeks of pregnancy presents with heavy vaginal bleeding and passage of clots. The cervical os is open with products of conception visible at the os, the uterus is smaller than the period of amenorrhoea, and she is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassurance, bed rest and repeat scan in one week
Suction evacuation of retained products of conception
questions.concept: An open os with products at the os and a uterus smaller than dates indicates INCOMPLETE miscarriage; with ongoing heavy bleeding, prompt surgical evacuation (suction) is appropriate. Reassurance/rest is for THREATENED miscarriage (closed os, live fetus); cerclage treats cervical insufficiency, not an incomplete miscarriage.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman requesting contraception has migraine WITH aura but no other risk factors. She is keen on the combined oral contraceptive pill. Which is the single most important reason to refuse the combined pill and offer an alternative?
options: Combined (oestrogen-containing) pills are contraindicated - migraine with aura markedly increases ischaemic stroke risk
Combined pills reduce menstrual bleeding, which would mask her migraine
Combined pills are simply less effective than a progestogen-only pill
Combined pills always cause weight gain in migraineurs
questions.concept: Migraine WITH aura is a WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria category 4 (unacceptable risk) condition for combined hormonal contraceptives because oestrogen further raises the already-elevated ischaemic stroke risk. Safer choices are progestogen-only methods, the copper IUCD or barrier methods. Efficacy and weight change are not the governing concern here.
questions.reference: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria 5e / DC Dutta's Gynaecology 7e (Contraception)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman who is 3 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding wants reliable ongoing contraception. Which is the most appropriate option, and why should the combined oral contraceptive pill be avoided at this time?
options: Combined oral contraceptive pill - it is fully safe immediately postpartum
No contraception is needed while she is breastfeeding
Progestogen-only pill or an intrauterine device - oestrogen this early postpartum carries a high venous thromboembolism risk
Only barrier methods are ever acceptable during lactation
questions.concept: In the early postpartum period (before ~6 weeks) and while breastfeeding, oestrogen-containing pills are avoided (WHO MEC category 4) because of high venous thromboembolism risk. Progestogen-only methods and the IUCD are preferred. Lactational amenorrhoea alone is not reliable ongoing contraception.
questions.reference: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria 5e / DC Dutta's Gynaecology 7e (Postpartum contraception)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A primigravida at term has been in labour for several hours; over 4 hours the cervix remains at 6 cm with ruptured membranes. Contractions are infrequent and weak (2 in 10 minutes), there is no fetal distress and no evidence of cephalopelvic disproportion, but the cervicograph has crossed the alert line. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.concept: This is primary dysfunctional (hypotonic) labour - inadequate uterine activity with no CPD and a reassuring fetus - so oxytocin augmentation (with amniotomy if needed) is appropriate. Caesarean/forceps are not justified without CPD, fetal distress or a fully dilated cervix; simple observation would prolong an already abnormal labour.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: During labour at 6 cm dilatation, shortly after spontaneous rupture of membranes, a loop of pulsating umbilical cord is felt in the vagina below the presenting part and the fetal heart rate falls to 80/min. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Knee-chest/Trendelenburg position, manually elevate the presenting part off the cord, and arrange immediate delivery (usually caesarean)
Reduce the cord above the presenting part and await vaginal delivery
Start oxytocin augmentation to hasten delivery
Continue labour and reassess in one hour
questions.concept: Overt cord prolapse with fetal bradycardia is an acute emergency: relieve cord compression (elevate the presenting part, knee-chest or Trendelenburg position, fill the bladder) and expedite delivery, almost always by immediate caesarean section. Handling the cord causes vasospasm, and oxytocin/waiting worsens hypoxia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 34-week primigravida with known pre-eclampsia develops right upper quadrant pain and nausea. Investigations show haemolysis (schistocytes on smear, LDH 700 U/L), AST 150 U/L and a platelet count of 78,000/microL. What is the diagnosis and definitive management?
options: Gestational thrombocytopenia; reassure and continue pregnancy
HELLP syndrome; stabilise the mother (including magnesium sulfate) and deliver
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura; give steroids and continue to term
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy; treat with antivirals
questions.concept: Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelets in a pre-eclamptic woman define HELLP syndrome, a severe variant of pre-eclampsia. Definitive treatment is delivery after maternal stabilisation (control BP, magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis). Gestational thrombocytopenia is mild and isolated without haemolysis or liver derangement.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Obstetrics 9e (Hypertensive disorders - HELLP syndrome)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 36-week woman with severe pre-eclampsia presents with sudden continuous abdominal pain and a tense, tender, 'woody' hard uterus. Vaginal bleeding is minimal, fetal heart sounds are absent, and she is in shock that seems out of proportion to the visible blood loss. What is the diagnosis and the key complication to anticipate?
options: Abruptio placentae with concealed haemorrhage; anticipate disseminated intravascular coagulation
Vasa previa; anticipate fetal exsanguination only
Uterine rupture; anticipate amniotic fluid embolism
questions.concept: A painful, tense, tender uterus with shock disproportionate to external bleeding indicates abruptio placentae with concealed haemorrhage (associated with pre-eclampsia). Retroplacental clot consumes clotting factors, so DIC is the key complication. Placenta previa is classically PAINLESS with a soft, relaxed uterus.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Obstetrics 9e (Antepartum haemorrhage - abruptio placentae)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old nulliparous woman with infertility has severe secondary dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and cyclical painful defaecation. On examination the uterus is fixed and retroverted with tender nodules palpable in the pouch of Douglas along the uterosacral ligaments. What is the diagnosis and the gold-standard method to confirm it?
options: Pelvic inflammatory disease; confirmed by high vaginal swab culture
Endometriosis; confirmed by diagnostic laparoscopy with visualisation and biopsy
Ovarian carcinoma; confirmed by serum CA-125
questions.concept: Secondary dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, cyclical dyschezia, infertility and tender uterosacral/pouch-of-Douglas nodules are classic for endometriosis; laparoscopy (with visualisation and histological confirmation) is the diagnostic gold standard. CA-125 may be raised but is non-specific, and endometrial biopsy diagnoses adenomyosis/endometrial pathology, not endometriosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 42-year-old parous woman has progressively worsening heavy, painful periods. The uterus is diffusely and symmetrically enlarged, tender and 'boggy'. Transvaginal ultrasound shows myometrial heterogeneity with a thickened, indistinct endometrial-myometrial junctional zone and no discrete mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A diffusely enlarged, tender, boggy uterus with menorrhagia and dysmenorrhoea, plus junctional-zone thickening without a discrete mass, is characteristic of adenomyosis (endometrial glands within the myometrium). A fibroid is typically a firm, discrete, whorled mass; endometrial carcinoma usually presents with postmenopausal bleeding.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 32-year-old asymptomatic, sexually active woman with no prior abnormal results attends for routine cervical cancer screening. According to current recommended screening for an average-risk woman aged 30 or older, which approach and interval is most appropriate?
options: Annual Pap (cytology) smear for life beginning at first intercourse
Primary HPV-DNA testing every 5 years (or HPV/cytology co-testing every 5 years, or cytology alone every 3 years)
No screening is required unless she becomes symptomatic
Colposcopy every year regardless of prior results
questions.concept: VERIFY: confirm the CURRENT nationally recommended cervical screening test and interval before shipping this item - guidance is guideline- and currency-dependent and differs between bodies (WHO 2021 favours primary HPV-DNA testing every 5-10 years from age 30; USPSTF/ACOG allow HPV, co-testing or 3-yearly cytology; and India's operational framework has historically used VIA-based screening). The stem's 5-yearly HPV-based answer reflects international guidance but must be checked against the latest MoHFW/ICMR program recommendation.
questions.reference: WHO Guideline for screening and treatment of cervical pre-cancer 2021 (CONFIRM current national/ICMR-MoHFW interval)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 50-year-old multiparous woman with biopsy-proven squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix has parametrial disease extending to the pelvic side wall. She now develops bilateral hydronephrosis with a rising serum creatinine. Which is the most common cause of death in advanced carcinoma cervix, exemplified by this patient?
options: Uraemia from bilateral ureteric obstruction (renal failure)
questions.concept: Carcinoma cervix spreads by direct/lateral extension into the parametrium and can encase both ureters, causing bilateral obstruction, hydronephrosis and death from uraemia (renal failure) - the classic commonest mode of death. Side-wall extension with hydronephrosis also defines advanced (stage IIIB) disease. Distant visceral metastases are comparatively late and less often the terminal event.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A pelvic ultrasound in a 55-year-old postmenopausal woman with abdominal distension shows a complex solid-cystic right adnexal mass with thick septations and papillary projections, ascites and omental 'caking'; serum CA-125 is markedly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis and the commonest histological type?
options: Epithelial ovarian carcinoma - serous cystadenocarcinoma is the commonest type
Dysgerminoma - the commonest ovarian malignancy overall
Bilateral Krukenberg (metastatic) tumours from the stomach
questions.concept: A complex solid-cystic adnexal mass with ascites, omental caking and a high CA-125 in a postmenopausal woman is typical of epithelial ovarian carcinoma, of which serous cystadenocarcinoma is the commonest histological subtype. Dysgerminoma and granulosa cell tumours occur in younger women; Krukenberg tumours are characteristically bilateral with signet-ring cells from a GI primary.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Gynaecology 7e (Ovarian tumours) / Robbins Pathology

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: After a vaginal delivery a woman has continuing atonic postpartum haemorrhage despite uterine massage, intravenous oxytocin, methylergometrine and carboprost. The genital tract has been fully explored with no trauma and no retained tissue, and she remains haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the same course of uterotonics and wait
Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade (e.g. condom/Bakri balloon)
Discharge to the ward for observation
questions.concept: When first-line uterotonics fail in atonic PPH and tissue/trauma are excluded, the next step in the stepwise ladder is a minimally invasive intrauterine balloon tamponade, followed if needed by surgical measures (B-Lynch suture, uterine/internal iliac artery ligation), with hysterectomy reserved as the last resort. Simply repeating uterotonics wastes time.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Obstetrics 9e / FIGO PPH management guideline

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A multigravida with two previous caesarean sections has an anterior placenta previa in this pregnancy. Antenatal ultrasound and MRI suggest the placenta has invaded the myometrium, placing her at high risk of torrential haemorrhage at delivery. What is this condition, and what is the most appropriate planned management?
options: Placenta accreta spectrum; planned caesarean hysterectomy leaving the placenta in situ (no forcible removal)
Simple uterine atony; plan oxytocin infusion alone at delivery
Placental abruption; plan expectant outpatient management
questions.concept: A previa overlying previous caesarean scars with myometrial invasion is placenta accreta spectrum. The safest plan is a scheduled caesarean, often with caesarean hysterectomy leaving the placenta in situ; attempting to forcibly separate an accreta provokes catastrophic haemorrhage. This is a Tissue (adherent placenta) cause, distinct from simple atony.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Obstetrics 9e (Morbidly adherent placenta / placenta previa)

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A WHO growth chart for a 9-month-old shows the weight-for-age curve falling from the 50th percentile to below the 3rd percentile over 3 months, while length-for-age and head-circumference-for-age remain steady on the 50th percentile. This pattern most strongly suggests:
options: Inadequate caloric intake / failure to thrive
questions.concept: In under-nutrition/failure to thrive, WEIGHT falters first, then length, and finally head circumference - exactly this pattern. Endocrine causes such as hypothyroidism impair LENGTH out of proportion to weight, and genetic/constitutional short stature affects length/height with a proportionate, non-crossing weight curve.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e (Growth & its assessment)

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A clinical video shows a 15-month-old who previously sat, babbled and smiled socially but now cannot sit unsupported, has stopped babbling and no longer smiles responsively; there is increasing limb stiffness with brisk deep tendon reflexes. Which single feature is the most concerning and mandates urgent neurological evaluation?
options: Loss of previously acquired milestones (developmental regression)
Not yet walking independently at 15 months
questions.concept: Developmental REGRESSION - loss of previously attained milestones - is a major red flag suggesting a neurodegenerative or metabolic disorder and needs urgent work-up. Not walking at 15 months can still be within normal limits (red flag is >18 months), and stranger anxiety is a normal finding around this age.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e (Development - warning signs)

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 2-year-old with severe acute malnutrition (weight-for-height below -3 SD with bilateral pitting pedal oedema) is admitted lethargic and cold to touch. During the initial stabilisation phase of WHO-based management, which pair of complications is the most important immediate threat to prevent?
questions.concept: In severe acute malnutrition the early killers are hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration and infection; management begins with frequent feeds, keeping the child warm, and treating/anticipating infection. High-protein diets and iron are deliberately withheld in the stabilisation phase (iron can worsen infection and free-radical injury; over-rapid feeding risks refeeding syndrome).
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e / WHO 10 steps for severe acute malnutrition

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 14-month-old exclusively breastfed child with minimal sun exposure has bow legs, a rachitic rosary, widened wrists, a delayed anterior fontanelle closure and delayed dentition. Wrist X-ray shows cupping and fraying of the metaphyses. Which deficiency is responsible and what is the characteristic biochemistry?
options: Vitamin D deficiency; low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, raised parathyroid hormone
Vitamin C deficiency; normal alkaline phosphatase with subperiosteal haemorrhage
Vitamin A deficiency; hypercalcaemia with normal phosphate
Vitamin K deficiency; low alkaline phosphatase with bleeding
questions.concept: Bow legs, rachitic rosary, widened wrists with metaphyseal cupping/fraying and delayed fontanelle closure define nutritional rickets from vitamin D deficiency (breastfed, low sun exposure). Biochemistry: low/normal calcium, low phosphate, HIGH alkaline phosphatase and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Scurvy (vitamin C) causes bleeding with a normal ALP.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e (Vitamin D deficiency / rickets)

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A chest radiograph of a 32-week preterm neonate who developed grunting, nasal flaring, tachypnoea and intercostal recession within hours of birth shows low lung volumes with a diffuse fine reticulogranular ('ground-glass') pattern and air bronchograms. What is the most likely diagnosis and its underlying cause?
options: Meconium aspiration syndrome; airway obstruction by meconium
Respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease); pulmonary surfactant deficiency
Transient tachypnoea of the newborn; delayed clearance of lung fluid
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia; abdominal viscera in the chest
questions.concept: A preterm neonate with early respiratory distress and a ground-glass, air-bronchogram X-ray has respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease) due to surfactant deficiency; treatment is antenatal steroids for prevention, plus surfactant and respiratory support. Transient tachypnoea is usually mild, in term/near-term babies, and shows fluid in the fissures rather than diffuse ground-glass change.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e (Respiratory distress in the newborn)

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A term neonate born after prolonged rupture of membranes (over 18 hours) develops temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy and reduced tone at 30 hours of life. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Reassure the mother and observe without intervention
Start oral antibiotics and discharge home
Delay all treatment until blood culture turns positive
Draw blood culture, CBC and CRP and start empirical intravenous antibiotics for early-onset sepsis
questions.concept: Prolonged rupture of membranes plus clinical deterioration in the first 72 hours signals early-onset neonatal sepsis; the standard is a septic screen (culture, CBC, CRP) with immediate empirical IV antibiotics, because delay markedly increases mortality. Waiting for culture positivity or using oral antibiotics is unsafe in a sick neonate.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: An unimmunised 5-year-old has a sore throat, low-grade fever and a greyish adherent membrane over the tonsils and pharynx that bleeds when scraped, together with marked 'bull-neck' cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the causative organism and its most dangerous systemic complication?
questions.concept: A bleeding, adherent grey pseudomembrane with a 'bull neck' in an unimmunised child is diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae). Its exotoxin causes myocarditis (the leading cause of death) and neuropathy such as palatal palsy; treatment is prompt antitoxin plus antibiotics. Forcible removal of the membrane causes bleeding, a useful distinguishing clue.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 1-year-old with acute watery diarrhoea is restless and irritable, has sunken eyes, drinks water eagerly when offered, and a skin pinch that goes back slowly. Using the WHO/IMNCI classification, what is the degree of dehydration and the appropriate treatment plan?
options: No dehydration; home fluids under Plan A
Some dehydration; supervised oral rehydration solution under Plan B
Severe dehydration; intravenous fluids under Plan C
questions.concept: Restlessness/irritability, sunken eyes, eager drinking and a slow skin pinch place the child in the 'some dehydration' category, managed with supervised oral rehydration solution (Plan B). 'Severe dehydration' (Plan C, IV fluids) requires signs such as lethargy/unconsciousness, inability to drink and a very slow skin pinch.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e / WHO-IMNCI diarrhoea management

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, not on anticoagulation, develops sudden severe, diffuse abdominal pain that is strikingly out of proportion to a soft, minimally tender abdomen. Over the next hours he passes bloody diarrhoea and develops a rising serum lactate with metabolic acidosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute mesenteric ischaemia (superior mesenteric artery embolism)
questions.concept: Pain out of proportion to examination findings in a patient with atrial fibrillation, progressing to bloody stool and lactic (metabolic) acidosis, is classic for acute mesenteric ischaemia, usually an SMA embolism from the fibrillating atrium. A perforated ulcer gives early board-like rigidity, not a deceptively soft abdomen.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love 27e (Intestinal ischaemia / the acute abdomen)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A patient being managed conservatively for adhesive small-bowel obstruction, initially with colicky central pain, now develops CONTINUOUS severe pain, tachycardia, fever, localised tenderness with guarding, and a rising white cell count. What does this change most likely indicate and what is the correct management?
options: Strangulation with bowel ischaemia; proceed to urgent surgery
Paralytic ileus; treat with prokinetics only
questions.concept: A shift from intermittent colic to continuous pain with fever, tachycardia, localised peritonism and leucocytosis signals strangulation/ischaemia of the obstructed segment - an indication for urgent operative intervention. These 'red flag' features distinguish a complicated obstruction from a simple one that may be managed conservatively.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A clinical photograph shows the breast of a 45-year-old non-lactating woman: it is diffusely erythematous, warm and oedematous with prominent 'peau d'orange' skin over more than a third of the breast, but no discrete lump is palpable. There has been no response to a course of antibiotics. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A rapidly progressive, warm, erythematous, oedematous breast with peau d'orange affecting a large area, no discrete mass and no response to antibiotics in a non-lactating woman is inflammatory breast carcinoma (T4d), due to tumour emboli obstructing dermal lymphatics. It is aggressive and needs urgent biopsy, not further antibiotics; true mastitis/abscess occurs typically during lactation and responds to treatment.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A woman with early invasive breast carcinoma that is clinically node-negative is planned for breast-conserving surgery. What is the standard method to stage the axilla while minimising the lymphoedema and morbidity associated with full axillary clearance?
options: Complete axillary lymph node dissection in every case
Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the primary tumour only
questions.concept: For a clinically node-negative early breast cancer, sentinel lymph node biopsy accurately stages the axilla while sparing most women the lymphoedema and morbidity of a full axillary dissection; completion clearance is reserved for significant sentinel-node involvement. Routine complete clearance in all cases is now avoided.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with known gallstones develops right upper quadrant pain, high fever with rigors and jaundice, and then becomes hypotensive and confused. What is the diagnosis, and after resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics, what is the definitive intervention?
options: Acute cholangitis; urgent biliary drainage, typically by ERCP
Uncomplicated acute cholecystitis; interval cholecystectomy in 6 weeks only
Acute viral hepatitis; supportive management alone
Amoebic liver abscess; oral metronidazole alone
questions.concept: Charcot's triad (RUQ pain, fever/rigors, jaundice) progressing to hypotension and confusion (Reynolds pentad) indicates acute cholangitis from an obstructed, infected biliary tree. After resuscitation and antibiotics, the definitive step is urgent biliary decompression/drainage, usually by ERCP. Delaying to a purely elective plan is inappropriate for a septic patient.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with severe alcohol-induced acute pancreatitis has persistent organ dysfunction; a contrast CT on day 4 shows extensive pancreatic necrosis that is not infected. Which early management approach best improves his outcome?
options: Prophylactic antibiotics for all sterile necrosis
Aggressive early fluid resuscitation with organ support, avoiding routine prophylactic antibiotics and early surgery
Prolonged complete starvation with no enteral nutrition
questions.concept: Early management of severe acute pancreatitis is supportive: aggressive fluid resuscitation, analgesia and organ support, with (where tolerated) early enteral nutrition. Routine prophylactic antibiotics for STERILE necrosis are not recommended, and surgery/necrosectomy is deferred and reserved mainly for infected necrosis, ideally after several weeks (step-up approach).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 30-year-old with a firm thyroid nodule reports episodic headaches, palpitations and sweating with paroxysmal hypertension, and has a family history of thyroid cancer. FNAC shows tumour cells in an amyloid stroma and serum calcitonin is markedly raised. What is the diagnosis, and which coexisting tumour must be excluded before any thyroid surgery?
options: Medullary thyroid carcinoma (part of MEN 2A); exclude and treat a phaeochromocytoma first
Papillary thyroid carcinoma; no additional work-up needed
Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma; proceed straight to surgery
questions.concept: Amyloid-containing FNAC with a high calcitonin indicates medullary thyroid carcinoma (from parafollicular C cells), here within MEN 2A. A coexisting phaeochromocytoma MUST be excluded (metanephrines) and, if present, resected FIRST - operating on the thyroid before controlling the phaeochromocytoma risks a fatal hypertensive crisis.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love 27e (The thyroid gland - medullary carcinoma / MEN 2)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: About 24 hours after a total thyroidectomy, a woman develops circumoral and fingertip tingling and painful carpopedal spasm. Tapping over the facial nerve produces twitching of the facial muscles. What is the most likely cause and the immediate management?
options: Hypocalcaemia from inadvertent parathyroid injury/removal; give intravenous calcium gluconate
Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy; immediate re-exploration
questions.concept: Perioral/peripheral paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm and a positive Chvostek's sign after total thyroidectomy indicate acute HYPOCALCAEMIA from damage to or removal of the parathyroid glands; management is intravenous calcium gluconate (with later oral calcium/vitamin D). Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy causes voice/airway problems, not tetany.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love 27e (The thyroid gland - complications of thyroidectomy)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy has sudden severe left testicular pain of 3 hours' duration with nausea. The left testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie and is exquisitely tender, and the cremasteric reflex is absent on that side. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Scrotal support and analgesia with review in 48 hours
Doppler ultrasound and reassess the following morning
Immediate surgical exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy
questions.concept: Sudden pain with a high-riding, horizontal, tender testis and an absent cremasteric reflex is testicular torsion - a surgical emergency requiring IMMEDIATE exploration and bilateral orchidopexy, since the testis is best salvaged within about 6 hours. When the picture is classic, do not delay for imaging; epididymo-orchitis is a dangerous misdiagnosis here.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has a reducible groin swelling that appears on standing or coughing and disappears on lying down. After it is reduced, occluding the deep inguinal ring (at the mid-point of the inguinal ligament) prevents it from reappearing on coughing. What type of hernia is this and what is the preferred repair?
options: Femoral hernia; a McVay repair is mandatory
Direct inguinal hernia; no repair is required
Indirect inguinal hernia; tension-free mesh hernioplasty (Lichtenstein)
Incisional hernia; conservative management with a truss
questions.concept: If occluding the DEEP inguinal ring controls the hernia (it does not reappear on coughing), it is an INDIRECT inguinal hernia passing through the deep ring; a DIRECT hernia would still bulge medially through Hesselbach's triangle despite ring occlusion. The standard elective treatment is a tension-free mesh (Lichtenstein) repair.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis vomits large volumes of fresh blood; endoscopy shows bleeding varices at the lower end of the oesophagus. The porto-systemic anastomosis that has opened up connects the portal-drained left gastric vein with which systemic vein?
options: Oesophageal tributaries of the azygos vein
questions.concept: Oesophageal varices form at the gastro-oesophageal porto-systemic anastomosis, where the left gastric (portal) vein communicates with oesophageal tributaries of the azygos (systemic) system; portal hypertension reverses flow into these thin submucosal veins, which rupture. The superior-to-inferior rectal channel instead produces rectal varices, not oesophageal ones.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 40-year-old develops hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, an absent gag reflex on the right and weakness of the right trapezius and sternocleidomastoid. A mass is found eroding the base of the skull. Injury to nerves passing through which foramen best explains this cluster (Vernet syndrome)?
questions.concept: The jugular foramen transmits cranial nerves IX, X and XI (with the internal jugular vein); a lesion here (e.g., a glomus jugulare tumour) causes Vernet syndrome - loss of gag, palatal/pharyngeal and laryngeal palsy, and trapezius/SCM weakness. The foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (V3), not this group.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 2-year-old passes brick-red painless blood per rectum. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan lights up an outpouching in the distal ileum containing ectopic gastric mucosa. This anomaly results from persistence of which embryonic structure?
questions.concept: Meckel's diverticulum is a true diverticulum from failed regression of the vitellointestinal duct (rule of 2s: ~2% of people, ~2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, ~2 inches long); its ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid, causing painless bleeding. Persistence of the urachus instead links the bladder apex to the umbilicus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The photograph shows the hand of a newborn delivered by breech with the arm forcibly pulled upward: the metacarpophalangeal joints are hyperextended and the interphalangeal joints flexed (a 'claw hand') with wasting of the small hand muscles, together with a drooping upper eyelid and a constricted pupil on the same side. The lesion is at:
questions.concept: Klumpke's palsy is a lower brachial plexus (C8-T1) injury from forcible upward traction on the arm; loss of the intrinsic hand muscles gives a total claw hand, and involvement of the T1 sympathetic fibres to the head produces an ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). Upper-trunk (Erb's) injury instead gives the 'waiter's tip' posture, without a claw or Horner's.
questions.reference: Vishram Singh, Clinical Anatomy - Upper Limb

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Lower limb: femoral/sciatic nerve, foot drop
questions.stem: A video shows a patient asked to stand on the right leg alone: the pelvis on the left (unsupported) side sags downward, and while walking the patient lurches the trunk toward the right. This positive Trendelenburg sign indicates weakness of which muscle group and nerve?
options: Gluteus medius and minimus - superior gluteal nerve
questions.concept: The gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve, L4-S1) abduct the hip and stabilise the pelvis over the stance limb; their weakness lets the opposite hemipelvis drop (positive Trendelenburg) with a lurching/waddling gait. The gluteus maximus (inferior gluteal nerve) is chiefly a hip extensor, so its loss impairs climbing stairs and rising, not pelvic stabilisation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 30-year-old reports painless burns on both hands and has lost pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders and arms in a 'cape' distribution, while light touch, vibration and joint-position sense are preserved. MRI shows a central cervical cord cavity. The sensory pattern is explained by damage to:
options: Decussating spinothalamic fibres in the anterior white commissure
questions.concept: Syringomyelia is a central cord cavity that first interrupts the second-order spinothalamic fibres crossing in the anterior white commissure, producing a segmental, suspended, dissociated sensory loss (pain and temperature lost, touch and proprioception spared) in a cape distribution. The dorsal columns lie posteriorly and are spared early, so vibration and position sense remain intact.
questions.reference: Vishram Singh, Textbook of Clinical Neuroanatomy

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A week after a difficult oesophagectomy, a patient's chest drain begins to yield about a litre a day of milky-white fluid that is rich in triglycerides and lymphocytes. Injury to which structure, which crosses from right to left at about the T4-T5 level, is responsible?
questions.concept: The thoracic duct ascends on the right, crosses the midline to the left around T4-T5, and drains into the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins; injury spills chyle into the pleura, producing a milky, triglyceride-rich chylothorax. The azygos vein carries blood, so its injury would cause a haemothorax.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A 55-year-old develops a coarse tremor of the right hand that worsens as it approaches a target, cannot perform rapid alternating movements on that side, overshoots when reaching, and has nystagmus and slurred, scanning speech. These signs localise the lesion to:
