questions.concept: Cerebellar hemispheric lesions cause ipsilateral limb signs: intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, dysmetria (past-pointing), nystagmus, hypotonia and scanning dysarthria. A basal-ganglia (nigral) lesion instead produces a resting (pill-rolling) tremor with rigidity and bradykinesia, worst at rest rather than on movement.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cardiac cycle, ECG basis, BP regulation
questions.stem: A rhythm strip from a patient in acute renal failure shows tall, narrow, symmetrically peaked ('tented') T waves, flattening of the P waves and progressive widening of the QRS complexes tending toward a sine-wave pattern. Which is the most appropriate immediate step to protect the myocardium?
questions.concept: These ECG changes are classic for hyperkalaemia, which raises the resting membrane potential and slows conduction; IV calcium gluconate does not lower potassium but rapidly restores the myocardial threshold gradient and stabilises the membrane against fatal arrhythmia. Insulin-dextrose and salbutamol then shift potassium into cells, and dialysis removes it.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A 45-year-old with resistant hypertension is found to have hypokalaemia, a metabolic alkalosis, a high plasma aldosterone and a suppressed plasma renin activity. Which is the most likely mechanism?
options: Renal artery stenosis with secondary hyperaldosteronism
questions.concept: Autonomous aldosterone excess (e.g., a Conn's adenoma) drives renal sodium retention (hypertension) with potassium and hydrogen-ion loss (hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis); the resulting volume expansion suppresses renin - hence high aldosterone with low renin. In secondary hyperaldosteronism (renal artery stenosis) renin is high, and Addison's disease causes hyperkalaemia with low aldosterone.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A 60-year-old smoker has proximal limb weakness and a dry mouth; power paradoxically improves after sustained exercise, and repetitive nerve stimulation shows an incremental (facilitation) response. In contrast to myasthenia gravis, the underlying defect is antibodies against:
options: Voltage-gated sodium channels of the muscle fibre
questions.concept: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is caused by antibodies to presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing acetylcholine release; sustained activity mobilises calcium and augments power, giving an incremental response on repetitive stimulation, and it is often paraneoplastic (small-cell lung cancer). Myasthenia gravis targets postsynaptic ACh receptors and shows a decremental response with fatigability.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A patient given intravenous furosemide for pulmonary oedema develops a low serum potassium with a metabolic alkalosis. Furosemide produces this electrolyte picture chiefly by inhibiting which transporter, and where?
options: Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
Epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct
Na-glucose cotransporter in the proximal tubule
questions.concept: Furosemide blocks the Na-K-2Cl (NKCC2) cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, so more sodium reaches the distal nephron, where it is reabsorbed in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions - producing hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis (compounded by volume contraction). Thiazides act on the distal Na-Cl cotransporter and are less potent diuretics.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Two hypoxaemic patients are each given 100% oxygen. Patient 1's arterial PaO2 rises substantially; Patient 2's PaO2 barely improves. Which mechanism best explains Patient 2's failure to respond to 100% oxygen?
questions.concept: A true right-to-left shunt (blood bypassing ventilated alveoli, e.g., consolidation or ARDS) does not correct with 100% oxygen, because the shunted blood never contacts the raised alveolar oxygen. Pure V/Q mismatch and hypoventilation both improve markedly with supplemental oxygen, so a poor response to 100% O2 is the hallmark of a shunt.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A tall adolescent with long thin limbs, a downward-and-inward dislocated lens and a history of deep-vein thromboses is found to have markedly elevated plasma homocysteine and methionine. Which enzyme deficiency underlies this inborn error?
questions.concept: Classic homocystinuria is due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency (a B6-dependent enzyme), raising homocysteine and methionine and causing a marfanoid habitus, ectopia lentis (typically downward), thromboembolism and intellectual disability. It is distinguished from Marfan syndrome (upward lens dislocation, normal homocysteine); some patients respond to high-dose pyridoxine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A breastfed neonate develops vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, bilateral lens cataracts and Escherichia coli sepsis after milk feeds. Reducing substances are present in the urine but the blood glucose-oxidase test is negative. The deficient enzyme is:
questions.concept: Classic galactosemia is deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase; galactose-1-phosphate accumulates (hepatorenal toxicity) and galactose is shunted by aldose reductase to galactitol in the lens, causing cataracts. Urinary galactose is a reducing sugar not detected by the glucose-specific oxidase strip; treatment is a galactose-free diet, and E. coli neonatal sepsis is characteristic.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has severe intellectual disability, choreoathetosis, spasticity and compulsive self-mutilation (biting his lips and fingers), with a high serum uric acid and orange urate 'sand' in his nappy. The X-linked defect is in which enzyme?
questions.concept: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked deficiency of HGPRT, the purine-salvage enzyme; loss of salvage drives purine overproduction and hyperuricaemia (gout, urate stones) with a characteristic neurological picture of dystonia/choreoathetosis and compulsive self-mutilation. Adenosine deaminase deficiency instead causes severe combined immunodeficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A child of Ashkenazi Jewish descent has massive hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia and bone pain; a marrow biopsy shows lipid-laden macrophages with a 'crumpled tissue-paper' cytoplasm. This most common lysosomal storage disorder is due to deficiency of:
questions.concept: Gaucher disease is deficiency of glucocerebrosidase, causing glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages (Gaucher cells with a 'crumpled tissue-paper' cytoplasm), hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias and bone crises; it is the commonest lysosomal storage disease and is treated with enzyme replacement. Hexosaminidase A deficiency instead causes Tay-Sachs disease (cherry-red macula, no organomegaly).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: After a positive HIV ELISA screening test, a confirmatory laboratory assay separates the patient's serum antibodies by their reaction to viral proteins that have been size-separated by electrophoresis and blotted onto a membrane. This technique, which detects specific proteins, is:
questions.concept: The Western blot detects specific proteins (or antibodies against them) after gel electrophoresis and transfer to a membrane, and is a classic confirmatory format for HIV antibodies. Southern blot detects DNA and Northern blot detects RNA; PCR amplifies nucleic acids rather than detecting proteins.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A strict vegan presents with a macrocytic anaemia plus paraesthesiae and an unsteady gait from dorsal-column and corticospinal involvement. Blood shows a raised methylmalonic acid AND a raised homocysteine. Which deficiency does the raised methylmalonic acid specifically point to?
questions.concept: Vitamin B12 is a coenzyme for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase, so its deficiency raises both methylmalonic acid and homocysteine and can cause subacute combined degeneration of the cord. Folate deficiency raises only homocysteine (methylmalonic acid stays normal) and does not cause the neurological cord signs, which is why the raised methylmalonic acid points specifically to B12.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A woman is found dead with crescentic nail-mark abrasions and finger-tip bruises on the front of the neck; at autopsy the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage are fractured with deep bruising of the neck muscles. Which mechanism of asphyxial death does this indicate?
questions.concept: Manual strangulation (throttling) is caused by pressure from the hands; crescentic nail abrasions and finger-tip bruises on the neck, with fractures of the hyoid and thyroid cartilage and deep muscle bruising, are characteristic - and it is almost always homicidal, since one cannot throttle oneself to death. Hanging shows an oblique ligature mark high on the neck, without hand marks.
questions.reference: Reddy, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: At autopsy a medical officer must decide whether a scalp laceration was inflicted before or after death. Which feature most reliably indicates that the wound was sustained during life (an antemortem injury)?
options: Vital reaction - marked haemorrhage into the wound margins with clotting and an early inflammatory infiltrate
questions.concept: Antemortem wounds show a 'vital reaction': haemorrhage into the surrounding tissues with coagulation, gaping/retraction and, over hours, an inflammatory cellular and enzymatic response - all requiring a living circulation. Postmortem wounds lack this reaction, bleed little, and their edges do not gape or inflame; parchmentisation is a postmortem drying artefact, not a sign of vitality.
questions.reference: Reddy, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A stabbing victim, fully conscious but dying, names his assailant to the attending doctor before he succumbs. At trial the defence objects that this statement was not made on oath and the maker could not be cross-examined. Which statement about the evidentiary status of a dying declaration in India is correct?
options: It is admissible even though not made on oath and untested by cross-examination
It is inadmissible unless recorded only by a magistrate
It is inadmissible because the maker cannot be cross-examined
It is valid only if the declarant was expecting to die
questions.concept: A dying declaration is admissible substantive evidence and may be recorded by a magistrate, a doctor or any person; it needs no oath and cannot be cross-examined, resting on the maxim 'nemo moriturus praesumitur mentiri', and in Indian law (unlike English law) the declarant need not have been under expectation of death. VERIFY: the governing provision was Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act 1872, now replaced by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 - confirm the current section number before relying on it, as this is law-currency-dependent.
questions.reference: Reddy, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology; Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (replaced Indian Evidence Act) - current section number to be confirmed

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A body recovered from a river has the fingers tightly gripping a tuft of aquatic weeds that cannot be prised open, and there was no preceding flaccidity of that muscle group. What is this finding, and what is its medicolegal significance?
options: Cadaveric spasm - the weeds were grasped at the moment of death, indicating the person entered the water alive
Rigor mortis - indicates death occurred about 12 hours earlier
Cold stiffening - due to freezing of tissues
questions.concept: Cadaveric spasm is an instantaneous rigidity of a group of voluntary muscles at the moment of death, without any preceding primary flaccidity; it cannot be reproduced artificially and so has great medicolegal value - weeds clutched in the hand show the person was alive on entering the water. Ordinary rigor mortis develops gradually after a flaccid interval and affects all muscles.
questions.reference: Reddy, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A young farm worker in rural India is brought in after swallowing a fumigant grain-preservation tablet; his breath smells of garlic/decaying fish, and he has refractory hypotension and severe metabolic acidosis. There is no specific antidote. The most likely poison is:
questions.concept: Aluminium phosphide ('celphos'/'rice tablet') is a common agricultural fumigant and a leading cause of fatal suicidal poisoning in India; it liberates phosphine gas, giving a garlic/decaying-fish odour, profound refractory shock and metabolic acidosis, with no specific antidote (management is supportive). Organophosphate poisoning instead causes a cholinergic crisis reversible with atropine and pralidoxime.
questions.reference: Reddy, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 25-year-old falls on the outstretched hand and has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox; the initial wrist X-ray appears normal. Why should this injury be immobilised and re-imaged rather than dismissed as a sprain?
options: A scaphoid fracture is likely, is often invisible on the first film, and risks avascular necrosis/non-union
It is certainly a simple wrist sprain needing no follow-up
It represents a Colles fracture requiring immediate reduction
questions.concept: Snuffbox tenderness after a fall on the outstretched hand suggests a scaphoid fracture, which may not be visible on the first radiograph; because the scaphoid's blood supply enters distally (retrograde), a proximal-pole fracture risks avascular necrosis and non-union, so the wrist is immobilised and re-imaged (or MRI obtained) at 10-14 days. A Colles fracture is a displaced distal-radius injury obvious on the first film.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 5-year-old refuses to bear weight, holds the hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated, has a temperature of 39C, an ESR of 60 and a WBC of 15,000; any movement of the hip causes severe pain. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Urgent joint aspiration and surgical drainage (arthrotomy) with antibiotics
Reassurance and oral analgesia, as this is transient synovitis
Apply a hip spica and review in one month
questions.concept: This picture (non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5C, ESR >40, WBC >12,000 - all four Kocher criteria) strongly indicates septic arthritis of the hip, a surgical emergency: pus under pressure and chondrolytic enzymes rapidly destroy articular cartilage and can cause avascular necrosis, so urgent aspiration/arthrotomy plus antibiotics is required. Transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion in an afebrile child with normal inflammatory markers.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A radiograph of the mid-shaft (diaphysis) of the femur in an 8-year-old with fever and a raised ESR shows a permeative lytic lesion with a laminated 'onion-peel' periosteal reaction. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Ewing's sarcoma arises in the diaphysis of long bones in children, causing an 'onion-peel' lamellated periosteal reaction and often mimicking osteomyelitis (fever, raised ESR); histology shows small round blue cells and it carries the t(11;22) translocation. Osteosarcoma is metaphyseal with 'sunburst' spiculation and a Codman's triangle, and giant cell tumour is epiphyseal in adults.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 25-year-old has years of scanty, foul-smelling ear discharge with progressive hearing loss; otoscopy shows a retraction pocket and perforation in the attic (pars flaccida) filled with white pearly debris. Why is this type of chronic otitis media termed 'unsafe'?
options: The keratinising squamous epithelium (cholesteatoma) erodes bone and can cause facial palsy or intracranial complications
It always resolves spontaneously without treatment
It is purely a cosmetic problem of the pinna
questions.concept: An attic (pars flaccida) retraction/perforation with foul scanty discharge and pearly debris indicates a cholesteatoma - a sac of keratinising squamous epithelium that releases bone-eroding enzymes; it is the 'unsafe' (atticoantral) type of CSOM because it can erode the ossicles, facial canal, labyrinth and tegmen, causing facial palsy, labyrinthitis and intracranial abscess, and needs surgery (mastoidectomy). The 'safe' (tubotympanic) type has a central perforation with mucoid discharge.
questions.reference: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy has recurrent profuse epistaxis and progressive nasal obstruction; a highly vascular mass is seen filling the posterior nasal cavity and nasopharynx. Why is an incisional biopsy in the clinic contraindicated?
options: It is a juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, and biopsy risks torrential haemorrhage; diagnosis is by contrast CT/angiography
Biopsy would spread a highly malignant carcinoma
The mass is a simple polyp needing no imaging
Biopsy is painless and always safe here
questions.concept: A vascular nasopharyngeal mass causing recurrent epistaxis and obstruction in an adolescent male is a juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma - benign but extremely vascular, so an office biopsy risks life-threatening bleeding; it is diagnosed by contrast-enhanced CT/MRI and angiography and treated by excision after preoperative embolisation. It is not a simple polyp and does not warrant blind biopsy.
questions.reference: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 45-year-old diabetic with a recent lower-molar infection develops a tense, tender, board-like bilateral swelling of the floor of the mouth and submandibular region, with the tongue pushed up and difficulty swallowing and breathing. The most appropriate priority is:
options: Securing the airway (with drainage and IV antibiotics), as this is Ludwig's angina
Reassurance and oral antibiotics at home
Antihistamines alone for an allergic reaction
questions.concept: Ludwig's angina is a rapidly spreading bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces, usually of dental origin, causing a woody floor-of-mouth swelling, tongue elevation and impending airway obstruction; the airway takes priority (early intubation/tracheostomy as needed) alongside IV antibiotics and surgical drainage. It is a life-threatening emergency, not a condition for home management.
questions.reference: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 50-year-old on long-term oral corticosteroids complains of glare and poor vision in bright sunlight and while reading, though vision is better in dim light. Slit-lamp shows an opacity just in front of the posterior capsule at the centre of the lens. This is which type of cataract?
questions.concept: Posterior subcapsular cataract lies centrally, just in front of the posterior capsule (in the visual axis), so it causes disproportionate glare and poor vision in bright light and on near work (pupillary constriction), with relatively preserved vision in dim light; it is associated with corticosteroids, diabetes and radiation. Nuclear sclerosis instead causes a gradual myopic shift with yellowing of the lens nucleus.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A patient with primary open-angle glaucoma is examined at the slit lamp. Which optic-disc finding is the most characteristic sign of glaucomatous optic-nerve damage?
options: Increased cup-to-disc ratio with thinning of the neuroretinal rim (violating the ISNT rule)
Optic disc swelling with blurred margins (papilloedema)
A pale, waxy disc with attenuated vessels
Peripapillary haemorrhages with cotton-wool spots and macular oedema
questions.concept: Glaucoma preferentially destroys retinal ganglion-cell axons, so the neuroretinal rim thins and the optic cup enlarges (increased cup-to-disc ratio), with loss of the normal ISNT rim-thickness pattern, bayonetting of vessels and sometimes a disc (Drance) haemorrhage - correlating with arcuate field loss. Papilloedema is bilateral disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure, a different entity.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 45-year-old emmetrope who has never needed glasses now has to hold the newspaper at arm's length to read, though his distance vision is normal. What is the underlying mechanism of this presbyopia?
options: Age-related loss of lens elasticity reducing the amplitude of accommodation
questions.concept: Presbyopia is the physiological, age-related decline in accommodation from about 40 years, mainly because the crystalline lens loses elasticity (and the ciliary muscle weakens), so the near point recedes and reading requires a convex (plus) 'add'. It is unrelated to axial length (myopia) or lens opacity (cataract), which alter distance vision or clarity.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 65-year-old with atrial fibrillation reports sudden, painless, total loss of vision in one eye. The fundus photograph shows a diffusely pale, oedematous retina with a bright 'cherry-red spot' at the fovea and segmented ('cattle-trucking') retinal arterioles. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden painless monocular blindness with a pale, oedematous retina and a cherry-red spot (the thin foveola still transmits the underlying choroidal colour); it is an ocular 'stroke' (often embolic, e.g., from atrial fibrillation) and an emergency (ocular massage, lowering IOP). Central retinal vein occlusion instead gives a 'blood and thunder' fundus with widespread haemorrhages and a less abrupt, less complete loss.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A 30-year-old has recurrent, unexpected episodes of intense fear peaking within minutes, with palpitations, chest tightness, sweating, trembling and a fear of dying, and now avoids public places for fear of an attack. ECG, thyroid function and examination are normal. Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
options: An SSRI combined with cognitive behavioural therapy
A long-term high-dose benzodiazepine as sole therapy
No treatment - reassurance alone, as it is not a disorder
questions.concept: This is panic disorder with agoraphobia; organic mimics (arrhythmia, hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma) having been excluded, the evidence-based long-term treatment is an SSRI plus cognitive behavioural therapy, with benzodiazepines used only briefly because of dependence. Antipsychotics are not first-line for uncomplicated panic disorder.
questions.reference: Niraj Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A 26-year-old is brought in after a week of little need for sleep, rapid pressured speech, grandiose plans, overspending and increased goal-directed activity; he is elated and irritable. He had a depressive episode two years ago. Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological management of this acute episode?
options: A mood stabiliser (lithium or valproate) or an atypical antipsychotic
A benzodiazepine as the sole long-term treatment
questions.concept: This is an acute manic episode of bipolar I disorder (elevated/irritable mood plus decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech and increased activity for at least a week), especially given the prior depressive episode. First-line treatment is a mood stabiliser (lithium or valproate) and/or an atypical antipsychotic; antidepressant monotherapy is avoided as it can precipitate or worsen mania.
questions.reference: Niraj Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A man with schizophrenia has failed to respond to adequate trials of two different antipsychotics, and clozapine is being considered. Which mandatory monitoring is required because of its most dangerous adverse effect?
options: Regular white-cell / absolute neutrophil count monitoring for agranulocytosis
questions.concept: Clozapine is the drug of choice for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of two or more antipsychotics) and reduces suicidality, but it can cause life-threatening agranulocytosis, so regular white-cell and absolute neutrophil counts are mandatory (weekly initially, then less frequently). Other important risks include myocarditis, seizures, weight gain and hypersalivation.
questions.reference: Niraj Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Two weeks after starting an anticonvulsant, a patient develops a painful dusky rash with targetoid lesions and extensive erosions of the lips, mouth and conjunctivae; gentle lateral pressure shears off the epidermis, and about 25% of the body surface is denuded. The most likely diagnosis and key first step are:
options: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis - stop the culprit drug and give supportive (burns-unit-type) care
Bullous pemphigoid - continue the drug and use topical emollients only
Contact dermatitis - patch test and reassure
questions.concept: Drug-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (a spectrum; SJS <10%, TEN >30% body-surface detachment) presents with painful mucocutaneous erosions, targetoid lesions and a positive Nikolsky sign after culprit drugs (anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, allopurinol, NSAIDs); immediate withdrawal of the drug plus supportive care in a burns/ICU setting is critical. Bullous pemphigoid is a chronic autoimmune blistering disease of the elderly, not this acute drug emergency.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient has numerous symmetrically distributed, poorly-defined shiny skin lesions, thickened earlobes with loss of the eyebrows, nasal stuffiness and a glove-and-stocking sensory loss; slit-skin smears teem with acid-fast bacilli and the lepromin test is negative. Which pole of leprosy is this, and what does the negative lepromin test signify?
options: Lepromatous leprosy - poor cell-mediated immunity (Th2), hence a high bacillary load and a negative lepromin test
Tuberculoid leprosy - strong cell-mediated immunity and a positive lepromin test
questions.concept: Lepromatous leprosy sits at the low-immunity pole: weak cell-mediated (Th2-biased) immunity allows uncontrolled bacillary multiplication, giving numerous symmetrical lesions, leonine facies, madarosis and a negative lepromin test (which reflects the host CMI response, not diagnosis). Tuberculoid leprosy has strong CMI - few well-defined lesions, scanty bacilli and a positive lepromin test.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A 22-year-old shows a single 2-cm oval, scaly, erythematous plaque on the trunk that appeared a week before a subsequent crop of smaller oval macules; the photograph shows these lesions running with their long axes along the skin cleavage lines in a 'Christmas-tree' pattern on the back, each with a fine peripheral 'collarette' of scale. Before diagnosing pityriasis rosea, which condition must be excluded?
options: Secondary syphilis (which involves the palms and soles and is confirmed serologically)
questions.concept: The herald patch followed by a 'Christmas-tree' distribution of oval, collarette-scaled plaques along cleavage lines is classic for pityriasis rosea, a self-limiting eruption. Because secondary syphilis can closely mimic it but characteristically involves the palms and soles and carries systemic implications, it must be excluded (with treponemal serology) before settling on the benign diagnosis.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: A ventilated trauma patient becomes acutely hypotensive with a raised jugular venous pressure. A portable chest film shows a hyperlucent left hemithorax with absent lung markings, a deep left costophrenic sulcus, a depressed left hemidiaphragm and the trachea and mediastinum shifted to the right. What is the immediate management?
options: Immediate needle decompression / chest drain - this is a tension pneumothorax
Await a CT scan to confirm before acting
Give a blood transfusion for a haemothorax
questions.concept: A hyperlucent hemithorax with absent lung markings plus contralateral mediastinal/tracheal shift and a depressed diaphragm indicates a tension pneumothorax, in which trapped air compresses the mediastinum and impairs venous return (shock, raised JVP). It is a clinical emergency treated by immediate needle decompression or chest drain - one must not wait for a CT. A haemothorax would appear opaque, not hyperlucent.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: A patient presents 90 minutes after sudden onset of right-sided weakness. A non-contrast CT head, done to exclude haemorrhage, is normal. Which imaging modality is most sensitive for detecting the early acute ischaemic infarct at this stage?
options: Carotid Doppler ultrasound of the neck
questions.concept: In acute ischaemic stroke a non-contrast CT is done first to exclude haemorrhage but is often normal in the first hours; diffusion-weighted MRI detects the cytotoxic oedema of infarction within minutes (restricted diffusion), making it the most sensitive test for early ischaemia. Carotid Doppler assesses a possible embolic source but does not image the brain infarct itself.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: A 10-week-pregnant woman has right-lower-quadrant pain and suspected appendicitis. To minimise fetal risk while investigating, which imaging strategy is most appropriate first?
options: Ultrasound first, then MRI if inconclusive - both avoiding ionising radiation
questions.concept: Ionising radiation is best avoided in pregnancy, especially during organogenesis, so ultrasound (no ionising radiation) is the first-line investigation and MRI (also non-ionising) is the preferred second-line problem-solver for suspected appendicitis; CT and plain films use ionising radiation and are reserved for when the benefit clearly outweighs the risk. This follows the ALARA principle.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: An unfasted patient with acute bowel obstruction needs emergency general anaesthesia. To minimise the risk of regurgitation and pulmonary aspiration during induction, the anaesthetist plans a rapid sequence induction. Which combination of steps is characteristic of this technique?
options: Pre-oxygenation, a rapidly-acting induction agent with suxamethonium, cricoid pressure, and avoidance of routine mask ventilation before intubation
Slow inhalational induction with prolonged bag-mask ventilation
Awake extubation before the airway is secured
questions.concept: A full ('unfasted') stomach carries a high aspiration risk, so rapid sequence induction is used: pre-oxygenation, a swift IV induction agent plus a fast-acting muscle relaxant (classically suxamethonium), application of cricoid pressure and prompt intubation while avoiding routine positive-pressure mask ventilation that could inflate the stomach. Aspiration of gastric acid causes Mendelson's syndrome.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: During an adult cardiac arrest, a rhythm check reveals an organised narrow-complex electrical rhythm on the monitor but no palpable pulse. What is the correct immediate action?
options: Continue high-quality CPR, give adrenaline, and search for and treat reversible causes - do NOT defibrillate
Stop CPR because there is electrical activity
questions.concept: Pulseless electrical activity is a non-shockable rhythm: there is organised electrical activity without a pulse, so defibrillation is not indicated. Management is uninterrupted high-quality CPR with adrenaline and an active search for reversible causes (the 4 Hs and 4 Ts - hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis). Only VF and pulseless VT are shocked.
questions.reference: Standard ACLS principles; Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Two days after an uncomplicated spinal anaesthetic for a caesarean section, a young woman develops a severe throbbing headache that is worst when she sits or stands and is relieved by lying flat, with neck stiffness and photophobia. Which is the definitive treatment if conservative measures fail?
questions.concept: A post-dural-puncture headache follows leakage of CSF through the dural puncture, causing low CSF pressure; it is characteristically postural (worse upright, relieved by lying down) and is commoner with larger/cutting needles and in young women. Initial care is conservative (bed rest, hydration, caffeine, analgesia), and the definitive treatment for a persistent or severe headache is an epidural blood patch.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Cell injury, adaptation, necrosis vs apoptosis
questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with an occluded coronary artery undergoes successful thrombolysis 3 hours after symptom onset, but his cardiac enzymes rise higher than expected and ventricular arrhythmias worsen soon after flow is restored. This paradoxical aggravation of injury on reperfusion is chiefly mediated by:
options: Generation of reactive oxygen species with mitochondrial calcium overload
Immediate coagulative necrosis from ATP depletion alone
p53-triggered apoptosis occurring only after 24 hours
questions.concept: Ischemia-reperfusion injury: reintroduction of oxygen generates reactive oxygen species and, with intracellular/mitochondrial Ca2+ overload plus neutrophil-driven inflammation, opens the mitochondrial permeability transition pore, worsening damage beyond that of ischemia alone. Simple ATP depletion does not explain the paradoxical post-reperfusion rise.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e (Cell Injury - Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Cell injury, adaptation, necrosis vs apoptosis
questions.stem: During hormone-deprived involution of an organ, individual cells shrink, show intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm with condensed, fragmented chromatin, and are cleared by neighbouring cells without any inflammatory reaction. Which statement about this process is correct?
options: It is caspase-mediated apoptosis with plasma-membrane integrity preserved until late
It is coagulative necrosis with early membrane rupture
It releases lysosomal enzymes causing liquefaction
It is always pathological and provokes acute inflammation
questions.concept: Apoptosis (programmed cell death) causes cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation/fragmentation and apoptotic bodies WITHOUT inflammation, because the plasma membrane stays intact until phagocytosis; it is executed by caspases. Necrosis instead ruptures membranes early and triggers inflammation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Ten days after receiving equine anti-snake-venom serum, a patient develops fever, urticaria, arthralgia and new proteinuria, with a low serum C3. Circulating antigen-antibody complexes are depositing in vessel walls, joints and glomeruli. This reaction is best classified as:
questions.concept: Serum sickness is the prototype systemic type III reaction: circulating immune complexes deposit in vessels, joints and glomeruli, fix complement (low C3) and recruit neutrophils, ~1-2 weeks after antigen exposure. Type I is immediate/anaphylactic; type IV is delayed and cell-mediated with no antibody.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A nurse develops an itchy, vesicular rash confined to the skin beneath her nickel watch strap, appearing about 48 hours after contact; patch testing reproduces the lesion at the same site. The immunological mechanism responsible is:
options: Type IV delayed hypersensitivity mediated by sensitized CD4+ T cells
Type I hypersensitivity mediated by IgE and mast cells
Type II hypersensitivity from anti-basement-membrane antibodies
questions.concept: Allergic contact dermatitis (e.g., to nickel) is a classic type IV delayed hypersensitivity; the 24-72 hour delay reflects antigen-specific CD4+ T-cell recruitment and cytokine release. No antibody mediates it, which is why it cannot be a type I, II or III reaction.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A lymph-node biopsy shows aggregates of epithelioid macrophages ringed by lymphocytes with occasional multinucleate giant cells but no caseation. Which cytokine, secreted by Th1 cells, is most critical for transforming macrophages into the epithelioid cells that build this lesion?
questions.concept: Granuloma formation is a Th1 (type IV) response: interferon-gamma activates macrophages into epithelioid and giant cells, while TNF maintains the granuloma (anti-TNF therapy reactivates latent TB). IL-4 and IL-5 instead drive Th2 / eosinophilic responses.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A wound healing by secondary intention shows, around day 3-5, a pink soft tissue bed with proliferating fibroblasts and abundant new capillaries. Which single cell type most orchestrates this transition by clearing debris and secreting growth factors such as VEGF, PDGF and TGF-beta?
questions.concept: The macrophage is the central cell of repair: it clears debris and secretes VEGF, PDGF and TGF-beta that drive the angiogenesis and fibroblast proliferation of granulation tissue. Neutrophils dominate only the first 24-48 hours of acute inflammation and do not orchestrate repair.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A 60-year-old smoker with a central lung mass has serum calcium 13 mg/dL, a suppressed parathyroid hormone but elevated parathyroid-hormone-related peptide (PTHrP). Which lung-cancer histology most classically produces this paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia?
questions.concept: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung classically secretes PTHrP, causing humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy (high calcium, low PTH, high PTHrP). Small cell carcinoma instead causes ectopic ACTH (Cushing) and SIADH, not PTHrP-driven hypercalcaemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear is shown from a boy who developed dark urine and jaundice two days after starting primaquine. It shows red cells with peripheral 'bite' defects and, on supravital staining, dark intracellular inclusions (Heinz bodies). The underlying enzyme defect is:
questions.concept: G6PD deficiency impairs NADPH/glutathione regeneration, so oxidant stress (primaquine, fava beans, infections) denatures haemoglobin into Heinz bodies that splenic macrophages pluck out, creating 'bite cells'. It is X-linked recessive. A spectrin defect instead causes hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has a mild normocytic anaemia. Serum iron is low, but serum ferritin is HIGH and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) is LOW. Which mediator drives this iron-restricted anaemia by upregulating hepcidin?
questions.concept: In anaemia of chronic disease, inflammatory IL-6 raises hepcidin, trapping iron within macrophages: the result is low serum iron with HIGH ferritin and LOW TIBC - the mirror image of iron-deficiency anaemia (low ferritin, high TIBC), which is the key distinguishing point.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A peripheral smear is shown from a woman with abruptio placentae who is now oozing from every venepuncture site; it reveals fragmented red cells (schistocytes) and scanty platelets. Labs show prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen and a raised D-dimer. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: DIC is a consumptive coagulopathy (obstetric catastrophe, sepsis, malignancy): widespread microthrombi consume platelets and clotting factors, giving prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer and microangiopathic haemolysis (schistocytes). ITP shows isolated low platelets with a normal PT/aPTT.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A young woman has easy bruising, prolonged bleeding after dental extraction and menorrhagia. Her platelet count is normal, bleeding time is prolonged and aPTT is mildly prolonged (correcting on mixing), while ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation is reduced. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder: deficient vWF impairs platelet adhesion (prolonged bleeding time, reduced ristocetin aggregation) and shortens factor VIII half-life (mildly prolonged aPTT). Mucocutaneous bleeding predominates. Haemophilia A gives isolated aPTT prolongation with a normal bleeding time.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A blood film is shown from a 45-year-old with massive splenomegaly and a very high leukocyte count; it displays the full spectrum of maturing granulocytes with basophilia and only rare blasts. Cytogenetics reveal t(9;22). Which fusion gene drives this disorder and is the target of imatinib?
questions.concept: Chronic myeloid leukaemia carries the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22), producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion - a constitutively active tyrosine kinase inhibited by imatinib. PML-RARA t(15;17) defines acute promyelocytic leukaemia; JAK2 V617F is seen in polycythaemia vera and other myeloproliferative neoplasms.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A lymph-node biopsy is shown from an African child with a rapidly growing jaw mass; it reveals sheets of intermediate-sized lymphocytes with numerous tingible-body macrophages producing a 'starry-sky' pattern and a near-100% Ki-67. Which translocation and virus are classically associated?
options: t(8;14) MYC translocation with Epstein-Barr virus
t(14;18) BCL2 translocation with hepatitis C
questions.concept: Burkitt lymphoma shows a 'starry-sky' pattern and extremely high proliferation (Ki-67 near 100%); it is driven by a MYC translocation, t(8;14), and the endemic (African, jaw) form is EBV-associated. t(14;18)/BCL2 defines follicular lymphoma; t(11;14)/cyclin D1 defines mantle-cell lymphoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presents with a single, rapidly enlarging nodal mass. Biopsy shows sheets of large lymphoid cells effacing the node architecture and staining strongly CD20-positive. Regarding the commonest non-Hodgkin lymphoma of adults, which statement is correct?
options: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is aggressive but potentially curable with R-CHOP
It is an indolent lymphoma best left untreated
It is a T-cell tumour that never expresses CD20
It is defined by Reed-Sternberg cells
questions.concept: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the commonest NHL in adults - aggressive (a rapidly enlarging mass) but potentially curable with immunochemotherapy (rituximab-CHOP). It is a CD20+ B-cell tumour; Reed-Sternberg cells define Hodgkin lymphoma, not DLBCL.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A contrast MRI is shown of a 50-year-old woman with a well-circumscribed, dural-based extra-axial mass showing a 'dural tail'. Histology reveals whorls of meningothelial cells with laminated calcified psammoma bodies. The most likely tumour is:
questions.concept: Meningioma is a benign, dural-based extra-axial tumour, commoner in women (often progesterone-receptor positive); histology shows syncytial whorls and psammoma bodies with a characteristic 'dural tail' on MRI. Glioblastoma is intra-axial and infiltrative, not dural-based.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has chronic sinusitis with nasal septal ('saddle-nose') collapse, haemoptysis with nodular cavitating lung lesions, and rising creatinine with red-cell casts. Renal biopsy shows pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis. Which serological test is most specific for his diagnosis?
questions.concept: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's) is an ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis affecting the upper airway (sinusitis, saddle nose), lungs (nodules/cavities) and kidneys (pauci-immune crescentic GN); it is strongly associated with c-ANCA / anti-PR3. p-ANCA / anti-MPO instead typifies microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic GPA.
questions.reference: Robbins 10e (Blood Vessels - Vasculitis: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with long-standing hepatitis-B cirrhosis develops right-upper-quadrant pain, weight loss and rapidly worsening ascites, with a markedly raised serum alpha-fetoprotein. Triple-phase CT shows a mass with arterial-phase enhancement and venous-phase 'washout'. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Hepatocellular carcinoma arises on a background of cirrhosis (HBV, HCV, alcohol, aflatoxin); the clues are a rising AFP and the classic arterial enhancement with venous 'washout' on triple-phase imaging. A haemangioma shows peripheral nodular enhancement with a normal AFP.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 20-year-old with tremor, dysarthria and deteriorating school performance is found on slit-lamp examination to have brown rings at the corneal limbus, along with deranged liver enzymes. Serum ceruloplasmin is low and 24-hour urinary copper is high. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Wilson disease (ATP7B mutation) causes copper accumulation in liver, brain (basal ganglia - tremor, dysarthria) and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings), with LOW ceruloplasmin and HIGH urinary copper. Haemochromatosis instead deposits iron (diabetes, bronze skin) and presents later in adult life.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with haemoptysis and acute kidney injury with red-cell casts. Renal biopsy shows crescents in most glomeruli, and immunofluorescence reveals LINEAR deposition of IgG along the glomerular basement membrane. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Linear GBM staining for IgG with crescentic (rapidly progressive) glomerulonephritis and pulmonary haemorrhage defines anti-GBM / Goodpasture disease (antibody to the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen). Post-streptococcal GN instead shows granular ('lumpy-bumpy') subepithelial humps, never linear staining.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 55-year-old with 15 years of poorly controlled type-2 diabetes has increasing proteinuria and hypertension. A renal biopsy performed for atypical features shows nodular, acellular, eosinophilic masses expanding the mesangium of the glomeruli. These nodules are known as:
questions.concept: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular glomerulosclerosis) are the hallmark of diabetic nephropathy, reflecting mesangial matrix expansion from chronic hyperglycaemia. 'Wire-loop' lesions occur in lupus nephritis; the 'spike-and-dome' pattern describes membranous nephropathy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 4-year-old develops bloody diarrhoea after eating an undercooked beef burger, and a week later has acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. Which organism/toxin is responsible, and why are antibiotics avoided?
options: Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli O157:H7 producing Shiga-like toxin; antibiotics may increase toxin release and HUS risk
Enterotoxigenic E. coli producing heat-labile toxin; antibiotics are curative
Vibrio cholerae producing cholera toxin; antibiotics are first-line
Enteropathogenic E. coli; antibiotics prevent HUS
questions.concept: EHEC O157:H7 (from undercooked beef) produces Shiga-like (vero)toxin, causing haemorrhagic colitis that can progress to haemolytic-uraemic syndrome (AKI + thrombocytopenia + MAHA). Antibiotics are avoided because they may increase Shiga-toxin release and the risk of HUS. ETEC causes watery traveller's diarrhoea.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e (Escherichia coli)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient in the SECOND week of a stepwise-rising fever with relative bradycardia and splenomegaly is being investigated for enteric fever. Regarding laboratory diagnosis, which specimen gives the HIGHEST yield in the FIRST week of illness?
questions.concept: In enteric fever the blood culture is positive earliest and has the highest yield in the first week (~90%); stool and urine cultures turn positive later (2nd-3rd week). The Widal test detects antibodies, rises only after the first week and has limited specificity, so it cannot confirm early disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: An unimmunized child has a grey pseudomembrane over the tonsils, bull-neck lymphadenopathy, and later develops myocarditis and palatal palsy. The exotoxin responsible kills cells by:
options: ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor-2, halting protein synthesis
Cleaving SNARE proteins to block acetylcholine release
Raising intracellular cyclic AMP via Gs stimulation
questions.concept: Corynebacterium diphtheriae toxin (phage-encoded) ADP-ribosylates elongation factor-2, inhibiting protein synthesis and causing the local pseudomembrane plus systemic myocarditis and neuropathy. SNARE cleavage is botulinum/tetanus toxin; cAMP elevation is cholera/pertussis; superantigens cause toxic-shock syndrome.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Pus from a post-operative wound grows golden colonies that are catalase-positive and coagulase-positive and ferment mannitol on mannitol-salt agar. Which organism is identified, and which single test best separates it from other staphylococci?
questions.concept: Staphylococcus aureus is catalase-positive (separating staphylococci from streptococci) and, crucially, coagulase-positive (separating it from S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus); it also ferments mannitol. Optochin and bacitracin sensitivity are tests used for streptococci, not staphylococci.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A BCG-vaccinated healthcare worker is screened for latent tuberculosis. An interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is chosen over the tuberculin skin test mainly because the IGRA:
options: Uses M. tuberculosis-specific antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10) absent from BCG, so it is not confounded by prior vaccination
Can reliably distinguish latent from active tuberculosis
Becomes positive within hours of primary infection
Detects the organism directly in sputum
questions.concept: IGRAs use M. tuberculosis-specific antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10) that are absent from BCG and most environmental mycobacteria, so - unlike the tuberculin skin test - they are not confounded by prior BCG vaccination. Neither test can distinguish latent from active disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Sputum smear microscopy by Ziehl-Neelsen staining is reported negative in a patient with clinically suspected pulmonary tuberculosis. Which statement about the sensitivity of smear microscopy is correct?
options: At least ~10,000 (10^4) bacilli per mL are needed for smear positivity, so smear-negative TB is common
A single negative smear reliably excludes tuberculosis
Smear microscopy can differentiate M. tuberculosis from atypical mycobacteria
Culture is less sensitive than smear microscopy
questions.concept: Ziehl-Neelsen smear microscopy requires roughly 10^4 acid-fast bacilli per mL to be positive, so paucibacillary and early disease are frequently smear-negative; culture (LJ medium / liquid MGIT) is far more sensitive (~10-100 bacilli/mL) and is the gold standard, and it - not smear - allows species identification.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A hospital's sterile-services department wants to validate that its steam autoclave achieves sterilization. Spores of which organism are used as the biological indicator to confirm the efficacy of moist-heat (autoclave) sterilization?
questions.concept: Spores of Geobacillus stearothermophilus are the biological indicator for moist-heat (autoclave, 121C) sterilization, being the most heat-resistant. Bacillus atrophaeus (subtilis) spores validate dry-heat and ethylene-oxide sterilization. Vegetative bacteria like E. coli are killed easily and are not used as indicators.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A flexible fibre-optic endoscope cannot withstand autoclaving. Which agent is most appropriate for high-level disinfection of such heat-sensitive instruments between patients?
questions.concept: Heat-labile instruments such as flexible endoscopes are high-level disinfected by immersion in 2% glutaraldehyde (or OPA), which is sporicidal with adequate contact time. Alcohol and quaternary compounds (cetrimide) are only low-to-intermediate level, and boiling is not sterilization.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A young man has recurrent episodes of non-pruritic, non-pitting swelling of the face and larynx without urticaria, often triggered by dental work, and made worse by ACE inhibitors. Complement studies show a persistently low C4. The deficient protein is:
questions.concept: Hereditary angioedema is C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency: uncontrolled activation of the classical complement and kinin pathways generates bradykinin, causing recurrent non-urticarial angioedema; C4 is characteristically low. Being bradykinin-mediated, it does not respond to antihistamines/adrenaline. CD55 deficiency underlies PNH.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Microbiology 11e (Complement System) / Abbas Cellular and Molecular Immunology

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: An India-ink preparation of cerebrospinal fluid is shown from an HIV patient (CD4 count 40) with subacute headache; it reveals round budding yeasts each surrounded by a wide clear (unstained) halo. The most likely organism is:
questions.concept: Cryptococcus neoformans causes subacute meningitis in advanced HIV; its thick polysaccharide capsule excludes India ink, giving a clear halo around budding yeasts. The cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) latex test is more sensitive. Candida forms pseudohyphae; Aspergillus forms septate acute-angle-branching hyphae.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A yeast isolated from blood culture is incubated in serum at 37C for 2 hours and forms short hyphal projections that show NO constriction at their point of origin (a positive germ-tube test). This rapidly identifies:
questions.concept: The germ-tube (Reynolds-Braude) test is positive for Candida albicans (and C. dubliniensis): serum induces true germ tubes with no basal constriction within 2 hours, distinguishing it from most other Candida species. Cryptococcus is capsulated and germ-tube negative.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A Giemsa-stained blood film is shown from a patient with tertian fever; the infected red cells are ENLARGED and pale, contain fine brick-red (Schuffner's) dots, and show amoeboid trophozoites. Which species is this, and which feature makes relapse possible?
options: Plasmodium ovale; relapse does not occur
questions.concept: Enlarged red cells with Schuffner's dots and amoeboid trophozoites indicate Plasmodium vivax (benign tertian, 48-hour periodicity). Relapses occur because vivax (and ovale) form dormant liver hypnozoites, requiring primaquine for radical cure. Falciparum forms no hypnozoites and infects red cells of all ages.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient from Bihar has months of irregular fever, massive splenomegaly, weight loss and darkening of the skin. A splenic/bone-marrow aspirate shows intracellular amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) within macrophages. The causative organism is:
questions.concept: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), endemic in Bihar, is caused by Leishmania donovani transmitted by the sandfly; diagnosis rests on demonstrating amastigotes (LD bodies) in splenic/marrow aspirate or by the rK39 serological test. It causes fever, massive splenomegaly and skin hyperpigmentation ('kala-azar' = black fever).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient with known chronic hepatitis B (HBsAg-positive for years) suddenly deteriorates with acute hepatitis and sharply rising transaminases; anti-HDV IgM is now positive. This scenario is best described as:
options: Hepatitis D superinfection, carrying a high risk of fulminant hepatitis and chronicity
Hepatitis D coinfection, which is usually self-limiting
Acute hepatitis E, which explains the chronic HBsAg
questions.concept: Hepatitis D is a defective virus that needs HBsAg to replicate. When it infects an established HBV carrier (SUPERINFECTION), it causes severe acute-on-chronic hepatitis with high rates of fulminant failure and chronicity. Simultaneous HBV + HDV COinfection is usually self-limited. HDV cannot replicate without HBV.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Microbiology 11e (Hepatitis Viruses - Hepatitis D)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A man presents 3 weeks after a high-risk exposure with a mononucleosis-like illness (fever, pharyngitis, rash, lymphadenopathy). A third-generation HIV antibody ELISA is negative. Which test is most appropriate to detect acute HIV during this 'window period'?
options: HIV RNA (viral load) or p24 antigen assay
Simply repeat the antibody ELISA once and, if negative, exclude HIV
questions.concept: In acute HIV (seroconversion illness) antibodies may not yet be detectable ('window period'), but HIV RNA and p24 antigen appear early; a fourth-generation antigen/antibody combination assay or nucleic-acid test detects infection soonest. The CD4 count is for staging, not diagnosis, and antibody tests can remain negative for weeks.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with cocaine-induced chest pain and severe hypertension is mistakenly given intravenous propranolol, after which his blood pressure rises even further. This paradoxical worsening is explained by:
options: Unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction once beta-2-mediated vasodilation is blocked
Beta-1 agonist activity of propranolol at high doses
questions.concept: A non-selective beta-blocker given in cocaine toxicity (or phaeochromocytoma) blocks beta-2-mediated vasodilation while alpha-mediated vasoconstriction continues UNOPPOSED, worsening hypertension and coronary spasm. Alpha-blockade (phentolamine) or benzodiazepines are preferred; this is the same reason alpha must be blocked before beta in a phaeochromocytoma.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e (Adrenergic Antagonists)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A myasthenia gravis patient on high-dose pyridostigmine develops INCREASING weakness with excessive salivation, sweating, miosis and muscle fasciculations. To distinguish a myasthenic crisis (needs more anticholinesterase) from a cholinergic crisis (needs less), the appropriate step is:
options: Give a short-acting anticholinesterase (edrophonium/neostigmine) test; worsening indicates a cholinergic crisis
Give atropine, which will reverse the weakness if it is a myasthenic crisis
Give a non-depolarizing blocker to test the response
questions.concept: The muscarinic excess (salivation, miosis, fasciculations) points to a cholinergic crisis from anticholinesterase overdose. A short-acting anticholinesterase (edrophonium/neostigmine) transiently WORSENS a cholinergic crisis but IMPROVES a myasthenic crisis, distinguishing them; in a cholinergic crisis the drug is withheld and airway support given.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with acute angle-closure glaucoma presenting with a red, painful eye and haloes around lights is given topical pilocarpine as part of initial management. By which mechanism does this muscarinic agonist lower the raised intraocular pressure?
options: Ciliary-muscle contraction opens the trabecular meshwork, improving aqueous outflow
It blocks beta receptors to reduce aqueous humour production
It causes mydriasis, which widens the angle
It osmotically draws fluid out of the vitreous
questions.concept: Pilocarpine (a muscarinic agonist) contracts the ciliary muscle and constricts the pupil (miosis); ciliary contraction pulls on the scleral spur to open the trabecular meshwork, enhancing aqueous outflow and lowering IOP. Beta-blockers (timolol) instead lower IOP by reducing aqueous production.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi 8e (Cholinergic Drugs; Drugs for Glaucoma)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: An intensivist switches a patient from thrice-daily to once-daily high-dose gentamicin for Gram-negative sepsis. Which pharmacodynamic property of aminoglycosides best justifies once-daily dosing?
options: Concentration-dependent killing with a prolonged post-antibiotic effect
Time-dependent killing requiring the level to stay above MIC continuously
Bacteriostatic action needing constant plasma levels
Extensive hepatic metabolism prolonging the half-life
questions.concept: Aminoglycosides show concentration-dependent bactericidal killing plus a long post-antibiotic effect, so once-daily high-dose regimens maximise the peak/MIC ratio while allowing the trough to fall, which actually reduces time-dependent nephro- and ototoxicity. Beta-lactams, by contrast, are time-dependent (time above MIC matters).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A neonate given high-dose chloramphenicol develops abdominal distension, vomiting, an ashen-grey cyanosis, hypotension and circulatory collapse ('grey baby syndrome'). This toxicity occurs because neonates:
options: Have immature hepatic glucuronyl transferase and reduced renal excretion, causing drug accumulation
Have accelerated hepatic metabolism of the drug
Excrete the drug renally faster than adults
Lack the ribosomal target of the drug
questions.concept: Grey baby syndrome results from chloramphenicol accumulation because neonates have deficient hepatic glucuronidation (UDP-glucuronyl transferase) and immature renal excretion; toxic levels then impair mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, causing circulatory collapse. Dose reduction or avoidance is required in neonates.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with invasive mould infection on conventional amphotericin-B deoxycholate develops fever with rigors during the infusion, plus hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and a rising creatinine. Which statement about this drug is correct?
options: It binds ergosterol to form membrane pores; nephrotoxicity and electrolyte wasting are dose-limiting, and liposomal forms reduce them
It inhibits fungal cell-wall beta-glucan synthesis
Its toxicity is unrelated to the dose
It is safe in renal impairment without monitoring
questions.concept: Amphotericin B binds fungal ergosterol, forming membrane pores; infusion reactions (fever, rigors) and dose-dependent nephrotoxicity with potassium and magnesium wasting are characteristic, and liposomal formulations lower these toxicities. Echinocandins (caspofungin), not amphotericin, inhibit beta-glucan synthesis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient on standard four-drug antitubercular therapy develops an acutely painful, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint, and serum uric acid is elevated. Which drug most likely precipitated this, and by what mechanism?
options: Pyrazinamide, which reduces renal tubular excretion of urate
questions.concept: Pyrazinamide (via its metabolite pyrazinoic acid) inhibits renal tubular secretion of uric acid, causing hyperuricaemia that can precipitate acute gout; it is also the most hepatotoxic first-line antitubercular. Isoniazid's classic ADR is instead peripheral neuropathy (preventable with pyridoxine).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Two patients on the same weight-based isoniazid dose fare differently: one develops peripheral neuropathy while the other clears the drug rapidly with subtherapeutic levels. This variability is best explained by genetic polymorphism in which metabolic process?
options: N-acetyltransferase-2 (NAT2) acetylation status (slow vs fast acetylators)
questions.concept: Isoniazid is metabolised by hepatic N-acetyltransferase-2; slow acetylators (genetically determined) accumulate INH and are more prone to peripheral neuropathy, whereas fast acetylators may have subtherapeutic levels and generate more hepatotoxic metabolites. Pseudocholinesterase variation instead affects succinylcholine.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A woman of childbearing age with generalized tonic-clonic and myoclonic seizures needs a broad-spectrum antiepileptic. Regarding sodium valproate, which counselling point is most important before prescribing it to her?
options: It is highly teratogenic (neural-tube defects) and should be avoided in women planning pregnancy where alternatives exist
It is completely safe throughout pregnancy
It is a potent enzyme inducer that accelerates its own metabolism
It has no hepatic adverse effects
questions.concept: Sodium valproate is a broad-spectrum AED but a major human teratogen (neural-tube defects, reduced childhood IQ), so it is avoided in women of childbearing potential when alternatives exist. It is actually an enzyme INHIBITOR (not inducer) and can cause hepatotoxicity, weight gain and tremor.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: During general anaesthesia with halothane and succinylcholine a patient develops rapidly rising end-tidal CO2, high fever, generalized muscle rigidity and a metabolic acidosis. What is the diagnosis and the specific treatment?
options: Malignant hyperthermia; dantrolene plus withdrawal of triggering agents
questions.concept: Malignant hyperthermia is a pharmacogenetic reaction (RYR1 mutation) to volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine, causing uncontrolled sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium release: rigidity, rising CO2, hyperthermia and acidosis. Dantrolene (which blocks the ryanodine receptor), plus stopping the triggers, is the specific treatment.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A video is shown of a patient on long-term typical antipsychotic therapy demonstrating repetitive involuntary chewing, lip-smacking and tongue-protruding movements. Regarding this late complication, which statement is correct?
options: It is tardive dyskinesia from chronic dopamine-receptor blockade/supersensitivity; raising the dose transiently masks but ultimately worsens it
It is an acute dystonia that resolves immediately with intramuscular anticholinergics
It is drug-induced Parkinsonism best treated with levodopa
It always resolves quickly once the drug is stopped
questions.concept: Tardive dyskinesia is a late, potentially irreversible movement disorder from chronic D2-receptor blockade (dopamine-receptor supersensitivity), classically orofacial (chewing, lip-smacking, tongue movements). Increasing the antipsychotic dose transiently suppresses but long-term worsens it; VMAT2 inhibitors help. Acute dystonia (early) is the one that responds to anticholinergics.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Amiodarone is grouped as a class III antiarrhythmic but is unusual in showing properties of all four Vaughan-Williams classes. Its principal (class III) antiarrhythmic action is to:
options: Block potassium channels, prolonging repolarization and the effective refractory period (lengthening the QT interval)
Block fast sodium channels only, shortening the action potential
Act purely as a beta-adrenergic agonist
questions.concept: Amiodarone's dominant class III effect is potassium-channel blockade, prolonging repolarization, action-potential duration and the refractory period (QT lengthening); it additionally blocks sodium (class I) and calcium (class IV) channels and has beta-blocking (class II) activity. Despite QT prolongation, torsades de pointes is uncommon with it.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 68-year-old with symptomatic heart failure and rapid atrial fibrillation is started on digoxin for rate control and inotropic support. Its positive inotropic (force-increasing) effect on the cardiac myocyte results from:
options: Inhibiting the Na+/K+-ATPase, raising intracellular Na+ and hence intracellular Ca2+ via the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger
Direct opening of L-type calcium channels
questions.concept: Digoxin inhibits the sarcolemmal Na+/K+-ATPase, raising intracellular Na+, which reduces Ca2+ extrusion by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger; the resulting rise in intracellular calcium enhances contractility. It also increases vagal tone, slowing AV conduction (useful in AF). Hypokalaemia potentiates its toxicity.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi 8e (Cardiac Glycosides / Drugs for CHF)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with a hypertensive emergency is put on an intravenous infusion of sodium nitroprusside. During prolonged, high-dose infusion he develops a metabolic acidosis with altered mental status. This toxicity is due to accumulation of:
options: Excess nitric oxide causing methaemoglobinaemia only
questions.concept: Sodium nitroprusside is metabolised to release nitric oxide (its vasodilator action) plus cyanide, which is normally converted to thiocyanate and excreted renally; prolonged/high-dose infusion or renal impairment leads to cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity (metabolic acidosis, altered sensorium). Co-administered sodium thiosulphate reduces the risk.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: An elderly hypertensive on long-term hydrochlorothiazide is reviewed. All of the following biochemical changes are typical of thiazide diuretics EXCEPT one. Which change is NOT expected?
questions.concept: Thiazides cause hypoKALAEMIA (not hyperkalaemia), together with the classic metabolic effects: hyperGlycaemia, hyperLipidaemia, hyperUricaemia and hyperCalcaemia (they reduce urinary calcium). Potassium-sparing diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs are the drugs that cause hyperkalaemia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: An elderly type-2 diabetic with mild renal impairment on glibenclamide (a long-acting sulfonylurea) is admitted with prolonged, recurrent hypoglycaemia. Which statement best explains the mechanism and the risk?
options: Sulfonylureas close beta-cell ATP-sensitive K+ channels to release insulin independent of glucose, so long-acting agents cause prolonged hypoglycaemia, especially in the elderly and in renal impairment
They only act when blood glucose is high, so hypoglycaemia is impossible
They work solely by increasing urinary glucose loss
They reduce hepatic glucose output without touching insulin
questions.concept: Sulfonylureas bind the SUR1 subunit and close beta-cell ATP-sensitive K+ channels, triggering insulin release REGARDLESS of blood glucose - hence a real risk of hypoglycaemia, worst with long-acting agents (glibenclamide) in the elderly and in renal impairment. SGLT2 inhibitors act by urinary glucose loss; metformin reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi 8e (Insulin and Oral Hypoglycaemic Drugs)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A young woman presents about 12 hours after a large intentional paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose, still asymptomatic but with a rising serum drug level. Which antidote, and by what mechanism, prevents the delayed hepatotoxicity in such a case?
options: N-acetylcysteine, which replenishes hepatic glutathione to detoxify the reactive metabolite NAPQI
Naloxone, which competitively blocks opioid receptors
questions.concept: In paracetamol overdose, saturation of conjugation diverts metabolism via CYP2E1 to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which depletes glutathione and causes centrilobular hepatic necrosis. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is most effective within ~8-10 hours. Naloxone and flumazenil are antidotes for unrelated poisonings.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi 8e (Non-opioid Analgesics; Treatment of Poisoning)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A drug has a volume of distribution of 40 litres and a target steady-state plasma concentration of 5 mg/L. Assuming complete bioavailability, what intravenous LOADING dose is required to rapidly achieve this concentration?
questions.concept: Loading dose = target concentration x volume of distribution / bioavailability = 5 mg/L x 40 L / 1 = 200 mg. The loading dose depends on the volume of distribution (to fill the compartment) and is independent of clearance and half-life; the MAINTENANCE dose, by contrast, depends on clearance.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi 8e (Pharmacokinetics) / Katzung Basic and Clinical Pharmacology

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes presents with 30 minutes of retrosternal chest pain radiating to the jaw, with sweating. Troponin is mildly elevated. His ECG rhythm strip is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: ST-segment depression with ischemic symptoms plus a raised troponin indicates a non-ST-elevation MI (subendocardial ischemia) — contrast with ST elevation in STEMI (transmural infarction). Management differs: no immediate thrombolysis; urgent risk stratification and often an early invasive strategy instead.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: In the graph, Drug Z (dashed curve) never reaches the maximal response of full agonist Drug X, even at very high concentration, and this ceiling is not overcome by adding more Drug Z. Given ALONE (no full agonist present), Drug Z still produces a measurable, submaximal response. Drug Z best exemplifies which category?
questions.concept: A partial agonist has intrinsic activity <1: it activates the receptor (unlike a pure antagonist) but cannot reach full Emax even alone, and when co-administered with a full agonist it competes for the same site and blunts the full agonist's effect (looks like competitive antagonism in that setting). The exam trick is distinguishing 'produces some response alone' (an agonist property) from 'has a capped ceiling' (submaximal efficacy) — both are true of a partial agonist simultaneously.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi 8e — General Pharmacology (agonists, partial agonists, antagonists)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The epidemic curve from a hostel gastroenteritis outbreak shows three successive waves of cases, each occurring roughly one incubation period apart, rather than a single sharp peak. This pattern is most consistent with which mode of spread?
questions.concept: Successive waves spaced roughly one incubation period apart reflect ongoing person-to-person transmission — each wave is a new generation of cases infected by the previous one. A point-source outbreak instead shows a single sharp peak with all cases clustered within one incubation period of the common exposure.
questions.reference: Park 27e — Epidemiology of communicable diseases (outbreak investigation)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A patient with progressive exertional dyspnea has the flow-volume loop shown: a narrow, tall-appearing loop with reduced lung volumes but a preserved (even supranormal) expiratory flow-to-volume relationship, unlike the scooped/concave pattern of airway obstruction. Which physiological pattern does this represent, and what happens to the FEV1/FVC ratio?
options: Restrictive pattern; FEV1/FVC normal or increased
questions.concept: Restrictive lung disease (e.g. pulmonary fibrosis, chest-wall disease) reduces FVC and FEV1 roughly proportionately, so the FEV1/FVC ratio stays normal or even rises, and the flow-volume loop is narrow/tall rather than scooped. This is the classic contrast with obstructive disease, where FEV1 falls more than FVC and the ratio drops.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A newborn delivered with shoulder dystocia has the right upper limb adducted, medially rotated at the shoulder, extended at the elbow and pronated (the 'waiter's tip' posture). Injury to which part of the brachial plexus is most likely?
questions.concept: Erb-Duchenne palsy is injury to the upper trunk (C5-C6), giving the classic 'waiter's tip' posture. Klumpke's palsy (C8-T1) instead causes a claw hand with small-muscle wasting.
questions.reference: Vishram Singh, Clinical Anatomy - Upper Limb

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A man with a mid-shaft fracture of the humerus cannot extend his wrist and fingers (wrist drop) and has sensory loss over the dorsum of the first web space. Which nerve is injured?
questions.concept: The radial nerve lies in the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus and is injured in mid-shaft fractures, producing wrist drop (loss of extensors) and sensory loss over the first dorsal web space.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: After a deep laceration at the wrist, a patient develops wasting of the thenar eminence, inability to oppose the thumb, and loss of sensation over the palmar aspect of the lateral three-and-a-half digits. Which nerve is affected?
questions.concept: The median nerve supplies the thenar (LOAF) muscles and sensation to the palmar lateral three-and-a-half digits; injury causes thenar wasting, loss of opposition ('ape hand'), and this sensory pattern.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Lower limb: femoral/sciatic nerve, foot drop
questions.stem: After a tight plaster cast around the neck of the fibula, a patient develops foot drop and loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot. Which nerve has been compressed?
questions.concept: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds superficially around the neck of the fibula, where it is easily compressed, causing foot drop (loss of dorsiflexors and evertors) and dorsal foot sensory loss.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Lower limb: femoral/sciatic nerve, foot drop
questions.stem: Which motor function is chiefly lost following a complete femoral nerve injury?
questions.concept: The femoral nerve supplies quadriceps femoris, the main knee extensor; its injury impairs knee extension and abolishes the knee jerk. Thigh adduction is supplied by the obturator nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The sternal angle (angle of Louis), at the level of the T4/T5 disc, marks which of the following?
questions.concept: The sternal angle marks the tracheal bifurcation (carina), the start and end of the aortic arch, and the T4/T5 level. The celiac trunk (T12) and aortic bifurcation (L4) are abdominal landmarks.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: During hernia repair the surgeon finds the hernial sac emerging medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, through Hesselbach's triangle. How is this hernia classified?
questions.concept: A direct inguinal hernia passes medial to the inferior epigastric vessels through Hesselbach's triangle; an indirect hernia enters the deep ring lateral to these vessels. A femoral hernia lies below the inguinal ligament.

questions.subject: Anatomy
