questions.stem: A patient has vertical diplopia that is worst when walking down stairs, and cannot depress the adducted eye. Which cranial nerve is most likely involved?
questions.concept: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) supplies superior oblique, which depresses and intorts the adducted eye; palsy causes vertical diplopia worst on downgaze (difficulty descending stairs).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: All of the following structures pass through the cavernous sinus EXCEPT:
questions.concept: The cavernous sinus transmits CN III, IV, V1 (ophthalmic), V2 (maxillary), VI and the internal carotid artery. The mandibular nerve (V3) leaves the skull via the foramen ovale and does not traverse the sinus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A stab wound causes hemisection of the spinal cord at T10. Below the lesion there is ipsilateral loss of motor power and of fine touch/proprioception, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature. This is:
questions.concept: Cord hemisection (Brown-Sequard) gives ipsilateral loss of motor and dorsal-column function and contralateral loss of pain/temperature, because spinothalamic fibres cross within one to two segments of entry while dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts remain ipsilateral until higher up.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The stapes, stylohyoid muscle and the muscles of facial expression (all supplied by the facial nerve) are derivatives of which pharyngeal arch?
questions.concept: The second pharyngeal arch (Reichert's cartilage), supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII), forms the stapes, styloid process, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric and the muscles of facial expression.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which neurotransmitter and receptor mediate transmission at the skeletal neuromuscular junction?
questions.concept: At the skeletal NMJ, acetylcholine acts on nicotinic (Nm) receptors of the motor end-plate. Myasthenia gravis is caused by autoantibodies against these nicotinic ACh receptors.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cardiac cycle, ECG basis, BP regulation
questions.stem: The first heart sound (S1) is produced by:
options: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
questions.concept: S1 marks the onset of ventricular systole and is due to closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves. S2 is due to closure of the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cardiac cycle, ECG basis, BP regulation
questions.stem: On a normal ECG, the QRS complex represents:
questions.concept: The P wave is atrial depolarization, the QRS complex is ventricular depolarization (which masks atrial repolarization), and the T wave is ventricular repolarization.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which substance is the ideal marker of glomerular filtration rate because it is freely filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the tubules?
questions.concept: Inulin clearance equals GFR because it is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted. PAH clearance estimates renal plasma flow; creatinine clearance slightly overestimates GFR due to minor tubular secretion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin) increases water reabsorption mainly by inserting aquaporin-2 channels in which part of the nephron?
options: Descending limb of loop of Henle
questions.concept: ADH acts on V2 receptors of the collecting duct to insert aquaporin-2 water channels, increasing water permeability and concentrating the urine. ADH deficiency causes central diabetes insipidus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: In actively exercising skeletal muscle the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve shifts to the right, favouring oxygen unloading. Which combination of changes is responsible?
options: Decreased CO2, decreased temperature, increased pH
Increased CO2, increased temperature, decreased pH and increased 2,3-BPG
questions.concept: A rightward shift (Bohr effect, reduced Hb-O2 affinity) results from increased CO2, increased temperature, decreased pH (increased H+) and increased 2,3-BPG - all present in exercising tissue - enhancing O2 delivery.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: The largest fraction of carbon dioxide is transported in the blood as:
questions.concept: About 70% of CO2 is carried as bicarbonate (formed by carbonic anhydrase in RBCs, with the chloride shift), roughly 20-23% as carbaminohaemoglobin, and about 7% dissolved in plasma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which hormones are released from the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis)?
questions.concept: The posterior pituitary stores and releases oxytocin and ADH, which are synthesised in the supraoptic and paraventricular hypothalamic nuclei. ACTH, TSH, GH, prolactin, FSH and LH are anterior pituitary hormones.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A patient on long-term high-dose oral corticosteroids has suppressed plasma ACTH. This is best explained by:
options: Negative feedback of glucocorticoid on the hypothalamus and pituitary
Direct stimulation of the adrenal cortex
questions.concept: Cortisol and exogenous glucocorticoids exert negative feedback on hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH. Chronic exogenous steroids suppress the HPA axis, causing adrenal atrophy and risk of crisis if stopped abruptly.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: The sensory receptor responsible for the monosynaptic stretch (myotatic) reflex, such as the knee jerk, is the:
questions.concept: The muscle spindle senses stretch; its Ia afferents synapse monosynaptically on alpha motor neurons to drive the stretch reflex. The Golgi tendon organ (Ib) mediates the inverse myotatic reflex, limiting excessive tension.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which enzyme catalyses the rate-limiting (committed) step of glycolysis?
questions.concept: PFK-1 (fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate) is the rate-limiting, committed step of glycolysis. It is activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by ATP and citrate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which enzyme is unique to gluconeogenesis and converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate, bypassing the irreversible pyruvate kinase step?
questions.concept: Gluconeogenesis bypasses the three irreversible glycolytic steps using pyruvate carboxylase, PEPCK (oxaloacetate to PEP), fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient is started on a statin, which inhibits HMG-CoA reductase. The resulting upregulation of hepatic LDL receptors chiefly clears which lipoprotein from plasma?
questions.concept: HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. Statins lower intracellular cholesterol, upregulating hepatic LDL receptors that clear LDL ('bad' cholesterol). HDL mediates reverse cholesterol transport; chylomicrons are the most triglyceride-rich lipoprotein.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The urea cycle, which detoxifies ammonia, occurs mainly in which organ, with its first step in the mitochondria?
questions.concept: The urea cycle operates chiefly in the liver; the first (rate-limiting) step is carbamoyl phosphate synthetase-I (CPS-I) in the mitochondria. Defects in urea-cycle enzymes cause hyperammonaemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Transamination reactions that transfer amino groups between amino acids and keto acids require which vitamin-derived coenzyme?
questions.concept: Aminotransferases (e.g., ALT, AST) use pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active form of vitamin B6, as coenzyme for transamination. B6 deficiency (e.g., with isoniazid) impairs these reactions.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A malnourished elderly man has swollen bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages and poor wound healing. Deficiency of which vitamin, needed to hydroxylate proline and lysine in collagen, is responsible?
questions.concept: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in collagen synthesis; deficiency causes scurvy - bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhage and impaired wound healing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: An alcoholic develops confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia (Wernicke encephalopathy). Deficiency of which vitamin, a coenzyme for pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase, is responsible?
questions.concept: Thiamine (B1), as thiamine pyrophosphate, is a coenzyme for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase. Deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, common in alcoholics.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: During DNA replication, short DNA segments (Okazaki fragments) are synthesised discontinuously on the:
questions.concept: Replication is semiconservative and bidirectional; because DNA polymerase synthesises only 5' to 3', the lagging strand is made discontinuously as Okazaki fragments (later joined by DNA ligase), while the leading strand is continuous.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Insertion or deletion of a single nucleotide (not a multiple of three) in a coding region produces which type of mutation?
questions.concept: Adding or deleting nucleotides not in multiples of three shifts the reading frame (frameshift), altering all downstream codons and often creating a premature stop codon. Point mutations may be silent, missense or nonsense.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Newborn screening flags a high blood phenylalanine. If untreated the child develops intellectual disability, a musty/mousy body odour and hypopigmentation. The deficient enzyme is:
questions.concept: Classic phenylketonuria (PKU) results from phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, causing phenylalanine accumulation (musty odour, hypopigmentation from reduced melanin, intellectual disability). Treated with a low-phenylalanine diet. Homogentisate oxidase deficiency causes alkaptonuria.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Regarding rigor mortis in temperate/average Indian conditions, which statement is correct?
options: It appears immediately at the moment of death
It begins about 1-2 hours after death, is fully developed by ~12 hours, and passes off over the next ~12 hours
It is identical to cadaveric spasm
questions.concept: Rigor mortis begins 1-2 hours after death (small muscles first, per Nysten's law), is complete by about 12 hours, persists ~12 hours, then passes off over ~12 hours. Cadaveric spasm is a separate, instantaneous phenomenon with no primary flaccidity.
questions.reference: Reddy, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A body recovered from a closed room with a running charcoal heater shows cherry-red postmortem lividity. This coloration of hypostasis is most characteristic of:
questions.concept: Cherry-red livor mortis is classic for carbon monoxide poisoning (carboxyhaemoglobin), with a charcoal source pointing to CO. Hydrogen sulphide gives greenish lividity and methaemoglobinaemia gives brown lividity.
questions.reference: Reddy, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In firearm injuries, 'tattooing' (stippling) from unburnt and semi-burnt powder grains embedded in the skin indicates a wound fired from:
options: Distant range, beyond the carry of powder
questions.concept: Tattooing/stippling indicates an intermediate (close) range wound, as powder grains travel only a limited distance. Contact wounds show muzzle imprint, singeing and blackening; distant wounds show only the bullet's mechanical effect without powder marks.
questions.reference: Reddy, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In a typical death due to hanging, the ligature mark is characteristically:
options: Horizontal, continuous and below the thyroid cartilage
Oblique, non-continuous and high on the neck above the thyroid cartilage
Multiple horizontal abrasions across the mid-neck
questions.concept: In hanging the ligature mark is oblique, incomplete (non-continuous, highest at the point of suspension) and lies high, above the thyroid cartilage. In ligature strangulation it is typically horizontal, continuous and low (at or below the thyroid).
questions.reference: Reddy, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In a decomposed body suspected of drowning, which test on the marrow of a long bone (e.g., femur) helps confirm antemortem drowning by demonstrating silica-walled algae carried in the circulation?
questions.concept: The diatom test detects silica-shelled diatoms in long-bone marrow; their presence implies the person was alive with a beating heart in the water (antemortem drowning), since diatoms reach the marrow only via circulation. The Gettler test compares chloride content of blood from the two sides of the heart.
questions.reference: Reddy, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A farmer who ingested an insecticide has pinpoint pupils, profuse salivation, lacrimation, sweating, bronchorrhoea and muscle fasciculations. The specific antidotes are:
questions.concept: This is organophosphate (anticholinesterase) poisoning - a cholinergic crisis (muscarinic SLUDGE features plus fasciculations). Atropine blocks muscarinic effects and pralidoxime (2-PAM) reactivates acetylcholinesterase, most effective before enzyme 'ageing'.
questions.reference: Reddy, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In chronic arsenic poisoning, which characteristic nail finding - transverse white bands across the nails - is seen?
questions.concept: Chronic arsenic poisoning classically causes Mees' lines (transverse white bands), along with 'rain-drop' pigmentation, hyperkeratosis and peripheral neuropathy. Hair and nails are used for postmortem detection of arsenic.
questions.reference: Reddy, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: Under Indian criminal law (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, which replaced the IPC), below which age is a child granted absolute immunity from criminal responsibility (doli incapax)?
questions.concept: A child under 7 years is doli incapax - absolutely incapable of committing an offence (BNS Section 20, formerly IPC Section 82). Between 7 and 12 years, immunity applies only if the child lacks sufficient maturity of understanding (BNS Section 21, formerly IPC 83).
questions.reference: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (in force 01-Jul-2024); Reddy, Forensic Medicine

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: In India, the minimum age generally taken as sufficient for a person to give valid consent to an ordinary medical examination (absent an overriding statute such as POCSO) is:
questions.concept: By convention a person aged 12 years or above can give valid consent for a general medical examination; below 12 guardian consent is required. Consent to procedures carrying a risk of harm requires 18 years, and statutes such as POCSO may override for minors in sexual-offence cases.
questions.reference: Reddy, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 65-year-old osteoporotic woman falls on her outstretched hand and presents with a 'dinner-fork' deformity of the wrist. X-ray shows a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal (posterior) displacement of the distal fragment. This is which fracture?
questions.concept: Colles fracture = fracture of the distal radius (within ~2.5 cm of the wrist) with dorsal displacement/angulation of the distal fragment, giving the 'dinner-fork' deformity; classic in elderly osteoporotic women after a fall on the outstretched hand. Smith fracture is the reverse (volar displacement).

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy falls on his outstretched hand; X-ray shows an extension-type supracondylar fracture of the humerus. A few hours after closed reduction and an above-elbow slab, he develops severe pain on passive extension of the fingers, refuses to move the hand, and the radial pulse is feeble. What is the most likely impending complication?
questions.concept: Supracondylar humeral fractures can injure the brachial artery and cause forearm compartment ischaemia. Severe pain on passive stretch of the fingers plus a diminished pulse signals impending Volkmann's ischaemic contracture (an acute compartment syndrome) - an emergency. Cubitus varus is a late malunion deformity, not an acute vascular event.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: An 8-year-old child presents with acute fever and severe pain around the knee, with tenderness over the metaphysis of the lower femur. Which is the most common causative organism of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children?
questions.concept: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in all age groups, typically affecting the metaphysis of long bones (rich blood supply with sluggish flow) in children. Salmonella osteomyelitis is characteristically associated with sickle-cell disease.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 30-year-old presents with chronic back pain, low-grade evening fever and weight loss. MRI shows destruction of two adjacent vertebral bodies with narrowing of the intervening disc space and a paravertebral (psoas) abscess. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Tuberculosis of the spine typically affects the paradiscal region of two contiguous vertebrae with disc-space reduction and a cold (paravertebral/psoas) abscess; the thoracolumbar region is the commonest site and a gibbus (angular kyphosis) is characteristic. Metastasis and myeloma classically spare the disc space.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 15-year-old presents with a painful swelling around the knee. X-ray of the lower femur shows a destructive metaphyseal lesion with a 'sunburst/sunray' spiculated pattern and a Codman's triangle. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Osteosarcoma occurs in adolescents at the metaphysis around the knee (lower femur/upper tibia), with 'sunburst' spiculation and Codman's triangle (elevated periosteum). Ewing's sarcoma shows an 'onion-peel' lamellated periosteal reaction and favours the diaphysis; giant cell tumour is epiphyseal/subarticular in the mature skeleton.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: During newborn examination the paediatrician flexes and abducts the hip and feels a palpable 'clunk' as the femoral head relocates into the acetabulum, suggesting developmental dysplasia of the hip. This manoeuvre is known as:
questions.concept: Ortolani's test relocates a dislocated hip (abduction with a palpable clunk of reduction), while Barlow's test is the provocative dislocation test (adduction plus posterior pressure). Both screen for DDH in neonates; ultrasound is the imaging of choice under 6 months of age.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: In a patient with unilateral hearing loss, the Rinne test is negative (bone conduction > air conduction) on the affected side and the Weber test lateralises to the same (affected) side. This pattern indicates:
questions.concept: In conductive hearing loss the Rinne test is negative (BC>AC) on the affected ear and the Weber test lateralises to the poorer (affected) ear. In sensorineural loss the Rinne stays positive (AC>BC) and the Weber lateralises to the better (normal) ear.
questions.reference: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman reports gradually progressive bilateral hearing loss that paradoxically seems better in noisy surroundings (paracusis willisii). Otoscopy is normal; audiometry shows conductive hearing loss with a dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Otosclerosis is fixation of the stapes footplate causing progressive conductive hearing loss in young adults; paracusis willisii and Carhart's notch (a dip in bone conduction at 2 kHz) are classic. Schwartze sign is a reddish tympanic membrane over an active focus. Treatment is stapedectomy or a hearing aid.
questions.reference: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has recurrent anterior nosebleeds. Bleeding most commonly arises from a vascular plexus in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum. This site is called:
questions.concept: Anterior epistaxis (the commonest type, especially in children) arises from Little's area on the anteroinferior nasal septum, where the anterior/posterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries anastomose to form Kiesselbach's plexus. Woodruff's plexus is the source of posterior epistaxis in the elderly.
questions.reference: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 35-year-old has facial pain over the cheek that worsens on bending forward, with purulent nasal discharge. The maxillary sinus is the most commonly involved sinus in sinusitis. This is largely because:
options: Its ostium lies high on the medial wall, so gravity-dependent drainage is poor
It is the smallest of the paranasal sinuses
It drains directly into the superior meatus
It is lined by keratinised squamous epithelium
questions.concept: The maxillary sinus is the largest paranasal sinus, but its ostium opens high on the medial wall into the middle meatus (via the hiatus semilunaris), so gravity-dependent drainage is poor and it is the most frequently infected sinus. Pain characteristically worsens on stooping forward.
questions.reference: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 22-year-old presents a few days after acute tonsillitis with severe unilateral sore throat, trismus, a muffled 'hot-potato' voice, drooling and the uvula pushed to the opposite side. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Quinsy is a collection of pus between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor. It presents with severe unilateral sore throat, trismus, a muffled 'hot-potato' voice and the tonsil/uvula pushed medially and to the opposite side. Management is incision and drainage plus antibiotics, with interval tonsillectomy.
questions.reference: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A purely glottic (true vocal cord) carcinoma of the larynx typically presents early and carries the best prognosis among laryngeal cancers. Which anatomical feature best explains both the early presentation and the good prognosis?
options: The glottis has a rich lymphatic supply causing early symptomatic nodes
The true vocal cords have sparse lymphatic drainage and hoarseness appears early
The supraglottis has no lymphatic drainage at all
The subglottis presents earliest, with stridor
questions.concept: The true vocal cords have very poor lymphatic drainage, so glottic cancers spread to nodes late (good prognosis) while causing hoarseness early (early presentation). Supraglottic tumours have rich lymphatics and therefore metastasise to nodes early with a worse prognosis.
questions.reference: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has gradually progressive, painless dimming of vision in both eyes with glare. Examination shows a grayish-white opacity of the lens. What is the definitive treatment of a visually significant senile cataract?
options: Surgical extraction with intraocular lens implantation
questions.concept: There is no proven medical therapy that reverses a cataract. The definitive treatment of a visually significant cataract is surgery - phacoemulsification (or extracapsular cataract extraction) with implantation of a posterior-chamber intraocular lens.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is found on routine examination to have an intraocular pressure of 26 mmHg, an enlarged optic disc cup (cup-to-disc ratio 0.7), open angles on gonioscopy and early peripheral field loss, with no pain. Which class of drug is generally first-line medical therapy for primary open-angle glaucoma?
questions.concept: Primary open-angle glaucoma is a chronic, painless optic neuropathy with raised IOP, disc cupping and peripheral (arcuate) field loss. Topical prostaglandin analogues (e.g., latanoprost) are usual first-line agents, lowering IOP by increasing uveoscleral outflow with once-daily dosing; topical beta-blockers are an alternative.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with sudden severe pain in one eye, coloured haloes around lights, nausea and vomiting. The eye is red, the cornea hazy, the pupil mid-dilated and fixed, and IOP is 50 mmHg. Which is the most appropriate immediate measure to lower the pressure?
options: Topical atropine to dilate the pupil
Intravenous acetazolamide (with osmotic agents) plus topical pilocarpine
Reassurance and review in one week
questions.concept: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency. Immediate IOP reduction uses IV acetazolamide (with IV mannitol if needed), a topical beta-blocker and topical pilocarpine (a miotic that opens the angle); definitive treatment is laser peripheral iridotomy. Atropine (a mydriatic) is contraindicated as it worsens angle closure.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A patient with diabetes of 15 years' duration is found on fundoscopy to have fragile new blood vessels growing on the optic disc and retina (neovascularisation), defining proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Which is the treatment of choice to induce regression of this neovascularisation?
questions.concept: Neovascularisation defines proliferative diabetic retinopathy, which risks vitreous haemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment. Pan-retinal photocoagulation ablates ischaemic peripheral retina, reducing VEGF drive and causing regression of new vessels; anti-VEGF injections are useful adjuncts.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A myopic patient suddenly notices flashes of light and floaters, followed by a 'curtain' descending across the vision of one eye. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Photopsiae (flashes), floaters and a progressive 'curtain/veil' over the visual field are classic for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, in which a retinal break lets fluid separate the neurosensory retina from the RPE. Myopia and posterior vitreous detachment are risk factors; urgent referral is required.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: In myopia (short-sightedness), parallel rays of light come to a focus in front of the retina. Which type of corrective lens is used to bring the focus onto the retina?
questions.concept: In myopia the image focuses in front of the retina (the eye is too long or too powerful); a concave (minus, diverging) lens spreads the rays so they focus on the retina. Hypermetropia is corrected with convex (plus) lenses and astigmatism with cylindrical lenses.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has 6 weeks of persistent low mood, anhedonia, early-morning awakening, poor appetite with weight loss and feelings of worthlessness, without psychotic features. Which is the first-line pharmacological treatment for major depressive disorder?
options: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (e.g., sertraline/fluoxetine)
A tricyclic antidepressant as the first choice
questions.concept: Major depressive disorder requires at least 2 weeks of depressed mood or anhedonia plus associated symptoms. SSRIs are first-line because of good efficacy and a favourable side-effect and overdose-safety profile compared with tricyclic antidepressants.
questions.reference: Niraj Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A patient on long-term lithium for bipolar disorder develops coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, vomiting and confusion soon after starting a thiazide diuretic. Which statement about lithium is correct?
options: Lithium has a wide therapeutic index and needs no monitoring
Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index; serum levels and renal/thyroid function must be monitored
Thiazide diuretics lower serum lithium levels
Lithium is the drug of choice for acute schizophrenia
questions.concept: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index (therapeutic ~0.6-1.2 mEq/L; toxicity above ~1.5). Thiazides reduce renal lithium clearance and precipitate toxicity (coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, seizures). Serum levels plus renal and thyroid function need regular monitoring.
questions.reference: Niraj Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A 24-year-old man believes his thoughts are being broadcast aloud so that others can hear them, and he hears voices discussing him in the third person. These are examples of Schneider's first-rank symptoms, most characteristically seen in:
questions.concept: Schneiderian first-rank symptoms - thought broadcasting/insertion/withdrawal, third-person auditory hallucinations, delusional perception and passivity phenomena - are highly suggestive of schizophrenia. They are characteristic though not, in isolation, absolutely diagnostic.
questions.reference: Niraj Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A young man on haloperidol develops high fever, severe 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity, autonomic instability, altered sensorium and a markedly raised creatine kinase. What is the most likely diagnosis and the key management step?
options: Serotonin syndrome; treat with an SSRI
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; stop the antipsychotic and give supportive care, with dantrolene or bromocriptine
Acute dystonia; add a second antipsychotic
questions.concept: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction to dopamine-blocking antipsychotics: hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental state and raised CK. Management is to stop the offending drug, give aggressive supportive/cooling care, and use dantrolene or bromocriptine.
questions.reference: Niraj Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man admitted after a road accident becomes, on day 3 without alcohol, disoriented, tremulous and diaphoretic, with visual hallucinations of insects and tachycardia. Which is the most appropriate first-line drug management?
questions.concept: This is delirium tremens (severe alcohol withdrawal, typically 48-72 h after cessation) with autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, disorientation and hallucinations. Benzodiazepines are first-line (cross-tolerance, seizure prevention), with parenteral thiamine to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy. Disulfiram and naltrexone are for maintaining abstinence, not acute withdrawal.
questions.reference: Niraj Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: According to the WHO operational classification (based on the number of skin lesions), a patient with 3 hypopigmented anaesthetic skin patches and a negative slit-skin smear is classified and treated as:
questions.concept: WHO operational classification: paucibacillary leprosy = 1-5 skin lesions (smear-negative), treated with 6 months of rifampicin + dapsone; multibacillary leprosy = more than 5 lesions (or a positive skin smear), treated with 12 months of rifampicin + dapsone + clofazimine.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD; WHO leprosy guidelines (verified 2026-07-04)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient with borderline leprosy on multidrug therapy develops, over a few days, acute painful swelling and redness of existing skin lesions together with sudden nerve pain, tenderness and a new nerve deficit. This is best described as:
questions.concept: A type 1 (reversal) reaction is a type IV cell-mediated reaction seen in borderline leprosy: existing lesions become acutely inflamed and nerves become tender with sudden deficit (neuritis) - a medical emergency treated with corticosteroids. Type 2 reaction (ENL) is a type III immune-complex phenomenon with crops of tender nodules and systemic upset, seen in lepromatous/borderline-lepromatous disease.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A young man has well-demarcated erythematous plaques covered by silvery-white scales over the extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees and the scalp. Gently removing the scale produces pinpoint bleeding points. This sign is called:
questions.concept: Auspitz's sign (pinpoint bleeding on removing the scale) reflects the thinned suprapapillary epidermis and dilated dermal papillary capillaries of psoriasis. Koebner's phenomenon (new lesions at sites of trauma) also occurs; Munro microabscesses are the histological hallmark.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A middle-aged woman has intensely pruritic, flat-topped, violaceous, polygonal papules on the flexor aspect of the wrists, with fine white lacy lines over the papules and on the buccal mucosa. These white lines are called:
questions.concept: Lichen planus is remembered by the '6 Ps': pruritic, purple (violaceous), polygonal, planar (flat-topped) papules/plaques. Wickham's striae (a fine white lacy network) are characteristic. The flexor wrists and buccal mucosa (reticular oral lichen planus) are typical sites, and the Koebner phenomenon is positive.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A 50-year-old presents with flaccid blisters and painful oral erosions; lateral pressure on normal-looking skin shears off the epidermis (Nikolsky's sign positive). Which set of findings correctly fits pemphigus vulgaris (rather than bullous pemphigoid)?
options: Subepidermal blister, Nikolsky negative, IgG against BP180/BP230
Intraepidermal (suprabasal) blister, Nikolsky positive, IgG against desmoglein 3
Subepidermal blister, linear IgA at the basement membrane
Intraepidermal blister, Nikolsky negative, no autoantibodies
questions.concept: Pemphigus vulgaris: intraepidermal (suprabasal) acantholytic blister, flaccid bullae, Nikolsky positive, autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (with a 'fish-net' intercellular IgG pattern on direct immunofluorescence). Bullous pemphigoid: tense subepidermal blisters, Nikolsky negative, antibodies against hemidesmosomal BP180/BP230 with linear IgG/C3 along the basement membrane.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A young man presents about 3 weeks after unprotected intercourse with a single, painless, indurated genital ulcer that has a clean base, together with non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Primary syphilis (Treponema pallidum) - a hard chancre
questions.concept: Primary syphilis presents as a solitary, painless, indurated ulcer with a clean base (the hard chancre) plus non-tender ('shotty') lymphadenopathy, roughly 3 weeks after exposure. Chancroid is painful with a ragged, undermined edge and tender suppurative nodes; herpes causes grouped painful vesicles and ulcers.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with acute head trauma and deteriorating consciousness needs urgent imaging to detect intracranial haemorrhage and skull fractures. Which is the imaging modality of choice in this acute setting?
questions.concept: Non-contrast CT is the first-line emergency investigation in acute head trauma - fast, widely available and excellent for acute blood (hyperdense) and bony fractures. MRI gives better parenchymal/posterior-fossa detail but is slower and less suited to the unstable acute trauma patient.
questions.reference: Cerebellum Radiology notes; standard radiology texts

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: Before giving an intravenous iodinated contrast agent for a contrast-enhanced CT, which factor is most important to check in order to reduce the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy?
options: Renal function (serum creatinine / eGFR) and hydration status
questions.concept: Iodinated contrast can cause contrast-induced nephropathy, especially with pre-existing renal impairment, diabetes or dehydration, so renal function (creatinine/eGFR) and hydration must be assessed first. Prior contrast reactions and metformin use are also checked. (Gadolinium, used in MRI, is linked to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in severe renal failure.)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: A chest X-ray in acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema classically shows bilateral perihilar alveolar opacities in a 'bat-wing' pattern, upper-lobe blood diversion and Kerley B lines. Kerley B lines represent:
options: Thickened interlobular septa due to interstitial fluid
questions.concept: Kerley B lines are short, horizontal peripheral lines abutting the pleura at the lung bases, caused by fluid or thickening of the interlobular septa - a sign of interstitial pulmonary oedema (and of other causes of septal thickening). 'Bat-wing' perihilar opacity and upper-lobe diversion accompany cardiogenic oedema.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: On an erect PA chest X-ray, which is the earliest and most characteristic sign of a moderate pleural effusion?
options: Blunting of the costophrenic angle with an upper concave meniscus
Deviation of the trachea towards the same side
Increased lucency of the affected lung
questions.concept: On an erect film, pleural fluid first blunts the costophrenic angle and forms a homogeneous opacity with an upper concave meniscus. A large effusion pushes the mediastinum and trachea to the opposite side. Roughly 200-300 mL is needed before blunting is visible on a PA film.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: The core principle of radiation protection, stating that radiation exposure should be kept 'As Low As Reasonably Achievable', is abbreviated as:
questions.concept: ALARA ('As Low As Reasonably Achievable') is the core radiation-safety principle: minimise dose using time, distance and shielding. Ionising radiation (X-ray/CT) is avoided in pregnancy where possible; ultrasound and MRI use no ionising radiation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: A patient with well-controlled hypertension on a single antihypertensive and no other systemic disease is scheduled for elective surgery. Under the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical-status classification, this patient is:
questions.concept: ASA II is a patient with mild, well-controlled systemic disease and no substantive functional limitation (e.g., well-controlled hypertension or diabetes, current smoker, mild obesity). ASA I is a normal healthy patient; ASA III has severe disease with functional limitation; ASA IV has severe disease that is a constant threat to life.
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology; ASA physical status

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: For a healthy adult undergoing elective surgery under general anaesthesia, standard preoperative fasting guidelines recommend a minimum fasting time of:
options: 2 hours for clear fluids and 6 hours for a light/solid meal
questions.concept: The '2-4-6' fasting rule reduces aspiration risk: 2 h for clear fluids, 4 h for breast milk, and 6 h for a light meal / formula / non-human milk (8 h for a large or fatty/fried meal). The concern is aspiration of gastric contents (Mendelson's syndrome).
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology; ASA fasting guidelines

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: What is the maximum recommended safe dose of lidocaine (lignocaine) WITH adrenaline (epinephrine) for infiltration anaesthesia in an adult?
questions.concept: Adrenaline causes vasoconstriction that slows systemic absorption, allowing a higher safe dose: lidocaine is limited to about 7 mg/kg WITH adrenaline versus about 4.5 mg/kg (often quoted as 3 mg/kg) plain. Exceeding this risks local anaesthetic systemic toxicity.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Shortly after a large-volume bupivacaine field block, a patient develops circumoral tingling and tinnitus, then a seizure and a cardiac arrhythmia. In addition to standard resuscitation and airway support, which specific therapy is indicated for this local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)?
questions.concept: LAST progresses from CNS excitation (perioral numbness, tinnitus, seizures) to cardiovascular collapse; bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic local anaesthetic. Management: stop injection, secure airway/oxygen, treat seizures with a benzodiazepine, and give IV 20% lipid emulsion ('lipid rescue') with prolonged, modified ACLS.
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology; ASRA LAST guidance

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: During adult basic life support for an unresponsive, pulseless patient (before an advanced airway is placed), the recommended chest-compression rate and compression-to-ventilation ratio are:
options: As fast as possible, with no ventilations
questions.concept: High-quality adult CPR uses compressions at 100-120 per minute to a depth of 5-6 cm (2-2.4 inches) with full recoil, and a 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio (single or two rescuers) until an advanced airway is placed. Interruptions should be minimised.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: During an adult cardiac arrest, a rhythm check shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the single most important immediate intervention?
questions.concept: Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless VT are 'shockable' rhythms - the priority is immediate defibrillation (an unsynchronised shock) followed by resumption of CPR; adrenaline 1 mg IV is given every 3-5 minutes and amiodarone after the third shock. Synchronised cardioversion is for unstable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse; atropine is used for symptomatic bradycardia.
